prompt: On DigitalOcean, what does "choosing a Droplet flavor" actually mean? Explain what the `size` slug prefixes (`s-`, `g-`, `c-`, `m-`, `so-`/`gd-`) mean, and explain clearly why picking a flavor is not "just pick the biggest one".
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Choosing a flavor on DO is literally changing one argument: `size`. The slug itself already encodes the entire flavor and spec — there's no "custom machine type" concept for freely choosing CPU/RAM like on GCP, DO only offers presets. The `s-` prefix is Basic shared-CPU; `g-` is General-Purpose with a balanced vCPU:RAM ratio (~1 vCPU : 4 GB), the default when the workload is unclear; `c-` is CPU-Optimized with **dedicated** vCPU, a 1 vCPU : 2 GB ratio, for CPU-heavy workloads; `m-` is Memory-Optimized, 1 vCPU : 8 GB, for RAM-hungry workloads; `so-`/`gd-` is Storage-Optimized with large-capacity NVMe. You shouldn't "pick the biggest" because picking the wrong flavor doesn't break anything but wastes real money: a single-threaded Node.js event-loop backend is a CPU-bound workload — choosing `g-4vcpu-8gb` General-Purpose pays for 8 GB of RAM while only using 1 GB; the right choice is `c-2`/`c-4` to get dedicated vCPU instead. Matching principle: CPU-bound (Node.js, build server, video encoding) → CPU-Optimized; memory-bound (Redis, OLTP Postgres, JVM heap) → Memory-Optimized; disk-heavy (ClickHouse, Elasticsearch, data lake) → Storage-Optimized; balanced or unclear workload → General-Purpose.

prompt: On DigitalOcean Spaces, is a bucket's ACL always the same as an object's ACL inside it? Explain Spaces' ACL mechanism (how many values, which levels it applies at) and give an example where a bucket is private but an object inside it is still publicly readable.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
No, bucket ACL and object ACL aren't automatically the same — they're two independent levels. Spaces supports exactly two canned ACLs: `private` and `public-read`, not the richer set S3 offers (no `authenticated-read`, no `aws-exec-read`, no canonical-id grantees). ACL applies at two separate places: one is the **bucket's** own ACL (set when `digitalocean_spaces_bucket` is created, defaulting to `private`), the other is each **object's** ACL (set at `digitalocean_spaces_bucket_object` PUT time, also defaulting to `private` if unspecified). Concrete example: a bucket `assets` set to `acl = "private"` (blocking public listing/reading of everything), but an object `logo.png` inside it uploaded with `acl = "public-read"` — that object is still directly readable via `bucket_domain_name/logo.png` even though the parent bucket is private. Conclusion: "public or not" on Spaces is a decision made by two combined layers (bucket ACL + object ACL), rather than one master switch controlling everything inside a bucket.

prompt: On GCP, granting a service account permissions is NOT "attaching a policy to an identity" the way you're used to on AWS IAM. Explain what GCP's actual model is, and why saying "a member's effective permission is the union of every binding at every level" matters.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
GCP doesn't let you "attach a policy to an identity" like AWS IAM does. Instead, a resource's (project, folder, organization) IAM policy is a list of **bindings**, each being a pair (role, one or more members). In other words: AWS attaches a policy TO the identity (user/role carries its own permissions as it moves); GCP does the opposite — roles and members are attached TO the resource, permission "lives" on the resource side, not the identity side. Because policy is inherited downward through organization → folder → project → resource, a member's true effective permission is the **union** of every binding applying to it at EVERY level — not just the binding at the project you're currently looking at. This matters because to know exactly what a service account can do, you can't just read the project's IAM policy — you must also check the folder and organization above it, since a binding at a higher level can silently grant additional permission that a project-level reviewer would never see.

prompt: You just SSH'd for the first time into an Ubuntu server running nginx that you've never touched. Your boss says: the nginx config is wrong somewhere, and the error log is ballooning. You are NOT allowed to use `find` or `locate` to scan the whole disk (the server is under heavy load). Walk me through how you'd navigate to the right config directory and log directory using only your knowledge of how Linux organizes files, and explain why you're confident those files live where you guess.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
I don't scan the disk; I reason from the **Filesystem Hierarchy Standard**. System config always lives under `/etc`, so nginx config is in `/etc/nginx/` — the main file `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf`, sites under `conf.d/` and `sites-enabled/`. Runtime data lives under `/var`, logs under `/var/log`, so nginx logs are at `/var/log/nginx/access.log` and `error.log`. To be sure rather than guess, I query the package directly: `dpkg -L nginx | grep -E 'etc|log'` lists every installed nginx file and where it went, because `apt`/`dpkg` records locations. In parallel I ask the running process itself: `nginx -T` dumps the config in use with each file's path, `systemctl cat nginx` shows `ExecStart` (the binary path), and `ss -tlnp` confirms nginx is listening. I'm confident because FHS is a standard every Debian package follows — locations are reproducible, so I never need `find`/`locate` on a loaded server.

prompt: You just moved from AWS to working on Azure infrastructure. A colleague asks: "Why do we always have to create this Resource Group first, then put the VM, network, and disk inside it — isn't it just a folder for tidiness?" Explain what a Resource Group actually is on Azure, why it's mandatory, and how it differs from how AWS organizes resources.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
A Resource Group isn't a decorative folder — it's Azure's mandatory **lifecycle and scope boundary**. Every resource (VM, network, disk...) must declare `resource_group_name` pointing at exactly one RG; you can't create a resource without one. Because everything lives inside an RG, deleting the RG deletes every child resource — the safest cleanup, one `az group delete` instead of remembering to delete each resource by hand and risking an orphaned disk or IP that quietly keeps billing. The RG is also where RBAC role assignment, resource locks, and cost views attach, so it's the natural isolation unit for one environment (dev/staging/prod) or one workload. This is the biggest difference from AWS: AWS has no mandatory RG layer — people group resources by tags or split accounts via Organizations, with no hard lifecycle boundary enforced. GCP has a project as its isolation boundary, but the project sits above Azure's RG. Azure's full hierarchy is Management Group → Subscription → Resource Group → Resource, and RBAC inherits down this tree.

prompt: Your team needs to store three kinds of data on Azure Blob Storage: (1) product images read constantly by a website, (2) last month's logs — occasionally looked up, (3) quarterly database backups — legally required to be kept for 3 years but almost never read again. Explain Azure Blob's three access tiers and which one fits each type of data.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
All three tiers — **Hot**, **Cool**, **Archive** — sit on one trade-off axis: **storage cost** versus **access (read/write) cost**. The less something is accessed, the more it should move to a lower tier to save on storage, at the cost of paying more for the rare read. **Hot** has the highest storage cost but the lowest access cost — right for product images since the website reads them constantly, so cheap reads matter more than cheap storage. **Cool** is cheaper than Hot to store but pricier to read, with a minimum storage duration (an early-deletion/tier-change penalty) — right for last month's logs since they're only occasionally looked up, no need for Hot-level read speed. **Archive** is the cheapest to store but the data sits **offline** — reading requires **rehydration** (a wait of hours) and it only accepts newly-written block blobs — a perfect fit for a legally-required 3-year backup that's almost never read again, since long-term storage cost dominates any concern about read speed. Access tier can be set as a default at the storage-account level and overridden per blob, or automated via a lifecycle policy that ages blobs down through tiers instead of doing it by hand.

prompt: Your company needs to store 100 TB of logs, with a compliance-mandated 7-year retention, but the data is almost never read after the first 90 days (except during an audit). A coworker suggests: "Just store it all in one Standard bucket, keep it simple." How do you push back, and how would you design the storage classes?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The "one Standard bucket" suggestion is wrong because it pays for something never used: GCS Standard is the most expensive class (optimized for frequent access, low latency), but logs are barely read after 90 days except during an audit — keeping 100 TB in Standard for 7 years costs hundreds of thousands of USD while the data mostly just sits there. The right design is a **lifecycle policy** cascading across the 4 storage classes matching decreasing access frequency: newly created objects land in **Standard** (heavily checked in the first 30 days), automatically move to **Nearline** after 30 days (accessed <1x/month, lower storage price), then **Coldline** after 90 days (accessed <1x/quarter, storage price drops further), then **Archive** after 1 year (almost never read, cheapest storage price, kept purely for compliance). Each tier trades in the opposite direction: retrieval price goes up, but since old logs are rarely read, the total 7-year cost drops more than 90% compared to leaving everything in Standard. This cascade is declared via `lifecycle_rule` with `action`/`condition` blocks on `google_storage_bucket`, running fully automatically — no manual cron job to switch classes. Finally, since this is compliance data, a second layer independent of picking the cheap class is needed: a **retention policy** configuring the minimum number of days data must be kept, combined with **bucket lock** to make that constraint **immutable** — nobody, not even the project owner, can delete/modify objects during the retention period. Storage class decides cost; retention + lock decide the legal/safety guarantee of compliance — two independent decisions, but both are required.

prompt: A new colleague says: "I gave user A the `Contributor` role, done with permissions." You notice this conflates two concepts. Explain precisely how role definition and role assignment differ in Azure RBAC, and why keeping these two concepts separate matters.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The colleague's statement conflates two separate concepts. **Role definition** answers "what can be done" — it's a list of `actions` (control-plane operations like creating/deleting/reading resources) and `dataActions` (data-plane operations like reading blob contents, reading a secret), either using a built-in role like `Contributor`/`Reader` or a custom-written one. The definition alone grants NOBODY any permission — it's just a "permission template" waiting to be used. **Role assignment** is what actually grants permission: it's a pairing of THREE pieces — a **principal** (who: user/group/service principal/managed identity, from Entra ID), a **role definition** (what: e.g. Contributor), and a **scope** (where: a specific point in the Management Group → Subscription → Resource Group → Resource tree). The statement "gave user A Contributor" is missing the single most important piece — WHAT SCOPE? Without it, nobody knows whether user A has Contributor across the entire subscription (very broad) or just on one specific Resource Group (much closer to least-privilege) — this is a huge difference in risk level. Keeping these two concepts separate matters because: a definition is reusable across countless different assignments (no need to redefine "what Contributor means" every time it's assigned to someone), which makes RBAC easier to audit — you can list every assignment (who, what permission, where) independently of re-understanding what each role means each time, and easier to standardize permissions across the organization.

prompt: You tell a new colleague: "I'm running 10 containers from the same `node:20-alpine` image, and disk usage only grew by a few dozen MB, not 10x the image size." The colleague doesn't believe it, thinking each container must have its own full copy of the image. Explain precisely how an image and a container differ, and what mechanism keeps 10 containers from costing 10x the disk space.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Your observation is entirely correct, and the reason is that an image and a container are fundamentally different things. An **image** is a set of IMMUTABLE filesystem layers plus metadata (env, entrypoint, history) — it has no state, can't run on its own, more like a static "mold" sitting on disk. A **container** is a PROCESS launched from an image, and Docker gives it its own writable layer (Copy-on-Write mechanism) sitting on top of the image's layer stack — this is the ONLY part each container owns individually; every change (new file, edited file) is written to this writable layer, never touching the image's original layers. The technical mechanism enabling sharing: Docker uses a **Union filesystem** (OverlayFS) so multiple containers can MOUNT the same read-only image layers — these layers exist ONLY ONCE on the physical disk no matter how many containers share that image; Docker never copies the whole image for each container. So when you run 10 containers from `node:20-alpine`, the extra disk usage is ONLY 10 times the size of each container's writable layer (usually a few MB if the container doesn't write much new data) — not 10 times the whole image's size. This is exactly why disk usage only grew a few dozen MB instead of several GB.

prompt: A coworker quickly deployed a service with `kubectl run web --image=nginx` (a bare Pod) and said "done — `restartPolicy: Always` means it'll bring itself back if anything goes wrong." That night the node got restarted for an OS patch, and by morning customers reported the service was fully down. Explain to the coworker exactly what `restartPolicy: Always` protects this Pod against, what it does NOT protect against, and what you'd change about the deployment so a node restart doesn't take the service down.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
`restartPolicy: Always` isn't wrong, but the coworker misjudged its scope. It's enforced by the **kubelet** on the node and only affects the **container inside a Pod that still exists**: if the container crashes, the kubelet restarts it in place, the Pod keeps its name and IP, and `RESTARTS` increments. It has nothing to do with whether a Pod that was deleted or lost along with its node gets recreated — that's a **controller's** job. A bare Pod (`kubectl run` without a Deployment) has empty `ownerReferences` — nobody owns it. When the node restarts for the OS patch, every Pod on it disappears; for a bare Pod that's the end, nothing rebuilds it, regardless of `restartPolicy`. The fix: wrap the service in a **Deployment**. The Deployment creates a **ReplicaSet**, and the ReplicaSet runs a continuous reconcile loop counting Pods matching the label selector against the desired `replicas` — if short, it creates more. When the node restart wipes out the Pod, the ReplicaSet notices the shortfall and creates a new Pod (different name/IP) on a surviving node, and the service self-heals without anyone intervening. General rule: a bare Pod should only ever be used for a one-off debug shell (`kubectl run -it --rm`); every real workload needs a controller behind it.

prompt: When you run `kubectl apply -f pod.yaml`, which control-plane components does the request pass through before the Pod actually runs on a node? Walk through the full path.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
`kubectl` calls the **apiserver** directly over HTTPS with a client cert. The apiserver runs a chain: **authentication** (verifying who via cert/bearer token/OIDC) → **authorization** (RBAC checking whether the subject has the right verb + resource) → **admission controllers** (mutating runs first and can modify the object, e.g. injecting defaults; validating runs after and only accepts/rejects) → **schema validation**, and only then writes the object to **etcd** under key `/registry/pods/<namespace>/<name>`. etcd is the single source of truth, using Raft consensus so every write is replicated across a quorum before being committed. **kube-scheduler** watches the apiserver for Pods without `spec.nodeName`, running two phases: predicate (filtering out nodes with untolerated taints, insufficient resources, or a non-matching nodeSelector) then priority (scoring 0-10 via plugins like `LeastAllocated`, `ImageLocality`) — the highest-scoring node wins, and the scheduler calls the apiserver to bind the Pod to that node via the `/binding` subresource. Finally **kubelet** on that exact node, watching the apiserver filtered by its own `nodeName`, sees the newly bound Pod and calls **CRI** (containerd over gRPC) to pull the image and actually start the container.

prompt: Your manager says: "just use the root account's access key for the Terraform provider, faster than creating an IAM user for this." How do you respond? Explain how the root account differs from an IAM user/role, and how the least-privilege principle should actually apply here.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
I'd decline this suggestion. The **root account** is the email that registered the AWS account — it holds absolute power (change billing, close the account, remove any security restriction), and the crucial point: it **cannot be restricted**, no policy can ever be attached to root to limit it. Because the risk is so severe, AWS recommends enabling MFA on root, **never creating an access key for root**, and only using root for the handful of mandatory actions like billing changes or closing the account. Everyday work — including Terraform calling the API — should go through **IAM**, a service built from four blocks: **user** (a person/service identity), **group** (a bucket of users for centralized group-based permission management), **role** (a temporary identity issuing short-lived credentials for services/cross-account access), and **policy** (a JSON document defining what actions are allowed/denied). An identity's effective permission is the sum of every policy attached to it, directly or via a group. Applying **least-privilege** to this exact situation: I'd create a dedicated IAM user (or role, if running from CI/EC2) for Terraform, attaching only the policy it actually needs for the resources it manages (e.g. EC2 + VPC + S3), absolutely not `AdministratorAccess`. Reason: if this user's access key leaks, the damage is bounded to exactly the granted scope — the attacker can't change billing, can't close the account, can't touch resources outside that scope. In contrast, leaking a root access key means losing the entire account, with no way to revoke or bound the damage afterward, because root simply doesn't accept a limiting policy.

prompt: You came from AWS, used to "attaching an IAM policy to a user/role". On GCP, a coworker tells you to "go find where to attach a policy for that service account" but you can't find that concept anywhere in the Console. Explain how GCP IAM actually grants permissions, and why the AWS "attach policy" mental model doesn't apply directly.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
There's no "place to attach a policy" on GCP because the permission-granting model is entirely different from AWS. On AWS, an IAM policy is a standalone JSON document that can be created and then "attached" to a user/role/group — people picture "the SA has a chunk of policy". On GCP, the unit of granting permission isn't a standalone document but a **binding**: attaching a **role** (a set of permissions, e.g. `roles/compute.instanceAdmin.v1`) to a **member** (user/group/service account) at a specific **level** in the resource hierarchy (resource → project → folder → organization). So looking for "where to attach for that SA" with an AWS mindset turns up nothing — instead you have to look the other way: open the IAM page of the **resource** (or project) and see "who has what role here", where your SA is one member row in that binding list. The effective policy on a specific resource is the ADDITIVE sum of every direct binding on that resource PLUS every binding inherited from folder/project/organization above it — there's no "deny" in ordinary bindings (only cumulative allow), unlike AWS where an explicit Deny can override an Allow within the same policy document. In Terraform, `google_project_iam_member` (adds one binding, additive, safe when multiple teams manage the same project), `google_project_iam_binding` (overwrites ALL members of ONE role, easy to accidentally wipe someone else's grant if you're not careful), and `google_project_iam_policy` (overwrites the ENTIRE policy of the resource, the riskiest) are all operating on this same binding concept at different additivity levels — not three different APIs for "policy" the way AWS thinking would expect.

prompt: Your team runs a 1000 RPS Node.js service on GCE using `n1-standard-2`. Your manager asks: "Why not switch to a different family to save money?" Which family would you propose, and how would you explain to your manager why `n1` is a poor choice here?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
I'd propose switching to `e2-standard-2`. Why `n1` is bad here: it's a **legacy** machine family running 2017-era Skylake CPUs, roughly 30% pricier than `e2` at the same spec while performing worse for general-purpose workloads — Google keeps `n1` mostly for backward compatibility, not as the optimal choice for new services. `e2` fits a 1000 RPS web service because web traffic always has peaks and troughs: `e2` uses shared CPU with **CPU bursting** (like AWS `t3`) — it can burst when needed then cool down, while staying the cheapest of the 4 families (e2/n2/c2/m2). I wouldn't jump straight to `n2` without evidence: if after switching to `e2`, production shows large P99 latency variance from CPU contention (other tenants on the same host fighting for CPU), that's when `n2` becomes worth considering — dedicated Cascade Lake CPU, predictable performance, but roughly 30% pricier than `e2`. `c2` (compute-optimized, high-clock) and `m2` (memory-optimized up to 12TB RAM) are only for workloads already profiled as extremely CPU-bound or memory-bound, which doesn't apply to an ordinary Node.js service. Bottom line: start with the cheapest fit (`e2`), measure for real, then upgrade with evidence.

prompt: `aws eks describe-cluster` reports `status: ACTIVE`, but `kubectl get nodes` comes back empty. A coworker says "the node's probably still booting, just wait a few more minutes." Explain why that advice is wrong, and what actually needs to happen to get a node.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
The "wait a few more minutes" advice is wrong because it assumes some background node-boot process is running — in reality, there's nothing to wait for. On EKS, the **control plane and data plane are completely decoupled**: `status: ACTIVE` only signals that the control plane portion (API server, etcd, scheduler), managed by AWS, has finished standing up and is ready to accept `kubectl` requests. Creating the cluster **never** triggers the creation of any EC2 worker node — that's a deliberately separate step in EKS's design. To get a node, you must explicitly declare either a **managed node group** (`aws_eks_node_group`) so AWS manages the EC2 lifecycle via an Auto Scaling Group, or a **Fargate profile** for a serverless data plane. With a node group, you also need exactly one **node IAM role** (trusting `ec2.amazonaws.com`) attached with all three required policies: `AmazonEKSWorkerNodePolicy` (basic kubelet operation), `AmazonEKS_CNI_Policy` (VPC CNI IP assignment), `AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryReadOnly` (image pulls). There's a more subtle near-miss to know: if a node group ALREADY exists but the role is missing one of those three policies, the EC2 instance boots fine (`kubectl get nodes` shows the node appearing) but it never turns `Ready` because the kubelet can't register or the CNI can't hand out IPs — very different from the no-node-group case (where the list is completely empty, nothing to "wait to become Ready"). So the right move here isn't to wait, but to immediately check whether an `aws_eks_node_group` resource has been declared at all, and if it has, whether the node IAM role really has every required policy.

prompt: A coworker says: "I know GitHub Actions, I push code and see the green checkmark." Explain this in more depth: what concepts make up the path from `git push` to a new image appearing on GHCR, and what role does `GITHUB_TOKEN` play in it without anyone creating a separate token?
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
The green checkmark is the final result of a clear chain of concepts, not GitHub "magic." When you `git push`, GitHub recognizes an **event**, and a **trigger** declared in a workflow (`on: push`) matching that event kicks off a **workflow** — a YAML file living in `.github/workflows/`. A workflow contains one or more **jobs**; each job is scheduled to run on its own separate **runner** — a VM (usually `ubuntu-latest`) freshly provisioned by GitHub for that job. Inside a job is a sequence of **steps** run in order: each step is either `run:` (a shell command executed directly on the runner) or `uses:` (calling a reusable **action** — from the GitHub Marketplace like `actions/checkout@v4` to clone the repo onto the runner, or a custom one). To build and push a Docker image, the workflow uses the `docker/build-push-action` action — but to actually push to **GHCR (GitHub Container Registry)**, it needs a credential to authenticate with. This is where `GITHUB_TOKEN` shines: GitHub **automatically generates and injects** this token into every job, scoped exactly to the repo and job that's running — nobody has to manually create or store a Personal Access Token. The only condition: the workflow must declare `permissions: packages: write` (the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` doesn't have write access to packages), after which `docker/build-push-action` uses that exact token to log into `ghcr.io/<owner>/<repo>:<tag>` and push the image. The whole chain — trigger → workflow → job → runner → step → action → GITHUB_TOKEN → GHCR — is exactly what produces the green checkmark on every merge.

prompt: A teammate says: "A Jenkinsfile is just a Groovy file — write `node { ... }` for flexibility, why bother distinguishing Declarative from Scripted?" Do you agree? Explain the structural difference between the two Pipeline types, and when (if ever) you'd actually need to drop down to Scripted.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
I don't fully agree. Declarative Pipeline has a fixed structure `pipeline { agent; stages; steps; post }` — this structure is exactly what lets Jenkins validate syntax up front, and it ships with `when`/`post`/`parallel` as declarative building blocks. Scripted Pipeline is plain Groovy, `node { stage('x') { ... } }` — genuinely more flexible (arbitrary loops, complex logic), but in exchange it's harder to read, harder to review in a PR, and easy to let sprawl into a script nobody dares touch. By default I use Declarative for roughly 90% of cases. I only drop to Scripted via a `script { }` block nested inside Declarative when there's dynamic logic that truly can't be expressed declaratively — say, computing an artifact name from several conditions at once. One more thing worth flagging: Scripted's freedom also makes it easier to accidentally call a Groovy method outside the sandbox allowlist, causing `RejectedAccessException` — a risk Declarative reduces since its built-in steps are already pre-approved.

prompt: A junior teammate says: "GitOps is just a fancy name for CI running `kubectl apply` after tests pass, what's actually different?" Do you agree? Explain the 4 GitOps principles and why the pull-based model differs from the push-based mechanism they're describing.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
I don't agree. What they're describing — CI running `kubectl apply` after tests pass — is **push-based**: CI holds the cluster's kubeconfig and credentials and actively pushes config out, and once the `apply` command finishes, CI considers its job done with no further monitoring. GitOps inverts this with 4 CNCF-standardized principles: **declarative** — the whole system is described by a declarative desired state, not a sequential script; **versioned and immutable** — desired state lives in git, every change is an auditable, revertible commit; **pulled automatically** — an agent (like ArgoCD's application-controller) running INSIDE the cluster pulls the desired state from git itself, nobody pushes from outside; **continuously reconciled** — the agent constantly compares actual state to desired state and self-heals drift, not a one-and-done action. Two concrete differences from push: on credentials, push-based CI needs to hold kubeconfig and network access to every cluster's apiserver (expanding the attack surface, especially across many clusters); a pull-based agent only needs read access to git, so no cluster credential ever leaves that cluster. On drift: a one-time `kubectl apply` from CI has no mechanism to detect someone `kubectl edit`-ing by hand afterward — whereas a GitOps agent reconciles continuously, detecting and (if selfHeal is on) self-healing that drift almost immediately. So the difference isn't just naming — it's a completely different security model and synchronization mechanism.

prompt: Your team's pipeline declares `stages: [build, test, deploy]`, and GitLab runs every job in `test` before moving to `deploy`, even though `deploy` really only depends on ONE job in `test`. A junior asks: "Why not let `deploy` start as soon as the job it needs finishes, instead of waiting for the whole `test` stage?" How would you answer — what mechanism actually solves this, and how does it differ from the default sequential stages?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
There is indeed a real problem here: by default GitLab runs pipelines by **sequential stages** — every job in `test` must finish completely before `deploy` starts, even when `deploy` really only needs the result of one specific job in `test`. If that stage has a slow lint job unrelated to `deploy`, it still blocks `deploy` pointlessly. The right solving mechanism is `needs`: declaring `deploy: needs: [test_integration]` turns the pipeline into a **DAG** (directed acyclic graph) — the `deploy` job runs AS SOON AS `test_integration` finishes, without waiting for other jobs also in the `test` stage (like lint) to complete. As for declaration, `deploy` still keeps `stage: deploy` — GitLab still uses this field to display the pipeline in columns on the UI and to validate structure — but the ACTUAL RUN ORDER is decided by `needs`, not by stage. That means two jobs both declared `stage: test` can run completely out of phase if one has a `needs` pointing earlier than the other. The real benefit: total pipeline time drops significantly when many jobs aren't truly sequentially dependent — here `deploy` no longer waits on lint (an unrelated task) but only on its real dependency.

prompt: A junior teammate proposes: "For GitHub Actions to deploy to AWS, let's just create an IAM user, grab the access key/secret key, and stash it in GitHub Secrets — quick and simple." Do you agree with this approach? Explain what problem OIDC federation solves that the long-lived access key approach doesn't.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
I don't agree with this "quick and simple" approach. Creating an IAM user with a static access key/secret key and stashing it in GitHub Secrets is exactly the classic CI/CD anti-pattern: this key never expires on its own. If it leaks — through an accidental log print, a workflow running on a fork PR, or simply a bad commit into history — the attacker retains AWS access PERMANENTLY until someone actively rotates it, and manual rotation is very easy to forget in practice. OIDC federation solves exactly this problem by replacing the static access key entirely with a SHORT-LIVED JWT: GitHub Actions signs a token representing the currently running workflow, AWS verifies that token's signature via the `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` mechanism (trusting GitHub as a registered IdP), then issues a set of temporary credentials that live for at most a few hours (default 1h, up to the role's `MaxSessionDuration`). The result: no static secret exists in GitHub Secrets to leak; and if some old token is exposed (e.g. in a debug log), it's completely useless since it expired (`exp`) long ago. That's exactly why OIDC federation is the mandatory standard for any modern keyless pipeline, rather than "quick and simple" via a static access key.

prompt: You just finished GCP, used to "project is the isolation boundary" — every resource, billing, quota, IAM is scoped to a project. Now moving to Azure, a coworker says "every Azure resource must live inside a Resource Group". Are these two concepts the same thing, just different names? Explain clearly.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Not the same concept with a different name — they sit at two different LEVELS in the hierarchy and solve different problems. On GCP, **project** is the hardest isolation boundary: billing, quota, AND IAM are all scoped to a project — two different projects are almost two separate "worlds". On Azure, the hierarchy is Management Group → **Subscription** → **Resource Group** → Resource. **Subscription** is the closest equivalent to a GCP project — this is where billing and quota are actually tracked. **Resource Group** sits ONE LEVEL LOWER than subscription — it's a **lifecycle boundary**, not a hard billing/quota/IAM boundary: the main purpose of an RG is to group resources sharing the same lifecycle or management purpose together (e.g. all resources of one app, or all resources of the staging environment), so they can be managed/deleted as ONE unit. The most important practical consequence: deleting an RG (`az group delete` or `terraform destroy` targeting the RG) deletes EVERY resource inside it, irreversibly — this is both an extremely powerful cleanup tool (wipe a whole test environment with one command) and a serious risk if accidentally applied to an RG holding production. On granularity: ONE subscription can absolutely hold MULTIPLE Resource Groups — teams commonly split dev/staging/prod into separate RGs BUT still within the same subscription (shared billing, separate lifecycle/management permissions), whereas on GCP environment separation is usually done at the PROJECT level (each environment its own entirely separate project, including billing). In other words: Resource Group is a more flexible, finer-grained layer that sits INSIDE GCP's project-equivalent concept (which is Subscription), not another name for the same thing.

prompt: A new teammate asks you: "Why not just write a bash script calling the AWS CLI to create everything, why do we need Terraform?". Explain how Terraform differs from a bash script (declarative vs imperative), and why `terraform.tfstate` is the mandatory piece that makes that mechanism work — if the state file were deleted, what would happen on the next `apply`?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The core difference is **declarative vs imperative**. A bash script is imperative: you write "call the API to create the VPC, then the subnet, then the EC2" — manually handling order, intermediate state, and if something fails midway you hand-write cleanup/rollback logic. Terraform is declarative: you only declare the **desired state** ("I want this VPC, this subnet, this EC2") in a `.tf` file, and Terraform builds a **dependency graph** from references (`aws_subnet.x.vpc_id` pointing to `aws_vpc.x.id`) to infer creation order, and handles **reconciliation** — comparing desired against current and fixing the gap. The mandatory piece that makes that comparison possible is `terraform.tfstate`: a JSON file recording the mapping between declarations in code and real-world resources (id, created attributes). If the state file is deleted, on the next `apply` Terraform no longer has any "memory" of what already exists — it will try to recreate resources from scratch: if the cloud allows duplicate names it creates a duplicate (waste + double cost), if the name must be unique (like an S3 bucket) it fails with "already exists" and you have to painfully `terraform import` each resource back manually. This is also exactly why Terraform achieves **idempotency**, which a raw API call from bash does not: because it always compares against state before acting, applying a second time when nothing changed reports "No changes" instead of calling the create API again.

prompt: Your manager asks: "What's the actual difference between SLSA Level 2 and Level 3, and why does our team need to climb from 2 to 3?" How do you answer in a way that proves you're not just reciting level names, but understand exactly what changes between the two levels — and why that specific change matters?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The core difference is **who gets to create provenance, and where**. Level 2 only requires provenance to be signed by a hosted build platform (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI) — but the MAIN build job can still generate and sign its own provenance, so if an attacker compromises that build job, they can forge provenance claiming "I built cleanly." Level 3 patches exactly this: it requires the build environment to be **ephemeral** (not reused across builds, avoiding state leaking from one build to the next), and critically, provenance must be generated by the build platform in a **separate, isolated** job that the main build job cannot read from or write to. This is why `slsa-github-generator` always runs two independent jobs: `build` and `provenance`. Tying to SolarWinds: the 2020 attacker compromised the internal build pipeline, not the source code, and the shipped binary still had a valid signature because the build system itself signed it. L3 doesn't prevent this 100% (if the GitHub Actions runner infrastructure itself were compromised, it would still fail), but it dramatically raises the attack cost — the attacker now has to compromise large-scale, heavily-audited build platform infrastructure instead of a lightly-watched internal build server.

prompt: You're instrumenting a new service and need to pick a metric type for three things: (1) total requests processed, (2) number of database connections currently open right now, (3) request processing latency. Which metric type do you pick for each, and why does using the wrong type (e.g. reading a counter's raw value, or averaging latency) give you misleading results?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The three types differ because the underlying data differs in nature. Total requests processed is a number that ONLY INCREASES over time (and resets to 0 on process restart) — this is exactly a **counter**; reading its raw value is meaningless (just a huge accumulated number), so you must wrap it in `rate(counter[5m])` to get "average rate of increase per second," and `rate()` automatically detects a counter drop (restart) so it doesn't produce a nonsensical negative number. The number of open database connections is a value that goes UP AND DOWN FREELY at a point in time — this is a **gauge**, read directly, no `rate()` needed. Request latency is a DISTRIBUTION, not a single number — it needs a **histogram**: it buckets observations cumulatively by the `le` label, enabling server-side quantile computation via `histogram_quantile()` and aggregation across instances. If you use an average (`_sum/_count` or an averaged gauge) for latency, you get fooled: latency has a long tail toward slowness (GC pauses, lock contention, cold cache misses) — the average gets pulled only SLIGHTLY by those slow requests but mostly still reflects the fast majority, so it looks "fine" while p99 might already be 4 seconds, and exactly that group of requests is what drives customers away. That's why SLOs/alerts are always written on p95/p99 (from a histogram), never on average. The key point: picking the wrong metric type at instrumentation time locks it in permanently — if latency was already exposed as a gauge holding an average value, there's no cleverer PromQL that recovers a quantile, because the raw individual observations were already lost at the app level.

prompt: A teammate says: "Free-text logging (arbitrary `printf`/`console.log`) has worked fine for 3 years, why bother switching to structured JSON?" How do you explain EXACTLY where free-text logging starts breaking as a system grows, rather than a generic "JSON is the industry standard"?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Free-text logging isn't "wrong" — it breaks at a SPECIFIC point: once a system grows large enough that no human reads the logs by eye anymore, and a MACHINE needs to automatically filter/aggregate/correlate. A free-text line like `"Error processing order 123 for user 456"` is plain text with no schema — to find "every error from the `checkout` service related to route `/pay` in the last hour," the logging system has to guess with a regex over the wording, and that regex BREAKS the moment someone changes the message to `"Failed processing order 123"` (one word changed, matching capability lost). By contrast, structured JSON logs — `{"level":"error","service":"checkout","route":"/pay","trace_id":"...","message":"..."}` — allow filtering/aggregation EXACTLY BY FIELD (`service="checkout" AND route="/pay"`), independent of whether the message wording changes. The more important point: this problem ONLY surfaces AT SCALE. With a single service and sparse logs, one person still reads them by eye, and "worked fine for 3 years" is genuinely true. But with dozens of services, a request crossing many services, and a need to AUTOMATICALLY stitch log lines from different services into ONE story (correlation) — free-text has no standard field to join on, while JSON's shared `trace_id` is an instant join key. Fair conclusion: JSON structured logging isn't "the industry standard so you must dogmatically follow it" — it's a solution to two specific problems (machine-parseability at scale, and cross-service correlation). If the system is genuinely small, with few services and no need for cross-service correlation, the cost of converting to JSON right now may genuinely not be worth it — but knowing the breaking point in advance helps you decide the RIGHT TIME to convert, rather than waiting until the system is already large and migrating the log format becomes far more painful.

prompt: Your manager asks: "You said a 'trace' is made of many 'spans' — so what exactly IS a span, and how does the system know which span is the child of which so it can reconstruct a request's entire call tree?" How do you answer with enough technical detail, not just "a span is a processing step"?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
A **span** is a TIMED unit of work — it can be an HTTP handler processing a request, a database query, or a call to another service. Each span carries: a name describing that piece of work, a start and end timestamp (to compute duration), a set of `attribute`s (arbitrary key-value context, e.g. `http.method=GET`, `db.statement=...`), and a `status` (success or error, with an exception if applicable). The identity mechanism for reconstructing the call tree lives in THREE values attached to every span: `trace_id` — THE SAME across EVERY span belonging to the same request, regardless of which service the span is in; `span_id` — UNIQUE to this specific span, never colliding with any other; and `parent_span_id` — pointing back to the `span_id` of the span that CALLED it (the parent). When a request travels from `gateway` to `orders` to `payments`, each service creates a new span for its own piece of work, reads the shared `trace_id` from the received context, generates a new `span_id` for itself, and sets `parent_span_id` to exactly the `span_id` of the span that called it. The tracing backend (Tempo, Jaeger) receives these spans — often arriving at different times, from different services, as DISCRETE records — then uses `trace_id` to GROUP every span belonging to the same request together, and uses the `parent_span_id` chain to ARRANGE them into a TREE (not a flat list), reflecting the correct nested call order: which span called which, which ran in parallel, which ran sequentially. A span with no `parent_span_id` (or an empty parent) is the ROOT SPAN — usually where the request first enters the system, e.g. at `gateway`.

prompt: Your team runs a video encoding job 24/7 on a `t3.large`, and there are reports the job "occasionally slows down for no clear reason" even though CPU utilization on CloudWatch doesn't look particularly high. Explain why choosing the `t3` family was wrong for this workload, what mechanism causes the slowdown, and which family it should move to.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Choosing `t3.large` for this job was wrong from the start because `t3` belongs to the **burstable** family — its CPU works on a credit mechanism: baseline is only 5-40% depending on size, and the instance accrues credits when running below baseline, spends credits when running above it. The `t` family is designed for UNEVEN workloads (dev/test, fluctuating web traffic), not a CPU-bound workload running continuously 24/7 like video encoding. The mechanism behind the "slows down for no clear reason": an encoding job sustained above baseline continuously burns `CPUCreditBalance` down to 0 after tens of minutes to a few hours depending on instance size, and at that point AWS **hard-throttles** the instance to exactly the baseline (5-40%) — CPU utilization then looks "not quite 100%" on CloudWatch, not because the job doesn't need much CPU, but because it's being capped at baseline, which is easy to mistake for "slow code" when it's actually the infrastructure choking it. The way to confirm the real cause: watch `CPUCreditBalance` on CloudWatch — if it drops toward 0 right when the job slows down, that's direct evidence of credit throttling. The real fix: move to the `c` family (compute optimized, vCPU:RAM = 1:2) — no credit mechanism, so it never throttles no matter how long it runs at full CPU, exactly matching a CPU-bound batch job like video encoding. If switching family isn't immediate, you could temporarily enable `credit_specification.cpu_credits = "unlimited"` to pay a surcharge instead of being throttled — but this is only a stopgap, costing extra per hour, not the right long-term direction for a workload already known to be continuously CPU-bound.

prompt: Your manager asks: "What's the difference between SLI, SLO, and SLA, and why must our internal SLO be STRICTER than the SLA signed with customers, instead of just being equal for simplicity?" Answer concretely with a numeric example, not just bare definitions.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The three concepts differ in ROLE, not just naming. **SLI** (Service Level Indicator) is an actual MEASURED number from the system — e.g. % of requests returning successfully over 28 days, or p99 latency. **SLO** (Service Level Objective) is an INTERNAL TARGET the team sets for that SLI — "this SLI must be ≥ 99.9%." **SLA** (Service Level Agreement) is the CONTRACTUAL version of that target, signed with an external customer, with PENALTY CLAUSES (refunds, credits) on violation. Why the SLO must be STRICTER than the SLA, not equal: if SLO = SLA, the team only realizes there's "a problem" exactly when the contract has ALREADY BEEN BREACHED — by then it's too late to fix, customers have already been affected, and the company already owes a penalty. Concrete example: the SLA signed with customers is 99.5% availability (with a refund clause on shortfall), but the team sets a stricter INTERNAL SLO of 99.9%. When the success ratio STARTS falling into the RANGE BETWEEN 99.9% and 99.5% — meaning the internal SLO has been breached but the SLA threshold has NOT been reached yet — an alert has already fired and the team has a TIME BUFFER to investigate and fix BEFORE actually breaching the customer commitment and owing a penalty. A stricter SLO is exactly an early-warning system, not an arbitrary number.

prompt: Your lead asks you to add a CPU-based `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` to a production Deployment, but that Deployment currently does NOT declare `resources.requests`. Can you add the HPA right away? If not, what's missing, and why does missing exactly that make HPA "blind"?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Not right away — `resources.requests.cpu` must be added to the container first. CPU-based HPA (`type: Resource`, `target.type: Utilization`) computes `currentUtilization = (average actual CPU used per pod) / requests.cpu × 100%`. Requests is the **denominator** of that formula; without it HPA has nothing to divide by, and `kubectl get hpa` will show the TARGETS column as `<unknown>/50%` forever — the HPA sits idle even though real CPU has spiked, because it can't "read" utilization. What needs to happen: add `resources.requests.cpu` (e.g. `100m`) to the container, ideally with `limits.cpu` as a ceiling so one pod can't eat the whole node's CPU — but `limits` is not HPA's denominator, only `requests` is. After adding it, reapply the Deployment then the HPA, and confirm via `kubectl get hpa` that TARGETS shows a real number (e.g. `1%/50%`) instead of `<unknown>` before trusting the HPA to work.

prompt: You just learned three deployment strategies: rolling update, canary, and blue-green. Explain to someone newer: how does each strategy shift traffic from the old version to the new one, and if the new version has a serious bug, how big is each one's "blast radius" compared to the others?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The three strategies differ in HOW they shift traffic and the CONSEQUENCE when the new version breaks. **Rolling update** (Kubernetes Deployment's default) replaces old pods with new ones in small sequential batches — at any point during the rollout, both old and new versions coexist and both receive traffic randomly via the Service. If the new version has a bug, some requests already "hit" the broken version starting from the very first pods replaced, and blast radius (the fraction of traffic hitting the bug) grows with rollout progress — nobody deliberately caps that number at a safe threshold. **Canary** solves exactly that problem: deliberately route a small, controlled slice of traffic (e.g. 5-20%) to the new version, keep most on the old one, and observe signals (error rate, latency) before gradually increasing the ratio. Blast radius here is DELIBERATELY CAPPED at exactly the percentage routed to canary — if a bug shows up at the 10% step, only 10% of traffic is affected, not 100%. **Blue-green** takes a different approach: stand up an entirely new version (green) running alongside the currently serving one (blue), then flip ALL traffic at once from blue to green. There's no prolonged "both versions receiving traffic" phase — it's either 100% on blue or 100% on green. If green has a bug, rollback is nearly instant by pointing traffic back at blue (already running, no restart needed). Trade-offs: canary is safest on initial blast radius but slowest (many observation steps before full rollout); blue-green rolls back fastest but costs double the resources since it must run 2x replicas in parallel during the switch; rolling is cheapest on resources (no extra capacity needed) but hardest to precisely cap blast radius at a desired percentage.

prompt: A junior teammate wrote a Helm chart but hard-coded `replicas: 3` and `image: myapp:1.2.0` directly in `templates/deployment.yaml`, not using `values.yaml` at all — and `helm install` still runs fine. Explain to them: what's wrong with doing it this way, and why is separating values into `values.yaml` the condition for "one chart runs across multiple environments"?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
It's true `helm install` still runs with hard-coded values, because Helm just renders the Go template into a YAML manifest and `kubectl apply`s it — it doesn't force you to use `values.yaml`. But this isn't a proper chart, and the problem shows up the moment you need that chart for a second environment: to deploy staging with 1 replica and a different image tag, the only option is to EDIT `templates/deployment.yaml` DIRECTLY — meaning the chart is no longer "one shared copy", each environment needs its own hand-edited version or you must remember to edit it before every install, extremely error-prone and a source of drift between environments. The right approach: move every value that differs between environments into `values.yaml` as defaults — `replicas: 3`, `image: { repository: myapp, tag: 1.2.0 }` — then the template only references them via the `{{ .Values.replicas }}` and `{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}` directives, with no hard-coded numbers or strings left. Then each environment just needs ONE values file of its own (`values-staging.yaml` with `replicas: 1`, `values-prod.yaml` with `replicas: 5`) to override the defaults via `helm install -f values-staging.yaml`, WITHOUT touching the original template. Core principle: the template is the FIXED, reusable part; only `values` CHANGES per environment. Correctly separating the two is the required condition for one chart to run across multiple environments without forking code or hand-editing before every deploy.

prompt: A junior teammate says: "RTO and RPO sound the same, they're both 'time', right?" Explain to them: what does each metric actually measure, and give a concrete example that makes the difference obvious.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
RTO and RPO measure two completely different AXES, even though both are expressed in time units. **RTO (Recovery Time Objective)** answers "how long is the system allowed to be DOWN?" — it measures the time from when the incident happens to when the system is FULLY RECOVERED and serving again, i.e. the DOWNTIME axis. **RPO (Recovery Point Objective)** answers a completely different question: "how much DATA are we allowed to LOSE?" — it measures the gap between the MOST RECENT backup and the moment the incident happens, i.e. the DATA-LOSS axis, unrelated to how fast or slow recovery is. A concrete example to separate the two: a system backs up every 24 hours (say at midnight), and an incident happens at 11pm the same day — the real RPO is nearly 24 hours: every data change since the last backup (midnight) up to the incident (11pm) is PERMANENTLY LOST when restoring from that backup, regardless of whether the team then finishes restoring in 10 minutes or 3 hours — restore speed is an RTO matter, entirely unrelated to how much data was already lost. Because these are two independent axes, a system can have a SHORT RTO (very fast restore, e.g. 10 minutes) but a LONG RPO (sparse backups, up to 24h of data lost) if backups are infrequent but the restore process is well-practiced; or the reverse, a SHORT RPO (near-continuous backups) but a LONG RTO if the restore process is manual, never tested, and takes hours to run correctly. To improve RPO, increase backup FREQUENCY (or switch to near-real-time replication); to improve RTO, optimize the restore PROCESS (automation, restore drills) — two different efforts; doing just one won't improve both.

prompt: A teammate proposes: "to save the most money, let's write a lifecycle rule that moves EVERY object to Glacier Deep Archive after just 1 day, including app logs the team usually deletes after a few days once processed." Do you agree? Explain the concrete risk of this proposal.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
I disagree with this proposal. The issue is the **minimum storage duration charge** concept: every storage class cheaper than Standard carries a mandatory minimum storage time — Standard-IA is 30 days, Glacier Instant/Flexible Retrieval is 90 days, and Deep Archive is 180 days. If an object is transitioned to a class and then deleted EARLIER than this minimum, AWS still charges for the FULL minimum duration as if the object sat there that entire time — deleting early does NOT "save money" as intuition might suggest. Applied to the log scenario: if the team habitually deletes app logs after a few days once processed (far shorter than Deep Archive's 180-day minimum), forcing ALL objects — including these short-lived logs — into Deep Archive after just 1 day makes the ACTUAL cost HIGHER than leaving them in Standard and deleting on schedule within a few days, since the team still pays for the full 180 days of storage despite the data actually existing for only a few days. On top of that, retrieval cost runs INVERSELY to storage cost: the cheaper the storage (Deep Archive), the more expensive retrieval gets and the higher the latency (12-48 hours) — if these logs occasionally need to be pulled for debugging, having them in Deep Archive means paying more and waiting much longer to read them back. The correct rule: only transition an object to a storage class when its expected lifetime is ≥ that class's minimum duration — short-lived logs should stay in Standard and use `expiration` (not `transition`) to delete on schedule when no longer needed; only data that genuinely needs long-term retention (audit trails, compliance backups, legal data) is worth transitioning to Glacier/Deep Archive. Lifecycle rules should be segmented by `filter.prefix` (e.g. `logs/app/` vs `logs/audit/`) instead of applying one blanket rule to every object in the bucket.

prompt: Your team needs a role in account B to read objects in an S3 bucket in account A, WITHOUT account B needing to attach anything else. A teammate asks: "just attaching an identity policy to the role in account B is enough, right?" How do you respond, and why?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The answer is NOT enough — attaching only an identity policy in account B doesn't solve the cross-account problem. The reason lies in the fundamentally different nature of the two policy types: an **identity-based policy** attaches to a principal (user/group/role) and answers "what can this principal DO" — it knows nothing about whether a resource in a DIFFERENT account agrees to let it touch anything. For cross-account to work, a **resource-based policy** is needed — attached to the resource itself, here the S3 bucket policy placed in account A, answering "WHO can touch this resource". This is the ONLY policy type capable of granting cross-account access without the other side (account B) needing to attach anything, because the resource itself (the bucket in account A) declares trust in a foreign principal (the role in account B). For cross-account, AWS applies exactly the "two-key model": the bucket policy in account A must name the specific role ARN of account B in the `Principal` block, AND at the same time that role in account B still needs its own identity policy allowing `s3:GetObject` — missing EITHER side still leaves the request `AccessDenied`, not "one side allowing is enough". This is entirely different from the SAME-account case: if the resource and principal belong to the same account, "resource policy allow OR identity policy allow" is enough to pass — neither one alone is required in the cross-account case, both are. The most common mistake is carrying "same-account" thinking into a cross-account situation and forgetting the other side. The concrete config needed: (1) in account A, create an `aws_s3_bucket_policy` with `Principal` being account B's role ARN (possibly with a condition like `aws:SourceIp` for tighter control); (2) in account B, attach an `aws_iam_role_policy` or `aws_iam_policy` to that role allowing `s3:GetObject` on the exact ARN of the bucket in account A. Only when BOTH steps exist together does the request pass.

prompt: You just moved from an AWS-based team to DevOps for a DigitalOcean team. Your manager asks: "On DO, who decides who can do what, and where does that live?" List the exact three access-control surfaces that really exist on DO, and explain which guardrail layers DO is missing compared to the AWS IAM you're used to.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
DO has exactly three access-control surfaces, no more. One, **PAT scope** — the token can be read-only or full-access, chosen at creation, stored in the `DIGITALOCEAN_TOKEN` env var, not a `.tf` resource, so you can't review its scope through a Terraform PR. Two, **Spaces key grant** — each Spaces key carries one or more `{bucket, permission}` pairs, permission being only `read`/`readwrite`/`fullaccess`; this is the real least-privilege surface for object storage, fully separate from the PAT. Three, **project** — just an administrative bucket grouping resources by environment/billing, carrying no permission field, so placing a bucket in a `Production` project does not tighten access on it at all. Compared to AWS, DO lacks assume-role/STS, instance profiles, workload-identity federation, permission boundaries, org SCPs, per-action policies with condition keys, and a dedicated KMS. Honest trade-off: fewer knobs means fewer places to get wrong (IAM misconfig is AWS's #1 vulnerability source), but also fewer defensive layers — so on DO, protecting access control is mostly about protecting and rotating the right token/key, not writing policy.

prompt: Your app has the domain `api.example.com`. External Internet users must resolve to the anycast IP of the public load balancer. But another service in the same VPC calling `api.example.com` should go straight through the internal load balancer, without going out to the Internet and back (wasting latency + egress). How do you design Cloud DNS to hit both goals at once, and what's the mechanism behind it?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
This is exactly the **split-horizon DNS** pattern. I'd create two `google_dns_managed_zone` resources, both with `dns_name = "api.example.com."` (trailing dot required) but different `visibility`: one zone with `visibility = "public"` holding an A record pointing to the anycast IP of a `google_compute_global_forwarding_rule` (external LB) — this is the answer for every query from the Internet. One zone with `visibility = "private"` holding an A record pointing to the internal load balancer's internal IP, and it's **mandatory** to set `private_visibility_config.networks` to my VPC — without this step, instances in the VPC still resolve through the public zone (Cloud DNS only prefers the private zone when the exact VPC is bound). Result: the same lookup of `api.example.com` returns the public anycast IP for external users and the internal LB IP for services in the VPC — not two different domain names. The main benefit: service-to-service traffic doesn't have to leave to the Internet and loop back through the external LB, saving latency, saving egress cost, and cleanly separating internal traffic from public traffic — safer since the internal service is never exposed externally.

prompt: A dev on your team runs a daily deploy script from their personal machine by downloading a JSON key for a service account that has `roles/owner` on the project, and setting `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` to point at that file. What's wrong with this approach, and what would you propose instead?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The current approach stacks two layers of risk. Layer 1 — a JSON key is a **long-lived credential that never expires on its own**: once downloaded to a personal machine, it exists forever until someone actively revokes it. If this file is accidentally committed to a git repo (even private), copied off a lost/compromised personal machine, or accidentally logged somewhere, an attacker gets that SA's permissions **indefinitely** — there's no self-expiry mechanism bounding the damage window, unlike a temporary token that invalidates itself after a short time. Layer 2 — overly broad scope: `roles/owner` is the highest permission on a project, granted for a task that's "just deploy" — a serious least-privilege violation; if the key leaks, the blast radius is the **entire project** (deleting resources, changing IAM, accessing all data), not limited to the deploy scope. Proposed replacement: **service account impersonation**. The dev signs in with their own personal identity (`gcloud auth login`, not a key file), granted exactly one permission — `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` on the target SA (the SA still holds the business permission needed for deploy, ideally narrower than `owner` — just enough for the actual deploy). When the script needs to run, the dev calls the `generateAccessToken` API to **mint a short-lived access token** (at most 3600 seconds) representing that SA, used once and gone — no file sits around on the personal machine for long enough to leak. The biggest benefit of this separation: business permission stays centralized on the SA (easy to audit, easy to review), while the dev's personal identity only holds "allowed to impersonate", never the business permission directly — revoking a dev's access is just removing the Token Creator binding on that SA, no key rotation/revocation dance needed.

prompt: You're used to AWS NACLs, where opening a port for an inbound client call requires writing BOTH inbound (for the request) AND outbound (for the response, usually opening the whole ephemeral port range 1024-65535) rules. Now you're writing a Network Security Group (NSG) on Azure for a VM that only needs to receive HTTP inbound on port 443 from the Internet. Do you need to write an extra outbound rule for the response? Explain the mechanism behind it.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
No extra outbound rule needed for the response — one inbound rule allowing HTTPS on port 443 covers the entire flow, both directions. The reason is that NSGs are **stateful**: once an inbound flow is allowed (tracked by 5-tuple: source IP, source port, dest IP, dest port, protocol), Azure automatically permits the RETURN traffic of that exact flow to go back out with no matching outbound rule needed — the connection-tracking mechanism recognizes "this is the response to an already-allowed request" and lets it through. This is the core difference from AWS **NACLs**, which are **stateless**: NACLs don't track connections, so each direction requires its own completely independent rule — allowing an inbound request does NOT automatically allow the outbound response. Since the client calls in from a **random ephemeral port** (usually within 1024-65535, chosen by the client OS), for the response to actually get out, NACLs require opening the WHOLE ephemeral range on the outbound rule — there's no way to know in advance which exact port the client will use. This is exactly why NSG rule sets end up much leaner than NACLs in practice: just ONE inbound rule covers this simple HTTPS-inbound use case, while the NACL equivalent needs at least two rules (inbound port 443 + outbound ephemeral range). A notable practical consequence: a leaner rule set means less chance of misconfiguring/forgetting to open the ephemeral range — a very common mistake when hand-configuring NACLs (forgetting the outbound ephemeral open blocks the response, "hanging" the connection even though inbound was correct) — NSGs eliminate this entire class of error via their stateful design.

prompt: You need to grant a service account rights to only `list` and `get` Compute instances, plus `list` objects in Storage — no create/update/delete at all. A teammate suggests granting `roles/editor` "to be safe, so we don't have to come back and ask for more later." Do you agree, and which of GCP's three role types (basic/predefined/custom) would you choose?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
I disagree with `roles/editor`. It's a **basic role** — extremely broad in scope, granting nearly full create/update/delete rights on most project resources, completely at odds with "only list/get, no create/update/delete." Granting `roles/editor` to an SA that only needs to read is a severe least-privilege violation — if that SA leaks, an attacker can modify/delete nearly everything. GCP's three role types in order of preference: basic (`owner`/`editor`/`viewer`, only for personal sandboxes) → predefined (Google-maintained, scoped to one service, preferred choice) → custom (you list permissions yourself, used when predefined is still broader than needed). Here, try predefined first: `roles/compute.viewer` + `roles/storage.objectViewer` might be enough if they match exactly — but check whether that predefined role includes any excess permission (predefined roles are sometimes slightly broader than "just list/get"). If it's still too broad, use `google_project_iam_custom_role` listing exactly `compute.instances.list`, `compute.instances.get`, `storage.objects.list` — maximum least-privilege, exactly the point of a custom role for a read-only SA. Trade-off of a custom role: you have to maintain it yourself as Google adds/removes/deprecates permissions, whereas predefined roles are updated automatically by Google.

prompt: A teammate says: "this is a public subnet because I named it `public-subnet-1a`." Do you agree with that way of determining it? What ACTUALLY decides whether a subnet is public or private on AWS, and why does choosing a `/16` CIDR for the VPC upfront matter?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
I disagree with determining it by name. A subnet is fundamentally just a CIDR range tied to an AZ — the name `public-subnet-1a` is only a naming convention for humans, it carries no technical meaning to AWS. What ACTUALLY decides whether a subnet is public or private is the **route table** associated with it. A subnet is public when its route table has `0.0.0.0/0 → Internet Gateway`, PLUS the subnet attribute `map_public_ip_on_launch = true` — without that attribute, even with the correct route, the instance doesn't automatically get a public IP so it still can't reach the internet (a nasty debugging trap because "the route looks right"). A subnet is private (egress) when its route table points `0.0.0.0/0 → NAT Gateway` — allowing egress (pulling images, calling outbound APIs) but not accepting direct inbound from the internet. And the data/isolated tier has NO default route at all, reaching only internal VPC traffic — this is where RDS/ElastiCache go for maximum isolation. Route tables also use **longest prefix match**: a more specific route always wins over a broader one, and a broad route wins over the default `0.0.0.0/0`; each subnet is associated with exactly one route table, and without an explicit association it falls into the main route table (usually with no internet route). On CIDR: you should choose a `/16` for the VPC upfront because the VPC's primary CIDR CANNOT be resized after creation — you can only add a secondary CIDR via `associate-vpc-cidr-block`, never change the original block. A `/16` gives enough of the 65k IPs to slice subnets by AZ × tier (public/private/data) without worrying about running out of room as the system grows.

prompt: Your web backend has 5000 concurrent users, each holding a Postgres connection. A teammate proposes: "Just tune Managed PostgreSQL's `max_connections` up to 5000 in the parameter group and we're done." Do you agree, and how would you actually solve this on DO?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
I disagree. DO Managed Database doesn't have a hundreds-of-options parameter group like AWS RDS to freely tune `max_connections` — and even if it did, opening 5000 direct connections to Postgres would consume enough RAM to crash a small node (each Postgres connection costs roughly 10MB RAM). The right approach on DO is `digitalocean_database_connection_pool` — PgBouncer running on port 25061, pooling thousands of clients into a much smaller `size` of real connections to Postgres, instead of each client holding its own connection. For production, choose `mode = "transaction"` — returns the connection to the pool right after each commit, the most connection-efficient, unlike `session` (holds it the whole session, less efficient) or `statement` (strictest, returns after each statement). The most important caveat: per the Registry, the connection pool is **PostgreSQL-only** — if the backend runs MySQL, DO has no equivalent built-in PgBouncer, you'd need to run an external pooler like ProxySQL yourself. Bottom line: this is a connection-load problem, solved with a **pool**, not by tuning `max_connections`.

prompt: Your `$6/month` Droplet only has a 25 GB boot disk, but your Postgres data needs 100 GB and is still growing. A teammate suggests: "Simple, just upgrade the Droplet to a bigger size for a 100 GB disk and we're done." Do you agree? If not, what would you use instead and why is it better?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
I disagree. Upgrading the Droplet for a bigger disk ties the disk tightly to CPU/RAM — needing more disk means swapping the whole flavor, and it's still the Droplet's **boot** disk, which can't be separated for independent backup/migration, and disappears when the Droplet is destroyed. The right approach is a **Block Volume**: a standalone resource, created ahead of time and attached later, with a lifecycle entirely decoupled from the Droplet — you can detach it and attach it to a different Droplet, snapshot it independently, and it keeps existing (and keeps billing) even after the original Droplet has been destroyed. That's exactly what "upgrade the Droplet for a bigger disk" can never give you. Use a Volume for data that must persist across repeated Droplet re-creation: Postgres/MongoDB data directories, log file streaming, application working set. Verify the independence with `terraform output volume_attached_droplet_ids` — showing exactly one Droplet ID at a time since Volumes are single-attach — and by checking the Volume still exists (and still bills) after the host Droplet was `terraform destroy`-ed.

prompt: Your workflow uses `uses: some-3rd-party/action@v4`. A security review asks you to pin it to a full SHA instead of the tag. Explain exactly why `@v4` is less safe, and what pinning to a SHA actually solves.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
The issue lies in the nature of a Git tag: `@v4` or `@main` are **mutable** names — they're just pointers to a commit, and that pointer can be **moved**. The action's legitimate maintainer (perfectly legally, when releasing a new version) or an attacker who has gained push access to that repo (a compromised account, or a malicious PR that got merged) can both make the `@v4` tag point at a different commit — including one containing malicious code — without anyone on your team knowing. The concrete consequence: the next time your workflow runs `uses: some-3rd-party/action@v4`, GitHub Actions pulls exactly whatever content that tag CURRENTLY points to — if it's been moved to malicious code, your runner will **automatically execute** it, with full access to secrets, the repo's source code, and anything else the runner can reach. This is precisely the kind of supply chain attack that has happened in the wild. Pinning to a **full SHA** (`@a1b2c3d4e5f6...`) solves it at the root because a SHA is **immutable** — it's a cryptographic hash of the exact content at one specific commit; there's no way for that same SHA to ever point at different content, since changing even a single byte produces a completely different SHA. When you pin by SHA, the workflow always runs EXACTLY the code your team reviewed and accepted once, no matter what anyone does to the tag afterward. To keep SHA pinning from turning into a "never update anything" burden, use **Dependabot** (or an equivalent tool) to automatically open a PR proposing a bump to the new SHA whenever a new release comes out — you still review every update, just without manually looking up SHAs by hand.

prompt: You need to grant a worker access to read files from exactly one Spaces bucket named `reports`, with no write/delete, and no access to any other bucket. A teammate suggests creating a `fullaccess` Spaces key "to keep it simple, so we don't have to redo it later." Do you agree, and how would you create the Spaces key correctly?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
I don't agree with `fullaccess`. Per DO's schema, `fullaccess` requires `bucket` to be an empty string — meaning the key gets access to the entire account's Spaces, not scoped to any bucket; if this read-only worker's key leaks, an attacker can write/delete on every bucket. The right fix: create a Spaces key with exactly one grant block `{bucket = "reports", permission = "read"}` — permission has only three valid values (`read`/`readwrite`/`fullaccess`), and I pick the lowest one that's sufficient. Each key has its own access_key/secret_key pair, so revoking exactly this worker's access is just deleting its key — other keys are unaffected, unlike editing a shared JSON policy the way IAM works. Verify by attempting a PUT with that key against the bucket: it must return `AccessDenied` since the key only carries read.

prompt: A teammate reports a bug: "I gave the CI pipeline `sts:AssumeRole` permission already, but `terraform apply` launching an EC2 with an instance profile still gets `AccessDenied`, I don't understand why." What do you diagnose, and explain the difference between `sts:AssumeRole` and `iam:PassRole`.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
This is a classic bug caused by confusing two permissions with similar-sounding names but completely different natures. `sts:AssumeRole` is the action for a principal (here, the CI pipeline) to itself BECOME another role — it calls STS, STS checks the target role's trust policy, then returns temporary credentials so the pipeline ACTS UNDER THAT ROLE'S IDENTITY. This permission lives in the target role's TRUST POLICY, and only makes sense when the pipeline itself wants to change its own identity. But the situation here is completely different: the pipeline doesn't need to BECOME the instance profile role, it's just ATTACHING that role to a newly launched EC2 instance, so the EC2 runs under the instance profile's own permission — the pipeline keeps its own identity throughout. The action "hand a role to an AWS service to use on its behalf" (EC2 running under an instance profile, Lambda running under an execution role, an ECS task using a task role) needs a SEPARATE permission: `iam:PassRole`. This permission lives in the IDENTITY POLICY of the pipeline itself (the principal performing `RunInstances`), having nothing to do with the STS flow. Granting the pipeline `sts:AssumeRole` only lets it change its own identity if needed, but does NOT allow it to attach any role to EC2 at all — that's why `terraform apply` still gets `AccessDenied` despite already having `sts:AssumeRole`. The correct fix: grant the pipeline `iam:PassRole` as well, and just as important — scope this permission's `Resource` down to exactly the ARN of the role being passed (never use `Resource: "*"`, since that would let the pipeline pass ANY role, including an admin role, to a service, opening a privilege escalation path), with a condition `iam:PassedToService = ec2.amazonaws.com` to ensure that role can only be passed to the EC2 service, not abused to pass it to some other unintended service.
