If team A runs `helm install team-a-release ./mychart` and team B runs `helm install team-b-release ./mychart` in the SAME namespace, both try to create a Deployment named `myapp` — causing a resource name collision: the release installed later errors that the resource already exists (owned by the other release), or worse, silently "takes over" and modifies the other release's resource if Helm can't detect the ownership mismatch. The problem extends to the label too: `app: myapp` is also hard-coded identically, so the `selector.matchLabels` of the Deployment, and any `Service` sharing this pattern, risk matching the WRONG pods belonging to a different release with the same label — causing traffic to be misrouted between two supposedly independent releases. The standard Helm fix (matching the default template `helm create` generates): add a `mychart.fullname` helper that combines `.Release.Name` with the chart name, e.g. using logic equivalent to `{{- if .Values.fullnameOverride -}}{{ .Values.fullnameOverride }}{{- else -}}{{ .Release.Name }}-{{ .Chart.Name }}{{- end -}}` (shortened if they match), then replace EVERY `mychart.name` reference with `mychart.fullname` in `metadata.name` and the `app.kubernetes.io/instance`/`app.kubernetes.io/name` labels. After the fix, each release will have a UNIQUE resource name and label tied to its own `Release.Name`. To verify, install two differently-named releases (`rel-a`, `rel-b`) in the same namespace on a test cluster, confirming `kubectl get deploy` shows two distinctly-named Deployments with no collision or cross-routing.

prompt: A coworker sends you the Terraform below for review before applying — the team wants to manage a GitLab project's CI/CD variables with Terraform instead of typing them into the UI by hand. Point out EVERY issue you see (not just one) and propose a fix.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
There are two serious issues and one loose configuration issue, ranked by priority to fix. Most severe: `DEPLOY_TOKEN` has `value = "abc"` — both hardcoded directly in HCL (goes into git history and Terraform state, the same mistake seen with hardcoded credentials in Jenkins) and too short to satisfy GitLab's masking requirements (a maskable value needs to be long enough, no whitespace, base64-friendly). With this 3-character value, `masked = true` will almost certainly make GitLab reject creating the variable (a validation error), or worse, accept it but fail to mask it in logs — both are bad outcomes. Fix: read `DEPLOY_TOKEN` from a Terraform variable injected via `TF_VAR_deploy_token` (the way `registry_password` already does it correctly), and make sure the real token is long enough (a GitLab token like `glpat-...` always satisfies this). Second issue: neither resource sets `protected = true` for a secret used to DEPLOY (`DEPLOY_TOKEN` explicitly sets `false`, `REGISTRY_PASSWORD` leaves it unset so it also defaults to `false`). `protected = false` means EVERY pipeline, even one running on any random feature branch from an MR, can read the production deploy secret — so `protected = true` should be set so only pipelines running on a protected branch (usually `main`/a release tag) can see these secrets, shrinking the risk surface to exactly where it should be. In short, before merging, I'd fix all three: `DEPLOY_TOKEN`'s value via `TF_VAR_*` instead of a literal, and `protected = true` on both resources.

prompt: A coworker sends you the Jenkinsfile below for review before merging — the pipeline deploys to a registry that needs a token, and runs directly on the controller "to save time, no need to set up an agent." Review it carefully, point out EVERY security issue you see (not just one), and propose a concrete fix for each.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
There are three issues, ranked by severity. The most severe: `REGISTRY_TOKEN = 'glpat-...'` hardcoded directly in `environment` — this value goes straight into git history permanently, so anyone with read access to the repo (even after the token is rotated) can see the old token. Fix: create a Secret text credential in the Jenkins credential store (via Terraform `jenkins_credential_username` or the equivalent secret-text resource), then wrap the step using it in `withCredentials([string(credentialsId: 'registry-token', variable: 'REGISTRY_TOKEN')]) { sh "docker login -u ci -p ${REGISTRY_TOKEN} registry.example.com" }` — never a literal in the Jenkinsfile. The second issue is subtler: even after switching to `withCredentials`, Jenkins ONLY masks secret values in the console log, not when you write it to a file yourself. The line `echo "Deployed with token ${REGISTRY_TOKEN}" > out/deploy-log.txt` followed by `archiveArtifacts` on that same file means the raw token sits in a downloadable UI artifact — a complete leak outside the reach of masking. Fix: remove the line writing the token to a file; if a deploy log is needed, only log `BUILD_NUMBER` and a timestamp, never a variable holding the secret. The third issue: `agent any` lets this stage run directly on the controller whenever it has a free executor — a build (even from an untrusted PR) running on the controller can read `JENKINS_HOME` and other system secrets. Fix: set `numExecutors: 0` on the controller to force every build onto an isolated agent, and specify `agent { label 'deploy' }` instead of `any`.

prompt: A coworker opened a PR adding Cloud Armor to block SQLi and asks you to review before merging. They're confident: "I already created a security policy with the OWASP CRS rule, it's definitely blocked." Reading the Terraform below, how do you review it — do you approve the merge, and what do you say in the comment?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
I would NOT approve this merge as-is. The OWASP CRS rule (`sqli-v33-stable`) in `google_compute_security_policy.waf` is syntactically correct, priority is sensible, and there's a default allow rule at the end — policy logic-wise it's fine. But the bug is elsewhere: `google_compute_backend_service.web` has **no** `security_policy` argument pointing to `google_compute_security_policy.waf.id`. On GCP, Cloud Armor isn't a standalone appliance that automatically blocks traffic — it must be **attached directly** to a backend service through that argument before it's evaluated in the data path at the edge POP. Without that line, `google_compute_security_policy.waf` still `apply`s successfully (Terraform reports no error, since the policy is a valid resource on its own), but it **enforces nothing** — all traffic flows straight through `google_compute_backend_service.web` without ever touching the SQLi rule. This is the #1 Cloud Armor trap: apply succeeding makes it easy to assume it's blocking, when actually 0% of requests are ever inspected by this policy. My review comment: "The policy is written correctly but never attached — add `security_policy = google_compute_security_policy.waf.id` to `google_compute_backend_service.web`. After applying, don't just trust that `apply` succeeded — verify with `terraform state show google_compute_backend_service.web | grep security_policy` to confirm the field is set, and send a fake SQLi request (`?id=1' OR '1'='1`) then check Cloud Logging filtered on `jsonPayload.enforcedSecurityPolicy.outcome=DENY` to see the policy actually block it."

prompt: A junior teammate asks you to review the `modules/app-stack` module below before it gets published to the internal registry for the whole company to use. Review it like a senior would: point out the design problems (not syntax errors), and propose how to split the module correctly.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The main problem isn't syntax, it's design: this is a textbook **God module** — a single module carrying networking (VPC/subnet), database (RDS), load balancer + compute (ALB/ECS), IAM, WAF, and DNS (Route53), essentially the entire application stack crammed into one place. The first consequence is 34 input variables: any consumer calling this module has to read and understand — and fill in — nearly the whole input surface even if they only need a part of it, e.g. a team that just needs a shared VPC still has to care about `db_engine`, `lb_type`, `enable_waf`. The guideline for an easy-to-use module is input ≤10, output ≤5 — one clear responsibility that can be tested and refactored. The second, more serious consequence for production is unbounded blast radius: a small change to WAF or Route53 forces `plan`/`apply` to touch every resource in the module, including the RDS/VPC already running live, increasing the risk that a small change accidentally affects an unrelated infrastructure layer. My proposal is to split it along clear responsibility boundaries: a `networking` module (VPC, subnet, route table), a `database` module (RDS/Aurora), a `compute` module (ECS + ALB), a `security` module (IAM role, WAF) — each exposing only what's needed (`vpc_id`, `subnet_ids`, `db_endpoint`, ...), with a root module orchestrating by wiring one module's output into another module's input via references, so Terraform can build an explicit dependency graph between modules instead of one inseparable block. Before publishing to the internal registry, each sub-module should version independently under semver, pinned via `version = "~> x.y"` at the consumer side — keeping one giant module means even a WAF-only change forces a version bump that affects the entire registry, for every team using that module for both VPC and RDS.

prompt: A coworker opens a PR adding an IAM Deny Policy to block EVERYONE (even admins) from modifying the project's IAM policy, aiming to prevent privilege escalation. They say: "Let's block it absolutely to be safe, nobody touches `setIamPolicy` anymore." Reading the Terraform below, how do you review it BEFORE merging — is there a serious risk left unhandled?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
I would NOT approve this merge as-is — the idea of "blocking `setIamPolicy` to prevent privilege escalation" is sound, but the implementation is missing exactly ONE line that can cause the most serious incident possible with IAM: **self-lockout**. `denied_principals = ["principalSet://goog/public:all"]` means this deny rule applies to **absolutely every principal**, with no exception since `exception_principals` isn't configured. After `apply`, once the deny propagates (up to ~7 minutes), **nobody** in the organization — not the org-admin, not even whoever just wrote this rule — will be able to call `cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com/projects.setIamPolicy` on that project anymore. The scariest part: editing THIS SAME deny rule (to loosen or remove it) ALSO goes through the same `setIamPolicy` permission — so once locked out, there's no way to self-rescue from inside the project; the only option left is contacting **Google Cloud Support** for manual intervention, a slow process that can take hours to days depending on the support tier. The mandatory fix before merging: add `exception_principals` containing at least one break-glass identity into the rule RIGHT NOW — this could be a dedicated service account used only for emergencies (tightly audited, never used day-to-day) or a pre-identified org-admin group — so that identity always retains the ability to call `setIamPolicy` even while this deny rule is active. Before applying to production, test on a separate project/sandbox: apply the rule, confirm the identity in `exception_principals` can still `setIamPolicy` (using `gcloud policy-troubleshoot` or attempting a small direct IAM change), while a DIFFERENT principal gets denied as expected — only once both are confirmed should this be applied to the real project.

prompt: A teammate wrote the `AnalysisTemplate` below so canary auto-rollbacks when p95 latency degrades. Review it carefully and point out every problem — including anything that "looks reasonable but will cause harm in production".
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
There are four issues. Most serious: the template has NO `failureCondition`. The goal is "auto-rollback when p95 degrades", but declaring only `successCondition: result < 500` means when p95 exceeds 500, the AnalysisRun isn't clearly defined as "failed" — per Argo Rollouts semantics, missing `failureCondition` leaves the system with no basis to transition to `Failed`; a bad result is simply "not success", very likely landing on `Inconclusive` and NOT triggering auto-rollback — the exact opposite of the intent. A `failureCondition: result >= 500` should be added (or a slightly stricter threshold than `successCondition` to leave a buffer zone). Second, a likely unit bug: the metric name `http_request_duration_seconds_bucket` indicates the histogram value is in SECONDS (Prometheus/OpenTelemetry convention), so `result < 500` is comparing against 500 SECONDS — almost certainly not the author's intent (500ms would need `result < 0.5`). Third, the `histogram_quantile` syntax is missing the standard aggregation step: the correct formula needs `sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{rollout="web"}[5m])) by (le)` before wrapping it in `histogram_quantile(0.95, ...)` — missing `rate()` over a time window and missing `by (le)` makes the quantile computed over the entire cumulative history instead of the correct canary observation window, producing a completely skewed number. Fourth, `interval: 30s` × `count: 3` gives only 1.5 minutes of total observation — too short to distinguish a transient latency spike (e.g. a random slow request, a GC pause) from a real regression caused by the new code; `count` should be increased or `consecutiveErrorLimit`/`failureLimit` used to require MULTIPLE consecutive threshold breaches before treating it as a real failure, reducing false-positive rollbacks. Before merging, it's mandatory to test-run this PromQL query directly against Prometheus to confirm syntax and units, then deliberately create a real latency regression in a lab environment to see whether the AnalysisRun actually transitions to `Failed` and the rollout truly auto-rolls-back — never trust YAML that "looks correct" without a test run.

prompt: A coworker sends you the Vault policy below for review, for a `checkout` service using KV v2 mounted at `secret/`, authenticating via AppRole. After applying it, the service reports `403 permission denied` even though the coworker insists "the path is right, I tested with `vault kv get secret/checkout/db` and saw the data." Point out the issue and propose a fix.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The coworker was misled by the very tool used to test. Root cause: KV v2 stores data at the REAL API path `<mount>/data/<key>` (metadata at `<mount>/metadata/<key>`) — the `data/` prefix is how the engine separates the data API from the metadata API. The current policy writes `path "secret/checkout/*"` — this matches `/v1/secret/checkout/*`, NOT `/v1/secret/data/checkout/*` which is what the app's real request actually calls, so Vault returns `403 permission denied`. Why the coworker saw `vault kv get secret/checkout/db` succeed: the `vault kv` CLI command is a wrapper that AUTOMATICALLY inserts the `data/` prefix when it calls the HTTP API underneath — the user types `secret/checkout/db` but the CLI actually calls `GET /v1/secret/data/checkout/db`. With the coworker's own token (possibly broader permissions or a different policy), the command succeeds, but that proves nothing about the `checkout` service's policy — the service calling directly via SDK/HTTP API (bypassing the `vault kv` CLI) will genuinely hit `secret/data/checkout/*` and gets blocked by the current policy. Fix: change the policy to `path "secret/data/checkout/*" { capabilities = ["read", "list"] }`. If the service also needs to view version history for rollback, add `path "secret/metadata/checkout/*" { capabilities = ["read", "list"] }` separately, since this is a completely different KV v2 API path, not automatically included in data-read permission. To verify correctly instead of trusting the CLI, use `vault kv get -output-policy secret/checkout/db` — Vault prints the exact policy path needed — or call the HTTP API directly with `curl` using the service's own token to reproduce the exact 403 the app is hitting.

prompt: The team reports the Docker build in CI always takes ~8 minutes even when only one line of application code changed, and never shows a single `CACHED` line in the log no matter how many times it's rebuilt on the same branch. Based on `givenCode`, pinpoint the cause and the fix.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
The cause is in the build command itself: `docker buildx build -t ... --push .` has **no `--cache-from`/`--cache-to` parameters at all**. With no cache backend declared, buildx defaults to **local** cache — layer cache stored right on the filesystem of the exact runner performing that build. The problem is that every GitHub Actions job runs on a completely fresh, **ephemeral runner**: GitHub provisions a clean VM for the job and destroys it right after the job finishes. The local cache created during build A **disappears along with A's runner** once that job ends — build job B (even just 5 minutes later, even changing only one line of application code) runs on an entirely different runner, with an empty filesystem, nothing to reuse. That's exactly why the log never shows `CACHED` no matter how many times it's rebuilt: it's not that the Dockerfile has the wrong layer order (layer order only matters when there's ONE persistent cache existing across builds to compare against and reuse — here no cache survives even a single build). The fix: switch to **registry** cache, which is genuinely persistent cross-run since it lives on the container registry itself, not on the runner:
```yaml
- name: Build image
  run: |
    docker buildx build \
      --cache-to type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:cache,mode=max \
      --cache-from type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:cache \
      -t ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }} \
      --push .
```
`--cache-to type=registry,...,mode=max` pushes ALL intermediate layers (including intermediate build stages, not just the final layer) to a dedicated cache tag on the registry after every build. `--cache-from type=registry,...` pulls that cache back at the start of the next build — since the registry exists independently of any runner, this cache survives every runner being destroyed and recreated. After adding these two parameters, subsequent builds (especially when only application code in the final layer changes, with no dependency changes) will show `CACHED` lines for the upper dependency-install layers, cutting build time from ~8 minutes down to a few dozen seconds.

prompt:
You inherit a script that collects errors from logs; it takes nearly 20 minutes on a directory with a few thousand log files:

```
find /var/log/app -name '*.log' > /tmp/files.txt
for f in $(cat /tmp/files.txt); do
  grep 'ERROR' "$f" -l >> /tmp/hits.txt
done
cat /tmp/hits.txt | awk '{print}' | sort | uniq
```

Point out what makes it slow and anti-patterns (more than one spot), explain mechanically WHY they're slow, then rewrite it as a much shorter and faster pipeline. Be explicit about why your version handles even a huge directory without blowing up RAM.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Several things are slow, not just one. First, the **fork-storm**: `for f in $(cat files.txt); do grep ...; done` spawns a separate `grep` process per file — a few thousand files means a few thousand `fork()`/`execve()` calls, and that spawn cost, not the log scanning, eats most of the 20 minutes. Second, the two temp files `/tmp/files.txt` and `/tmp/hits.txt`: they serialize the pipeline (write fully, then read back) and waste disk IO; the data should flow straight through a kernel pipe with the stages running in parallel. Third, the no-ops: `cat hits.txt | awk '{print}'` is both useless-use-of-cat and an `awk '{print}'` that transforms nothing; `$(cat files.txt)` word-splits and breaks if a filename has a space; `sort | uniq` should be `sort -u`. I'd rewrite it as one line: `grep -rl 'ERROR' /var/log/app --include='*.log' | sort -u` — or `find /var/log/app -name '*.log' -exec grep -l 'ERROR' {} +`. The key point: `grep -r` (and `-exec {} +`) passes MANY files to a single grep invocation, erasing the fork-storm; `-exec {} +` self-batches by `ARG_MAX`, so it stays safe with tens of thousands of files. On RAM: grep streams line by line, holding only the current file in its buffer instead of loading the whole tree; there's no `$(cat)` loading the whole list into shell memory and no temp files — so even a huge directory runs in near-constant memory. I'd verify with `time` on both versions and test a filename with a space to prove the new one doesn't word-split.

prompt: Several different Terraform modules each grant `roles/viewer` to different members on a shared project. Your team's module (module A) was just updated to add a new viewer. How do you review this PR?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Serious issue: `google_project_iam_binding` is **authoritative for the whole role** — applying it sets the entire member list of `roles/viewer` on the project to EXACTLY what's listed in `members` (here, only `alice@example.com`), and DELETES every other member currently holding `roles/viewer` that isn't in this list — including members added by module B, module C from other teams entirely outside this PR's scope. Since the situation here is multiple different Terraform modules each granting `roles/viewer` to different members on ONE shared project, using `_binding` is a ticking time bomb: the PR "looks like" it just adds one new viewer, but it actually silently revokes everyone else's viewer access — a "permissions mysteriously vanished" incident that's extremely hard to debug because the Terraform diff doesn't clearly state who will lose access. The correct fix: switch to `google_project_iam_member`, a **non-authoritative** resource — it only ADDS exactly one (role, member) pair to the policy without touching any other member holding the same role, absolutely safe when multiple teams/modules grant the same role on the same resource in parallel. Verify before merging: run `terraform plan` and read the proposed changes carefully — if the plan shows it would DELETE any member outside this PR's intended change, that's a clear sign of misusing an authoritative resource.

prompt: A coworker opens a PR creating a BigQuery table `events` (100 TB, partitioned by `event_date`) for the analytics team's daily queries. They ask for a quick review before merging, saying: "The table is already partitioned by day so cost should be fine." Reading the Terraform schema and a sample query the team commonly runs below, how do you review it?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
I would NOT approve this merge as-is — "already partitioned by day" is a NECESSARY condition, not a SUFFICIENT one for cost optimization. There are two compounding bugs. Bug 1 is in the schema: `time_partitioning` doesn't set `require_partition_filter = true` (defaults to `false`), meaning BigQuery still ALLOWS a query with zero filter on `event_date` — the table is correctly partitioned in storage, but nothing forces a query to actually take advantage of it. Bug 2 is right in the team's sample query: it filters on `user_id` and sorts by `event_date`, but **has no** `WHERE event_date = ...` or any condition at all on the partition column — for a 100 TB table, missing that condition means scanning every partition. Add `SELECT *` on top: since BigQuery storage is **columnar**, `SELECT *` scans EVERY stored column, while the dashboard actually only needs a few displayed fields — if the table has dozens of columns, this scans many times more than listing the exact columns needed. Combined: every run of this sample query scans nearly the full 100 TB × every column — a few hundred USD, repeated **every morning**, that nobody notices because the query still returns correct results, just invisibly expensive. Fix: (1) add `require_partition_filter = true` to the schema — any query missing a filter on `event_date` gets REJECTED by BigQuery immediately instead of silently being charged, forcing the team to write correct queries from day one; (2) fix the sample query: list the exact columns the dashboard needs instead of `SELECT *`, and add a `WHERE event_date >= ...` condition matching the dashboard's needed time window; consider adding `cluster_by` on `user_id` too if filtering by user is a common pattern, letting BigQuery further shrink the scan within each partition. My review comment would spell out both points explicitly, not stop at "already partitioned, looks fine".

prompt: A mid-level teammate asks you to review a DynamoDB single-table schema for an order management system. Review it as a senior: point out the design problems (not syntax errors), explain the concrete cost/performance consequences, and propose a fix.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
This schema violates a core DynamoDB single-table design principle: "create a GSI ONLY for a validated access pattern, never speculatively". Of the four GSIs, only `GSI1-status` is valid because it's tied to a real access pattern (the dashboard needs to filter by status) — the other three (`GSI2-email`, `GSI3-city`, `GSI4-category`) were added "just in case", meaning NO actual query/access pattern is currently using them. The cost consequence is concrete and immediate, not a future risk: EVERY GSI turns a write to the base table into a DOUBLED cost — DynamoDB must write both the base table AND sync-write every GSI containing the relevant attribute. With 3 redundant GSIs, every order create/update pays 3 extra write costs for zero query value — money paid for something nobody uses. The second issue is `projection_type = "ALL"` on ALL FOUR GSIs: `ALL` copies EVERY base table attribute into each GSI, doubling storage once more per index — with 3 redundant GSIs using `ALL`, storage is wasted many times over compared to using just `KEYS_ONLY` or `INCLUDE` with the few attributes actually needed for that access pattern (which here doesn't even exist). Putting it together: a table with exactly ONE real access pattern is paying write cost + storage cost as if it had FOUR — a silent form of waste, especially dangerous because DynamoDB never warns "this GSI has never been queried"; the cost just silently accumulates every month until someone digs into the bill. My proposed fix: delete `GSI2-email`, `GSI3-city`, `GSI4-category` NOW — GSIs can be added anytime later (unlike LSIs, which must be created at table creation), so there's no reason to add them speculatively. When a real access pattern actually shows up (say, a concrete business requirement to look up orders by customer email), create the matching GSI then, and consider `projection_type = "INCLUDE"` with only the few attributes that pattern needs, instead of defaulting to `ALL` for every GSI.

prompt: A newly created PVC on EKS sits stuck at `Pending` forever. A coworker suspects the wrong StorageClass or capacity exhausted in that AZ. Based on the `givenCode` below, pinpoint the REAL cause, explain why this isn't a storage bug, and how to fix it.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
This is **not a storage bug** — it's an **IAM/IRSA** bug. The evidence is right there in the log: `csi-provisioner` reports `is not authorized to perform: ec2:CreateVolume because no identity-based policy allows the ec2:CreateVolume action`. If the real problem were a wrong StorageClass or AZ capacity, the log would show a completely different kind of error about parameters or capacity (`InvalidParameterValue`, `no available zones`), not a clear **authorization** message like this one — this message points in exactly one direction: the CSI controller has no AWS permission to call the EC2 API. Confirm it further with the second piece of evidence: `kubectl get sa ebs-csi-controller-sa -n kube-system` shows `annotations: {}` — the EBS CSI controller's own ServiceAccount has **no** `eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn` annotation. That annotation is exactly the IRSA wiring: without it, the EKS Pod Identity Webhook never injects `AWS_ROLE_ARN` plus a projected OIDC token into the controller Pod, so the AWS SDK inside it has absolutely no credentials to call `ec2:CreateVolume` with — it's not "missing permission because the role is wrong," it's "no role at all" to even check permissions against. The result: the PVC hangs at `Pending` forever at the "Provisioning" step because the controller never manages to actually create the volume, not because of missing capacity or a wrong StorageClass. The fix: reattach the correct annotation `eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn=<ARN of the IRSA role for EBS CSI>` to the `ebs-csi-controller-sa` ServiceAccount — do this via Terraform (so it isn't lost again on the next apply) rather than a one-off manual `kubectl annotate`; then `kubectl rollout restart deployment ebs-csi-controller -n kube-system` so the new controller Pod actually receives the IRSA token. Verify by watching the PVC turn `Bound` within a few seconds, and confirm the `csi-provisioner` log no longer shows any `is not authorized` lines.

prompt: A teammate wrote the PromQL recording rule below to compute a 30-day availability SLI for `checkout`, based on the `http_requests_total{status}` counter. The team finds this SLI ALWAYS reports ~100% even though there were serious 5xx incidents last week. Review it carefully and point out the bug.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The core bug: the formula directly divides `http_requests_total{status!~"5.."} / http_requests_total` — both are COUNTERS, whose raw values are ACCUMULATED numbers since the process (or target) started, NOT a measurement over any specific time window. The rule is named `checkout:sli_availability:ratio30d` — implying a ratio over a 30-DAY window — but the formula has no `[30d]` or any range vector at all; it computes the process's LIFETIME ratio, not the last 30 days. This is exactly why "the SLI always reports ~100% despite last week's incident": if the service has run stably for MONTHS with the vast majority of historical traffic succeeding, a few hours of 5xx errors from ONE incident last week is only a TINY fraction of the total ACCUMULATED requests over its lifetime — the overall ratio barely moves, even though that incident was SEVERE to real users during the time it happened. "SLI computed over the process's entire history" and "SLI over the last 30-day window" are TWO entirely different quantities, and the rule's name promises the second while the formula computes the first. Fix: use `increase()` (turning a counter into the NUMBER of increments within a SPECIFIC window, similar to `rate()` but WITHOUT dividing by seconds) over the exact `[30d]` window matching the rule name's meaning, applied to BOTH numerator and denominator:
```yaml
- record: checkout:sli_availability:ratio30d
  expr: |
    sum(increase(http_requests_total{status!~"5.."}[30d]))
      /
    sum(increase(http_requests_total[30d]))
```
`increase(...[30d])` counts the ACTUAL number of requests occurring in the last 30 days (not the entire history), `sum(...)` aggregates across instances/labels if there are several. With this formula, a 5xx incident within the 30-DAY WINDOW directly pulls down the NUMERATOR (fewer successful requests within that exact 30 days), correctly reflecting how much that incident affects the SLI — instead of being diluted across the process's entire history as in the old formula. Verify: after fixing, simulate a period with a spike in 5xx error traffic (test by generating fake errors), confirm the 30-day SLI DROPS CLEARLY corresponding to the error rate just generated — unlike the old formula which barely reacted at all to a new incident.

prompt: Two things happen the same week: (1) Trivy reports 7 CVEs, Grype reports 9 for the SAME SBOM — the team doesn't know who to trust; (2) a CRITICAL CVE blocks the gate but the team confirms the vulnerable code path is never actually called. For EACH situation, how do you handle it, and why are "lower the threshold" or "add it to `.trivyignore` with no reason" both bad choices?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The two situations are different in nature and need different handling, but share one principle: never lower the GLOBAL security bar to solve a SPECIFIC problem. Situation 1 — Trivy and Grype disagree because they use **different vulnerability databases**: Trivy aggregates NVD + GitHub Advisory Database + distro security feeds (Debian/Alpine/Red Hat), Grype uses Anchore's own database. A mismatch doesn't mean one is "wrong" — each catches a set of CVEs the other may miss. The correct handling is to treat the **union** of both as coverage: the gate should fail if EITHER scanner reports CRITICAL, and CVEs only one scanner sees should be investigated separately to understand why (usually distro-specific detection or version mismatch). Picking the scanner that reports fewer findings to make the gate "easier to pass" is a self-inflicted security downgrade — you're choosing to let through a CVE the other scanner correctly flagged. Situation 2 — a CRITICAL that's genuinely not exploitable needs **VEX**: write a statement declaring that CVE `status: not_affected` with a standardized `justification` (e.g. `vulnerable_code_not_in_execute_path`), then pass `--vex vex.json` to the scanner on rescan — the CVE gets suppressed from the gate report BUT with evidence, machine-readable, and reviewable via PR. Compared to the two bad options: lowering the severity threshold (e.g. only gating on even-more-severe CRITICALs, or dropping CRITICAL from the gate entirely) loses the ability to catch EVERY future CRITICAL including real ones; adding to `.trivyignore` with no reason is a blind suppression nobody reviews again, easy to abuse to hide a real vulnerability under deadline pressure. VEX keeps the threshold strict for every OTHER CVE, justifies exactly one specific CVE with evidence, and gets audited periodically to confirm the justification still holds as code changes.

prompt: You need to write the trust policy (Terraform) for an IRSA IAM role, allowing ONLY the exact ServiceAccount `s3-reader` in namespace `default` to assume the role via the cluster's OIDC provider (already exists as `aws_iam_openid_connect_provider.eks`). Write the `data "aws_iam_policy_document"` for `assume_role_policy`, making sure both the `sub` and `aud` conditions are correctly pinned.

Your system has two services: `app` (web UI, path `/app/*`) and `api` (REST backend, path `/api/*`), currently sitting behind a SINGLE `azurerm_application_gateway` that uses a `url_path_map` to route these two paths to two different backend pools (see the current config below). Your manager complains the `Standard_v2` App Gateway bill is unusually high because it's billed hourly + capacity unit 24/7 even though there's almost no traffic at night. Propose an architecture that optimizes cost while keeping path-based routing, and clearly explain the trade-offs.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
First, separate two questions: "we need path routing" and "we're paying for App Gateway 24/7" aren't necessarily the same problem. Path routing (`/app/*` → app-pool, `/api/*` → api-pool) is **Layer 7** behavior — reading the HTTP path — so it must go through a layer that understands HTTP; `azurerm_lb` is L4 (5-tuple IP/port/protocol) and can't read the path, so "downgrade to a cheaper LB" doesn't keep the current capability — it's not a free choice. There are two genuine optimization directions. Direction (a) — keep App Gateway but change how it's billed: switch from fixed capacity to `autoscale_configuration { min_capacity = ... max_capacity = ... }` on the `Standard_v2` SKU, so capacity units scale with real load instead of paying for peak capacity 24/7 — at night with almost no traffic, autoscale pulls capacity down to the minimum, while `url_path_map`/`request_routing_rule` stay exactly as they are, no architecture change. Direction (b) — if the `app`/`api` services already run, or could run, on a platform with a built-in L7 layer (AKS Ingress Controller, Azure Container Apps ingress), move path routing to that layer and drop App Gateway for this case entirely — considerably cheaper since you no longer pay Azure's separate hourly + capacity-unit fee, but the trade-off is losing the managed WAF rule set and Azure's other built-in L7 features (session affinity, centrally managed SSL policy...), so it only makes sense when the threat model doesn't require WAF at the Azure edge or WAF already exists elsewhere. Concrete recommendation: if the system runs on plain VM/VMSS (as here), keep App Gateway but enable `autoscale_configuration` to cut off-peak cost without changing the architecture; if it's moving or already moved to AKS/Container Apps, drop App Gateway, use that platform's built-in L7 Ingress, and only put Front Door/App Gateway at the edge if global WAF is genuinely required.

prompt: This month's DigitalOcean bill is unusually high. Investigation shows the autoscale pool below keeps adding and removing Droplets all day long, even though average load is fairly stable around the target. How would you optimize this config to stop the flapping while still being able to scale for real traffic spikes?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Main cause: `cooldown_minutes = 1` is too low — the pool never gets to breathe between scale events, so any mild natural fluctuation in traffic around the target keeps triggering add/remove cycles. Secondary cause: `target_cpu_utilization = 0.5`/`target_memory_utilization = 0.5` sit close to the system's normal average load, so traffic only needs to nudge up/down slightly to cross above/below target, triggering constant scaling even though load is "fairly stable on average." Optimization: raise `cooldown_minutes` to a reasonable value, e.g. 5-10 minutes, giving the pool time to stabilize before considering another scale; also consider raising the target to around 0.6-0.7 to build in headroom before hitting the threshold, avoiding natural traffic variance triggering unnecessary scaling. Flapping costs real money because every scale-out Droplet is billed hourly the moment it's created, even if it lives only a few minutes before being removed by scale-in — wasteful and destabilizing for traffic being routed to a node mid-creation/removal. Verify after the fix by monitoring `terraform output autoscale_current_utilization` and `doctl compute droplet list --tag-name <pool-tag>` over several hours: node count should stay stable around `min_instances` under normal load, only rising for a genuine traffic spike sustained long enough to clear the cooldown.

prompt: The team reports that `terraform plan` keeps proposing changes on every run even though nobody edited anything — sometimes it "will attach" a bucket to the project, sometimes "will detach" it. The code below is the source of the drift. Diagnose the cause and optimize the config so `plan` is clean (0 to change) when nothing has actually changed.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The cause: both bucket URNs are declared in TWO places at once — directly in `digitalocean_project`'s `resources`, AND again in a standalone `digitalocean_project_resources`. Both resources believe they own the bucket-to-project association, so on every `plan`, Terraform sees one resource's apply and the other "wanting" to correct it back — producing an oscillating attach/detach even though nobody changed anything. `digitalocean_project_resources` exists exactly to solve "attach a Terraform-managed resource into a project that may be managed elsewhere" — that is, to separate grouping from project definition, not to run alongside a direct `resources` declaration. Fix: pick exactly one approach. If multiple teams/Terraform modules attach resources into the same shared project, drop `resources` from `digitalocean_project` and keep only `digitalocean_project_resources` (more flexible, decoupled lifecycle). If a single module owns the whole project and its buckets, keeping `resources` directly in `digitalocean_project` and deleting the `digitalocean_project_resources` resource entirely works fine too. Verify by running `terraform plan` twice in a row with nothing changed — the second run must print `No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration`; if it still proposes changes, some other place is still fighting over URN ownership.

prompt: Your team has 40 shared config values (feature flags, static third-party API endpoint URLs, a few threshold values) all stored in AWS Secrets Manager, each as its own separate secret. NONE of these 40 values needs automatic rotation — they barely change over months. The Secrets Manager bill has become a significant expense. Propose a cost optimization without reducing security.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The cost cause lies in Secrets Manager's billing model: it charges by the NUMBER of secrets (roughly $0.40/secret/month) REGARDLESS of whether rotation is enabled — with 40 config values, even though none needs automatic rotation, the team is still paying that full charge 40 times a month for a feature (automatic rotation with a 4-step Lambda) they never use at all. This is exactly the scenario where **SSM Parameter Store SecureString** should replace it: it also encrypts values with KMS — the same security level as Secrets Manager, no reduction at all — but at the standard tier it's entirely FREE, with no per-secret monthly charge whatsoever. The general decision rule between the two services: if a secret NEEDS scheduled automatic rotation (DB credentials that must change their password periodically, API keys rotated per compliance requirements) then Secrets Manager is worth its cost since it has a built-in 4-step rotation Lambda mechanism (`createSecret` → `setSecret` → `testSecret` → `finishSecret`) plus versioning staging labels for zero-downtime rollover; but for STATIC or rarely-changing config that never needs rotation — exactly like these 40 feature-flag/endpoint-URL/threshold values — Parameter Store SecureString is entirely sufficient and saves substantial cost. Before migrating, note a few Parameter Store limitations: a 4KB max size at standard tier (8KB with advanced tier, at extra cost), NO versioning staging label mechanism (`AWSCURRENT`/`AWSPREVIOUS`) like Secrets Manager, and no cross-account sharing support — confirm these 40 values (mostly short strings like feature flags/URLs/thresholds) don't hit any of those limits. Safe migration process: keep the KMS encryption mechanism intact (no security downgrade), create the corresponding values in Parameter Store in parallel, update the IAM permission of the service reading the secret from `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` to `ssm:GetParameter` (with `WithDecryption = true`), test a successful read from the actual service, then delete the old secret in Secrets Manager to avoid paying for both simultaneously.

prompt: Your team has a Lambda running every 5 minutes to find all orders with `status = "PENDING"` for more than 30 minutes (to send alerts). The `orders` table currently holds 100GB of data and the current code uses `Scan` with a `FilterExpression`. The DynamoDB bill has spiked and the Lambda frequently times out. Looking at the code below, identify the problem and rewrite it.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The core problem is using `Scan` for an access pattern that's entirely servable by `Query`. `Scan` reads the ENTIRE table before applying the `FilterExpression` — meaning DynamoDB scans through all the data first and only then filters out matching items, with cost calculated on the size of the WHOLE TABLE (roughly table_size / 4KB RCU units), not on the number of items ultimately returned. For a 100GB table, one `Scan` costs roughly 25 million RCU — even though only a handful of orders actually satisfy `status = PENDING` and being older than 30 minutes. The problem is much worse because of how often it runs: this isn't a single scan, it repeats EVERY 5 MINUTES, 24 hours a day — multiplying that enormous cost roughly 288 times a day, exactly why the DynamoDB bill spiked and the Lambda keeps timing out (reading 100GB of data every single run can never be fast). The correct fix: redesign so `Query` can serve the "orders PENDING for over 30 minutes" access pattern — create a new GSI with `hash_key = status` and `range_key = createdAt` (or a similar time field supporting range comparisons). With this GSI, the code becomes a `Query` with `KeyConditionExpression = "#s = :pending AND createdAt < :cutoff"` run against that GSI — DynamoDB now reads ONLY the items with `status = PENDING` matching the time condition, never touching the 100GB of unrelated data, with cost proportional to the number of matching items (usually a handful to a few hundred) instead of the whole table. To confirm the improvement, compare `ConsumedCapacity` in the response between the old `Scan` and new `Query` for the same run — you'd see a massive difference (from millions of RCU down to tens/hundreds), and watch DynamoDB CloudWatch billing before/after to confirm the cost drops as calculated.

prompt: The company's payments system currently uses a plain "backup-restore" DR strategy: everything only exists in the primary region, and only when that region goes down does it start building new infrastructure in a secondary region from backups. A test failure was measured once: the actual RTO measured was 4 HOURS (rebuilding infrastructure + restoring data + DNS cutover), while the business just lowered the requirement to RTO ≤ 30 minutes since this is a high-revenue payments service. Optimize the DR strategy: explain why "backup-restore" no longer meets the bar, and propose which DR tier to move to (with reasoning) on the scale from backup-restore → pilot light → warm standby → multi-site active-active.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
"Backup-restore" can't meet a 30-minute RTO because of its inherent nature: during failover, most of the measured 4 hours isn't from slow DATA restore (backup + WAL shipping already give a fine 15-minute RPO), but from having to BUILD THE ENTIRE INFRASTRUCTURE from zero — creating a new EC2/K8s cluster from Infrastructure as Code, waiting for nodes to boot, configuring networking, then restoring data, and finally switching DNS. This from-scratch provisioning process inherently takes hours no matter how fast data restore is — it's a CORE LIMITATION of the lowest DR tier, not a configuration bug fixable by optimizing the backup itself. With the new RTO ≤ 30 minutes requirement, the right move is to jump to the next tier: **pilot light**. The idea behind pilot light is to keep a MINIMAL copy of the core infrastructure already running in the secondary region — typically a database replica that's ACTUALLY RUNNING (continuously receiving WAL/binlog, staying near-synchronized), plus core networking/VPC already configured — but WITHOUT full compute/service capacity (kept at a minimum or entirely off). On failover, instead of building the ENTIRE infrastructure from scratch, you only need to SCALE UP the compute/service layer (add replicas, start the application) on top of an already-ready core — cutting out most of the provisioning time that dominated the previously measured 4 hours. There's no need to jump straight to warm standby (running a meaningful chunk of capacity 24/7, considerably more expensive) or multi-site active-active (running FULL capacity in both regions, the most expensive), because pilot light is usually ENOUGH to reach an RTO of a few dozen minutes — exactly matching the 30-minute requirement — while costing significantly less than the two higher tiers. Tier selection principle: cost increases along backup-restore → pilot light → warm standby → multi-site active-active, with RTO decreasing correspondingly; pick the LOWEST tier that just meets the actual RTO needed, don't jump to the most expensive tier "to be safe" if a near-zero RTO isn't actually required. After deploying pilot light, it's mandatory to run a REAL restore/failover drill on an environment close to production to MEASURE the actual RTO (not just theoretical calculation), confirming it's truly under 30 minutes before reporting to the business that the requirement is met.

prompt: Your team's CI/CD pipeline uses the `helm upgrade` command below to deploy to production. Last week a bad deploy (broken image) left the Deployment stuck half-old/half-new for 20 minutes until someone manually intervened with `helm rollback`. Optimize the command and process so a bad deploy next time self-heals without needing an on-call human.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
```bash
# ci/deploy-prod.sh (optimized)
helm upgrade myapp ./chart \
  -f values-prod.yaml \
  --set image.tag="$IMAGE_TAG" \
  --namespace prod \
  --atomic \
  --timeout 5m
```
The core gap in the old command: no `--atomic` (and no `--wait`) means Helm considers `helm upgrade` "successful" the moment the API server ACCEPTS the new manifest (returns 200 OK), WITHOUT waiting to see if the new pods actually become `Ready`. If the new `IMAGE_TAG` points at a broken image (wrong tag, bad entrypoint, crashes on startup), the rollout creates a new ReplicaSet stuck in `CrashLoopBackOff` while Helm already reported the pipeline "deploy successful" long ago — the Deployment gets stuck half-old/half-new (the rolling update stalls because the new pods never become Ready) until SOMEONE notices and manually runs `helm rollback myapp <old-revision>`, exactly like last week's incident. Main fix: add the **`--atomic`** flag — it does two things: (1) it implicitly enables `--wait`-equivalent behavior, forcing Helm to WAIT until every resource (Deployment, pods) reaches ACTUAL Ready state before considering the upgrade successful; (2) if the rollout still isn't Ready after the wait period (treated as failed), Helm **AUTOMATICALLY rolls back** to the immediately prior revision — no on-call human needed. Because `--atomic` will WAIT until `--timeout` expires before declaring failure, an explicit `--timeout` (e.g. `5m`) must be set instead of relying on Helm's default — too short a timeout will wrongly roll back a rollout that's just slow-but-fine to start; too long delays how long production stays broken before self-healing. Pick a number based on the app's actually-measured startup time (readinessProbe + warm-up time). To verify, deploy a deliberately-broken `IMAGE_TAG` on staging with the new command, confirming Helm auto-rolls-back to the correct old revision (cross-checked via `helm history myapp` showing the new revision marked then reverted) with zero manual steps.

prompt: Your team set an `AnalysisTemplate` with a fixed ABSOLUTE threshold: `failureCondition: result >= 0.05` (5% error-rate). After a few weeks in production, the team notices the rollout gets auto-rolled-back WRONGLY during low-traffic windows (normal system error-rate fluctuates 3-4% because of old clients retrying), while a real regression only needs to add 1-2 percentage points over baseline to hurt the business. Optimize the measurement strategy: what's the root problem with the absolute threshold, and how would you redesign it toward a "baseline" approach, including how to configure `failureLimit`/`consecutiveErrorLimit` to reduce false-positives while still catching real regressions?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The root problem with the absolute threshold `result >= 0.05` is that it assumes a "clean", stable-near-zero baseline error-rate for EVERY time window — but this system actually has 3-4% background noise (old clients, retries) that fluctuates by time of day. An absolute threshold cannot distinguish two entirely different situations: (a) the whole system has higher-than-usual background noise (baseline naturally drifts to 4%, unrelated to canary) and (b) canary is REALLY worse than stable (a real regression, where just +1-2 percentage points is enough to hurt the business). A fixed 5% threshold accidentally catches both the same way — causing false-positives in case (a) and potentially missing (b) if baseline is already close to 5%. The correct fix is to switch to a **live-baseline relative comparison**: run a parallel measurement of the **stable** ReplicaSet's error-rate at the SAME time (not a fixed historical number), then set the condition based on the gap between canary and stable — for example `successCondition: resultCanary <= resultStable + 0.02` (canary allowed to be up to 2 percentage points worse than stable) and `failureCondition: resultCanary > resultStable + 0.05` (a clear regression). This is far more robust because both canary and stable experience the same traffic conditions at measurement time — if error-rate rises for BOTH (retry storm, off-peak hours, old clients), the gap between them stays small and doesn't trigger a wrong rollback; only when canary specifically is worse than stable by a meaningful margin is that a genuine regression signal from the new code. In parallel, configure `consecutiveErrorLimit` (or `failureLimit`) to require MULTIPLE consecutive measurements (e.g. 3 of 5 cycles) to all breach the relative condition before transitioning to `Failed` — a single noisy measurement (one random slow request) isn't enough to trigger rollback; it must be a sustained TREND. To verify, replay the exact low-traffic window that previously caused false-positives with the new config and confirm no more wrong rollbacks, while also creating a deliberate real regression in a lab (e.g. noticeably raising canary error-rate) to confirm the new mechanism still catches it — don't just trust the theory that "baseline is better" without re-measuring in practice.

prompt: Your team just ran a k6 ramping test for the payments service. During the steady high-load stage, k6 reported p95 = 480ms (SLO is under 500ms) at 500 RPS with 5 pods running. The production target is to sustain a 4,000 RPS peak. The current HPA config below was set purely by feel, not from measurement. Optimize the whole thing: point out the problems with the current config, recompute the `maxReplicas` actually needed, and propose sensible `averageUtilization`/stabilization values for a payments service (high risk when short on pods).
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The current config is wrong in three places, all dangerous for a payments service. First, use the actual measurement instead of feel: the steady high-load stage measured 500 RPS with 5 pods at p95 480ms (already close to the 500ms SLO) → `RPS/pod ≈ 100`. For a 4,000 RPS peak target with 30% headroom (reasonable for a high-risk service), pods needed is `ceil(4000 / 100 / 0.7) = ceil(57.1) = 58`. The current `maxReplicas: 8` is nearly 7x below real demand — near real peak load, the HPA will hit its ceiling at 8 pods while needing 58, p95 will blow up badly and requests will fail en masse; this is the most serious issue, `maxReplicas` must go to at least 58 (round up with margin, e.g. 64). Second, `averageUtilization: 90` sits too close to the ceiling: at 90% average CPU, the service has almost no room to absorb a burst before p95 degrades (and pods may get CPU-throttled if they hit `limits`). For a payments service, lower it to 50-60% to leave a reaction margin — the trade-off is needing more pods at the same load, exactly the point of headroom. Third, `scaleUp.stabilizationWindowSeconds: 60` is a serious misconfiguration: it makes the HPA WAIT 60 seconds before reacting when load increases — the opposite of "scale-out must be instant" (usually set to 0). This is most likely a copy-paste of the value meant for `scaleDown`; fix it to `scaleUp.stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0` so new pods are added the instant CPU exceeds target, and keep `scaleDown` at a window of a few minutes (not 30s, too short and prone to thrashing) to guard against flapping when load fluctuates. After fixing all three, rerun the k6 ramping test simulating peak load, confirm p95 stays under SLO, and watch `kubectl get hpa -w` to see replicas climb fast enough before shipping to production — never trust numbers on paper without re-measuring.

prompt: A VM has an NSG attached at BOTH the subnet (`nsg-subnet`) AND its own NIC (`nsg-nic`) — the team did this wanting "double safety". `nsg-subnet` allows all HTTPS traffic from the Internet. `nsg-nic` only allows HTTPS from a specific internal IP range (set up for some other purpose by a different engineer a while back, nobody remembers exactly why). Result: every HTTPS request from the Internet gets denied, even though `nsg-subnet` clearly allows it. Explain the mechanism blocking the request, and the correct debugging process when TWO NSGs both apply to one traffic flow.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
This isn't a bug in either NSG individually — it's a direct consequence of having TWO NSGs both applying to one traffic flow, each attached at a different point (subnet and NIC). For **inbound**, the filtering order is: traffic from the Internet passes through the **subnet-NSG FIRST**, and only if it passes does it continue to the **NIC-NSG SECOND** — the request must clear BOTH stages, essentially AND logic, to actually reach the VM. The important consequence: EITHER NSG denying is ENOUGH to block everything entirely, regardless of how permissive the other one is — `nsg-subnet` allowing all HTTPS from the Internet means nothing if `nsg-nic` denies it at the later stage. Applied to this scenario: the HTTPS request from the Internet PASSES stage 1 (`nsg-subnet` lets it through, as designed), but at stage 2 (`nsg-nic`), the request's source IP (a real Internet IP) is NOT within the specific internal IP range `nsg-nic` allows — so it gets DENIED right there. End result: the request is blocked entirely, even though `nsg-subnet` was never wrong and worked exactly as designed — the bug is in `nsg-nic`, a rule configured for a DIFFERENT purpose (an internal IP range) accidentally imposing itself on exactly the traffic flow the team never intended to block. The correct debugging process with two NSGs: DON'T stop after checking one NSG and concluding — trace BOTH stages independently. The most effective tools are `az network nic list-effective-nsg` (shows the NIC's merged effective security rules, accounting for the subnet-NSG's influence too) or Azure Network Watcher's **IP flow verify** (directly answers "is traffic from IP X to port Y allowed, and which rule of which NSG decides it") — both tools point straight at which stage is blocking, instead of manually reading each NSG and reasoning by hand. After confirming `nsg-nic` is the culprit, the fix direction: if nobody remembers why `nsg-nic` restricts that IP range (a typical sign of outdated "double safety" causing more trouble than protection), REMOVE it and let `nsg-subnet` be the single control point; if that IP range still serves a legitimate purpose, EDIT `nsg-nic` to add an allow-HTTPS-from-Internet rule, matching the system's real intent instead of letting two NSGs silently contradict each other.

prompt: `checkout`'s SLO is 99.9% availability over 30 days (error budget = 0.1%). The team wants to replace a static threshold with **burn rate** alerting: one rule PAGES IMMEDIATELY when burning budget at 14.4x (enough to exhaust a whole month's budget in 2 days) over a 1-hour window, and another rule opens a TICKET (no page) when burning at 3x over a 6-hour window. Write these two PromQL alerting rules, using the metrics `checkout:sli_availability:ratio1h` and `checkout:sli_availability:ratio6h` (already available from another recording rule).
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
```yaml
groups:
  - name: checkout-burn-rate
    rules:
      # Fast burn -- severe outage, page immediately
      - alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetFastBurn
        expr: |
          (1 - checkout:sli_availability:ratio1h) / 0.001 > 14.4
        for: 2m
        labels:
          severity: critical
        annotations:
          summary: "checkout is burning error budget at 14.4x (exhausted in ~2 days if sustained)"

      # Slow burn -- sustained degradation, no immediate page, opens a ticket
      - alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetSlowBurn
        expr: |
          (1 - checkout:sli_availability:ratio6h) / 0.001 > 3
        for: 15m
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: "checkout is burning error budget at 3x, sustained — needs investigation before the monthly budget runs out"
```
The general burn rate formula: `(1 - SLI) / (1 - SLO)`. With SLO = 99.9% (0.999), the denominator `1 - SLO = 0.001` is exactly the allowed error budget. The numerator `1 - SLI` is the ACTUAL error ratio measured over the window. Dividing these two gives the "burn rate" — a number representing "how many times FASTER is budget being spent than the rate that would exhaust it exactly at the end of the SLO window (30 days)." A burn rate of 1 means spending at exactly the rate to run out after 30 days; a burn rate of 14.4 means CURRENTLY spending 14.4 times faster, meaning at this rate the WHOLE MONTH's budget would be exhausted in only about 30/14.4 ≈ 2 DAYS — this is a SEVERE level needing an immediate page. The first rule uses a SHORT window (1h) + a HIGH threshold (14.4x) to catch a genuinely SEVERE OUTAGE as fast as possible while staying reliable (`for: 2m` filters transient spikes that aren't real incidents, without delaying so much it misses the response window for a fast-burning outage). The second rule uses a LONGER window (6h) + a LOWER threshold (3x) to catch a DIFFERENT kind of degradation: slow-burning but SUSTAINED — a static threshold (e.g. "error rate > 1%") often misses this type because at ANY single point in time, the error rate might not be high enough to cross the threshold, but IF SUSTAINED continuously over several hours, it's still enough to exhaust the monthly budget before anyone notices. This rule carries `severity: warning` and does NOT page immediately — it just opens a ticket for the team to investigate during business hours, since "slow burn" by nature means there's still time to act, no need to wake anyone at 3am. The two windows complement each other: short window + high threshold catches acute outages, long window + low threshold catches chronic degradation — both anchored to ONE shared concept (burn rate of the same error budget), instead of two disconnected static thresholds with no relation to each other.

prompt: Your team has a CloudFront distribution serving both static assets (`.js`/`.css`/images) and an API. After launch, the dashboard reports a cache hit rate of only about 2% — nearly every request is a cache MISS, even static assets that should cache well. Looking at the config below, identify the cause and optimize it.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The main cause of the 2% hit rate is that the current cache policy puts the **`Authorization`** header into the cache key (`headers_config.header_behavior = "whitelist"` with `items = ["Authorization"]`). Since `Authorization` is almost always different across requests — each user has their own token/session — CloudFront treats every request with a different `Authorization` value as a completely different cache key, even if the URL path and everything else is identical. The result: despite `default_ttl = 86400` (1 day) being set, caching is effectively BYPASSED almost entirely because almost no two requests ever share the exact same cache key. The second, smaller but compounding issue: `query_string_behavior = "all"` puts every query string into the cache key — if any query string varies between loads (a tracking param, a random cache-buster) on static assets, each variant generates yet another cache key, further reducing the hit rate. But the real root cause is ARCHITECTURAL: using exactly ONE shared cache policy for both `/static/*` and `/api/*` is wrong from the start — the two traffic types have completely opposite caching requirements. Static assets (`.js`/`.css`/images) want the HIGHEST POSSIBLE hit rate, no need to distinguish by user, and with a hash-filename convention (`bundle.a3f5c2.js`) don't even need invalidation when content changes — you just rename the file. API traffic, on the other hand, usually NEEDS `Authorization` in the cache key to distinguish responses per user, and depending on the business logic may need a short TTL or even no caching at all. My proposed optimization: split into TWO `ordered_cache_behavior`s by path pattern — one for `/static/*` using a cache policy that does NOT whitelist `Authorization`, keeping a long TTL; one for `/api/*` using its own cache policy that still keeps `Authorization` in the cache key (correctly matching the API's real need) but with a short/zero TTL depending on the endpoint. After splitting, confirm with CloudWatch: the hit rate specific to `/static/*` should jump to near 100% (since static assets with hash filenames don't change between requests), while `/api/*` keeps its no-cache behavior as originally designed — not a bug, but the intended behavior.

prompt: Your team just deployed a Global External HTTP(S) Load Balancer in front of a regional MIG. The backend app runs fine — SSH into any VM and `curl localhost:80/healthz` returns 200 OK every time. But hitting the anycast IP of the LB ALWAYS returns `502 Bad Gateway`, and every backend shows `UNHEALTHY` on `backend-services get-health`. What order do you debug in, and what's the number-one suspect to rule out first?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
`curl localhost:80/healthz` passing on every VM immediately rules out an app-level bug — if the app itself were broken, `curl` from inside the VM would fail too. The problem lives in the gap between "the app is running" and "the LB sees the app running" — two different things, because Cloud LB health checks don't probe from localhost; they probe remotely over the network, specifically from two fixed Google IP ranges: `130.211.0.0/22` and `35.191.0.0/16`. This is the number-one suspect and also the most common pitfall when first setting up a GCP LB: if the VPC firewall only opens the port for internal traffic, or has no rule at all for these two ranges, every probe from Google gets DROPped at the network layer — the instance/app is completely healthy but the LB never receives a probe response, so it marks the backend `UNHEALTHY` and pulls it out of rotation. When ALL backends are unhealthy, the LB has nowhere left to route requests and returns `502 Bad Gateway` to every client — even though the app is perfectly fine at the OS/process layer. Confirmation step: run `gcloud compute firewall-rules list` to check for a rule allowing ingress TCP on the backend port (e.g. 80) from `source_ranges = ["130.211.0.0/22", "35.191.0.0/16"]` with `target_tags` matching the instance's actual tag (usually `["http-server"]`) — this rule being entirely missing, or `target_tags` not matching the real instance tag, are the two most common causes. After adding/fixing the `google_compute_firewall` correctly, verify with `gcloud compute backend-services get-health <name> --global` to see each backend flip from `UNHEALTHY` to `HEALTHY`, then re-test through the anycast IP to confirm the `502`s are gone — don't conclude it's fixed just because the firewall rule was edited without seeing health flip color.

prompt: Security asks: instances tagged `locked-egress` should only be allowed to call out over HTTPS (443), every other port should be blocked for egress. A teammate wrote the rule below and reports "done, only 443 is open." You double-check and find there's still a hole — how do you optimize/fix this config?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The hole: the config only has one `allow` rule for egress 443, no `deny` rule at all. Every GCP VPC has two default implied rules at priority 65535: allow egress all + deny ingress all. So "just declaring one allow rule for 443" does NOT mean every other port is blocked — traffic to other ports (e.g. 80, or anything else) simply doesn't match the priority-900 rule (which only covers 443), so it falls through to the default implied **allow egress all** rule and still gets out normally. The teammate mistakenly assumed a low-priority allow rule would automatically "lock down" everything else — actually an allow rule only OPENS exactly what it lists; to BLOCK the rest, a separate `deny` rule is required. Optimization: add a second `google_compute_firewall` — same `direction = "EGRESS"` and same `target_tags = ["locked-egress"]`, but `priority = 1000` (a LARGER number than 900, so LOWER precedence) with `deny { protocol = "all" }`. The first-match-wins mechanism by increasing priority: a packet to port 443 matches rule 900 first, so it's ALLOWED; a packet to any other port (e.g. 80) doesn't match rule 900, falls through to rule 1000, and is DENIED. Verify: from an instance tagged `locked-egress`, `curl`-ing an HTTP endpoint (80) must time out/be fully blocked, while `curl`-ing HTTPS (443) still succeeds normally — exactly matching the "egress allow-list, 443 only" requirement.

prompt: You need to write manual instrumentation for a function `apply_discount(cart_id, coupon_code)` — a critical, error-prone business function; auto-instrumentation doesn't create a span for it since it's not an HTTP/DB call. Write Python code using the OTel SDK to: open a span named `apply_discount`, attach `cart_id` and `coupon_code` attributes, record an event when the coupon is invalid (not an exception, just a noteworthy milestone), correctly handle when the inner function throws an exception, and ensure the span always closes properly.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
```python
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.trace import Status, StatusCode

tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__)

def apply_discount(cart_id, coupon_code):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("apply_discount") as span:
        span.set_attribute("cart_id", cart_id)
        span.set_attribute("coupon_code", coupon_code)

        coupon = lookup_coupon(coupon_code)
        if coupon is None or not coupon.is_valid():
            # Noteworthy milestone in normal flow -- NOT a technical error
            span.add_event(
                "invalid_coupon",
                {"cart_id": cart_id, "coupon_code": coupon_code},
            )
            return apply_no_discount(cart_id)

        try:
            result = charge_discount_engine(cart_id, coupon)
        except Exception as e:
            span.record_exception(e)
            span.set_status(Status(StatusCode.ERROR, str(e)))
            raise

        return result
```
Uses the context manager `with tracer.start_as_current_span("apply_discount") as span:` instead of calling `start_span()`/`end()` manually — this guarantees `span.end()` is ALWAYS called automatically when exiting the block, EVEN IF an exception is thrown from any line inside, avoiding exactly the "span never closes" bug common with manual handling. The two `set_attribute` calls sit RIGHT AT THE TOP of the block — before any logic that could fail runs — ensuring `cart_id`/`coupon_code` ALWAYS appear on the span regardless of whether something later throws; putting attributes at the END of a function is a common mistake because if an error occurs midway, execution never reaches the attribute-setting line. The invalid-coupon case uses `span.add_event("invalid_coupon", {...})` — this is a noteworthy MILESTONE in NORMAL PROCESSING FLOW (applying a bad coupon isn't a system error, could just be a user typo), so `record_exception`/`set_status(ERROR)` should NOT be used here — an event differs from an exception in that it doesn't mark the whole span as an error, it just records a noteworthy detail happening AT a point in time within the span. Conversely, when `charge_discount_engine` genuinely THROWS AN EXCEPTION (a technical error, e.g. a downstream service is down), the code wraps it in `try/except`, calls `span.record_exception(e)` to record the exception as an event with its stack trace, and `span.set_status(Status(StatusCode.ERROR, str(e)))` to mark the WHOLE span as an error — then RE-RAISES that exception (not swallowing it) so the error-handling logic at the layer calling this function still works normally; tracing only OBSERVES, it doesn't change business behavior.

prompt: The `payments` service logs JSON with a `level` field (already a Loki label) and a message containing "gateway timeout" whenever a call to an external payment gateway times out (the message is NOT put into a label because its content isn't stable cardinality). Write a LogQL query to: (1) retrieve ALL error log lines containing "gateway timeout" in the last 15 minutes, and (2) a separate METRIC query computing the RATE this error occurs per second over a 5-minute sliding window — clearly explain the difference between the two kinds of queries.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Two queries:
```logql
# 1) Log query — list "gateway timeout" log lines from the last 15 minutes
{job="payments", level="error"} |= "gateway timeout"

# 2) Metric query — rate of this error per second, 5-minute sliding window
sum(rate({job="payments", level="error"} |= "gateway timeout" [5m]))
```
Both share a common structure starting with a **stream selector** `{job="payments", level="error"}` — a CHEAP filtering step because Loki only needs to look up the label INDEX, not read any log line content. Then the **line filter** `|= "gateway timeout"` actually scans CONTENT of lines WITHIN the range already narrowed by the stream selector — this is a MORE EXPENSIVE step (regex/string matching per line), so the "labels first, content second" order isn't arbitrary: if `level="error"` were dropped from the stream selector, Loki would have to scan the content of EVERY `payments` log line (including info/debug) looking for "gateway timeout," much slower than having already narrowed to just `error` lines. The first query is a pure **log query** — the result is a LIST of raw log lines, used to READ directly while investigating (viewing details of each timeout occurrence). The second is a **metric query** — wrapping the same stream+line-filter expression in a `range vector [5m]` then applying `rate()`, turning a DISCRETE set of logs into a NUMERIC TIME SERIES (exactly how Prometheus handles a counter), giving "gateway timeout errors per second, 5-minute sliding average" — used to GRAPH a trend or as an ALERT CONDITION (e.g. `> 0.1`), not to read individual lines. `sum(...)` wraps the outside to aggregate results if logs come from multiple `payments` instances/pods into a single overall number. The key point: this isn't "the same question with `rate()` added" — the log query answers "WHAT happened, in what specific detail," while the metric query answers "HOW OFTEN does it happen over time" — two different questions serving two different purposes (reading detail vs. monitoring trend/alerting).

prompt: The `checkout` service exposes two standard metrics: counter `http_requests_total{route,method,status}` and histogram `http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route,method}`. Your manager wants a dedicated RED dashboard for route `/checkout/pay` — since it's the most critical route and the team wants it isolated from the whole-service aggregate. Write 3 PromQL queries: Rate, Errors (as a %), Duration (p95), ONLY for the `/checkout/pay` route, and explain each part of the formula.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Three RED queries for the `/checkout/pay` route alone:
```promql
# Rate — req/s for the /checkout/pay route only
sum(rate(http_requests_total{route="/checkout/pay"}[5m]))

# Errors — error ratio (0..1 fraction) for the /checkout/pay route only
sum(rate(http_requests_total{route="/checkout/pay", status=~"5.."}[5m]))
  /
sum(rate(http_requests_total{route="/checkout/pay"}[5m]))

# Duration — p95 latency for the /checkout/pay route only
histogram_quantile(
  0.95,
  sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route="/checkout/pay"}[5m]))
)
```
The key point running through all three: the `{route="/checkout/pay"}` label selector must be applied RIGHT ON the raw metric (`http_requests_total{route="/checkout/pay"}` or `..._bucket{route="/checkout/pay"}`) — BEFORE `rate()` and before `sum`/`histogram_quantile` aggregate series together. If done in reverse — `sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m]))` aggregating every route first and then trying to filter — the route information is already permanently lost in the `sum`, with no way to "filter afterward." For Rate, `sum(...)` aggregates the remaining dimensions (method, status) into a single throughput number for this route. For Errors, both the numerator (`status=~"5.."`) and the denominator must filter the SAME route `/checkout/pay` AND the same `[5m]` window — if only one side filters the route, numerator and denominator won't correspond to the same set of requests. For Duration, `sum by (le)` is still mandatory as in the standard formula (keeping the `le` label so `histogram_quantile` interpolates correctly), while the route label selector filters BEFORE `rate()` on the bucket series itself.

prompt: Your team suspects that after an RCE into a container, an attacker will try to write a new binary into `/usr/bin` or `/bin` to install persistence (e.g. a reverse shell disguised as a system binary). Falco's default ruleset has something similar, but the team wants its own custom rule, scoped only to the `production` namespace (excluding `kube-system` to avoid false positives from legitimate system init containers), with priority `Critical`. How do you write that rule, and explain how each part of condition/output/priority ties to the detection goal?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
```yaml
- rule: Write below binary dir in production
  desc: >
    Detect a process writing to a binary directory (/usr/bin, /bin, /usr/sbin, /sbin)
    inside a container running in the production namespace — a common persistence
    technique after RCE (dropping a disguised reverse-shell binary).
  condition: >
    open_write
    and container
    and k8s.ns.name = "production"
    and fd.name startswith "/usr/bin" or fd.name startswith "/bin"
       or fd.name startswith "/usr/sbin" or fd.name startswith "/sbin"
  output: >
    Binary directory write detected (user=%user.name command=%proc.cmdline
    file=%fd.name container=%container.name k8s.ns=%k8s.ns.name k8s.pod=%k8s.pod.name)
  priority: CRITICAL
  tags: [production, persistence, filesystem]
```
The `condition` composes the built-in `open_write` macro (any `open`/`openat` syscall with a write flag), plus `container` (only applies inside a container, not host processes), plus a `fd.name` check matching one of the standard binary directories — exactly the malware behavior of dropping a new binary. Adding `k8s.ns.name = "production"` SCOPES the rule to the sensitive namespace, naturally excluding `kube-system` (legitimate system init containers writing to binary dirs during bootstrap is normal, and matching this rule there would create meaningless alert fatigue). The `output` fills in enough fields to investigate immediately without cross-referencing: who (`user.name`), what command (`proc.cmdline`), which file was written (`fd.name`), which container/pod/namespace — missing any of these forces on-call to manually cross-reference, slowing response. `priority: CRITICAL` is justified because writing to a system binary directory from inside an ordinary application container is almost always a compromise signal, not normal operational behavior. Before applying, always run `falco --validate custom-rules.yaml` to make sure the syntax doesn't break the whole ruleset — one bad rule can make Falco fail to load everything, blinding the cluster at runtime.
