Test: exec into a demo pod in `production`, `touch /usr/bin/test-persist` to trigger the Critical alert; also exec into a `kube-system` pod doing the same thing to confirm the namespace scope works correctly — it should NOT produce an alert (negative test), proving the rule doesn't create fatigue for system components.

prompt: Your team discovers `pg_roles` on production PostgreSQL has accumulated hundreds of `v-app-xxx` roles that never get dropped even though Vault "revoked" those dynamic credentials long ago. The current `db_role` config is below. Point out what causes the accumulation, and rewrite `revocation_statements` to fix it thoroughly (not just a one-time manual cleanup).
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The root problem is that `revocation_statements` is NOT idempotent. Vault has a RETRY mechanism when a revoke hits an error (e.g. a temporary database connection timeout) — if the first call to `DROP ROLE "{{name}}"` actually succeeded but Vault never got the response (a network glitch), Vault retries, and that retry hits PostgreSQL reporting `ERROR: role "v-app-xxx" does not exist` because the role was already dropped last time. With a statement lacking `IF EXISTS`, PostgreSQL treats this as a real error, and Vault can't tell "already deleted, this retry is redundant" apart from "a genuine error to handle" — in some scenarios the lease gets stuck in an unclear state and the role isn't cleaned up correctly in Vault's tracking even though it's already gone from PostgreSQL, or conversely a role gets left behind if a real revoke failure goes unmonitored during retries. The core fix: change `revocation_statements` to `DROP ROLE IF EXISTS "{{name}}";` — with `IF EXISTS`, a retry after already-deleted returns success (no thrown error), so Vault always confirms revocation is complete no matter how many times it's called, matching the idempotency required of any distributed system. Another accumulation source that also needs handling: if the role still OWNS objects (tables, sequences it created) or has an active session/connection at the moment Vault attempts `DROP ROLE`, PostgreSQL may refuse to delete it with "role still has dependencies" — so add `REASSIGN OWNED BY "{{name}}" TO someadmin; DROP OWNED BY "{{name}}";` before the `DROP ROLE IF EXISTS "{{name}}";` line to make sure the role has no remaining bindings before deletion. To clean up the orphan roles already accumulated (which this fix alone won't retroactively remove), run a periodic query looking for `v-app-%` roles no longer tracked by Vault, and for any lease Vault still holds where the DB revoke keeps failing, use `vault lease revoke --force` to force Vault to clean up its own side independent of the database execution result.

prompt: Your team is about to package a Python worker as a service running on an Ubuntu VM, managed by systemd. Security requirement: if an attacker gets RCE inside the worker process, the damage must be limited as much as possible. Design the identity and permission configuration for this service: which user runs it, what the permissions on the code/config/secret/log files should be and why, where umask should be set, and — a junior proposes setting setuid on the worker script itself so it can 'self-elevate when needed' — how do you rebut that?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The guiding principle is **least privilege** and blast-radius reduction: assume the attacker can run arbitrary commands as the worker identity, so they should read/write as little as possible. Identity: create a dedicated, non-login service account (`useradd -r -s /usr/sbin/nologin appworker`) with its own group — not root, not shared with any other service. Code files: owned by a deploy identity (root or a deploy user), group `appworker`, permission `750` or `640` — the service can READ/EXECUTE but NOT write its own code, so even with RCE the attacker can't rewrite code to persist. Config: `640` owner root/deploy group `appworker` → the service reads, other gets nothing. Secrets: `600` (or `640` owner root group appworker), never for other; better still, use systemd `LoadCredential=`/credentials so secrets aren't spread across the filesystem. Log directory: `750`, owned by `appworker` so the service can write. umask: set `UMask=0027` in the unit's `[Service]` section — NOT in `.bashrc`, because services don't load a shell profile — so every file the worker creates defaults to `640`/`750`, never exposed to other. On the setuid proposal: it's wrong twice over. First, the Linux kernel DELIBERATELY ignores the setuid/setgid bit on interpreted scripts (`#!/usr/bin/python3`) for security — it simply has no effect. Second, even on an ELF binary, setuid works AGAINST the goal: it RAISES the process's privileges, widening exactly the blast radius we're trying to shrink. If the worker needs one specific privileged action, grant a sudo NOPASSWD rule for that ONE command, or a targeted Linux capability — never blanket setuid. Bonus: add `NoNewPrivileges=yes`, `ProtectSystem=strict`, `PrivateTmp=yes`, `ReadOnlyPaths=` so RCE can neither escalate nor write outside its allowed area.

prompt: Your team has many branches running pipelines in parallel. Recently there's a strange report: branch A's build fails because it's missing a package that branch B just removed from ITS `package-lock.json` — but branch A never touched that file. The current `cache` config is below. Point out the problem and rewrite it.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
This isn't a random failure — it's the inevitable consequence of the current cache config. `key: build` is a FIXED string — not tied to the branch, not tied to dependency content — so EVERY branch running the pipeline (A, B, and any other) reads and writes exactly the SAME `node_modules/` cache. When branch B removes a package from its `package-lock.json` and runs `npm ci`, the resulting `node_modules/` (missing that package) gets saved over the same `build` cache that branch A is also using. The next time branch A's pipeline runs, even though A's OWN `package-lock.json` still declares this package, GitLab restores the `build` cache — which branch B just overwrote — so A's `node_modules/` is missing exactly the package B removed, causing a build failure even though A never touched its own lockfile. This is exactly the "cross-branch cache contamination" scenario. The rewrite: change the cache key from a fixed string to one derived from the lockfile's CONTENT: `cache: key: files: [package-lock.json], paths: [node_modules/]`. With this config, GitLab automatically computes a different key (based on a hash of `package-lock.json`'s content) for each distinct lockfile state — branches A and B with different lockfiles automatically get two separate caches that never overwrite each other; if a branch's lockfile doesn't change across runs, it still hits the same cache (no loss of the speed benefit). To verify, I'd run A's and B's pipelines in parallel with different `package-lock.json` files, check each job's cache log printing a different key (due to the different lockfile hash), and confirm each branch's `node_modules/` matches its own lockfile, no longer depending on which branch ran previously.

prompt: Your team's canary keeps aborting randomly at the first step (20% traffic) even though the build is genuinely fine — manually promoting it afterward runs fine all day. The current `AnalysisTemplate` is below. Point out the issues in this config (not just one) and rewrite it to reduce false aborts while still catching real failures.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The current config has three compounding issues. First, the Prometheus query doesn't filter by a label distinguishing canary from stable (missing `rollouts-pod-template-hash` or equivalent) — meaning `error-rate` measures MIXED traffic from both canary and stable, so a single error spike on stable (unrelated to the new canary build) is enough to push the combined ratio over threshold. Second, `failureLimit: 0` is extremely sensitive: a SINGLE reading (every 30 seconds) exceeding 5% aborts immediately, with zero buffer for one isolated spike like a network blip. Third, there's no `initialDelay` — a freshly started canary Pod has a few seconds of higher-than-normal latency/error due to cold cache/JIT, and since analysis starts measuring right at second 30, it catches exactly this warm-up phase and mistakes it for a real failure. I'd rewrite it as follows: add a label filter to both numerator and denominator of the query (e.g. `{status=~"5..", job="checkout", rollouts_pod_template_hash="<canary-hash>"}`) so it measures ONLY canary, never mixing in stable; change `failureLimit: 0` to `failureLimit: 2` so it takes a few consecutive threshold breaches to abort, tolerating one isolated spike; add `initialDelay: 30s` to skip exactly the warm-up phase before scoring begins; and change the measurement window from `[1m]` to `[5m]` to smooth out instantaneous noise. To verify, I'd re-run the canary several times with a stable build — there should be no more random aborts; and I'd also deliberately deploy a build with a genuine bug (a real elevated error rate on the canary, not warm-up) to confirm `AnalysisRun` still aborts correctly — proving the change reduces false positives without blinding real-failure detection.

prompt: A service account that's been running fine for 3 months suddenly starts getting `403 PERMISSION_DENIED` on an API it's always called, with no code changes, no recent deploys, and `terraform plan` showing zero state drift. The team checked the role binding in the Console and confirmed the SA still has the right role, clearly visible. Which direction do you investigate next, and what's your leading hypothesis?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The symptom "ran fine, then suddenly broke, nobody changed code, no deploy, `terraform plan` shows no drift" is a classic sign of something **silently expiring over time** rather than an active configuration change — and on GCP IAM, that thing is a time-bound **IAM Condition**, e.g. `request.time < timestamp("2026-04-01T00:00:00Z")`. The key thing to understand: the team checked "the role binding is still present in the Console" and confirmed it's there — but a binding EXISTING doesn't mean it's currently IN EFFECT. If that binding carries a condition, the table-view Console sometimes only shows the role name without clearly surfacing the `expression` inside — so "seeing the role is still there" easily leads a debugger to overlook the possibility that it was time-limited and that deadline just passed. No `apply`/change event happened because there genuinely was NO ACTION — the permission simply stopped being effective the moment the clock crossed the pre-set timestamp, entirely "silently", leaving no trace in a change audit log (since the binding itself was never edited). Investigation direction: (1) read the full JSON policy via `gcloud projects get-iam-policy <project> --format=json` instead of the collapsed UI, directly inspecting the `condition` block of every binding relevant to that SA; (2) use the faster official tool — `gcloud policy-troubleshoot iam` — which directly answers "does this SA have permission to call that API on this resource, and why", immediately pointing to an expired condition instead of manually reading JSON and reasoning by hand. After confirming the real cause, the prevention measure for the future: for any binding carrying a LONG-duration time-bound condition (not a temporary few-hour grant for a specific action), set an alert/calendar reminder far enough BEFORE the expiry date (e.g. 2 weeks) to proactively renew or move to a properly controlled permanent grant, rather than letting the system error with `403` first and only then tracking down the cause.

prompt: Your team has one fixed static agent VM, always on, labeled `builder`. The Jenkinsfile below builds a Docker image on that agent by mounting the host's `docker.sock` directly. Recently 20 builds arrived at once and the agent choked hard because there's only one VM. Point out the problems (not just one) and rewrite the approach so it scales with load while dropping the privileged requirement.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
There are two separate problems here, not one. Scaling issue: `agent { label 'builder' }` always points at the same static VM — its executor count is fixed, so 20 concurrent builds have to queue, with no way to "add capacity" except manually standing up another VM. Security issue: for `docker build`/`docker push` to work, the agent needs a live Docker daemon, which forces mounting the host's `/var/run/docker.sock` into the container or running directly on the host VM — granting the job control over the node's Docker daemon, equivalent to granting privileged access; a malicious job (or a compromised dependency) could run a container that escapes out to the host. The rewrite: move the build onto Kubernetes via the Jenkins Kubernetes plugin. The controller declares, via JCasC, a kubernetes cloud with a `kaniko-builder` podTemplate: any build labeled `kaniko` makes the plugin call the Kubernetes API to spawn a single ephemeral agent pod containing a `jnlp` container (dials back to the controller) and a `kaniko` container (image `gcr.io/kaniko-project/executor`) mounting the registry secret at `/kaniko/.docker`. Kaniko reads the `Dockerfile` and builds the image entirely in the pod's userspace — no Docker daemon, no privileged mode, just registry credentials to push. On scaling: the pod lives for exactly one build then gets destroyed (`Terminating`); a `containerCapStr` limit (say 10) allows up to 10 build pods in parallel — 20 simultaneous builds run in batches instead of queuing behind a single VM, and when idle there are 0 pods, costing no background resources. Verify with `kubectl -n cicd get pods -w` showing pods named `kaniko-builder-<random>` transition Pending → Running → Terminating per build, and the `kaniko` container's log reporting a successful build/push with no `dockerd` process ever present in the pod.

prompt: You need to write the trust policy (Terraform `data "aws_iam_policy_document"`) for an IAM role that a GitHub Actions workflow will assume via OIDC to deploy, but ONLY when the workflow runs from the exact `main` branch of repo `my-org/my-app` — no other branch or repo should be able to assume this role. Assume `aws_iam_openid_connect_provider.github` already exists.

Your team has an EC2 fleet in a private subnet that only calls three services: S3 (reading config), DynamoDB (storing sessions), and SSM (patching/connect). All traffic to these three services currently goes through a NAT Gateway, and the NAT bill (hourly + per-GB) is the second-largest cost line in the account. Optimize the networking to cut NAT cost while keeping functionality intact, explaining clearly which endpoint type each service should use.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
These three services split into two different endpoint groups. **S3 and DynamoDB** can use a **Gateway Endpoint** — the only mechanism supporting exactly these two services: AWS doesn't create an ENI, it inserts a managed prefix-list route (the service's IP range) into the subnet's route table; when an instance calls S3/DynamoDB, traffic matches the prefix-list and goes STRAIGHT through the endpoint, never touching the NAT Gateway or Internet Gateway. The biggest benefit: a Gateway Endpoint is **entirely free** — no hourly charge, no per-GB. **SSM** is different — it's not on the Gateway-supported list, so it must use an **Interface Endpoint** (powered by AWS PrivateLink): AWS creates an ENI with a private IP right inside the subnet, this ENI is attached to a security group (only needing 443 open since every AWS API is HTTPS), and crucially you must set `private_dns_enabled = true` to create a private hosted zone so the canonical DNS name `ssm.<region>.amazonaws.com` automatically resolves to the ENI's private IP — meaning code using the SSM Agent/SDK doesn't need any endpoint URL change. An Interface Endpoint does incur cost (hourly per ENI/AZ plus per-GB), but it's still far cheaper than routing that traffic through a NAT Gateway. After adding all three endpoints (2 Gateway for S3/DynamoDB, 1 Interface for SSM), all traffic to these three services no longer needs the NAT Gateway. If the fleet has no other need to reach the Internet (no third-party API calls), the team could seriously consider removing the NAT Gateway entirely — eliminating that hourly + per-GB cost line that's currently the second-largest expense. To confirm, use VPC Flow Logs to verify traffic to S3/DynamoDB/SSM no longer passes through the NAT Gateway's ENI, and compare the "NAT Gateway" line in Cost Explorer before/after applying this.

prompt: A teammate created a standalone PVC (no Pod attached yet) to "pre-provision storage," and reports it's stuck at `Pending` forever, while last week another PVC they created with the same StorageClass became `Bound` almost instantly. Based on the info in `givenCode`, pinpoint the cause, and explain why the behavior differed between the two even though the StorageClass is the same.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
This isn't a bug — it's the correct designed behavior of the `local-path` StorageClass: `volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer` deliberately **delays** creating the PersistentVolume until a **Pod actually references (consumes)** that PVC. The event `WaitForFirstConsumer ... waiting for first consumer to be created before binding` means exactly what it says: the PVC is waiting, not failing. Why last week's PVC bound almost instantly while this one sits `Pending` forever: it's very likely the earlier PVC was applied **at the same time** as a Pod referencing it (via `volumes.persistentVolumeClaim.claimName`), so as soon as the scheduler bound the Pod to a node, the provisioner immediately knew where to create the volume and did so right away. This one was created **standalone**, "pre-provisioned" with no Pod using it — by design under `WaitForFirstConsumer`, it must wait until a first consumer exists. Why Kubernetes designed this delay mechanism: if the PV were provisioned immediately at PVC creation time (`volumeBindingMode: Immediate`), on a multi-zone cluster the provisioner could pick the wrong zone with no suitable node for the Pod that later needs the volume — leaving that Pod permanently unschedulable (`FailedScheduling` because the volume isn't in the same zone as any available node). Delaying until the first consumer exists lets the provisioner know exactly which node/zone the Pod will run in and create the PV there directly. The fix: apply a Pod mounting `data-claim` via `claimName: data-claim`; as soon as the Pod is bound to a node by the scheduler, the PVC will turn `Bound` almost instantly. Don't switch `volumeBindingMode` to `Immediate` just to avoid this wait — that throws away the zone-aware benefit this design provides.

prompt: After a label change in a Deployment, customers report every request through the Ingress returns `503`. `kubectl get pods` shows every Pod `Running` and `1/1`, and `kubectl get svc` shows the Service still has a normal ClusterIP. A coworker is confused: "all the Pods are running, why 503?" Walk through where you'd look FIRST to find the cause, and explain the mechanism behind why green Pods + an existing Service can still lead to a 503.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
The first thing to look at is **`kubectl get endpoints <svc>`**, not the Pod or the Service. Reason: a Service doesn't **"contain"** any Pods — it's just a declaration of a `selector` (e.g. `app: web`); Kubernetes continuously scans for every Pod that's **`Ready`** and matches that label, and writes their IP:port into a separate **Endpoints** object attached to the Service. `kubectl get pods` being green and `kubectl get svc` showing a ClusterIP tell you **nothing** about whether Endpoints is empty — those are two independent layers of information. After changing labels in the Deployment template, two things can cause empty Endpoints: (1) the Service's `selector` (immutable, doesn't auto-update) no longer matches the new `labels` the Pods now carry — the most common cause when someone changes labels without checking the Service; (2) the Pod's `STATUS` is `Running` but its `READY` column isn't `1/1` — meaning the readiness probe is failing, and the endpoints-controller has **excluded it from Endpoints** even though it's still running, so it doesn't count as a backend. The concrete way to verify: run `kubectl get pods --show-labels` and cross-check against `kubectl get svc <svc> -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'` to see whether they match; also check the Pod's `READY` column, not just `STATUS`. If `kubectl get endpoints <svc>` returns `<none>`, that's the proof: the Ingress returns `503` because it can't find any upstream to route traffic to — the Ingress itself isn't broken, the problem is that the Service/Pod layer below has no valid backend.

prompt: Finance requires invoices be kept for 10 years by law, fully immutable (even admins can't delete/modify during the first 10 years). A junior teammate proposes: "Let's just have a lifecycle rule move every object straight to Archive on upload for the cheapest storage, and turn on `lock_retention = true` right away to be safe." How do you review this proposal — what risks are being missed, and how would you redesign it?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The junior's proposal has two flaws — one about cost, and a much more serious one about the inability to undo mistakes. Flaw 1 — "move to Archive on upload": each storage class (Nearline/Coldline/Archive) has its own **minimum storage duration** (Nearline 30 days, Coldline 90 days, Archive 365 days) — if an object is deleted or CLASS-SWITCHED earlier than that threshold, GCS still charges for the **remaining** time of the term even though the object is no longer there (the **early-delete penalty**). Real financial invoices often need correcting or voiding within the first few months (before the customer's dispute window closes) — if objects jump straight into Archive on upload, EVERY edit/delete within the first 365 days gets hit with the full penalty, turning "saving on storage" into "extra penalty fees" during precisely the phase that needs the most editing. Flaw 2 — much more serious — is enabling `lock_retention = true` **from day one**: bucket lock is an **IRREVERSIBLE** action; once locked, the retention policy can never be shortened or removed by any means, not even by the project owner — if the retention period was entered wrong (a wrong day count from a legal misunderstanding, or because the final compliance requirement wasn't settled yet), the team is stuck FOREVER with that wrong config until the full 10 years elapse, with no way back. The correct redesign: (1) a lifecycle matching an invoice's real phases — keep Standard/Nearline for the first 90–180 days (matching the business dispute/correction window), then cascade to Coldline afterward, and Archive once the invoice is guaranteed fully "frozen" (usually after 1 year) — avoiding the early-delete penalty exactly during the still-volatile phase. (2) For retention: set `retention_policy` with the required day count BUT DO NOT lock it, let the system run for a while, review with legal/finance whether the day count and behavior are correct, and ONLY once absolutely certain, enable `lock_retention = true` — never lock on the very first apply, since that decision has no undo button.

prompt: Your CI pipeline currently signs images using **key-based** cosign: a private key stored in an internal shared secret manager, and every engineer with read access to that secret (even if unrelated to releases) can sign any image and push it to the registry with no way to audit WHO signed it. Security's manager wants the process optimized so that: (1) it's known exactly which image was signed by which CI workflow, (2) nobody can "sneak-sign" even with registry read access, and (3) Kubernetes automatically blocks improperly signed images. Propose a redesign and state the trade-offs.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The root problem with the current key-based architecture is that the private key is a SHARED, STATIC secret: any engineer who can read the secret manager (even unrelated to releases) can sign on the pipeline's behalf, and since the key isn't bound to a specific identity, there's no way to audit "who actually signed image X" — violating both requirements (1) and (2) at once. The optimization direction: switch to **cosign keyless**. Every time CI needs to sign, cosign generates an EPHEMERAL ECDSA keypair that only exists in that job's RAM, obtains an OIDC token from GitHub Actions itself (the identity of the specific WORKFLOW, not a generic shared account), sends the token + public key to **Fulcio CA** — Fulcio verifies the token and issues a short-lived x509 certificate (about 10 minutes) with a SAN bound to that exact workflow's identity (e.g. `https://github.com/org/repo/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main`). Cosign uses the ephemeral private key to sign the image digest, pushes signature + cert to the registry, and writes an entry to **Rekor** — a PUBLIC, IMMUTABLE transparency log. This correctly solves requirement (1): knowing exactly WHICH workflow signed, not guessing from a shared key. Requirement (2) is also solved because there's no more static private key to steal — to sign, an attacker would need a valid OIDC token from the EXACT right identity provider for the EXACT right workflow, no longer obtainable from the internal secret manager. For requirement (3), install an admission controller on Kubernetes — Kyverno or cosign policy-controller — with a `ClusterImagePolicy` specifying `issuer: https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com` and a `subjectRegExp` matching EXACTLY the allowed workflow/branch pattern (e.g. only the `release.yml` workflow on `refs/heads/main`); any Pod referencing an image signed by a non-matching workflow is rejected at the control plane immediately, no human intervention needed. Trade-off to clearly report to the manager: Rekor is a PUBLIC log — every entry contains the signer's OIDC email and the image digest, so anyone can look up "which workflow signed what image when"; for a truly sensitive organization/image (a secret product name, an unannounced release date), this could be an unwanted metadata leak. If privacy matters more than public auditability, there are two alternatives: (a) self-host the entire Sigstore stack (private Fulcio + Rekor, not public) — requires running your own infrastructure; or (b) go back to key-based but replace the shared secret manager with a cloud KMS (AWS KMS/GCP KMS) that has its own IAM-based audit log — losing Rekor's public transparency but keeping tighter control over who can sign. Neither option is "free" — it must be weighed against how sensitive the product actually is.

prompt: A security audit finds that the user-assigned Managed Identity used by the "billing" team's CI pipeline is granted the `Contributor` role at SUBSCRIPTION SCOPE (the entire subscription, dozens of Resource Groups belonging to every other team). This pipeline actually only needs to: deploy a Function App, read/write blobs in ONE storage account, and read a secret from ONE Key Vault — all inside one Resource Group owned by the billing team. Optimize the permissions per the least-privilege principle, and state clearly which Terraform resources you'd use.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
This is a very common double mistake: both SCOPE and ROLE are wrong, and both axes need fixing. Scope axis: `Contributor` assigned at the subscription lets the pipeline reach EVERY Resource Group of every other team, while its actual work is confined to one Resource Group owned by the billing team — lowering every role assignment's scope down to that exact Resource Group is the first step, immediately reducing the blast radius if this identity is compromised (only one RG exposed instead of the whole subscription). Role axis: `Contributor` allows creating/editing/deleting NEARLY ANY resource type, while the pipeline only needs exactly three things: deploy a Function App, read/write blob in one storage account, read a secret in one Key Vault. Replace it with narrow roles scoped to the exact resource where possible (not just the right RG but down to the specific resource): `Storage Blob Data Contributor` assigned at the scope of THAT storage account itself (not the whole RG) for blob read/write; `Key Vault Secrets User` assigned at the scope of THAT Key Vault itself (read-only secrets, no need for the Officer role if the pipeline never creates new secrets); and a role for Function App deploy permission — the built-in `Website Contributor` if narrow enough, or if it still grants unneeded permission (e.g. it also allows operations on the App Service Plan that the pipeline never touches), write a custom `azurerm_role_definition` with `permissions { actions = [...] }` listing ONLY the exact ARM actions needed for deployment (e.g. `Microsoft.Web/sites/write`, `Microsoft.Web/sites/config/write`), with `assignable_scopes = [resource_group_id_billing]` restricting it to only be assignable within the billing team's RG, never spilling into other scopes. Each of these role assignments (Terraform via `azurerm_role_assignment`, `scope` pointing at the exact resource ID instead of subscription or RG) looks like "more to manage" compared to one single `Contributor`, but that's exactly the nature of least-privilege: many narrow permissions matched to actual need are SAFER than one broad permission at a high scope, because each role assignment now explains its own reason for existing (the right resource, the right behavior), instead of one vague `Contributor` where nobody knows how much of the granted permission the pipeline actually uses.

prompt: You inherit a Terraform config managing 40 sub-modules, each independently declaring the same `data` source to look up the latest AMI, plus a manual `depends_on` even though a natural reference already exists. Every `plan` takes over 3 minutes just refreshing data sources, and there are occasional reports of hitting an API rate limit. Point out why it's slow, and rewrite the organization so it's faster while staying correct.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
There are two separate issues in this config. The main cause of slowness is **duplicated data source lookups**: every `data` block gets refreshed on EVERY `plan`/`apply` — since all 40 sub-modules declare the exact same `data "aws_ami" "app"` to ask the same question ("what's the latest AMI named `app-*`"), Terraform makes 40 separate API calls for an answer that only needed to be asked once, which is why plan takes over 3 minutes and occasionally hits the rate limit. The fix: look up the AMI ONCE at a higher layer — either right in the root module, or in a dedicated shared lookup module — store the result in `locals` (or that lookup module's output), and have every sub-module receive `ami_id` via `variable "ami_id" {}` instead of declaring its own `data` source. The result: only ONE AMI API call for the entire `plan`, while the 40 sub-modules just read a value already computed for them. The second, smaller issue is a code smell: `depends_on = [data.aws_subnet.selected]` is redundant, because the line right above, `subnet_id = data.aws_subnet.selected.id`, already creates an **implicit dependency** — Terraform reads the reference automatically and knows to resolve the subnet before creating the instance, no manual declaration needed. Keeping this redundant `depends_on` only makes the code harder to read and misleads future readers into thinking "there must be something special here" — it should be removed entirely. After the fix, you can verify by enabling `TF_LOG=DEBUG` and counting AMI API requests: from 40 down to 1, while `terraform plan` still creates exactly the same resources as before, only faster.

prompt: Your team shares ONE Azure Managed Redis instance for both (1) API result caching (has a TTL, safe to lose and recompute) and (2) logged-in user sessions (NO TTL, losing one force-logs-out the user unexpectedly). Recently, right at peak hours, a batch of users got unexpectedly logged out even though their sessions hadn't expired. Read the current config below, diagnose the cause, and propose an architecture that optimizes both cost and reliability.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The cause is `eviction_policy = "AllKeysLRU"` applying to the ENTIRE database, including TTL-less sessions. `AllKeysLRU` evicts the least-recently-used key regardless of whether it has a TTL — correct for pure caching since cache always needs room for new keys, but when mixed with sessions (no TTL because a session must survive the whole login lifecycle), a quiet session (a user leaving a tab idle for a while) can absolutely be evicted to make room for new cache entries — right at peak hours, when the volume of cache writes spikes, memory fills faster, eviction happens more aggressively, and a few unlucky sessions get swept away even though they haven't logically expired. This is NOT a Redis bug but an architectural flaw: sharing ONE database/policy for two data types with wildly different durability SLAs (cache = disposable, session = must not be lost) is the root cause; tweaking one parameter on a shared database doesn't fully solve it. The optimal architecture: split the two use cases into two separate Redis databases (Managed Redis supports multiple databases on one instance) or two separate instances if resource isolation/independent scaling is needed — the cache database/instance keeps `eviction_policy = AllKeysLRU` as before, the session database/instance switches to `eviction_policy = NoEviction`: when memory is full, Redis REJECTS THE WRITE instead of silently evicting — a failed new-session write is at least detectable (logs/alerts), unlike an old session vanishing silently. If splitting into separate instances, further optimize cost by choosing different `sku_name`s per workload: the session instance usually needs less RAM (session count is bounded by online users, with a natural ceiling), so a small `sku_name` suffices, while the cache instance may need to scale bigger or use a `ComputeOptimized`/`MemoryOptimized` class depending on the workload — splitting is often cheaper than one large shared instance since each part only pays for the resources it actually needs, and it also completely removes the risk of one use case "stealing" resources from the other.

prompt: The team uses a Kafka topic to publish "order placed" events for multiple independent consumers (billing, email, inventory). Each event only needs to be processed once and can be deleted after 7 days. The topic config below is causing messages to linger too long, and new consumers joining can't read enough recent history. How would you optimize it?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The current config is wrong on both critical fields for this use case. One, `cleanup_policy = "compact"` only keeps the **latest record per key** — appropriate for changelog/materialized state (e.g. an entity's latest state keyed by ID), but "order placed" is an **event stream**: each order is a distinct event, and billing/email/inventory all need to read ALL events, not just the latest per key — using `compact` here would silently lose old events if they happen to share a key. Two, `retention_ms = "-1"` means no time limit on retention at all, directly contradicting the "delete after 7 days" requirement — the topic grows unboundedly over time. Optimization: switch `cleanup_policy` to `"delete"` (matches event-stream semantics: retain by time then delete) and set `retention_ms = "604800000"` (7 days = 7×24×60×60×1000 milliseconds) instead of `-1`; keeping `retention_bytes = "-1"` is fine if only a time limit is desired, not a size cap. Verify: after applying, `doctl` confirms the topic is still `state = active`; monitor over more than 7 days to confirm old messages disappear automatically without manual intervention; and test that a newly joined consumer can read exactly the last 7 days of history before catching up to live.

prompt: You need to build a `primary`/`secondary` Droplet pair sharing the tag `web`, a Cloud Firewall protecting both by tag, and a Reserved IP attached to `primary` such that when `primary` dies, you only need to change ONE line of Terraform to fail traffic over to `secondary` without the public IP changing (DNS doesn't need to know anything). Write the HCL for the Reserved IP + assignment part, and explain why you'd separate the assignment into its own resource instead of setting `droplet_id` directly on `digitalocean_reserved_ip`.

You have a `base/` containing a `web` Deployment (1 replica, image `myapp:latest`, reading config from ConfigMap `app-config`). Write `overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml` that satisfies: (1) change replica count to 5, (2) change the image tag to `2.0.0` WITHOUT writing a dedicated patch for the image field, (3) add a `prod-` prefix to the NAME of every resource, (4) create a new ConfigMap overriding `app-config` with `LOG_LEVEL=warn`. Explain which `kustomization.yaml` field correctly handles each requirement.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
```yaml
# overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
resources:
  - ../../base

namePrefix: prod-

images:
  - name: myapp
    newTag: "2.0.0"

configMapGenerator:
  - name: app-config
    behavior: merge
    literals:
      - LOG_LEVEL=warn

patches:
  - target:
      kind: Deployment
      name: web
    patch: |-
      - op: replace
        path: /spec/replicas
        value: 5
```
Explaining each field: `resources: [../../base]` loads the entire original manifest from base as the foundation. Requirement (1) changing replicas uses `patches` with JSON6902 `replace` at `/spec/replicas` — a specific, simple field, so a direct patch is reasonable (alternatively, a strategic merge patch with `spec: {replicas: 5}` is equally correct). Requirement (2) changing the image tag uses the DEDICATED **`images`** field: declaring `name: myapp` (matching the original image name in the base, not the container name) and `newTag: "2.0.0"` — Kustomize automatically finds AND REPLACES every reference to the `myapp:*` image across all resources, without needing to know exactly which path it lives at in the YAML (unlike having to write a JSON6902 patch pointing at the correct container index by hand). Requirement (3) adding a prefix uses **`namePrefix: prod-`** — Kustomize automatically prepends `prod-` to `metadata.name` of EVERY resource listed in the overlay (Deployment becomes `prod-web`, Service becomes `prod-web` if present, etc.), no need to manually edit each file, and it also auto-updates internal references (e.g. a `configMapRef` pointing at the correctly-renamed ConfigMap). Requirement (4) creating/overriding the ConfigMap uses **`configMapGenerator`** with `behavior: merge` (merging into the existing `app-config` ConfigMap from base, only adding/overriding the `LOG_LEVEL` key) and `literals: [LOG_LEVEL=warn]`. An important thing to know: by default, Kustomize generates the ConfigMap's NAME with a content-based HASH SUFFIX (e.g. `app-config-a1b2c3d4`) and auto-updates every `Deployment` referencing that ConfigMap — this mechanism ensures that when the ConfigMap's content changes, its name changes too, forcing Kubernetes to treat it as a change and triggering a pod rolling restart to pick up the new config (unlike editing a ConfigMap in place under the same name, which the Deployment has no way of knowing to restart for). Using dedicated fields for all three cases (`images`, `namePrefix`, `configMapGenerator`) is far better than hand-written patches: less risk of a wrong path/index, and applied CONSISTENTLY across every related resource automatically instead of having to remember each spot.

prompt: Write a multi-stage Dockerfile for a simple Go service (`main.go` makes outbound HTTPS calls): a build stage compiling a static binary, and a runtime stage using the smallest possible image. Explain your choice of runtime base image and ONE thing you must manually add for HTTPS to work, since the base image doesn't include it.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
```dockerfile
FROM golang:1.22 AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux go build -o server .

FROM scratch
COPY --from=builder /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt
COPY --from=builder /app/server /server
ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]
```
The builder stage uses `golang:1.22` for the ready-made compile toolchain, and `CGO_ENABLED=0` is required to produce a STATIC binary — with no dependency on any dynamic C library (glibc/musl) at runtime, a prerequisite for running on an absolutely minimal base. The runtime stage uses `FROM scratch` — not `distroless` or `alpine` — since the Go binary is already fully static and needs no libc at all; `scratch` is an absolutely EMPTY image (0 layers, 0 bytes beyond whatever you copy in yourself), giving a final image just a few MB (exactly the binary's size), with almost no CVEs from the OS since there's no OS. Only copy what's needed: the built binary. What MUST be manually added since `scratch` has nothing at all: **CA certificates** — if `main.go` makes outbound HTTPS calls (e.g. to a third-party API), the Go runtime needs to verify the target server's certificate chain, and the root CA list normally lives at `/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt` on a regular OS — `scratch` doesn't have this file, so you must `COPY --from=builder /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt ...` (pulled from the builder stage itself, where `golang:1.22`'s Debian base already has it). Skipping this step makes every outbound HTTPS request fail with something like "x509: certificate signed by unknown authority" even though the code is entirely correct. Similarly, if the app needs timezone handling (`time.LoadLocation`), you'd also need to copy tzdata since `scratch` doesn't have that either.

prompt: The team enabled `enable_cdn = true` on a backend service serving static product images (JPEG/PNG, never change after upload). The Cloud Monitoring dashboard shows a cache hit ratio of only **~12%** — nearly every request is a `MISS` and goes to origin, even though the images never change. Reading the config below, optimize it to reach a high cache hit ratio, and explain WHY each change is necessary.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The 12% cache hit ratio comes from TWO stacked causes, not one. Cause 1 — origin header: every image response returns `Cache-Control: no-cache`, and `cache_mode = USE_ORIGIN_HEADERS` means the CDN **absolutely respects** the origin's instruction — origin says "don't cache" so the CDN doesn't cache, regardless of whether the content is actually static. Fix: change the image service's response to `Cache-Control: public, max-age=604800` (7 days, or longer depending on the invalidation policy when an image changes) — this is the right fix because it fixes at the source and keeps `USE_ORIGIN_HEADERS`, rather than jumping to `FORCE_CACHE_ALL` (extremely dangerous if this same backend service also serves other dynamic endpoints, since `FORCE_CACHE_ALL` caches EVERY response indiscriminately). Cause 2 — cache key: the actual client URL has a query string `?session=a92f...&ts=1737020000`; by default `cache_key_policy` INCLUDES the query string in the cache key, so `sku-8231.jpg?session=X&ts=1` and `sku-8231.jpg?session=Y&ts=2` are treated by the CDN as **two different objects** despite being the same image file — every session/every reload is a new cache key, causing constant misses. Fix: add `cache_key_policy { include_query_string = false }` to strip the query string out of the cache key entirely (correct for static images with no query-based variants); if a legitimate parameter later affects content (e.g. `?size=thumb`), use `query_string_whitelist = ["size"]` instead of turning it off completely. After both fixes, verify by calling the same image URL twice in a row — the second call should show an increasing `Age:` header (real proof of a HIT, not a guess), and watch the Cloud Monitoring `cache_result=HIT` metric climb over time on the dashboard rather than trusting a single percentage right after the config change (the CDN needs warm-up time for the cache to fill).

prompt: You need a subnet of multiple VMs with no external IP to egress to the internet under ONE fixed static IP (for a third-party partner to allow-list), and need to proactively guard against port exhaustion since these VMs call external APIs at a high frequency. Write the HCL for the Cloud Router + Cloud NAT + static IP, and explain your port-exhaustion-avoidance decisions.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
```hcl
resource "google_compute_address" "nat" {
  name         = "egress-nat-ip"
  address_type = "EXTERNAL"
  region       = var.region
}

resource "google_compute_router" "nat" {
  name    = "egress-nat-router"
  network = google_compute_network.main.id
  region  = var.region
}

resource "google_compute_router_nat" "nat" {
  name   = "egress-nat-gw"
  router = google_compute_router.nat.name
  region = var.region

  nat_ip_allocate_option             = "MANUAL_ONLY"
  nat_ips                            = [google_compute_address.nat.self_link]
  source_subnetwork_ip_ranges_to_nat = "LIST_OF_SUBNETWORKS"

  subnetwork {
    name                    = google_compute_subnetwork.private.id
    source_ip_ranges_to_nat = ["ALL_IP_RANGES"]
  }

  min_ports_per_vm              = 256
  enable_dynamic_port_allocation = true
  max_ports_per_vm               = 4096

  log_config {
    enable = true
    filter = "ERRORS_ONLY"
  }
}
```
Design decisions: (1) `google_compute_address` with `address_type = "EXTERNAL"` reserves a regional static IP — this is the IP the third-party partner will allow-list. (2) Cloud NAT on GCP **doesn't stand alone** like an AWS NAT Gateway — it must be attached to a `google_compute_router` (Cloud Router), a regional control-plane object; the `bgp` block isn't needed since this is NAT-only, no on-prem connection. (3) `nat_ip_allocate_option = "MANUAL_ONLY"` plus `nat_ips` pointing to the just-created static IP — using `AUTO_ONLY` would have GCP assign an ephemeral IP that changes over time, which the third-party partner couldn't reliably allow-list. (4) Guarding against port exhaustion — since the VMs call APIs at high frequency: raise `min_ports_per_vm` from the default 64 to 256 so each VM starts with more source ports for concurrent connections, and enable `enable_dynamic_port_allocation = true` with `max_ports_per_vm = 4096` so NAT can grant additional ports on demand when a VM needs to exceed the minimum, instead of a rigid fixed allocation. Verify: enable `log_config { enable = true, filter = "ERRORS_ONLY" }` to catch `OUT_OF_RESOURCES` errors (a sign of port exhaustion) early, before users report the issue; and from the third-party partner's side, confirm the observed source IP matches exactly the reserved static IP, not each VM's own IP (proving SNAT is working correctly).

prompt: A dev reports: 'I deployed my API to the server but calling into it from my machine just doesn't work.' When you probe further, sometimes it says `connection refused`, sometimes `connection timed out`. Walk me through how you'd layer this problem: how do those two error messages differ in nature, and which direction does each point you to debug? List at least three plausible root causes, and for each, which command you'd use to confirm it right on the server.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
I split the two error messages first, because they point at different layers. `connection refused` means the dev's SYN DID reach the host and the OS returned **RST** immediately — either no process is `listen()`ing on that port, or a firewall uses a `REJECT` rule; that's a service/socket-layer problem, investigated on the server. `connection timed out` means the SYN was **DROP**ped with no reply — usually a firewall DENY, a black-hole route, a security group, or a dead host; that's a network/firewall-layer problem, investigated along the path. Three root causes and how to confirm each on the server: (1) service not listening / crashed — `ss -tlnp` (or `ss -tlnp 'sport = :PORT'`) to see if any process holds the port, plus `systemctl status <svc>`; symptom is refused. (2) service bound to `127.0.0.1` instead of `0.0.0.0` — `curl 127.0.0.1:PORT` on the box works but from outside it's refused; confirm via the Local Address column of `ss -tlnp`. (3) firewall/security group blocking — `ufw status` / `iptables -L -n` on the host and the cloud security group; `ss` still shows it listening but from outside it times out (DROP). Fast bisect: from the server itself `curl 127.0.0.1:PORT` — if it works the service is fine and the bug is in bind-address or firewall/network; if it's refused locally the service isn't listening. Work inside-out so you don't blame the network when the service never came up.

prompt: The company's Loki bill tripled in 6 months as the fleet grew, and leadership demands a 60% cut in log storage cost next quarter WITHOUT losing the ability to investigate an incident that happened 2 weeks ago, and while still keeping compliance audit logs per legal requirements (minimum 1-year retention for financial-transaction-related logs). How do you design a tiered retention strategy that hits the cost target without breaking either constraint?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Cutting 60% of cost without breaking either constraint (investigating a recent incident, 1-year audit compliance) requires tiering by the VALUE of each log type, not uniformly cutting one shared retention. Step one, BEFORE cutting anything: measure where the 60% of cost actually comes from — almost certainly the bulk of it comes from high-volume, low-value logs (verbose DEBUG, detailed per-request access logs), NOT audit logs (which are usually far fewer lines than access logs). Cutting blindly without measuring first risks accidentally reducing retention on exactly the log type needed for investigation or compliance. Tiered design: (1) DEBUG and verbose access logs — SHORT retention (a few days), since their value drops off very quickly once a deploy stabilizes; (2) INFO and above (high-value events: request errors, important state changes) — MEDIUM retention, long enough to investigate an incident from 2 weeks ago (e.g. 3-4 weeks "hot" retention, fully indexed, fast queries); (3) audit logs related to financial transactions — a SEPARATE rule, DECOUPLED from the general policy, keeping a minimum of 1 year per legal requirements, NEVER sharing a retention policy with ordinary logs. Technically, Loki supports **per-tenant or per-stream retention** via `compactor` configuration (retention overrides by label or tenant) — this is exactly the mechanism to split audit logs into their own stream with its own policy, instead of one SHARED retention applied across the whole instance. For logs past the "hot" phase (recent investigation) but still needed for compliance, you don't need to keep them in the expensive fully-indexed tier — move them to a cheaper object-storage ARCHIVE, stored raw without needing fast queries (since old audit-log access frequency is VERY LOW, only on a specific legal request). Combined: cut the "hot" retention of noisy logs to the minimum needed for investigation, push rarely-accessed-but-mandatory logs (audit) into a cheap long-term storage tier — hitting a substantial cost cut without trading away recent investigation capability or breaching compliance obligations.

prompt: A junior sends you the manifest below for review before merging: a Deployment running a metrics-reading job, a ServiceAccount + binding for it, and namespace `team-a` already has a `ResourceQuota` on `requests.cpu`/`requests.memory` (no `LimitRange` alongside it). The junior explains: "namespace `team-a` and `team-b` are already isolated so we don't need a NetworkPolicy, and I gave the ServiceAccount `cluster-admin` just to make sure the job never hits a permission wall." Review it: list EVERY problem you see in the manifest and in the junior's explanation, ranked by severity, and state the fix for each.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
Three issues, ranked by severity. **Most severe — `ClusterRoleBinding` granting `cluster-admin`:** a job that only needs to read metrics has no reason to need cluster-wide admin; this is a textbook least-privilege violation — if the job's image or a dependency is compromised (supply-chain attack, RCE), the attacker instantly gets admin over **every** namespace and resource. Fix: create a namespaced `Role` inside `team-a` listing exactly the verbs/resources needed (e.g. `get, list, watch` on `pods`, `nodes/metrics`), then bind it with a `RoleBinding` (not a ClusterRoleBinding) — scoping the permission to the right namespace and the right job. **Second — missing `resources` on the container:** the namespace already has a `ResourceQuota` on `requests.cpu`/`requests.memory` with no accompanying `LimitRange` to fill in defaults; under Kubernetes' rules, once a quota exists on `requests.*`, ANY Pod that doesn't declare resources gets admission-rejected immediately with an error like `must specify requests.cpu` — meaning this Deployment will never get a single Pod created, the job dies at admission, not at runtime. Fix: explicitly declare `resources.requests`/`limits` on the container, or (better for the whole namespace) add a `LimitRange` supplying default/max values for every container in `team-a`. **Third — the junior's misunderstanding about namespaces:** a namespace only isolates **names** and serves as the scope for RBAC/ResourceQuota/LimitRange — it does NOT isolate network by default. A Pod in `team-a` can still `curl` a Service in `team-b` over ClusterIP without a NetworkPolicy. If real isolation is the intent, add a default-deny ingress/egress NetworkPolicy for `team-a` and then selectively open only the traffic that's actually needed. On priority: fix `cluster-admin` first (security risk that spans the whole cluster), then the missing resources (blocks functionality outright, caught right at apply time); the NetworkPolicy can follow since it doesn't block functionality immediately, but it's still a gap that needs patching.

prompt: The team configured `rotation` on a secret holding a database password in Secret Manager, believing "GCP will automatically change the password for us on schedule". After 90 days, the real database password did NOT change — it's still the same password from setup. Looking at the config below, explain why it doesn't work as expected, and redesign the rotation pipeline correctly.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The current config is doing EXACTLY what it was designed to do — the problem is the team misunderstood the scope of GCP Secret Manager's `rotation` feature. The `rotation` + `topics` block has exactly ONE job: every `rotation_period` (90 days), Secret Manager **publishes a message to the declared Pub/Sub topic**, announcing "this secret is due for rotation". It does NOT call any API to change the real database password, and does NOT add a new secret version on its own — the entire task of "actually making rotation happen" is the user's responsibility, not GCP's. In this case, the specific gap is: `google_pubsub_topic.rotation_notify` exists and correctly receives a message every 90 days, but has NO subscriber listening to it — the message publishes on schedule and falls into the void, unhandled. So the behavior "password never changed after 90 days" isn't a mysterious bug — it's the direct, entirely logical consequence of missing the second half of the pipeline. The correct redesign: implement a **Cloud Function** subscribed to `rotation_notify`, which on receiving a message performs three steps in order — (1) generate a new, sufficiently strong random password; (2) call the Cloud SQL Admin API (`instances.patch` or the equivalent password-change call) to actually change the password on the database; (3) call `secretmanager.projects.secrets.addVersion` to add a NEW secret version holding the just-changed password, so the next time the app reads the secret it gets a value matching the real database. This is a clear architectural difference from AWS: AWS Secrets Manager rotation calls a Lambda DIRECTLY through a standardized 4-step protocol (`createSecret` → `setSecret` → `testSecret` → `finishSecret`) with framework support; GCP only stops at publishing a signal, with all the password-change logic being hand-written, no equivalent 4-step framework built in. Finally, to avoid repeating the current "silent" failure, active monitoring is needed: set an alert on the Pub/Sub dead-letter queue (or on the unacknowledged-message rate on the subscription), to detect IMMEDIATELY if the Cloud Function subscriber errors out or stops running, instead of waiting 90 days to discover the password was never actually rotated.

prompt: Write an SCP using the **deny-list** strategy (keeping the default `FullAWSAccess`, only adding deny statements) to block two things on EVERY account in an OU: (1) nobody can leave the organization (`organizations:LeaveOrganization`), (2) nobody can disable CloudTrail (`cloudtrail:StopLogging`, `cloudtrail:DeleteTrail`). Write a `variable "environment"` for a Terraform module with these requirements: type `string`, accepting exactly 3 values — `dev`, `staging`, `prod` — no more, no less, and if someone passes any other value Terraform must fail immediately at the `plan` step with a clear message, WITHOUT letting it slip down to the cloud API where it would fail with a confusing error. Write the code, then explain why this approach is called "fail-fast".
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The code to write:

```hcl
variable "environment" {
  type        = string
  description = "Deployment environment"

  validation {
    condition     = contains(["dev", "staging", "prod"], var.environment)
    error_message = "environment must be one of: dev, staging, prod."
  }
}
```

`type = string` locks down the data type upfront. The nested `validation` block inside the variable has two parts: `condition`, an expression returning a boolean — here `contains(["dev", "staging", "prod"], var.environment)` checks whether the passed-in value is exactly one of the 3 allowed choices; and `error_message`, the string displayed when `condition` evaluates to `false`, which should clearly list the valid values so the user can fix it right away instead of guessing. This is called **fail-fast** because Terraform evaluates `validation` right at the `plan` step — before any request is ever sent to the cloud API. Without validation, a bad value like `"qa"` would slip all the way down to `apply`, and only then would the cloud provider return an error (often confusing, something generic like "InvalidParameterValue" that doesn't say the root cause is the `environment` variable) — wasting a real apply round-trip (which can take from minutes to tens of minutes depending on the resource) just to catch an error that could have been caught in seconds at `plan`. To self-verify, run `terraform plan -var="environment=qa"` — Terraform blocks it immediately and prints the exact message written, without creating any resource.

prompt: The BigQuery table `events` currently holds 50 TB, has NO partitioning, NO clustering, and uses on-demand pricing. 90% of the team's queries filter by `event_date` (roughly the last 1–7 days) AND a specific `customer_id`. The team pays an average of $8,000/month in query cost, running continuously during business hours (~10 TB/month of new data ingested, a stable and predictable workload). Propose a redesign of the table + billing model to cut cost, explaining each decision.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The first and cheapest step is **partitioning + clustering that actually matches the real access pattern**, done before considering any billing-model change. Since 90% of queries filter on `event_date` within a short 1–7 day window, adding `time_partitioning { type = "DAY", field = "event_date" }` lets BigQuery cut most of the 50 TB entirely out of the scan scope — a query asking for "the last 7 days" now only scans exactly 7 partitions instead of the entire history. Since queries further filter by a specific `customer_id` within each day, adding `clustering = ["customer_id"]` lets BigQuery keep shrinking what it reads inside each partition — not reading every customer's data for that day just to filter down to one. Alongside this is a mandatory `require_partition_filter = true`: without this line, the entire partition/cluster optimization can be silently undone by ONE query that forgets to filter by date — BigQuery still runs it and silently rescans all 50 TB, wiping out the design's benefit. On the billing model: the data shows a workload with ~10 TB/month of new data, running continuously and predictably during business hours — this IS a good signal to consider switching from on-demand to a **slot reservation** (fixed cost per slot-hour, effective at high, steady utilization, ineffective for erratic spiky workloads). But the correct order is: apply partition + cluster FIRST, re-measure real bytes-scanned/cost AFTER optimizing, and only then decide on a slot reservation commitment based on the NEW baseline — committing a reservation sized off the old baseline (when the table was unoptimized and the $8,000/month cost mostly came from unnecessary full scans) would lock the team into paying a fixed price for phantom demand, higher than what's actually needed once queries are optimized. How to measure the effect: run `bq query --dry_run` (or inspect `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS`) on the same set of common queries, comparing `totalBytesProcessed` before and after adding partition/cluster — this is direct evidence, not waiting until end of month to check the bill to find out whether the optimization actually worked.

Write the `strategy.canary.steps` section of an Argo `Rollout` for the `checkout-api` service, matching exactly these requirements: start at 20% traffic, pause for 5 minutes for manual observation; then increase to 50% and automatically run an `analysis` (referencing template `error-rate-check`) — auto-rollback if it fails; if it passes, go to 100%. No need to write the full `AnalysisTemplate`, just the correct `steps` structure with an explanation of each step.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
```yaml
strategy:
  canary:
    steps:
      - setWeight: 20            # Step 1: route 20% of traffic to canary
      - pause:
          duration: 5m            # Step 2: pause 5 min for MANUAL observation (timed, not waiting for approval)
      - setWeight: 50            # Step 3: raise to 50% BEFORE analysis
      - analysis:                 # Step 4: run an inline AnalysisRun right in this step
          templates:
            - templateName: error-rate-check
      - setWeight: 100           # Step 5: only reached if the prior analysis returned Successful
```
Explaining the order: step 1 `setWeight: 20` immediately shifts 20% of traffic to canary through whichever traffic-shaping mechanism is in use (ingress/SMI/Gateway API). Step 2 `pause: { duration: 5m }` is a TIMED pause — very different from `pause: {}` (an infinite pause, waiting for someone to run `kubectl argo rollouts promote` before continuing) — matching "pause for 5 minutes" automatically then auto-advancing, with no human approval needed. Step 3 `setWeight: 50` MUST come BEFORE the analysis step: `analysis` measures signals (error-rate, latency) against the REAL traffic running at that moment, so weight must be raised to 50% first, then measured — not measured at the old 20% then raised, which would evaluate against the wrong load level. Step 4 `analysis: { templates: [...] }` references `error-rate-check` to run an `AnalysisRun` RIGHT IN the rollout (inline), not a standalone AnalysisTemplate that nothing calls. This is an automatic gate: Argo Rollouts waits for this AnalysisRun to finish before deciding whether to proceed. Step 5 `setWeight: 100` is only reached IF the AnalysisRun in step 4 returns `Successful`. If it returns `Failed`, per Argo Rollouts' default behavior, the rollout HALTS progression immediately — never running `setWeight: 100` — and automatically scales the canary ReplicaSet down to 0 while keeping/restoring the stable ReplicaSet at 100% traffic, i.e. a full rollback with no human intervention. This is what "progressive delivery" really means: combining a human-gated step (a timed pause early, when risk is lower) with an automatic SLI-based gate (analysis later, when risk is higher because traffic has increased).

prompt: You inherit a 60-panel Grafana dashboard that nobody knows how to prioritize. Last week, during a severe checkout slowdown at 2am, on-call spent 15 minutes just SCROLLING through 60 panels looking for something red, while the real cause (an exhausted database connection pool) sat in panel 47. How do you redesign the dashboard around RED and USE so on-call can diagnose in under a minute next time, and how do the two frameworks complement each other in that design?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The root problem with the 60-panel dashboard isn't "missing data" — it's MISSING HIERARCHY, forcing on-call to visually hunt through flat, undifferentiated data. Redesign around two complementary frameworks, PLACED where their role actually belongs. **RED** (Rate, Errors, Duration) answers "is the user in pain" for a request-facing service — this is the signal on-call MUST see FIRST, so a RED row for `checkout` (and every other important service) must sit AT THE TOP of the dashboard, not after scrolling past dozens of panels. Directly below a service's RED row, place the **USE** (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) rows for the EXACT resources that service depends on — CPU, memory, and most importantly here, the database connection pool. This is exactly how you fix last week's incident: when `checkout`'s RED panel flags a p99 spike, on-call just needs to LOOK DOWN, right below it, to see the database connection pool's USE — not scroll through an unstructured 60-panel wall hoping to stumble onto panel 47. The most important technical point for a connection-pool-exhaustion case: **Saturation** — one of the three USE signals — is the EARLIEST warning indicator, because the queue of requests WAITING for a connection from the pool grows RIGHT AS the pool starts straining, BEFORE Utilization (the % of the pool that's busy) even pins at its maximum. If the dashboard only has a Utilization panel and no Saturation, on-call sees "pool is 70% busy" looking fine while requests have already started queueing — Saturation is the panel that catches the problem EARLIEST. End result: the dashboard is organized into BLOCKS per service, each block with RED on top (the user-facing symptom) and USE right below it (the corresponding resource for diagnosis) — on-call only needs to read the ONE block relevant to the firing alert, instead of scanning all 60 flat panels as before.

prompt: A platform team sends you a `ValidatingWebhookConfiguration` for review before merging, meant to enforce that every Pod declares `resources.requests`. They're running `webhook-server` with `replicas: 1` (no PodDisruptionBudget), and no `namespaceSelector` at all on the webhook rule. Review it: list EVERY operational risk you see in the manifest, explain a concrete scenario that could "lock" the entire cluster, and propose a fix for each risk.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
Two severe issues that compound into a genuinely dangerous self-lockout scenario. **Issue 1 — single point of failure with `failurePolicy: Fail`:** webhook-server runs with only `replicas: 1` and no `PodDisruptionBudget`. `failurePolicy: Fail` means that if the webhook can't respond (timeout, crash, network issue), the apiserver treats it as a **reject** rather than a pass — matching the original "enforce this" intent, but with just 1 replica, any ordinary restart (a rolling update of the webhook itself, a node drained for maintenance, an OOMKill) creates a window where **no replica is alive**, and during that window **every Pod-creation request cluster-wide is blocked**. **Issue 2 — missing exclusion `namespaceSelector`:** the `rules` apply to `resources: ["pods"]` in EVERY namespace, without excluding `kube-system` or `webhook-system`. Combining both issues: when the single `webhook-server` Pod dies (issue 1), its own Deployment tries to create a replacement Pod in `webhook-system` — but that `CREATE Pod` request also has to pass through the very webhook that's dead, and `failurePolicy: Fail` blocks it. The result: **complete deadlock** — the webhook can't heal itself since its own replacement Pod is blocked by itself, and no other Pod on the cluster (including CoreDNS, CNI needing a restart) can be created either. This requires emergency intervention via `kubectl delete validatingwebhookconfiguration require-resources.example.com` to unlock things first, then fixing the config. The fix: (1) raise `replicas` to at least 2-3, add a `PodDisruptionBudget` with `minAvailable: 1` (or 2), and spread Pods across multiple nodes with `topologySpreadConstraints`/`podAntiAffinity` so one dead node doesn't take down every webhook replica at once; (2) add a `namespaceSelector` to the rule excluding at least `kube-system` and `webhook-system` (`matchExpressions: kubernetes.io/metadata.name NotIn [kube-system, webhook-system]`), guaranteeing the cluster always has a self-recovery path even while the webhook is having problems.

prompt: Your team plans a canary deploy for a service with 2 characteristics: (1) this release changes the database schema (adds a required column), and (2) the current load balancer has session affinity (sticky session) enabled to keep logged-in users on the same Pod. The diagram below shows the team's initial canary plan. Point out ALL the problems in this plan and propose a redesign.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
This plan has two independent problems, both severe enough to block the canary before it runs. Problem 1 — DB migration: the diagram runs `ADD COLUMN NOT NULL` BEFORE the canary goes live, while Stable v1 (95% traffic, completely unaware of the new column) is STILL writing to the same database. If v1's code inserts a row without setting a value for the new NOT NULL column, that insert FAILS IMMEDIATELY — and since v1 serves 95% of traffic, this bug affects nearly ALL users, not just the intended 5% canary. Fix with **expand-contract**: the "expand" step adds the new column as NULLABLE (or with a `DEFAULT`), so both v1 (unaware of the column) and v2/canary (aware and using it) can write normally while running side by side; only in a LATER release — once 100% of traffic has fully moved to v2 — do you "contract": convert the column to truly NOT NULL and clean up the old logic. Problem 2 — sticky sessions: the load balancer pins users to a specific Pod to preserve sessions. For canary, this breaks a fundamental assumption: if a user gets pinned to the canary Pod from the start, they stay there for their ENTIRE session — not a random sample representing real traffic, and if the canary has a bug, that exact user is affected for the whole session instead of just one request. Conversely, the measured 5% traffic percentage is also no longer accurate, since the distribution depends on when a NEW user got pinned, not the real request ratio. The right fix: the app needs to be stateless — session stored in an external store (Redis) instead of tied to a specific Pod — so the load balancer can route by REQUEST for canary instead of by session; if the architecture can't change in time, the team must at least know the measured canary percentage is unreliable and consider delaying the canary until session affinity is resolved. Correct order: fix the migration to expand-contract FIRST, address (or knowingly accept the risk of) sticky sessions, and only then run the canary per the original diagram — neither of these problems is independent of whether the canary is meaningful at all.

prompt: You have an `aws_instance` running a web app with a public endpoint. Write a `metadata_options` block to enforce IMDSv2 (no unauthenticated IMDSv1 allowed), and limit the hop count so a container running ON that instance can't request the IMDS itself. Briefly explain what each field protects against.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The code to write:

```hcl
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  # ... ami, instance_type, subnet_id, etc.

  metadata_options {
    http_tokens                 = "required"
    http_put_response_hop_limit = 1
  }
}
```

`http_tokens = "required"` is the core field enforcing **IMDSv2**: instead of a plain `GET http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/...` like IMDSv1 (requiring no authorization step at all), IMDSv2 requires a `PUT` request first to obtain a session token, then a `GET` for metadata carrying that token. This layer protects against **SSRF** (Server-Side Request Forgery): if the app has a vulnerability tricking it into making an HTTP request to an attacker-chosen URL (a very common bug class for apps processing URLs from user input), with IMDSv1 the attacker just needs to trick the app into a GET to instantly obtain the `iam_instance_profile`'s credentials — no authentication step to bypass. With `http_tokens = "required"`, a simple SSRF-style GET request gets rejected for missing the token, and generating that token needs a PUT request with conditions a classic SSRF scenario typically can't satisfy. `http_put_response_hop_limit = 1` handles a different risk: if the instance runs containers (Docker), a container's network namespace counts as ONE additional hop compared to the host itself — setting the hop limit to exactly 1 means only a process running DIRECTLY on the host (0 additional hops) can successfully call metadata; a request originating from INSIDE a container (already adding at least 1 network hop) gets its response dropped before arriving, even though it's running on the same physical instance. These two fields together: `http_tokens` blocks the classic SSRF-from-the-app-itself attack, while `hop_limit` restricts who on the instance can successfully call metadata at all.

prompt: You have two existing Security Groups: `aws_security_group.app` (an auto-scaling fleet) and `aws_security_group.db` (RDS Postgres). Write an ingress rule for `db` that allows ANY instance belonging to `app` to reach port 5432 — mandatory requirements: the rule must survive auto-scaling (IPs changing constantly), and it must be a separate resource rule (not inline inside `aws_security_group`).

The code to write:

```hcl
resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "db_from_app" {
  security_group_id            = aws_security_group.db.id
  referenced_security_group_id = aws_security_group.app.id
```

This is a SEPARATE resource (`aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule`), not an inline `ingress {}` block inside `aws_security_group.db` — matching the requirement that each rule be an independent resource, easy to plan/tag/destroy on its own. `security_group_id = aws_security_group.db.id` identifies that this rule belongs to the database's SG — i.e. it defines "who is allowed into db". The key to surviving auto-scaling is `referenced_security_group_id = aws_security_group.app.id` instead of `cidr_ipv4`: this is the **SG-to-SG reference** mechanism, allowing by IDENTITY (any instance currently carrying the `app` SG at the exact moment the packet passes) rather than a specific IP range.
