Your team put the production website behind Azure Front Door for WAF and global caching. A security audit finds that hitting the origin server's public IP (the VM behind Front Door) directly still serves normal content — meaning an attacker can completely bypass WAF and cache by going straight to the origin. Based on the diagram below, redesign this to block the bypass path, and explain how the mechanism you use actually works.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The diagram shows exactly the vulnerability: the origin VM still has a Public IP directly open, so requests that don't go through Front Door still reach the origin — Front Door's WAF and cache only apply to whoever "goes through the front door," while an attacker who knows the IP bypasses everything cleanly. Azure's standard lock uses two layers together. Layer one — identification: the Front Door profile exports `resource_guid`, and this is exactly the value Front Door automatically stamps into an **X-Azure-FDID** header on every request it forwards to the origin — a normal client (including an attacker hitting the IP directly) has no way to fabricate this header correctly, since it's generated by your specific Front Door instance. Layer two — enforcement: configure the origin (NSG rule, firewall, or application middleware) to accept ONLY requests satisfying both conditions simultaneously — coming from the `AzureFrontDoor.Backend` service tag (narrowing source IPs to the whole Front Door infrastructure's range) AND carrying an FDID header matching your profile's `resource_guid` (narrowing it down to your exact Front Door instance, not some other organization's Front Door also sharing that service tag) — rejecting everything else, even requests that know the origin IP. On the Premium SKU, there's a much stronger option: use **Private Link** to connect Front Door to the origin, so the origin needs no Public IP at all — eliminating direct-IP access entirely instead of only relying on header/NSG blocking (which still leaves a Public IP as an attack surface). On Standard SKU without Private Link, the two-layer combo of NSG service-tag filtering plus an application-level FDID check is the required minimum — missing either one still leaves a gap, e.g. filtering by service tag alone while forgetting the FDID check still lets a different organization's Front Door call your origin directly since it shares the same `AzureFrontDoor.Backend` IP range.

prompt: Your lead messages: "The deploy from 10 minutes ago has a bug, roll back to the previous one!" You've never run `helm rollback` before. Walk through exactly what you'd do: what to check first, which command to run, and how to be sure the rollback actually succeeded.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
First step: don't roll back right away without knowing exactly where you are — run `helm history <release-name>` to see the full list of REVISIONS over time, each line with a revision number, timestamp, description (chart version, app version), and status. From that, identify precisely: which number is the CURRENT (broken, deployed 10 minutes ago) revision, and which number is the one RIGHT BEFORE IT (the good version to return to) — don't guess "probably the previous one", look at the exact numbers in the output. Once certain, run `helm rollback <release-name> <revision-number>` with the SPECIFIC revision number just identified — being explicit is safer than running `helm rollback <release-name>` without a number (this is STILL valid and defaults to the immediately prior revision, but being explicit avoids confusion when multiple people are operating). An important thing to understand correctly: rollback does NOT delete history or "rewind time" literally — it creates a NEW REVISION (the next incrementing number) with CONTENT identical to the selected old revision, then applies it like a regular upgrade. Running `helm history` afterward shows a NEW line added, not the old revisions being erased. To confirm the rollback succeeded: check `helm history` shows the newest revision with status `deployed` and the expected description, cross-check `kubectl get pods` to see the new pods `Running`/`Ready`, and most importantly — verify the application in practice (call the API, check logs, or whatever way the team verifies the bug) to be sure it's actually gone, not just trusting Kubernetes' reported state.

prompt:
Your app just crashed on startup with: `Nest can't resolve dependencies of the OrderService (?). Please make sure that the argument PaymentService at index [0] is available in the OrderModule context.`

The diagram below shows how the modules are currently declared. `OrderService` injects `PaymentService`, and `PaymentService` is decorated with `@Injectable()` and sits in `PaymentModule`'s `providers`.

Read this error out loud: what does the `?` mean, why can't Nest resolve it even though `PaymentService` is already `@Injectable()`, and where EXACTLY do you fix it — not by copying `PaymentService` into `OrderModule`'s `providers`?
ideal:
:::muted
TL;DR
:::
`(?)` = a token Nest can't resolve in `OrderModule`'s context. It's not a missing `@Injectable()` — `PaymentService` was never `exports`-ed by `PaymentModule`, and `OrderModule` never `imports: [PaymentModule]`. A provider is encapsulated inside the module that declares it; using it elsewhere requires export + import.

:::muted
How it works
:::
`@Injectable()` only registers the class as a provider under a token. Visibility is a module concern: `exports` opens that token to whichever module `imports` it. Importing a module means REUSING the SAME instance (singleton), not creating a new one.

:::muted
Common pitfall
:::
Copying `PaymentService` into `OrderModule`'s `providers` "to make the error go away" creates 2 separate instances — breaks any service with state (cache, connection, counter). The correct fix is export/import.

prompt: You're handed a piece of code: a component keeps `query` in `useState`, and also keeps a **separate** `filtered` in a second `useState`, syncing it with `useEffect(() => setFiltered(filterUsers(users, query)), [query])` every time `query` changes. Explain to the interviewer: why `filtered` shouldn't be state here, the measurable cost (extra renders, a visibly wrong frame or not) of writing it this way, and how to write it correctly.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
`filtered` here is redundant state: it's just a copy of `filterUsers(users, query)`, a value already fully computable from the `query` you already have. Because it's stored in state, you're forced to add `useEffect([query])` to "patch" it back in sync every time `query` changes — creating two sources of truth for the same information. The measurable cost: typing a key first calls `setQuery`, and render #1 happens while `filtered` still holds the *previous* query's value; React commits, runs the effect, and `setFiltered` triggers render #2 to catch `filtered` up. One change costs two renders, and there's a window (between those two renders) where the user sees the wrong result for a query that's already stale. The correct fix is to drop the second `useState` and the effect entirely: compute `const filtered = filterUsers(users, query)` directly in the component body — no extra state, no effect, exactly one render per `query` change, and `filtered` always matches `query` within that very render, never out of phase. If `filterUsers` were genuinely expensive (filtering tens of thousands of rows), wrap it in `useMemo(() => filterUsers(users, query), [users, query])` to cache by dependency — this is still derived-in-render, not a fancier way of writing `useEffect`. The general lesson: an Effect exists to synchronize with something *outside* React's render model; an effect whose only job is reading state/props and setting another piece of state is almost certainly unnecessary and should be replaced by a plain computation in render.

prompt: A fellow junior on your team asks: "Why doesn't Zustand need a `<Provider>` wrapping the app like Context does — do all components just magically read the same store?" Explain to them: where a Zustand store lives once it's created with `create()`, why every component that `import`s it sees the same instance, and what the core difference is versus `useContext` when state changes — which component re-renders and why.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
A Zustand store doesn't live inside the React tree the way `useContext` state does — it's a singleton at module scope. `create(...)` runs exactly once, the first time the file containing it is imported, and because of JavaScript's module cache, every `import { useStore }` from any other file later resolves to that same instance. That's why no `<Provider>` is needed wrapping the app: components just import the hook directly, with no context tree to read through. The core difference from `useContext` is in re-render scope: Context has a single value shared by every consumer, so when that value changes, all consumers re-render — narrowing that means wrapping every consumer in `React.memo`, which patches the symptom rather than stopping the signal at its source. Zustand solves this differently: each component calls the hook with a selector, e.g. `useStore((s) => s.count)`, and after every state change Zustand re-runs the selector and compares the old result to the new one with `Object.is` — only when they differ is the component notified to re-render. That's how two components reading the same store with two different selectors can end up with completely different re-render scopes, with no `memo` or Provider involved. One practical thing to remember: calling the hook without a selector subscribes to the entire state object, so any change (even to an unrelated field) triggers a re-render — losing all the selective-render benefit Zustand provides.

prompt: You're designing an avatar-upload API with Multer in NestJS. A colleague proposes `memoryStorage` because "it's easier to validate before saving," while you lean toward `diskStorage` to "avoid burning RAM." Analyze the trade-off between the two storage engines: where does the data actually live while Multer is receiving the stream in each case, what happens if an extra validation step (say, a magic-byte check) fails AFTER `diskStorage` has already written the file to disk, and in which pipeline does `memoryStorage` become the better choice instead?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
This isn't "which one is better" — it's "which one is correct for your destination and file size." `diskStorage` pipes the stream to disk as Multer receives each chunk — RAM never holds the whole file, so it fits large files or many concurrent uploads. The cost: the file is already on disk before any later validation (say, a magic-byte check in the controller) gets to run. If that step fails, you must `fs.unlink(file.path)` yourself in the catch block before throwing; skip it and you leave an orphan file taking up space indefinitely, since Multer doesn't clean up automatically. `memoryStorage` flips this: the whole file sits in RAM as a `Buffer`, so you can read/inspect/transform it before deciding whether to keep it at all — no orphan file, because nothing was ever written anywhere. The trade is RAM growing linearly with file size and concurrent upload count, so it can become a bottleneck under load. `memoryStorage` makes the most sense when the final destination isn't local disk but object storage: validate, then stream that same `Buffer` straight to the S3/MinIO SDK — no need to write to disk and read it back just to relay it onward, saving a whole I/O round trip. Bottom line: `diskStorage` defaults well for large files kept locally, `memoryStorage` fits small-to-medium files that need validation before being relayed elsewhere — the decision lives in your storage architecture, not personal preference.

prompt: A junior teammate says: "I'd pick Vite for a public storefront that needs SEO, because Vite is faster — the dev server starts instantly and hot reload is smoother." Explain to them: what kind of "fast" they're actually talking about, why it has nothing to do with whether SEO bots can read the content, and which tool you would pick for this storefront — based on what criterion, not just a feeling of speed.
ideal:
:::muted Bottom line ::: The "fast" the junior is referring to is developer-experience speed at dev time — Vite's dev server uses esbuild and starts almost instantly with very smooth HMR. That's *development* speed, completely different from the speed at which the *end user* sees content and what a *search bot* can actually read. A Vite app defaults to client-side rendering as an SPA: the server returns an almost-empty `index.html` (just `
`) plus a JavaScript bundle; the browser has to download the JS, run React, fetch data, and only then paint the content. An SEO bot visiting usually sees only that empty shell, because it doesn't execute JavaScript the way a real browser does. The real question isn't "which tool feels faster" — it's where rendering happens: on the server (HTML already has content, good for SEO and first paint) or in the browser (empty HTML, waiting on JS). For a public storefront that needs SEO, I'd pick Next.js with SSR/SSG: the server renders full HTML content before sending it down, so bots read it straight from the first HTML response and LCP improves because there's no wait for JS to load and fetch to resolve before anything shows up. If this were an internal dashboard behind login with no SEO need, a Vite SPA would still make sense — but for a public storefront, the deciding criterion is always "where does render happen," not how fast the dev server feels.

prompt: You're handed a `ProductCard`: placed in a wide main column it must show a large image, description, and buy button; placed in a narrow sidebar it must collapse to just a small image and a name — at the SAME viewport. Explain what fundamentally distinguishes a **container query** from a media query, and why only a container query lets the component truly adapt on its own, without a `variant`-style prop passed in by the caller.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
A media query only knows one thing: how wide the viewport is. At the same viewport it cannot tell "the card sitting in a 260px sidebar" from "the card sitting in a 720px main column" — so the old approach had to push the layout decision outward via a `variant` prop that every call site must remember to pass correctly. A **container query** flips that: once a wrapper declares `container-type: inline-size`, the browser establishes containment on the inline axis and turns that wrapper into a query container its children can query. From there, `@container (min-width: 320px)` doesn't ask the viewport — it asks that container's own width. The consequence: the same `ProductCard`, placed in a narrow sidebar, sees a narrow container and falls into the compact layout; placed in a wide main column, it sees a wide container and switches to the rich layout — at the same viewport, with no `variant` prop at all. The component holds its own entire responsive logic and is correct wherever it's dropped. The one trade-off: an element can't query its own width, so it always needs an ancestor wrapper declaring `container-type` — usually one thin extra DOM layer.

prompt: A colleague used to writing forms with one `useState` per field (controlled) asks you: "React Hook Form defaults to `register()` — how is that different from the `useState` + `onChange` everyone else does?" Explain: where the field value is held in each model, why `register()` doesn't cause the component to re-render on every keystroke, and what trade-off you pay when you need the UI to react to a field's value (e.g. disabling the submit button while a field is empty).
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
The difference is where the field value is held. A controlled form keeps each field's value in a `useState`; every `onChange` calls `setState`, and every state change triggers a re-render of that component (and usually sibling fields too) — meaning **one re-render per keystroke**. `register()` in React Hook Form goes a different route: it attaches a `ref` to the input's DOM node and lets the browser itself hold the current value; React Hook Form only *reads* `ref.current.value` at the moments it needs to (when `handleSubmit` runs, when `getValues()` is called). Because no field state variable changes as the user types, no `setState` is called, and therefore no re-render happens on every keystroke. This is why React Hook Form is noticeably faster on forms with many fields: it fully decouples rendering from typing. The trade-off: if you need the UI to react to a field's current value — disabling submit while it's empty, showing a live preview, or changing another field's rule based on it — the component will **not** automatically re-render, since React Hook Form doesn't track that value by default. You must subscribe explicitly with `watch("field")` or `useWatch({ name: "field" })`, and ideally call `useWatch` in the specific child component that needs the value (not `watch()` at the form root), so only the part that actually needs to react re-renders — preserving the original benefit of the uncontrolled model.

prompt: In an interview, you're shown a `MailService` where every time a request comes in to send an email, the handler calls `nodemailer.createTransport(...)` to build a brand-new transporter and immediately calls `sendMail` on it, instead of holding a singleton transporter injected via dependency injection. Explain to the interviewer: where exactly this wastes network resources, and why reusing a single shared transporter matters even more once email volume grows.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Calling `createTransport` on every send turns what should be a one-time cost into a repeated cost on EVERY request. Each call opens a new TCP socket to the SMTP server, and if `secure: true` there's also a TLS handshake round — together potentially costing 100–200ms just to "shake hands", before a single byte of the email body is sent. A singleton transporter fixes exactly this: it holds one persistent TCP socket (or a connection pool if `pool: true, maxConnections: N` is set) created exactly once at app startup, and every subsequent `sendMail` reuses that existing connection — no repeated handshake cost. This is precisely why the transporter should be registered as a provider in the dependency injection container: DI guarantees the whole app has exactly ONE transporter instance with exactly ONE SMTP configuration, instead of risking someone `new`-ing a transporter ad hoc in multiple places with mismatched host/port. As traffic grows, the gap widens further: with a per-request transporter, 1,000 requests/second means 1,000 parallel TCP opens — easily hitting the SMTP server's concurrent-connection limit and slowing down the very response being awaited; with a shared transporter, the connection count stays fixed and small, and every request just queues to reuse that pool. One good companion practice: call `transporter.verify()` once at startup to fail fast on a bad SMTP config (wrong host, wrong auth), instead of letting the first real user discover the bug.

prompt: A new teammate proposes: "Let's just keep sessions in server RAM, it's simple — we look it up whenever we need it." You're asked to explain why the team chose JWT over server-side sessions instead: walk through what goes wrong with session-based auth on server restart or across multiple instances behind a load balancer, how JWT solves it (what the server does when issuing the token, and what it does on every subsequent request), and what trade-off the team accepts in exchange.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
With RAM-based sessions, the server has to *remember* "who is logged in" in an internal store; that store is wiped on restart, and when running multiple instances behind a load balancer, a given user's request can land on an instance that never held that session — forcing sticky sessions or a shared session store, adding a dependency and a lookup on every request. JWT flips the approach: at sign-in, the server signs a self-contained token — say, a `sub` claim carrying the user id — with its own secret, and hands it to the client to hold. On every subsequent request, the server doesn't look anything up; it just verifies the signature: recomputes it from header + payload using the secret, compares it to the token's signature, and checks the expiry (`exp`). That's a cheap local cryptographic operation. Because of this, JWT scales horizontally with ease: every instance behind the load balancer only needs to know the same secret to verify the same token — no sticky sessions, no shared session store. In exchange, the server loses the ability to revoke a token instantly — since it holds no state, it has nowhere to mark a token as "revoked"; the token stays valid until it naturally expires. This is a deliberate trade-off of statelessness, not a flaw to patch immediately, and it's exactly why access tokens should be short-lived with a separate refresh mechanism.

prompt: A dev wrote the checkout flow so the frontend totals the cart and sends that `amount` straight up to create the payment intent, and the server just charges whatever number it receives. Explain to them: what exactly is the vulnerability here, where should the amount actually be computed, and if the client still sends an `expectedAmount` field, what should the server use it for instead of letting it *decide* the amount charged?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
That approach has a serious hole: the client runs on the user's machine, so any value it sends up — including `amount` — can be edited via DevTools or an intercepting proxy before it ever reaches the server. If the server trusts that number outright, anyone can turn `38.99` into `0.01` and clean out the store for pennies. The amount must be computed by the server, never received from the client: the client should only send `productId` and `quantity`; the server looks up the unit price in its own internal catalog, multiplies by quantity, and that is the *only* place the amount is ever produced — an unknown product (not in the catalog) is rejected right there. The computed amount is written to an internal ledger before any gateway call happens, so the gateway always receives the server's `record.amount`, never whatever the client sent. So what is the `expectedAmount` field for, if the client still sends one? It's not there to *set* the price — it's there for the server to *reconcile against*: the client sends the number it thinks it owes (based on what it displayed), the server compares that to the already-computed `record.amount`, and rejects before any money moves on a mismatch (a stale cart from a price change between creation and confirmation, or outright tampering). The general principle: any data that decides an amount must live entirely on the server side; client-supplied data only has value for detecting a mismatch, never for making the decision.

prompt: A dashboard ships a 250KB initial JavaScript bundle even though most users never open the chart or code editor sitting below the fold. You're asked: what mechanism actually removes a component from the initial bundle when you write `React.lazy(() => import("./Heavy"))`, what role does `import()` play differently from a static import at the top of the file, and what problem does `<Suspense>` solve that this creates? Talk through the mechanism yourself, don't just list API names.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
A static `import` at the top of a file is a compile-time edge in the dependency graph: the bundler sees it at build time and must place that module into whichever chunk imports it — even if the component only ever renders below the fold or after a click. `lazy(() => import("./Heavy"))` changes the game: instead of a static import, you pass a function that returns `import()` — an expression evaluated only at runtime. Vite/Rollup treats this as a **split point**, emits `Heavy` into its own chunk, and React only loads that chunk when `<Heavy />` actually mounts. `<Suspense fallback={...}>` is the mandatory companion piece: when a lazy component renders before its chunk has arrived, React suspends that subtree and renders the nearest `fallback` instead of leaving a gap, then swaps in the real component once the `import()` resolves; without a `<Suspense>` boundary wrapping a lazy component, React throws immediately. The measurable payoff: the initial chunk (now only carrying first-paint code) shrinks meaningfully — in an example like this it might go from ~250KB down to ~50-80KB — because the heavy chart/editor library moved to an on-demand chunk, improving LCP (painting from a small bundle) and INP (the main thread frees up earlier, not blocked by a long compile task on the first interaction). The one trade-off: the first time the widget appears it pays a network round-trip to fetch its chunk — which is exactly why `fallback` exists, so the user sees a smooth placeholder instead of a bare blank spot while waiting.

prompt: In your GraphQL schema you declared `id: String!` for one field and `publishedYear: Int` (no `!`) for another. A colleague asks: what's the actual difference between these two declarations, and what happens if the resolver for the non-null `id` field accidentally returns `null`? Explain properly — don't just say "one is required, one isn't."
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The difference isn't syntax — it's the nature of the contract. `String!` is non-null: a promise that this field's resolver always returns a valid value, never `null`. `Int` (no `!`) is nullable: `null` is a legitimate value, not an error. If the resolver for a non-null field (like `id: String!`) accidentally returns `null`, GraphQL does not silently set `data.id = null` — it treats this as an execution error and triggers "null-bubbling": the error propagates up to the nearest non-null parent field; if that parent is also non-null, it keeps propagating, potentially collapsing the entire `data` at the root to `null` even though sibling fields resolved successfully. This is why nullability isn't a minor syntactic detail but a design decision: only declare non-null for a field you're certain the resolver always has a value for (a system-assigned id, for example); fields that can legitimately be absent (an unknown publication year, an unset avatar) should be nullable so a harmless missing value doesn't collapse the whole response branch. When "absence is actually a domain error" (e.g. looking up a nonexistent id), the field still stays non-null, but the resolver actively throws a typed exception so the error goes into `errors[]` explicitly, instead of letting `null` bubble up in a confusing way.

prompt: A dev on your team writes a hand-rolled reorder by attaching `onMouseMove` on document and computing the new index from cursor coordinates. The board reorders perfectly with a mouse. Explain to them: how @dnd-kit splits the problem into a **Sensor** (how an input starts/moves a drag) and a **sortable strategy** (how position is computed), why that split lets a single `DndContext` serve both mouse and keyboard from the same `onDragEnd`, and which accessibility requirement the hand-rolled `onMouseMove` version fails. Don't just list API names — explain *why* splitting those two halves actually solves the problem.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The hand-rolled `onMouseMove` version tracks the cursor and only serves exactly one persona: a sighted mouse user. There's no way to `Tab` to focus a card, no key to pick it up or drop it, and no announcement telling a screen reader user what just happened. This isn't an optional polish gap — **WCAG 2.1.1 (Keyboard)** makes keyboard operability a hard requirement, and a pointer-only reorder fails that criterion outright. @dnd-kit fixes this by splitting the problem into two independent halves: a **Sensor** decides *how an input starts and moves a drag*, while a **sortable strategy** decides *how position is computed* as items shift. A `PointerSensor` and a `KeyboardSensor` are two implementations of the exact same contract — "tell the context when a drag starts/moves/ends" — and both hand off to the same `SortableContext` + `onDragEnd`. Because of that separation, `onDragEnd` (which calls `arrayMove`) never needs to know whether the drag came from a mouse or a keyboard: you write the reorder logic exactly once and get every input for free. `KeyboardSensor` uses `sortableKeyboardCoordinates` to turn discrete `Arrow` key presses into the coordinate deltas the strategy expects, so the keyboard "moves" the active item exactly like the pointer does. The trade-off to remember: the abstraction never adds a sensor you didn't register — dropping `KeyboardSensor` still leaves the board working perfectly with a mouse while silently failing WCAG 2.1.1, a failure no visual test would ever catch.

prompt: A junior teammate wants to build a chat endpoint calling an LLM the simplest way possible: wait for the model to finish generating the whole answer, then return a normal JSON response. Explain to them: for a model that takes several seconds to finish, why is that "buffered response" model bad for user experience, what does Server-Sent Events (SSE) fundamentally change about the data-transfer model, and what role do the `Content-Type: text/event-stream` and `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform` headers play in actually making that work.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The problem isn't the model's speed, it's the data-transfer model. With a buffered JSON response, the server must gather the entire answer before it can `return` once — if the model takes 8 seconds to finish, the user stares at a blank screen for the full 8 seconds even though data was actually available incrementally from the first second. SSE changes that fundamentally: it turns the response into a ONE-WAY event stream over a kept-open HTTP connection, where the server actively writes each chunk (each token) the instant it's generated and the client consumes and renders it incrementally — no more "wait until enough, then return", but "push whatever arrives, as it arrives". The two headers are the mandatory contract that makes this actually work: `Content-Type: text/event-stream` tells the browser this is an event stream rather than a normal response, so the browser keeps the connection open and reads incrementally instead of waiting for the full body to parse as JSON at once; `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform` blocks any proxy or CDN sitting in the middle from buffering or re-compressing the content — if a proxy buffers the response until it's "big enough" to forward, every token gets stuck and arrives at the client as a single lump, defeating exactly what we're trying to do. Compared to WebSocket: SSE is only a one-way server-to-client channel over plain HTTP (easy to traverse proxies, auto-reconnects), while WebSocket is full-duplex over its own protocol; since streaming LLM tokens to the client only needs to flow one direction, SSE is the simpler, sufficient choice — standing up WebSocket for a stream that's inherently one-directional is wasted effort.

prompt: A new dev on the team asks you: "Why not just call `fetch` inside `useEffect`, store it in `useState`, instead of learning `useQuery`?" Explain to them: why `useQuery` is a subscription into a shared cache layer rather than a shorter way to write a fetch call, what happens when two different components call `useQuery` with the same `queryKey`, and why "the data is stale" needs an explicit concept (`staleTime`) that the old approach never had.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
`useQuery` isn't "a tidier way to write `useEffect`" — it's a subscription into a cache layer sitting between the component and the network. When a component calls `useQuery({ queryKey: ["users"], queryFn })`, it registers interest in the `["users"]` entry inside `QueryClient`; the cache itself decides whether to call `queryFn` (based on whether data already exists and whether it's still fresh), and the component just reads the result through status flags. With `useEffect`+`useState`, each component fetches on its own — if the same list is shown in two places on the page, that's two duplicate requests, no shared layer between them, and no concept of "the data is stale" to know when to fetch again. When two different components call `useQuery` with the same `queryKey`, they read the same cache entry: only one request goes out, and both receive the same data — that's deduplication, and it isn't a feature you "turn on", it's the natural consequence of multiple subscribers pointing at the same entry. Finally, "the data is stale" needs an explicit concept because without it the system is stuck between two extremes: always refetch (wastes network, causes UI jank) or never refresh (data goes stale and drifts from the server). `staleTime` fills exactly that gap — it defines "fresh for how long", after which a trigger (re-mount, tab regains focus) is needed before a refetch happens. The condition for this whole model to work is a stable `queryKey`: it's the address of the entry in the cache, and a wrong or constantly-changing key on every render breaks sharing and makes deduplication meaningless.

prompt: In an interview, you're shown an API with exactly one endpoint, `POST /doThing`, for every operation (creating, updating, deleting a user), and every response — even a successful create or a successful delete — returns `200` with body `{ "ok": true }`. Explain to the interviewer: why this design throws away the contract REST already gives you through the HTTP verb and the status code, what the difference is between `PUT` (full replace) and `PATCH` (partial update), and what **idempotent** means — why it decides whether a client or proxy can safely retry when the network is flaky.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Collapsing every operation into one `POST /doThing` that always returns `200` throws away exactly the two things REST gives you for free: semantics through the HTTP verb and an outcome signal through the status code. On verbs: REST fixes the *verb* at the HTTP method and the *noun* at the URL — `POST` creates a resource (returns `201 Created`), `GET` reads (`200`), `PUT` replaces the whole representation, `PATCH` updates part of it, `DELETE` removes (`204 No Content`). That's what lets shared tooling (cache proxies, API gateways, client generators) understand the API without reading per-action documentation. The `PUT` vs `PATCH` difference is about *write scope*: `PUT` overwrites everything — the client sends every field and the server assigns it directly onto the resource, and any missing field is treated as removed (you don't fall back with `??` to keep the old value, because that would turn `PUT` into `PATCH`'s behavior); `PATCH` only touches the fields present in the payload, leaving the rest untouched. Idempotent means calling a request once or repeatedly always leaves the server in the same final state — `GET`/`PUT`/`DELETE` have this property, `POST` does not (calling `POST /users` twice creates two users). That's exactly why idempotency matters for retries: in a distributed system, a request may have already been fully processed by the server but its response got lost to a flaky network — if the verb is idempotent, the client or a proxy can safely resend it without fearing a duplicated side effect (resending the same `PUT` body always yields the same result); with `POST`, blind retries can create duplicate resources, so you need an idempotency key or a de-duplication mechanism elsewhere. A `POST`-only, always-`200` API wipes out both signals — you lose the ability to cache by verb, you lose the ability to decide "is it safe to retry here", and the client has to guess the outcome from the body instead of reading the status code.

prompt: You're handed a Dockerfile with a single `FROM`: it installs every dependency (dev included), copies all the source, builds right there, and `CMD`s the app — the image comes out at about 1.4 GB. Explain: what is this image carrying that production runtime never needs, why that's not just a disk problem but a real cost (pull time, attack surface), and what specific mechanism multi-stage builds use to fix it — don't just say "it's smaller".
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
A 1-stage Dockerfile installs every dependency (dev included), keeps `.git`, the build cache, and every tool used to compile — but runtime only ever needs prod `node_modules` and the already-built `dist/`. That extra weight isn't just a disk concern: every extra MB of image is added pull-time latency on pod scale-out, added registry egress cost, and every extra binary/tool (compiler, package manager, shell) is a potential CVE surface waiting to be exploited. Multi-stage builds fix this with a concrete mechanism: a Dockerfile with multiple `FROM` instructions, each stage using the right base image for its own job (`deps` installs prod dependencies, `builder` runs the build to produce `dist/`, `runner` only assembles the final image), and `COPY --from=<stage>` transfers only the needed artifact — build tooling, dev dependencies, and `.git` are entirely excluded from the final image, not compressed into it. Because each stage is also its own independent cache chain, putting rarely-changing files (`package.json`, lockfile) before the source copy lets the dependency-install layer be reused across builds, only rebuilding what actually changed. The essence: multi-stage separates "what it takes to build the runnable thing" from "the thing that actually runs" — it's not an image-compression trick.

prompt: A junior teammate asks you: "Why not just use NoSQL for everything and skip the whole SQL-vs-NoSQL decision?" Explain to them: the core difference between the two models isn't "which one is faster" — it's where the schema is kept (database or application) and what transactional guarantee you get (ACID vs BASE) — then give a concrete example of a business case that requires SQL and one where NoSQL is the better fit.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
"Use NoSQL for everything" skips the actual question worth asking. The core difference isn't "which is faster" — speed depends on the workload: reading one small document can be fast on Mongo, but a complex relational query with several `JOIN`s is SQL's home turf. The real difference sits on two axes. First, where the schema lives: SQL forces columns and types to be declared up front, and the database enforces that constraint right at write time — a mistyped record gets rejected at the storage layer. NoSQL pushes that responsibility to the application — the engine accepts a document of any shape, and whatever structure exists is enforced by code, so changing shape needs no migration but the code must keep consistency itself. Second, the transactional guarantee: traditional SQL gives you **ACID** — atomic, consistent, isolated, durable — critical when a half-finished state is unacceptable (transferring money, placing an order). NoSQL documents usually lean **BASE**, eventually consistent, trading that for availability and horizontal scalability. Concrete example: a banking transaction system requires SQL because it cannot tolerate a write that commits halfway and then fails midway — it must be atomic and fully consistent. Conversely, a product catalog with attributes that vary by item type, or that changes shape by season, and needs to scale reads horizontally, is a much better fit for NoSQL — you don't have to force every product into the same fixed column set. Bottom line: choosing an engine means choosing where schema lives and which transactional guarantee matches the business, not picking off a generic benchmark number.

prompt: Your team proudly reports 92% coverage, yet a dumb bug (an unhandled empty array) still shipped straight to production. Your manager asks: "Coverage is that high, so why did the bug still ship?" Explain to them: what line coverage actually measures, why a high number can still hide a brittle, low-value test suite, and what criteria (including a tool other than coverage) you'd use to judge whether a test suite is genuinely good.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
92% coverage only says that 92% of lines ran at least once during testing — it says nothing about whether every logic branch or data situation was actually checked. A test that mocks the repository to return exactly one row and then asserts the result can touch every line of a function, yet the empty-array branch, the negative-input branch, the not-found branch may never have been triggered — the bug shipped precisely because those branches were "covered" in the line-execution sense but never tested in the scenario sense. A good unit test needs to hit the **F.I.R.S.T.** criteria: Fast (runs in under a second), Isolated (no shared state), Repeatable (no dependence on the clock or randomness), Self-validating (pass/fail on its own, no eyeballing output), Timely (written alongside or before the code, not bolted on afterward). Missing any of these, a test gradually loses the team's trust until it gets ignored. To measure "does the test actually catch bugs" more precisely than coverage, use **mutation testing** (e.g. Stryker): it automatically introduces small code mutations (turning `>` into `>=`, deleting a line) and reruns the tests — if the test still passes, it isn't actually verifying that logic, even though the line stays "covered". The practical conclusion: use coverage as a warning floor (flag red under a threshold like 60-80%), not a target to chase toward 100% — a high coverage number does not by itself mean the test suite is trustworthy.

prompt: In an interview, someone hands you a service that calls `new` to instantiate its own dependencies right inside the constructor. Explain to them: what problems this style causes as the system grows (hard to test, hard to swap implementation, loss of sharing, fragile initialization order), and what you gain instead by letting an IoC container create and wire the dependencies for you. Talk through each benefit yourself — don't just rattle off buzzwords.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Calling `new` on dependencies inside the constructor turns the consumer into something that both *uses* and *creates* its dependencies — and that is the root of every problem as the system scales. First, it hard-wires the consumer to one concrete implementation: swapping to another forces you to edit the consumer, i.e. tight coupling. Second, tests are bound to the real object because the dependency is created inside, so you can't inject a mock/stub from outside to isolate the unit. Third, every `new` yields a separate copy, so you lose sharing — no shared state or expensive resource. Fourth, once the dependency graph grows, hand-wiring the correct initialization order becomes fragile and brittle. Letting an IoC container create and wire things, the consumer only *declares* "I need a CatService" via the constructor parameter type; the container reads that type, builds the dependency graph, creates instances in the right order, and injects them. In return you get testability (natural mocking in tests), loose coupling (swap implementation without touching the consumer) and lifecycle management (the container owns lifecycle and shares a singleton). That is exactly inversion of control: the power to create objects inverts from the consumer to the container.

prompt: A junior teammate wants to attach a `requestId` to every log line of a request. They propose two options: first, add a `requestId` parameter to EVERY function on the call path (controller → service → repository → logger); second, stash the `requestId` in a module-scope `let currentRequestId` and reassign it whenever a new request arrives. Explain to them where each approach breaks down when two requests run concurrently or when code crosses multiple `await` boundaries, and why AsyncLocalStorage solves both problems without changing a single function signature.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Both proposed approaches are wrong, but in different ways. Passing the parameter through every function is prop-drilling: a `requestId` has to snake through every function signature on the call path even though most of them never use it, and if the path crosses a third-party library function whose signature you can't change, manual passing hits a dead end. Stashing it in a module-scope `let` is worse: that's ONE memory cell shared by the entire process. When two requests run concurrently (completely normal in Node.js with async I/O), request B reassigns `currentRequestId` right in the middle of request A's processing — request A reads the variable again after an `await` and sees B's value instead, so its logs get tagged with the wrong ID. AsyncLocalStorage solves both problems with one mechanism: calling `requestContext.run({ reqId }, () => next())` attaches `{ reqId }` to the entire async call tree inside `next()` — including code that runs after `await`, inside `Promise.then`, or inside a callback — without changing a single function signature; anywhere in that tree, calling `getStore()` returns the correct context for that specific request. The key is that each `run()` call creates its own "execution context": two concurrent requests live in two fully independent stores, so IDs never mix — unlike a module-scope variable, which is one shared cell. This is also why AsyncLocalStorage beats `req.locals`: `req.locals` can only be accessed while holding the `req` object, so a deep util function (say, inside a logger or repository) still needs `req` passed down through every layer — right back to the original prop-drilling problem — whereas `getRequestId()` reads from the store anywhere in the call tree without anyone passing `req` down.

prompt: A teammate tests the API with curl and Postman, sees every cross-origin request succeed just fine, and concludes: "CORS isn't a real issue then, my tool can call it, the security team is overreacting." Explain to them: where CORS is actually enforced and by whom, why curl/Postman are never blocked even with the exact same server allowlist that runs in production against a real browser, and what a request actually blocked by CORS looks like from the client side.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Your teammate is confused about who actually enforces CORS. CORS isn't a security layer the server erects to reject requests — the server always receives the cross-origin request, runs its logic, and returns a response just like any other request. The only thing the server does is attach an `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header declaring "which origin may read this response." The actual enforcement happens in the browser: after receiving the response, if it was requested by JavaScript running on a different origin and the permitting header is missing, the browser blocks that code from reading the response's contents — even though the response already arrived on the client machine. That is exactly why curl and Postman "always work": they aren't JavaScript running in the context of some web page, so no same-origin policy applies to them at all. They send the request, receive the response, print it — nobody stands in between to block anything. Seen from a real page that IS blocked, the symptom looks very different from an ordinary failed request: the Network tab shows the request went out, the status code can be a perfectly fine 200, yet the console reports something like "blocked by CORS policy" — because the browser received the response but refuses to hand it to the calling JavaScript. The practical takeaway: a server allowlist only does anything when a browser sits in the middle enforcing it. A real attacker exploiting CORS doesn't use Postman — they lure the victim into opening a page containing malicious script, that script runs inside the victim's browser and tries to read data from your API using the victim's own cookies/session. That is exactly the scenario CORS exists to block, so "Postman can call it" says nothing about whether the allowlist is actually correct.

prompt: A user uploads a 2GB video that needs compressing. A dev proposes two options: (1) bump the HTTP request timeout to a few minutes and compress right inside the handler, or (2) `spawn` a thread/Promise running in the background inside the current process. Explain to them why neither option actually solves the problem, and what a durable job queue like BullMQ on Redis changes fundamentally compared to running a background task inside the process itself.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Both options attack the wrong symptom. Raising the timeout doesn't make the task lighter — compressing the video still eats CPU and blocks the thread of the very web process serving other requests, and stretching the timeout just moves the problem elsewhere (a load balancer or the client may time out first anyway). Spawning a thread or Promise in-process is worse: it only exists in that process's RAM, so when the process restarts — a new deploy, a crash, an OOM kill — the in-flight job vanishes completely with nobody aware it needs to be redone. A durable job queue like BullMQ on Redis changes the nature of the problem: the job is written to Redis, a durable backing store living outside the web process, so it survives restarts/crashes of both the API and the worker. The producer (API) now does exactly one thing: `add` the job to the queue and return immediately (fire-and-forget, typically HTTP 202) without waiting for it to finish. A worker is a completely separate process that actively pulls jobs from the queue to process in the background; the API never calls it directly. Because the producer and consumer only communicate through Redis rather than calling functions directly, you can run several workers in parallel to share load, or restart a worker to deploy a new version, while the API keeps serving requests normally — something impossible if the heavy task ran inside the web server's own process.

prompt: A junior teammate proposes having the client call an API every 2 seconds to fetch new messages for a chat feature, reasoning "it's simple, no new API to learn." Explain to them: what's the essential difference between the polling model (client asks periodically) and the WebSocket model (server actively pushes events), and why this choice directly affects both latency and server cost once client count reaches thousands?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The difference isn't "how fast you poll" but the essential communication model — who initiates. Polling is a request/response model: the client asks the server on a fixed cycle, each round costing a full HTTP request/response (headers, a TCP round trip), and the server stays entirely passive — only answering when asked. With a 2-second poll interval, average latency to learn about new data is roughly 1 second (half the cycle), worst case close to 2 seconds. WebSocket is the opposite: after an initial HTTP Upgrade handshake, both sides hold a persistent full-duplex connection, and the server listens for events and actively pushes as soon as something happens — latency drops to milliseconds because there's no next poll cycle to wait for. Cost scales very differently too: with 1000 clients polling every 2 seconds, the server receives 500 requests/second forever, even when nothing new happened; with WebSocket, the server only spends resources exactly when there's a real event to push — cost scales with actual message volume, not with client count times poll frequency. The fair trade-off: WebSocket requires extra handling for reconnect and heartbeats (`ping/pong`) that a plain REST endpoint doesn't need, so if a few seconds of latency is acceptable (e.g. a stats dashboard that doesn't need to be tightly realtime), polling remains a reasonable choice because it's simpler to operate.

prompt: Writing a unit test for `OrdersService`, one teammate only mocks `OrderRepository` (where it touches the database) with `vi.fn()`, while another teammate figures "to be safe" they'll also mock an internal helper `calculateTotal()` that lives in the same module as the service. Analyze it: why is mocking only `OrderRepository` correct while also mocking `calculateTotal()` is the wrong call, what happens to the test's reliability once you over-mock, and what role does NestJS's dependency injection play in making this clean mocking possible?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Only mocking `OrderRepository` is correct because that's the boundary — where the service touches the database, an expensive and non-deterministic I/O that a unit test needs to isolate from. `calculateTotal()` is a collaborator — pure logic living in the same module, with no I/O, so there's no reason to mock it. If you also mock `calculateTotal()`, the test stops verifying `OrdersService`'s real behavior; it only asserts whatever value the test author happened to assign the mock — if `calculateTotal()` has a real pricing bug, the test stays green because it never actually ran that code. That's exactly a false positive: the test passes not because the code is correct, but because the mock was configured to match what the test wants. Mechanically, `Test.createTestingModule({...}).compile()` still builds the real constructor wiring — if you only override the `OrderRepository` token via `useValue: mockRepo`, the internal call to `calculateTotal()` inside `OrdersService` still runs for real, which is exactly what you want to verify. NestJS's dependency injection is what makes this clean: the container knows how to swap one specific token (`OrderRepository`) for a mock without touching the rest of the dependency graph, with no monkey-patching or re-requiring modules needed. The general rule of thumb: mock where the system reaches outward, keep internal logic real — only then does the test still reflect the service's actual behavior as it changes.

prompt: Your team runs 5 services, each printing logs as free-text strings via `console.log("user 42 failed at 10:03")`. When production breaks, whoever's on call has to SSH into each box and `grep` around by hand. A junior teammate suggests: "Let's just print more logs, add more detail to the string so it's easier to read." Push back: why doesn't "print more" fix the root problem, what does structured logging (JSON) fundamentally change compared to free-text strings, and what mechanism would you add so secrets (tokens, passwords) never leak into a centralized log store that many people can read?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
"Print more logs" doesn't touch the root problem, because the problem isn't QUANTITY — it's FORMAT. A line like `console.log("user 42 failed at 10:03")` is free text: no matter how much detail you cram into that string, filtering "every error on route /orders" still means writing a fragile `grep` regex, and you can't aggregate by field — the more services and the more lines, the slower manual digging gets. Structured logging changes something fundamental: each log line stops being a sentence and becomes a JSON object with explicit fields (`level`, `msg`, `route`, `requestId`, `latencyMs`...). Because there are fields, a log aggregator like Loki/Elasticsearch/CloudWatch can index by field and answer a query like `level=error AND route=/orders AND requestId=...` in milliseconds — same event, but one side is human-readable text and the other is machine-queryable data; at multi-service production scale, only the latter is actually debuggable. When logs flow into a centralized system many people can read, secrets (a token in the `authorization` header, a `password` in the body) must be scrubbed BEFORE the line leaves the process. The right approach is to configure redaction right at the logger layer: declare a list of sensitive paths up front (`req.headers.authorization`, `*.password`) so they're automatically replaced with `"[Redacted]"` before serializing to JSON. This has to be centralized in ONE place — the logger — because every log line passes through it; if you rely on every developer remembering to scrub secrets at each call-site, one forgotten spot is all it takes for a token or password to leak into the centralized log store.

prompt: Your Trello-style board lets cards be dragged via `PointerSensor`, but users complain that just clicking to select a card (no intent to drag) makes it jump around, and clicking a button inside a card is sometimes "swallowed" into a drag. Reason through it: exactly what problem does `activationConstraint: { distance: 5 }` solve, what happens if you set that number too high, and why would you consider a `delay` constraint instead of `distance` on touch devices?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Without `activationConstraint`, dnd-kit treats every `pointerdown` on a draggable element as the start of a drag — including a plain click to select a card, focus it, or press a button inside it. That's why the list feels "sticky": any click risks being swallowed into a drag. `activationConstraint: { distance: 5 }` fixes exactly that by requiring the cursor to travel at least 5 px after `pointerdown` before dnd-kit commits to a drag gesture; a plain click barely moves, so it never escalates. The trade-off is in picking the number: set the threshold too high (say 20 px) and small, deliberate drags — a user nudging a position by a few pixels — feel sluggish, sometimes as if they "can't pick it up"; 4—8 px is the common sweet spot because it's large enough to filter hand jitter yet small enough to stay responsive. On touch devices, `distance` is actually a worse fit: a finger touching the screen already has small inherent jitter, and a low `distance` can turn an ordinary tap or scroll into an unintended drag. A `delay` constraint (long-press) fits that context better — waiting for a held duration before activating, matching the familiar "press and hold to drag" convention on mobile. Zooming out, an activation constraint is the boundary between two different interaction intents competing for the same physical event (`pointerdown`): "I want to click/select" and "I want to drag to reorder" — without that boundary, the framework has to guess, and a wrong guess breaks the UX.

prompt: A teammate puts all input-validity checking inside the service — that is, after the request has already entered the business logic. Analyze this: why is it better to place the validation layer BEFORE the handler (fail-fast right at the boundary), what happens to server resources when input that is certainly invalid is still pushed deep inside, and how does the handler's own code quality change once it is guaranteed to receive only clean, correctly-typed data?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Validating inside the service is too late. The fail-fast principle says: reject bad input *at the boundary*, before spending effort. In the request lifecycle the validation layer (pipe) runs before the handler, so when input is certainly invalid it throws early (HTTP 400) and short-circuits — the request never reaches business logic. If you validate late in the service, that same bad request is still pushed deep inside: you may have opened a transaction, queried the DB, called another service before noticing it's wrong — burning CPU/IO on something guaranteed to be discarded, and widening the failure surface. On code quality: the validation layer doesn't just *check* but also *transforms* input, so the handler receives the right type (`number` instead of `string`) and clean data. Its body can then assume "the input is valid" — no scattered defensive `if (!id)`, fewer branches, fewer places to go wrong. More deeply, this is separation of concerns: validation is its own concern, living in the layer with the right context (it sees each parameter's type and value); pushing it into the service makes the service lose single responsibility and forces duplicated validation in every handler. Doing it at the boundary also gives a consistent error contract instead of each service returning errors its own way.

prompt: You need to run async initialization before the app accepts its first request — e.g. warming a cache, or calling an external API to verify an API key is valid. Which NestJS lifecycle hooks fit this, and why is doing it directly in the service's `constructor` more dangerous?
