:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The current model is missing exactly one thing to make "log out everywhere" real: the ability to represent multiple concurrent refresh sessions. A single `refreshTokenHash` column only tracks exactly ONE session at a time per user — there's nowhere to say "this user is logged in on three devices at once", so there's nothing to "revoke all" beyond that single existing hash. The needed change on the refresh side: move from a single column to a multi-row table, one hash per device/login session. Then "log out everywhere" becomes a clean operation: delete or null-out ALL rows belonging to that `userId` in one transaction, so every subsequent refresh from every device returns `401`. But refresh only solves half the problem — access tokens are different: they verify entirely locally (only checking the signature + `exp`, never touching the DB), so on their own they have NO mechanism to be cut before they naturally expire. To make "log out everywhere" cut access nearly instantly too, you need a shared revocation check point that every instance behind the load balancer can consult — e.g. a Redis set/key by `userId` marking "every token issued before time T is no longer trustworthy" — and `JwtAuthGuard`/`RolesGuard` checks this before accepting an access token. This is exactly where you need to clearly name the trade-off: pure stateless access verification buys near-free horizontal scaling — no extra lookup at all; but "log out everywhere" taking instant effect requires giving some of that back, adding exactly ONE shared lookup at the access layer. What matters is making it a deliberate, narrowly-scoped exception (just one fast cache lookup, not a full return to a session store), not an excuse to drop the stateless architecture for the whole system. The added cost stays controlled: one O(1) cache call, not a table scan or a heavy DB round-trip, so this is a carefully weighed trade-off, not an architectural step backward.

prompt: Your chat app has run stably on a single backend instance for months: `server.to(room).emit(...)` always works correctly because every socket lives on the same process. The infra team just scaled the backend to 3 instances behind a load balancer to handle increased traffic — immediately users report a bug: two people in the SAME room stop seeing each other's messages if (and only if) they happen to be routed to two different instances. Explain precisely why room-based broadcast "breaks" under horizontal scaling, design the complete fix (not just one line of code), and point out the RISK still left over if you only fix half of it.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
This bug isn't a code mistake — it's an implicit assumption that stopped holding once the infrastructure topology changed. On a single instance, a Socket.IO `room` is a data structure living in that process's own memory, and `server.to(room).emit(...)` simply walks the list of sockets that process is directly holding connections to — this was always correct because EVERY socket, regardless of client, connected to the same single process. Scaling out to 3 instances behind a load balancer breaks that assumption: alice might get routed (randomly or round-robin) to instance 1, bob to instance 2. Both correctly call `client.join('X')` and are logically "in room X," but these are two COMPLETELY SEPARATE room `X` data structures living in the memory of two different processes — instance 1 has no idea instance 2 has any socket in room `X`. When alice sends a message, `server.to('X').emit(...)` running on instance 1 only fans out to its own LOCAL sockets, and bob never receives it. The correct solution has two complementary parts, not one line of code: (1) attach an ADAPTER that shares broadcast state across processes — e.g. the Socket.IO Redis adapter — turning Redis into an intermediary message bus: when instance 1 calls `server.to(room).emit(...)`, the adapter publishes that message to a Redis pub/sub channel; EVERY other instance (including instance 2) already subscribed to that channel receives it and forwards it to its own LOCAL sockets in that room — the application code calling `server.to(room).emit(...)` stays exactly the same, only the underlying adapter layer changes. (2) Configure STICKY SESSIONS at the load balancer (routing by cookie or IP hash) — this solves a DIFFERENT but related problem: if the transport falls back to long-polling (Socket.IO auto-falls-back when WebSocket is blocked), one logical "connection" is actually a series of discrete consecutive HTTP requests — if the load balancer routes those requests to different instances, the session breaks because each instance lacks the state from previous requests. Sticky sessions don't replace the Redis adapter (they don't solve cross-instance broadcast) and the Redis adapter doesn't replace sticky sessions (it doesn't guarantee requests from one long-polling connection always land on the same instance) — you need both. The risk of only fixing "half": if the team only adds the Redis adapter to the ChatGateway but forgets that other features (the presence Set backing the online list, the reconnection-replay ring buffer message log) are STILL storing per-instance in-memory state, those features will keep breaking through the exact same mechanism — presence will misreport "who's online" depending on which instance a socket is routed to, and replay-since will only see the history held by whichever instance happens to handle that particular request. One way to audit the whole system: enumerate EVERY piece of per-instance in-memory state across the entire realtime system, not just chat room broadcast, then decide for each whether it should move to a shared store (Redis) or whether degraded/eventual behavior is acceptable.

The `postCreated` subscription works perfectly in dev (a single process). After going to production with 3 replicas behind a load balancer, the team reports a bug: a client subscribed on replica A never receives the event when a new post is created by a request that landed on replica B — but if both requests happen to land on the same replica, it works fine. Read the PubSub configuration below, explain exactly why it only scales to a single process, and give the optimized version that works correctly across multiple replicas.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The root cause lies in the very nature of `new PubSub()` from the `graphql-subscriptions` package: it's a PURELY IN-MEMORY event bus, living entirely inside the heap of the Node process running it. `publish` writes the event into that instance's internal data structure, and `asyncIterator` reads from that same structure — the two only "see" each other when they're in the SAME process. With 3 replicas behind a load balancer, each replica has its OWN `PubSub` instance, with zero communication between them. When the `createPost` mutation runs on replica B, it `publish`es to replica B's `PubSub`; but the subscribing client holding a WebSocket connection open to replica A registered its `asyncIterator` on replica A's `PubSub` — the two are completely isolated. The event "disappears" not because of any mutation/subscription logic bug, but because they're talking to two different event buses entirely. The bug only "sometimes" works correctly when both requests (the subscription and the mutation) happen to land on the same replica — exactly matching the reported symptom. The optimization: replace the in-memory `new PubSub()` with an adapter backed by a store OUTSIDE any single process — the standard choice is `graphql-redis-subscriptions`, wired to a Redis instance every replica connects to. Now `publish`ing from any replica pushes the event onto a shared Redis channel; every replica with an active subscriber on that channel (regardless of which replica the subscriber's client is WebSocket-connected to) receives the event via Redis pub/sub, no longer dependent on "did they happen to land on the same replica." To verify correctly, run at least two backend processes pointing at the same Redis, open a subscription against process 1, call the mutation against process 2, and confirm the event still arrives — this test is guaranteed to FAIL against the original in-memory `PubSub` setup. One operational caveat worth flagging: Redis backing a realtime feature should be highly available (to avoid becoming a single point of failure), and Redis's pub/sub mechanism gives no delivery guarantee — if a subscriber is offline exactly when something publishes, that event is lost forever (no replay); acceptable for nice-to-have notifications, but not appropriate if that data absolutely must reach the client.

prompt: (Illustrated via TypeScript/NestJS — the concept applies to any stack.) The app registers two interceptors: one measures handler time and writes `executionMs` onto the request object, the other wraps the final response and reads that `executionMs` to return it to the client. But in the response, `executionMs` is ALWAYS `null`. Diagnose it: what does it mean that interceptors run as a LIFO stack on the way out, how did the wrong registration order make the response-wrapping layer read `executionMs` BEFORE the timing layer got to write it, and how do you reorder the registration to fix it?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The bug is in the interceptor registration order, not in either interceptor's logic. An interceptor wraps the handler like a decorator, so it sees both the inbound and outbound legs; several interceptors form a stack and run LIFO on the way out: registering `[A, B]` gives A.before → B.before → handler → B.after → A.after — the LATER-registered layer (B) runs FIRST on the way out. Here the order is `[ExecutionTimer, ResponseTransform]`. So on the way out, ResponseTransform.after (reads `req.executionMs` to wrap into the payload) runs FIRST, and only then does ExecutionTimer.after (writes `req.executionMs`) run — too late. ResponseTransform reads while the value is still `null`, so the client always gets `executionMs: null`. This is exactly the principle "a later layer can only read what an earlier layer already wrote": on the outbound leg, the WRITING layer must run before the READING layer. The fix: reorder registration to `[ResponseTransformInterceptor, ExecutionTimerInterceptor]`. Then on the way out ExecutionTimer.after (writes `executionMs`) runs first, and ResponseTransform.after (reads + wraps) runs after and sees the real value. Verify by re-calling the endpoint: `executionMs` is now a positive number, no longer `null` — and confirm with real logs *what* you're actually measuring (pure handler time vs including the wrapping layer), since the order also decides the measurement's scope.

In an interview, you're shown a design: the `users` table has a single extra boolean column `unsubscribed`; when a user clicks unsubscribe on ANY email, this column is set to `true`, and every subsequent notification (email and SMS, marketing and transactional) is blocked for that user. Explain: where does a single boolean column fall short compared to splitting a preference table along two axes, `channel` (email/sms) and `category` (marketing/transactional), and what are the real-world consequences of keeping this boolean design in production?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
A single `unsubscribed` boolean column completely loses the CONTEXT of an opt-out: it can only answer the binary question "does this user still receive notifications at all" across the WHOLE system, whereas real users almost always want a selective opt-out — for example turning off marketing email while still wanting an SMS alert about a suspicious login. The most serious consequence of keeping this design in production: if `unsubscribed = true` blocks every channel and category indiscriminately, a user who only clicked to unsubscribe from marketing email will accidentally lose the ability to receive an SMS OTP or an important security alert too — turning a harmless action (not wanting ads) into a serious incident (unable to log in due to a missing OTP). The right fix is to split preferences into a dedicated table along two independent axes: `channel` (email or sms) and `category` (marketing or transactional), with a mandatory composite key on `(userId, channel, category)` — each meaningful combination is ONE row with its own `enabled` flag. As a result, turning off `email × marketing` only affects that one row, while the other three combinations (`email × transactional`, `sms × marketing`, `sms × transactional`) keep their previous state untouched. Operationally, setting a combination should use UPSERT (`ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`) to guarantee idempotency — sending the same request multiple times doesn't create duplicate rows for the same combination. This fine-grained design also correctly reflects a legal constraint a boolean column simply cannot encode: `category=marketing` requires explicit consent and must always allow opt-out, while `category=transactional` (OTP, order confirmations) is typically allowed to be sent based on contractual obligation or legitimate interest — a properly designed production system usually REJECTS an opt-out request for the transactional category rather than silently turning it off.

A junior teammate asks: "I think a page can only be static (fast, cacheable) or dynamic (personalizable), not both at once. If a page has one part that needs personalization (like a cart), don't we have to set the whole page to dynamic?" Explain to them: how Partial Prerendering (PPR) breaks that assumption, what unit PPR actually decides static/dynamic at (the whole route, or something smaller), and why forcing the whole route to dynamic for one small personalized piece is wasteful.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The assumption "a route must be static OR dynamic" is exactly what Partial Prerendering breaks. PPR shifts the static/dynamic deciding unit from the **route** level down to the **component boundary** level — specifically, the `<Suspense>` boundary. For a route with `experimental_ppr = true`, Next.js looks at the component tree: any JSX that is **not** inside any `<Suspense>` and doesn't touch a dynamic API (`cookies()`, `headers()`, `searchParams`) is evaluated as the **static shell** — Next.js prerenders it **once** at build time and serves it from a CDN with near-zero latency. Anything wrapped in `<Suspense>` (like a cart reading a cookie) is a **dynamic hole** — only valid at request time, so it's rendered when the request arrives and streamed into its slot. Importantly, both the static shell and the dynamic hole arrive in **one single HTTP response** thanks to HTTP streaming, not two separate fetches. Forcing the whole route to `force-dynamic` because one small piece needs personalization is wasteful because most of a real page (header, title, product description, footer) **doesn't change between requests** — it deserves to be cached and served instantly. Setting the whole route dynamic means sacrificing static speed for 95% of the content just because 5% (the cart, personalized recommendations) genuinely needs to render per request. PPR lets you keep static speed for the static part and only "pay the dynamic cost" for the part that actually needs it — that's why a page can be both fast like static and personalized like dynamic.

A teammate proposes splitting the storefront experience into many fine-grained tiers: 6 tiers by `deviceMemory` (0.25/0.5/1/2/4/8GB) times 4 tiers of `effectiveType` (`4g`/`3g`/`2g`/`slow-2g`), each combination serving a different asset set for "maximum personalization." Push back: why do the adaptive-loading APIs themselves deliberately round/limit signal granularity, what does branching too finely cost (UI stability + fingerprinting surface), and what branching granularity would you propose to still respect progressive enhancement.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The "24-combination asset matrix" proposal runs against exactly the reason these APIs were designed coarse. `navigator.deviceMemory` only ever returns a rounded set of values (0.25/0.5/1/2/4/8), not the machine's exact RAM — that's a deliberate decision to shrink the fingerprinting surface, not a technical limitation. `effectiveType` is even coarser in nature: it's a FLUCTUATING engine estimate based on recent network conditions, not a constant measured once and fixed. Branching too finely pays two costs. First, stability: because `effectiveType` fluctuates in real time, a 4×6 = 24-combination grid means two consecutive requests from the same user could land in different tiers just from measurement noise — the UI "flickers" between asset sets, far worse than holding a single consistent experience. Second, fingerprinting: the more tiers a signal combination can distinguish, the smaller the pool of users sharing the same "signature" becomes, increasing device/cross-session identifiability — exactly what rounding `deviceMemory` in the first place was meant to prevent. I'd propose folding every signal into one derived binary flag, matching the lesson's own model: `constrained` = (`effectiveType` in {2g, slow-2g, 3g}) OR `saveData` OR `prefers-reduced-data`; otherwise `capable`. At most add one middle tier if truly needed (e.g. serving a medium-res image), but never more than three tiers total. Back to the core principle: optimizing on a capability signal is progressive enhancement — a REWARD when a signal is measurable, not the main axis deciding whether the experience runs at all. Adding detail beyond two-three tiers doesn't add value proportional to the UI-stability and fingerprinting cost it incurs — "maximum personalization" here is optimizing the wrong thing.

You're tasked with redesigning how a service pulls its DB password from Vault at startup. A colleague proposes: "Just let the loader retry forever if Vault isn't ready at boot, so the app always starts and the health check passes early — it's fine if there's no secret yet." Push back on this: why must the CORRECT behavior at bootstrap differ sharply from the behavior when a runtime secret refresh fails, and what mechanism authenticates the service with Vault from the very first moment so a static token never sits on disk?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The "retry forever to pass health check early" proposal confuses two kinds of failure that must be handled completely differently: a bootstrap failure and a runtime refresh failure. At bootstrap, the service has no secret yet to serve real traffic with — no DB password means it can't connect to the database, no JWT signing key means it can't authenticate requests. If the loader silently retries forever while still letting the health check pass, the orchestrator (k8s or cloud) believes the service is ready and routes real traffic to it — the result is that the very first request touching the database fails, at a layer much deeper and much harder to diagnose than simply seeing "couldn't reach Vault at boot" right away. The correct behavior is fail-fast: if Vault isn't reachable within a reasonable timeout at startup, the service should crash or fail its health check explicitly, so the orchestrator knows and reacts (restart, keep it Pending, never route traffic). Conversely, once the service ALREADY has a valid secret in memory and is serving traffic normally, a periodic refresh call to Vault failing (due to a temporary network blip or overload) should not crash the service — it's still holding a known-good secret from the last successful load, so the correct handling is to log a warning, keep serving with the old secret, and try again on the next refresh cycle. Reversing these two behaviors (retry-forever at boot, crash on a runtime refresh failure) produces exactly the hardest kind of incident to diagnose: an app that's "healthy" but useless at startup, and an app crashing unnecessarily just because Vault had a brief blip. On never using a static token for the initial authentication: the right pattern is AppRole, which splits authentication into two artifacts of different sensitivity — `role_id` is just the role's identity, low-sensitivity, safe enough to place in an environment variable; `secret_id` is the genuinely sensitive one, short-TTL, and should never sit pre-existing on disk. The service logs in with both artifacts to receive a short-lived `client_token` scoped to that session, not a static token used forever. What remains is the chicken-and-egg problem: where does the first `secret_id` come from if not a file? The answer is to push the root of trust to the infrastructure the service is already running on: in Kubernetes, use the pod's service-account JWT via Vault's Kubernetes auth method (this JWT is issued and rotated by k8s itself, nobody commits it); on cloud, use the instance's IAM role. Both are identities issued by a trusted platform at runtime, not a secret sitting pre-existing on disk.

The `GET /cats/search?breed=X` endpoint just got a `CacheInterceptor` added with a FIXED `CacheKey` to speed up lookups. After shipping to production, users report: searching `breed=Persian` and then immediately switching to `breed=Siamese` still returns the exact same Persian results, for the entire 30-second TTL. Optimize the caching strategy here: where's the problem in how the key is set, is the layer currently used (Response layer) still the right fit for a parameterized endpoint, and how would you redesign it to keep the speed-up without returning the wrong result for the parameter?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The root cause is a key collision — a form of over-caching. `@CacheKey("cats_search")` is a fixed string that never embeds the `breed` value into the Redis key, so EVERY different `breed` value reads and writes exactly the same cache entry. Here's the exact sequence producing the symptom: the first call with `breed=Persian` MISSes, `CacheInterceptor` runs `findByBreed("Persian")` and stores the result under key `cats_search`; the next call with `breed=Siamese`, within the 30-second TTL, sees `cats_search` already populated and returns it straight away — that's the stale Persian data, never re-calling `findByBreed` for Siamese at all. The second problem is layer choice: the Response layer caches the whole output at the entry point, which fits when the output is near-STATIC and identical regardless of who calls it — but `search`'s `breed` parameter changes the output entirely per value, so caching the whole response under ONE static key is the wrong tool for this problem: a parameterized endpoint needs a key that DISTINGUISHES by parameter, not a shared entry. The optimized redesign: either (a) keep the Response layer but replace the static `@CacheKey` with a mechanism that builds a DYNAMIC key from the query string (NestJS lets you override `trackBy` in a custom `CacheInterceptor` to build a key like `cats_search_${breed}`), or (b) — clearer and easier to control — move down to the Logic layer entirely: the service does its own `cacheManager.get(`cats_search_${breed}`)`, and on MISS calls `findByBreed(breed)` then `set`s that same key with a TTL. Either approach guarantees each `breed` value gets its own cache entry, so it never reads back another parameter's data. Verification: call `search` with `breed=Persian` then immediately `breed=Siamese`, and confirm the second call returns the CORRECT Siamese result (not leftover Persian) — checking behavior matches the parameter, not just an HTTP 200.

prompt: A new dev edits the webhook endpoint: when it detects a duplicate event (already processed earlier), they make it return `409 Conflict` "because the data conflicts with what's already there." Explain to them: why a webhook endpoint should ALWAYS return `200` for a valid duplicate event rather than an error code, and what will happen on the payment gateway's side if they keep that `409` behavior?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The problem is misunderstanding what a duplicate event actually is. A payment gateway (Stripe, SePay, or any gateway) operates on a simple contract: it sends a webhook and waits for the status code to decide whether to resend — only on `2xx` does it consider delivery "successful" and stop; any other code (`4xx`/`5xx`) is read as "not processed", so it resends on its own retry schedule (usually with increasing backoff). A duplicate event — the same `eventId` sent a second time — is not a real error: it's a valid re-delivery of an event the server already finished processing earlier, sent again by the gateway itself (either because it wasn't sure the server received it the first time, or per its at-least-once delivery policy). The correct behavior is simply to recognize "ah, I've already processed this" and skip it (no-op) — nothing like the "conflicting data" that `409` implies. If the `409` behavior stays: the gateway gets an error, understands it as unprocessed, and keeps resending that exact event on its retry schedule. But every time it resends, the server still sees it as a duplicate and still returns `409` — an infinite loop that never stops until the gateway gives up after its max retry count (and possibly fires an alert for a webhook failing repeatedly, adding on-call noise). The correct fix: return `200` for EVERY event that passes signature verification, even when it's a duplicate — optionally with a `duplicate: true` flag in the response body for logging/observability without affecting the status code. Reserve real error codes for cases that genuinely need a different reaction from the gateway: `401` on a bad signature (a real error, and having the gateway stop resending a forged event is appropriate), `404` when the corresponding order isn't found. Conversely, a genuinely transient error (a dropped DB connection) SHOULD return an error code so the gateway keeps retrying — that's fundamentally different from "duplicate", and the two shouldn't be handled the same way just because both aren't the happy path.

prompt: The interviewer asks: 'Our team keeps the database password in a `.env` file committed to a private repo — that's safe, right? Who can read a private repo?'. Explain why using a Secret Manager like Vault is still better, even when the repo is already private.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The essence of a Secret Manager like Vault is not "hiding the password better" but a CENTRALIZED secret store, fetched AT RUNTIME through an authenticated API, fully decoupled from any artifact (image, env file, repo). The problem with `.env` in a repo — even a private one — is that the secret ends up SCATTERED across many places: every clone of the repo, every CI runner that ever checked out the code, every Docker image that COPYs `.env` in, every dev machine that ever pulled it. Each of those is an independent potential leak point, regardless of the repo being private: a dev who left the company still has an old clone on their personal machine, a CI log accidentally prints the `.env` contents to public output, a laptop gets stolen. The core benefit of Vault is that blast radius (the scope of damage if the secret leaks) shrinks to exactly ONE place instead of being scattered across every copy — and rotating the password becomes changing ONE Vault entry, instead of hunting down and fixing every place the secret was previously embedded (every image, every CI, every machine). It's worth acknowledging that Vault still needs ONE initial credential for the app to authenticate to Vault itself (called secret-zero) — Vault doesn't eliminate the bootstrap problem entirely, but it SHIFTS TRUST from "one DB password living scattered everywhere, forever" to "one Vault token with a TTL and a revoke endpoint," meaningfully shrinking the risk surface. For a tiny personal project, `.env` in a private repo may be acceptable for now; Vault's benefit is clearest once multiple services, environments, and people all need access to the secret.

prompt: A junior teammate designs a video-upload API: the handler calls FFmpeg directly and waits for the encode to finish before responding to the client. Short clips are fine, but a few-minute clip starts causing client timeouts. Explain why this approach breaks at scale, and how you would split the processing to avoid it.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The problem isn't FFmpeg — it's merging "accept the request" and "do the heavy work" into one request. Re-encoding takes seconds to minutes, far beyond the gateway's timeout (30–60s), so a synchronous request is guaranteed to time out on longer clips, and if the process crashes mid-flight there's no checkpoint telling you where to resume. The fix is to split the two phases with a **job record**: the ingestion step does `INSERT status=PENDING` into the DB and returns HTTP 202 immediately with an `id`; the transcoding step runs **fire-and-forget** — not awaited in the handler — moving the job through `PROCESSING` then `COMPLETED`/`FAILED` once FFmpeg finishes. The client polls `GET /jobs/:id` until it sees `COMPLETED`. The DB is the **source of truth**: a service restart doesn't lose state, because the job is still there to recover — unlike keeping state only inside one hanging HTTP request.

prompt: The interviewer asks: 'Postgres can also search text with `LIKE '%apple%'`, so why do we still need Elasticsearch for search?'. Explain how Elasticsearch stores data differently to search faster, and why `LIKE '%X%'` doesn't scale.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Elasticsearch is not "a faster `LIKE`" but an **inverted index**: when indexing a `text` field, ES runs an analyzer (tokenize → lowercase → remove stopwords → stem) then builds a table mapping EACH TERM to the list of documents containing it (a posting list). At search time, ES splits the query into terms and looks up each posting list — at near O(1) per term — instead of sequentially scanning every row like a full-table scan. This is a fundamental difference from SQL's B-tree index: a B-tree is optimized for prefix/range matches (`LIKE 'X%'` can leverage a B-tree because the sought string is always at the START), but `LIKE '%X%'` (wildcard on BOTH ends) doesn't leverage the B-tree's sort order at all — Postgres is forced into a full scan to find a substring that could appear ANYWHERE within each row. Concretely: searching ES's inverted index over 1 million documents still takes only tens of ms, while a full-scan `LIKE '%X%'` at the same scale can take 5-10 seconds. It's worth acknowledging nuance: for a small table, or when only exact/prefix matching is needed (not free-text search with relevance ranking), Postgres with the right index (B-tree for prefix, `pg_trgm` for fuzzy matching) can still be sufficient without needing to add a whole Elasticsearch system.

prompt: The interviewer asks: 'Your producer emits click events with `key = adId` to Kafka, and the producer itself does NOT check for or remove any duplicates — it just writes and returns immediately. Is this design okay, and what does `key = adId` actually solve?'. Explain.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
This design is entirely fine and a standard pattern for high-throughput ingestion systems. `key = adId` makes Kafka hash this value to CHOOSE THE PARTITION for each record — so every click for the SAME ad always lands in the SAME partition, preserving RELATIVE ordering among that ad's clicks (Kafka only guarantees ordering WITHIN a partition, never ACROSS multiple partitions). The producer not deduping and not waiting for the consumer to process is an INTENTIONAL design decision, not an oversight: the producer only confirms it has APPENDED the event to the end of the log (an append-only operation, returning HTTP 202 'accepted') — it neither knows nor needs to know how the consumer will count/process it. By cleanly separating 'logged' from 'counted', the producer stays extremely lightweight (only writes, never reads back to check for duplicates), so it can sustain very high throughput — forcing the producer to check for duplicates before writing would slow it down significantly and turn it into a bottleneck at exactly the point receiving the system's highest traffic. The `clickId` field attached to every event is exactly the piece that enables dedup to happen AT THE CONSUMER LEVEL: the client generates it itself (or the API generates a UUID when absent) so each click carries a stable id, and the consumer uses this exact id to detect duplicates — even though the producer has no concept of 'duplication' at all. The prerequisite for this whole design to be correct: the consumer MUST actually perform the `clickId` check before counting — skip that step and the system will count INCORRECTLY under Kafka's at-least-once delivery semantics, since a record can genuinely be delivered more than once during a rebalance or consumer restart.

prompt: Your transfer endpoint must debit a wallet on service A and credit a wallet on service B, each with its own database. A colleague proposes wrapping both calls in a two-phase commit (2PC) distributed transaction: a coordinator asks both participants to "prepare", then sends "commit". Push back on this proposal — where can the coordinator crash, what happens to the participants, and why do modern wallet systems usually choose Saga over 2PC?
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
2PC puts every participant into a **prepared** state in phase 1 — locked but not yet committed — then waits for the coordinator to send commit/abort in phase 2. If the coordinator crashes right between the two phases, the participant is stuck prepared **forever**: the wallet row keeps its lock, nobody can write to it, and the only way out is a human manually resolving the in-doubt transaction. For a wallet system, that means money frozen mid-transfer — a violation of any serious fintech SLA. Saga solves exactly this by giving up the global lock: each step is an optimistic local transaction, and when one fails it runs a compensating transaction — an ordinary forward operation that reverses the business effect (the compensation for a debit is a credit) — to converge the system to a consistent state without a coordinator holding a cross-service lock. Saga's price is weaker isolation: the intermediate state (sender already debited, receiver not yet credited) may leak out, so the design must guarantee that intermediate state is safe to observe. Bottom line: 2PC only makes sense when participants are co-located and the workload tolerates blocking; a cross-service transfer in a money system always needs liveness, so Saga is the right choice.

prompt: A flash sale of 1,000 phones just ended and the team discovers 1,043 orders went through — stock is -43. The current code is simple: `if (stock > 0) { stock = stock - 1; save() }`. Explain precisely why this seemingly correct logic causes oversell when many requests run concurrently.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
This is a classic check-then-set **race condition**. The code `if (stock > 0) { stock = stock - 1 }` splits "read" and "write" into two separate application-level steps, leaving a gap between them. When stock is down to 1 and dozens of requests arrive concurrently, ALL of them read `stock = 1` before any single one manages to write back — so all of them pass the `stock > 0` check and all of them decrement, pushing stock negative even though each request's logic looks correct on its own. The problem isn't the if-check reasoning — it's that read-then-write isn't an indivisible unit. Fix it by merging check-and-decrement into ONE atomic operation the storage engine itself serializes: `UPDATE inventories SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = ? AND stock > 0` — the condition lives right inside the write, so even with many concurrent requests, the engine guarantees exactly one request wins a given row at a time; losing requests see `rows affected = 0` and know safely they're out of stock, without anyone decrementing incorrectly.

prompt: The interviewer asks: 'Your team already has Prometheus + Grafana with CPU/RAM/p95 latency dashboards — what more do you need Observability for?'. Distinguish Monitoring from Observability, and explain why having full dashboards still isn't enough when facing a production incident you've never seen before.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Monitoring addresses 'known unknowns' — problems anticipated in advance: collecting Metrics, comparing against thresholds to fire Alerts, with the core question being whether the SLI (measured indicator) meets the SLO (committed target), e.g. p95 latency or error rate. Observability addresses 'unknown unknowns' — problems NEVER anticipated: inferring the system's internal state from emitted signals (Metrics, Logs, Traces) to answer WHY the system is failing, even when no alert has fired. Having full CPU/RAM/p95 dashboards still has a classic blind spot: aggregate system-wide dashboards stay green while a specific user still hits errors (e.g. a localized DNS issue, or a single shard/instance having trouble) — because thresholds/alerts are designed for known failure patterns and don't cover every unusual case. When facing a never-seen-before production incident, the right process is: the metric signals 'something is off' (e.g. p95 spikes), then pivot to Logs and Traces, correlating them via `trace_id` to reconstruct a specific request's journey and pinpoint exactly which service/hop is the cause — something you cannot do by only looking at pre-defined dashboards. That's why Monitoring and Observability are complementary: without Observability, MTTR (mean time to recovery) drags on because you have an alert but no way to trace back the root cause.

prompt: A junior teammate asks: 'I see both API Gateway and Load Balancer sitting in front of the backend spreading requests around — what's the difference?'. Explain the different responsibilities of each clearly, and why a client shouldn't call individual microservices directly.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
These two sit at different layers of responsibility even though they look similar at a glance. A Load Balancer spreads traffic across multiple IDENTICAL instances of the same service, operating mainly at layer 4/7 based on host, indifferent to the request's business content. An API Gateway routes based on the CONTENT of the request — path, headers — to DIFFERENT services (order-service, payment-service...), while also handling cross-cutting concerns like authentication, rate limiting, CORS, and logging. Clients shouldn't call individual microservices directly because that forces the client to know each service's address — every topology change (a new service, merging/splitting services, an address change) forces a client change, an unnecessary hard coupling; also, auth/rate-limit/CORS logic would get duplicated across every service instead of being centralized. In practice, these two tools usually go TOGETHER: production often puts a load balancer in front of multiple API Gateway replicas, both to balance load for the gateway itself and to let the gateway handle business routing and cross-cutting concerns behind it.

prompt: The interviewer asks: 'In the worker that handles notification-sending jobs, you never call an explicit `ack()` or `nack()` — so how does BullMQ know whether a job succeeded or needs to be retried?'. Explain that mechanism, and why it produces an at-least-once guarantee.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
BullMQ has no explicit ack/nack API to call — the ack-versus-retry decision relies entirely on whether the processor function (the job-handling callback) returns NORMALLY or THROWS an exception. If the processor finishes and returns a normal value (no throw), BullMQ treats this as 'successfully processed', implicitly acks it, and removes the job from the queue — that job will never be re-queued for another send. Conversely, if the processor throws an exception (say, the provider returns a 503), BullMQ records this as one failed attempt and automatically re-queues the job according to the configured backoff policy, repeating until the maximum `attempts` is exhausted. This is exactly the AT-LEAST-ONCE guarantee, not exactly-once: BullMQ holds a Redis lock for each job a worker is currently processing; if that worker crashes suddenly AFTER actually sending the notification successfully through the provider but BEFORE the processor function manages to return (so BullMQ never received the 'success' signal), the lock expires and the job reappears in the queue for another worker to pick up and process again — resulting in the SAME notification potentially being sent more than once. Precisely because of this, the queue's own ack/retry mechanism is NOT enough to guarantee 'exactly one send' — the system needs an additional, separate dedup layer (an idempotency-key checked via `SET NX` before actually calling the provider) at the dispatch layer to absorb exactly the resends caused by at-least-once delivery.

prompt: The interviewer asks: "You sign webhooks with HMAC over the body — so what happens if an attacker captures a valid request (correct signature) and replays the exact same request many times?" Explain why signing the body alone isn't enough, and what mechanism actually blocks this kind of replay.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
Signing the body alone isn't enough because HMAC only binds the body bytes to a secret — it stops tampering (content modification) but a valid `(body, signature)` pair can be captured by an attacker and replayed identically an unlimited number of times, since the signature itself carries no notion of "time". The correct mechanism is to put the timestamp INSIDE the signed string, not just attached alongside it: `signature = HMAC(secret, "${timestamp}.${body}")`. Because the timestamp is part of the HMAC input, the signature is now bound to a specific moment. The receiver verifies in two steps: first checking whether the timestamp falls within a valid window (e.g. ±300 seconds), then recomputing the HMAC and comparing signatures. Doing the window check first rejects stale payloads immediately — even if their signature is still mathematically correct — and avoids wasting CPU computing HMAC for a request that will be rejected regardless. As a result, a captured payload can only be replayed successfully for a few minutes instead of forever. The trade-off: a narrower window is safer but more prone to false-rejecting legitimate requests when the two sides have significant clock skew — which is why every retry must re-sign with a FRESH timestamp rather than reusing the original one.

prompt: A junior teammate proposes: "Let's store every driver's raw lat/lng in a table, and when we need to find drivers near a rider, compute the Haversine distance to every row and filter." With millions of drivers and thousands of find-a-ride requests per second, explain why this doesn't scale, and what problem H3 (hashing coordinates into hexagon cells) actually solves.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The naive approach computes Haversine to every driver — O(N) per request — and with N in the millions and thousands of requests/second, the cost explodes along both dimensions. The core issue is that lat/lng are continuous and can't be indexed: no B-tree helps "only read rows near point X" when the comparison is a `sqrt`/trig function. H3 solves exactly this by discretizing space: `latLngToCell` hashes a coordinate into a stable cell id (the same coordinate always yields the same cell id) — turning "find nearby drivers" into a lookup on a list already indexed by cell id (one lookup, not a scan), and "how many drivers are in this area" into an O(1) read on a fixed key. Real distance (Haversine) doesn't disappear entirely — it only gets recomputed on the SMALL set of candidates inside the neighboring cell/k-ring after the coarse cell-based filter, cutting cost from O(entire table) down to O(candidates in a small local neighborhood).

prompt: A junior teammate proposes a rate limiter by splitting time into fixed 1-minute blocks, counting requests per block, rejecting over the threshold, and resetting the counter to 0 when the minute ends. Explain the flaw in this approach and how the token bucket refill model fixes it.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Fixed window has a boundary burst flaw: because each block resets its counter independently, a user can send up to `limit` requests in the last second of this block, then another `limit` in the first second of the next block — nearly double the quota in a very short span while the algorithm still considers each block valid. Token bucket fixes this by dropping the "block reset" concept entirely: the bucket has a `capacity` and refills continuously at `refillPerSec`, computing refill as a function of elapsed time (`delta_ms/1000 * refill_per_sec`) lazily at consume time — no active background job needed. Because there is no hard boundary to time an exploit around, token bucket still allows one instant burst up to `capacity`, but that burst is a fixed ceiling, not something that compounds across two consecutive cycles the way fixed window does. The cost is nearly nothing: the bucket only needs two stored numbers, `{tokens, ts}`, so it stays lightweight and distributes well.

prompt: The interviewer asks: 'You keep connected sockets in an in-memory `Map` on the server, and when a message arrives you look up the recipient's socket and emit directly to it — what breaks when you run multiple instances behind a load balancer?'. Explain exactly where it breaks, and what mechanism actually solves the problem.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
This approach works for a single instance but breaks immediately when scaling horizontally. A WebSocket is a stateful connection: a socket lives in the memory of exactly one process, so the socket `Map` is local per instance rather than cluster-wide shared state. When the sender connects to instance A and the recipient connects to instance B, A's `Map` simply never contains the recipient's socket — the `emit` call falls into the void even though the code logic is entirely correct. This isn't a programming bug but an inevitable consequence of splitting stateful connections across multiple nodes: any solution needs an inter-node channel to unify that fragmented state. The correct mechanism is a backplane — e.g. Redis pub/sub — where every node both publishes to and subscribes to a shared channel. When a node receives a message from a client, it doesn't emit in-memory right away; it publishes the envelope to the backplane. Every node (including the one that just received it, to keep a single code path) receives that envelope back via its subscription and decides which local sockets in the room to deliver to. As a result, cross-node routing becomes the default behavior instead of a special case that needs separate handling.

prompt: The interviewer asks: 'RabbitMQ has three main exchange types: direct, fanout, topic — what message-routing mechanism differs between them?'. Explain each type's mechanism clearly and give an example of when to use which.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
All three exchange types receive messages from the producer, but differ in HOW they ROUTE to the bound queues. `direct` matches the routing key EXACTLY against each queue's binding key — precise 1:1 routing; if the routing key doesn't match any binding, the message is dropped, no queue receives it. `fanout` COMPLETELY ignores the routing key, broadcasting the message to EVERY queue bound to that exchange — suited when every consumer needs to know about one event (e.g. a config-change notification that every service needs to refresh its cache for). `topic` is the most flexible: matches the routing key by PATTERN, using the wildcard `*` to match EXACTLY ONE token and `#` to match ZERO-OR-MORE tokens — e.g. the routing key `logs.error.payment-service` could be received by a queue bound to `logs.error.*` (all errors, regardless of service) and also by another queue bound to `logs.#` (all logs, every level, every service). Common thread: producers always publish to an EXCHANGE, never directly to a queue — it's the exchange TYPE (plus bindings) that decides where a message goes.

prompt: A mid-level developer says: 'SQL has constraints and transactions, NoSQL is faster and more flexible, so I'd default to NoSQL.' Push back on this: point out what's wrong with 'NoSQL is faster', and explain what you actually base a SQL-vs-NoSQL decision on for a real system.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
The mid-level answer is wrong to treat 'faster' as a fixed property of a database type — it's actually a property of a specific query shape running on a specific storage model. On the same dataset, a key-based point lookup or reading one pre-gathered aggregate (document) is usually fast on NoSQL because there's no JOIN; but a filter on a B-tree-indexed column, an ordered range query, or a many-to-many relation is fast on SQL thanks to indexing and normalized JOINs. Beyond speed there's a second axis: consistency model — SQL typically guarantees ACID/strong consistency (good for money, inventory), while many NoSQL stores favor eventual consistency for easier horizontal scaling; this is exactly CAP theorem showing up at the database-choice layer. The real decision should rest on: what is the system's dominant query shape (point lookup, range, aggregate, or many-to-many), and what are the consistency requirements — then measure on the same dataset to confirm, instead of assuming 'X is always faster than Y'.

prompt: A junior teammate asks: 'I see each Pod has its own IP — why doesn't the backend just call that IP directly, why bother going through a Service?'. Explain why hardcoding a Pod's IP is a bad idea, and what mechanism the Service uses to solve that problem.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
You shouldn't hardcode a Pod's IP because Pods are ephemeral resources: they get created and destroyed constantly due to scaling, rolling updates, or node failures — each time a Pod is recreated it gets a new IP, so hardcoding that IP breaks the connection the moment that Pod dies. The Service solves exactly this by providing a stable address — a virtual IP (ClusterIP) plus a DNS name that doesn't change over time — acting as an abstraction layer between the client and the actual set of Pods behind it. The update mechanism: the Service uses a `selector` matching labels to automatically track and maintain the list of currently healthy Pods in its Endpoints; when an old Pod dies and a new one comes up, the Service updates its Endpoints automatically without anyone intervening. So the backend only needs to know the Service's NAME (e.g. `order-service`), and Kubernetes fully handles resolving that to whichever Pod is currently alive.

prompt: A junior teammate proposes: "Let's just use `WHERE content LIKE '%term%'` in SQL to find documents containing a keyword, no need to build a complicated inverted index." With a corpus of several million documents, explain why this is both slow and inadequate for real search, and what problem an inverted index actually solves.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
`LIKE '%term%'` breaks on both fronts: performance and semantics. On performance, the leading `%` makes an ordinary B-tree index useless — the engine has to scan the entire table for every query, so cost grows linearly with corpus size and never scales to several million documents. On semantics, `LIKE` only answers the binary question "does this term appear in the document" — it has no idea which document is MORE relevant than another, so it can't rank results, only list every document that matches. An **inverted index** solves both problems: it maps each term to a **posting list** — the list of documents containing that term along with frequency data — so a multi-term query only needs to read a few posting lists for the query's terms and merge them, with cost scaling with the NUMBER OF QUERY TERMS, not corpus size. And because each posting list already carries frequency/position data, that's precisely the input needed to compute a relevance score (like BM25) — something `LIKE` can never have, since it stores nothing beyond a yes/no match.

prompt: Peak-hour traffic spikes 10x and the website starts slowing down and timing out. A teammate proposes: 'Just upgrade the current server to the beefiest tier, pile on lots of RAM and CPU and we're done'. Rebut this proposal: explain why it is only a temporary fix, distinguish vertical scaling from horizontal scaling, and argue why horizontal is the only path that survives in the long run.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The "add more RAM/CPU" proposal is vertical scaling — it fails for two walls it cannot cross: (1) a physical ceiling — every machine has a max core/RAM limit and high-end hardware costs grow exponentially, so it only delays the problem; (2) SPOF — it is still one machine, and if it dies the whole system dies. Horizontal scaling is the survival path: put many commodity machines behind a Load Balancer, the LB spreads requests round-robin so total throughput sums nearly linearly with node count, and if one node dies the rest keep serving — redundancy eliminates SPOF. The precondition for valid horizontal scaling is a stateless service: push session to Redis so any node can serve any request. Verdict: vertical buys time early, but horizontal is the mandatory condition to handle million-user load and reach high availability.

prompt: Two differently-named files happen to share one chunk with identical content. If the system names storage objects by `userId/filename`, do those two chunks get stored once? If it switches to using the chunk's SHA256 as the storage key (content-addressing), what changes?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Under `userId/filename` naming, two chunks with identical content but living in different files still get two different keys (since the key depends on a user-chosen location, not on content), so the system stores two separate physical copies even though there's really only one piece of content — the duplication is completely undetected. Switching to content-addressing by using the chunk's SHA256 as the key changes everything: a chunk's "address" is now its content itself, so two byte-identical chunks — regardless of which file they belong to or who uploaded them — always produce the same key. The direct consequence is that the storage layer only needs to keep exactly one physical copy per unique piece of content; every referencing file points at the same object, and dedup happens naturally without ever comparing files pairwise. This comes with an immutability guarantee: once a chunk is written under its SHA256 key, it's immutable — "editing content" really means creating a new object under a new key, there's no concept of an in-place update.

prompt: Redlock uses quorum (`SET NX PX` on a majority of nodes) to grant a distributed lock. Many people assume quorum alone is enough to make the lock absolutely safe. Explain what quorum actually guarantees (liveness or safety), and why a fencing token is still needed.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Quorum `SET NX PX` on a majority of nodes only guarantees LIVENESS: at any given moment, at most one client wins quorum and is considered the lock's owner — that's basic mutual exclusion. But quorum does NOT guarantee SAFETY: a client that once won the lock, if paused (for any reason — GC, network delay) longer than the lock's TTL, wakes up still holding what it believes is a "valid" client object and can absolutely send a write request, even though the server considers its lock long expired and may have already granted it to another client. This is exactly Kleppmann's critique of Redlock: quorum alone is liveness-only. A fencing token patches that exact gap: each lock grant produces a monotonically increasing integer (a token); the storage layer — where data is ACTUALLY written — keeps a watermark of the highest token ever seen, and rejects any write request carrying a token less than or equal to that watermark. Since storage only needs to compare two integers, it can reject a stale writer WITHOUT knowing anything about the lock mechanism above it — this is the final safety line. In short: quorum solves "who holds the lock at a given moment" (liveness), fencing token solves "only the valid writer actually gets to write" (safety) — two layers for two different problems; missing either one isn't enough.

prompt: The interviewer asks: 'When a user posts, should the news feed system immediately write that post into EVERY follower's timeline, or just store one post and compute the feed whenever each follower opens the app?'. Explain the fanout-on-write and fanout-on-read models, and the core trade-off of each.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
**Fanout-on-write (push model)**: when a user posts, the system IMMEDIATELY writes the postId into EVERY follower's materialized timeline — a cost of O(F) writes per post, F being the follower count. Benefit: reading a feed is extremely fast, since it just reads the ALREADY-SORTED timeline, with no JOIN or aggregation needed at read time. Trade-off: **write amplification** — the more followers, the higher the write cost; for a celebrity with F = 10 million, one post spawns 10 million writes. **Fanout-on-read (pull model)**: the opposite — nothing extra is written when posting (just a single insert); when a user opens their feed, the system THEN finds the authors they follow and filters/aggregates their posts AT READ TIME. Benefit: writes are extremely cheap. Trade-off: **read amplification** — the more people a user follows, the heavier the feed query gets, latency scaling with the number of followees and the posts table's size. Neither model is absolutely "correct" — the choice depends on three factors: the read:write ratio (social feeds typically read far more than they write, often 10:1 or higher, favoring push for high read throughput); follower distribution (a celebrity/KOL with millions of followers completely breaks pure push's "F is small" assumption); and the desired latency SLA for opening a feed. Large production systems usually don't pick one exclusively but use a **hybrid**: push for ordinary users, pull for celebrities.

prompt: The interviewer asks: 'You need a real-time top-10 leaderboard for millions of players. Why not store scores in a SQL table and run ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 10 whenever you need the top-10?'. Explain how a Redis sorted set is stored internally, and why it beats the SQL approach for this problem.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
A Redis sorted set attaches a `score` to each member and keeps every member pre-sorted internally in a **skip list**. `ZADD` inserts or updates a member in O(log N) because it only needs to locate the right position in the skip list, not re-sort the entire set. `ZREVRANGE key 0 N-1` reads the top-N directly, **already sorted by descending score** — no scan, no re-sort, no pulling extra data to the client. That is the core difference from SQL: `ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 10` on a table with millions of rows must re-sort (or lean on a B-tree index and scan) on every call, and there is no cheap way to ask "what is user X's rank" — whereas `ZREVRANK` answers that in O(log N). At the scale of millions of players continuously updating scores, the sorted set gives stable read/write throughput and rank lookups for free, while SQL pays the re-sort cost on every read.

prompt: The interviewer asks: 'Kafka and a traditional message queue like RabbitMQ/SQS are both used to send messages between services — what's the fundamental difference between them?'. Answer this and state a capability Kafka has that a traditional queue doesn't.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
The fundamental difference is in how messages are stored. Kafka is an append-only commit log: messages are written sequentially to the log and are NOT deleted when a consumer reads them — the consumer only advances its own offset to mark 'how far it has read.' A traditional message queue (RabbitMQ classic queue, SQS) is consuming: the message is deleted from the queue as soon as a consumer acks it, whoever reads it first makes it disappear for good. The direct consequence: since Kafka doesn't delete messages, each consumer group keeps its own offset on the same topic — two different groups can read the same data independently without contention or affecting each other. The standout capability Kafka has that a consuming queue doesn't: REPLAY. A brand-new consumer group (e.g. a newly formed analytics team) can read the ENTIRE event history from the start of the topic (within configured retention), or an existing consumer can actively rewind its offset to reprocess a past window — something a traditional queue can't do since its messages are permanently deleted once consumed.

prompt: A crawler uses a bloom filter to check "has this URL been crawled" before enqueueing. Explain why a bloom filter is suitable here even though it can answer incorrectly — and which kind of wrong answer a crawler absolutely cannot accept.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
A bloom filter is asymmetric: it can produce a **false positive** (claiming "this URL has been seen" when it's actually brand new) but NEVER a **false negative** — if `BF.EXISTS` returns 0, the URL is 100% guaranteed to have never been `BF.ADD`ed, since each add only flips a bit from 0 to 1 and never flips it back. This is exactly why it's a good dedup pre-filter for a crawler: the one error type a crawler absolutely cannot accept is a false negative — claiming "not seen" for a URL that was actually already crawled would cause a re-fetch, wasting bandwidth and violating the host's "only knock once per URL" policy. A false positive, in contrast, only makes the crawler skip one NEW URL at a small, configurable rate (e.g. 1%) — the cost of missing a few pages is far cheaper than repeatedly re-fetching already-crawled pages at a scale of hundreds of millions of URLs. Because the bloom filter's one and only error mode happens to be exactly the error type a crawler can tolerate, it's the ideal choice over a `HashSet<string>`, which is RAM-hungry and can't be shared across workers.

prompt: A teammate proposes: 'For simplicity, let's configure ONE Keycloak client shared by both the browser-based single-page app AND the backend service calling internal APIs, and require both to send `client_secret` when exchanging tokens, for consistency.' How do you push back on this proposal?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The difference between a public and a confidential client is NOT "a higher or lower security level of the same thing" but two different TRUST BOUNDARIES, determined by WHERE THE CODE RUNS. A single-page app running in a browser is a **public** environment: everything shipped to the browser — including the entire JavaScript bundle — can be read by the user (or anyone who opens DevTools). Forcing it to send a `client_secret` only creates a false sense of security, since that secret is effectively already sitting in public inside the bundle sent to every browser — it's no longer a "secret" in any meaningful sense. Conversely, the backend service running on a trusted server is a **confidential** environment: the server can safely keep a `client_secret` (never exposed, only the ops team can access the machine), so requiring the secret when exchanging tokens is reasonable and adds a genuinely useful authentication layer. The right proposal is to create TWO separate clients in the same Keycloak realm: a `public` client for the single-page app (no secret configured, none sent) and a `confidential` client for the backend service (secret required) — choose the client type based on WHERE THE CODE RUNS, not "for consistency" or by business unit. One more modern note: for the single-page app (public client), the standard flow is no longer password grant but Authorization Code + PKCE — PKCE protects the authorization code from being stolen mid-flow without needing any client secret at all, matching exactly the fact that "a public client cannot keep a secret."

prompt: The interviewer asks: 'Why does adding an index make a SELECT run faster, and is adding indexes always a good idea?'. Explain the mechanism that makes an index speed up reads, and point out the cost of overusing indexes.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
An index speeds up reads because it's a secondary structure (usually a B-tree) holding sorted keys, so the database looks things up at roughly O(log n) instead of scanning the whole table sequentially at O(n). But this is fundamentally a trade-off, not magic: the index doesn't make data 'faster' on its own — it just lets the database find the exact rows to read without scanning everything — and the price is that every write (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) must update every relevant index, so indiscriminate indexing slows writes down and bloats disk usage. Having an index doesn't guarantee the planner uses it: if a filter still keeps most of the table (low selectivity), random I/O through the index can be more expensive than a sequential scan, so the planner deliberately picks a sequential scan instead. That's why you need to monitor created indexes via system statistics (e.g. `pg_stat_user_indexes` in PostgreSQL) — an index with a usage count of 0 is a candidate to drop, since it only costs write overhead without ever serving a read.

prompt: A teammate asks: "Why does H3 use a hexagon grid instead of a simple square grid like geohash, which would be easier to compute?" Explain the real technical reason behind this choice, not just "it looks nicer."
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
It's not aesthetics — it's real geometry. A square grid (like geohash) has TWO kinds of neighbors: 4 edge-adjacent and 4 corner-adjacent, and the distance from the center to these two kinds differs by a factor of √2 — meaning "neighbor" isn't uniform in every direction, distorting the notion of "radius of k cells" (a diagonal neighbor is "farther" than an edge neighbor despite both being "1 cell away"). A hexagon grid solves exactly this: each cell has only ONE kind of neighbor — exactly 6 edge-adjacent cells, and all 6 are EXACTLY the same distance from the center. As a result, expanding k layers around a hex cell (k-ring) approximates a real circle far better than a square k-ring, which approximates a distorted square. For ride-hailing, this matters when computing surge/demand per cell or expanding the driver-search radius: a square grid can make one direction look artificially "closer" than another (a geometric bias), while hexagons give even distance/area error in every direction.

prompt: A teammate proposes: 'For each user's feed, just query Postgres `SELECT * FROM posts WHERE author_id IN (...) ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20` on every page load, no need for a separate cache to complicate things.' With a feed that's already materialized (each user has a list of posts from the people they follow), how do you push back on this proposal based on using a Redis sorted set (ZSET)?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The problem with "just query Postgres every time" is: `ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT N` still has to JOIN through the follows table then the posts table, filter by user, and RE-SORT for EVERY user on EVERY page load — even though the result barely changes between nearby loads (a feed doesn't change millisecond by millisecond). Using an epoch timestamp as a Redis sorted set's (ZSET) `score` solves exactly this: Redis ALWAYS keeps every `postId` pre-sorted in a skip list by ascending score, so `ZADD` (adding a new post) is O(log N), and reading the latest top-N (`ZREVRANGE key 0 19`) is O(log N + N) WITHOUT re-sorting on every read — the skip list is pre-sorted by design. An important point to emphasize: this isn't "caching a query result" like an opaque blob, but MATERIALIZING data into a structure that allows ordered reads — the ZSET is a pre-computed PER-USER projection (`feed:{userId}`), fundamentally different from caching a raw SQL result verbatim. Postgres remains the SOURCE OF TRUTH holding the original posts; the ZSET is just a RECONSTRUCTABLE materialized projection — if Redis loses the cache (restart, eviction), you just call the re-materialize function (`seedTimeline`) again from Postgres, no original data is lost. One mandatory note: the ZSET must be TRIMMED (e.g. `ZREMRANGEBYRANK key 0 -(MAX+1)` keeping exactly the latest N elements) right after every insertion, to avoid unbounded memory growth for a user following many active accounts — without trimming, the feed cache gradually loses its very "cheap reads" advantage as the ZSET grows to tens of thousands of entries.

prompt: Your client has retry logic for flaky networks: if it doesn't get a response within 3 seconds, it automatically POSTs the same create-transcode-job request again. If the server has no special handling, what happens when both the original request and the retry actually reach the server? How would you design `createJob` to avoid that outcome?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Without a guard, both the original request and the retry each create their own job row and spawn their own FFmpeg run for the same `inputPath` — double the resources and two records for what was one user intent. `createJob` needs an **idempotency** check before inserting: look for an existing job with the same `inputPath` and `status != FAILED`; if found, return that job immediately without creating a new one or spawning FFmpeg again. The key detail is excluding only `FAILED` — a job that already failed should let the next POST be treated as a legitimate retry attempt and be allowed to create a fresh job, whereas `PENDING`/`PROCESSING`/`COMPLETED` should just point retries back at the job that's already running or done. The result: however many times the client retries with the same `inputPath`, it always gets back the same `id`, with no need for complex client-side dedup logic.

prompt: A junior teammate asks: 'We already have an HTTP API — why do we still need a job queue (BullMQ)? Can't we just send emails right inside the request?'. Explain why handling a slow/failure-prone task inside the request itself is risky, and how a job queue solves that.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
Processing a slow or failure-prone task (sending email, calling an external API) RIGHT IN THE REQUEST has two clear risks. First, HTTP requests have a finite timeout (usually around 30 seconds) — if the task is slower than that, the client gets a timeout error even though the task might still be running server-side. Second, if the handler dies mid-way (server restart, crash, deploy) while processing, that task is LOST FOREVER — there's no record to know it needs retrying, the work data only existed in that request's memory. A job queue solves both problems by splitting into two steps: the request only WRITES the job to a DURABLE store (e.g. Redis via BullMQ) and returns IMMEDIATELY to the client, without waiting for the actual work to finish. The real processing is handled by a WORKER — a COMPLETELY INDEPENDENT process that pulls jobs from the store and runs them, entirely unbound by the original HTTP request's lifecycle or timeout. Alongside that come capabilities plain HTTP doesn't have out of the box: workers can SCALE SEPARATELY (increasing/decreasing worker count independently of API instance count), and the job queue has built-in RETRY/DELAY/PRIORITY per job — if relying only on request/response, all of that would have to be hand-built and error-prone.

prompt: A teammate suggests: "To stop the flash sale from crashing, just put a rate limiter at 500 requests/second in front of checkout — anything over that gets a 429." Explain why a rate limiter alone doesn't correctly solve the flash-sale problem, and how a virtual waiting room differs in kind.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
A rate limiter only solves half the problem: it **rejects** everything past the threshold with a 429, unfairly — whoever retries faster or has a better connection gets through, while someone who arrived earlier but on a slow connection gets wrongly dropped. Worse, a 429 usually triggers an immediate client retry, turning a spike into a retry storm that amplifies load instead of reducing it. A virtual waiting room solves a genuinely different problem: it **enqueues** everyone by their true arrival time (typically a durable sorted set with score = timestamp, preserving FIFO order), then **admits batches** of N people at exactly the rate checkout can actually sustain. The core difference: a rate limiter drops the excess, a waiting room keeps everyone and just delays them in an orderly way — for a flash sale, where millions compete for a few thousand spots, keeping a fair, predictable queue (knowing your position) matters far more than hard-blocking on an instantaneous QPS threshold.

prompt: A developer declares the product's `category` field with mapping `type: "text"` (to "be safe for search"), then tries running a `terms` aggregation to count products per category for a dashboard, and hits an error: 'Fielddata is disabled on text fields'. Explain this error, and how would you fix the mapping so it can both search AND aggregate?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The 'Fielddata is disabled' error happens because `category` is declared `text` — every `text` field gets torn apart by an ANALYZER into small terms (tokenize, lowercase, remove stopwords, stem) then stored in an inverted index; ES no longer keeps the original value to group/count by the exact original string. So a `terms` aggregation on a `text` field is BLOCKED BY DEFAULT (fielddata disabled) — running it would eat significant RAM if fielddata were enabled (it must reload all terms back into memory), so ES refuses by default to avoid trouble. A `keyword` field solves the opposite need correctly: it indexes the value AS-IS (no analyzer term-splitting), enabling exact match, `term` filters, and aggregation — but in exchange does NOT support full-text search (can't find a keyword buried inside a longer string). The correct fix is a MULTI-FIELD: declare `category` as `text` (keeping full-text search) and also add a `category.keyword` sub-field (`type: "keyword"`) in the same mapping — syntax `{ category: { type: "text", fields: { keyword: { type: "keyword" } } } }`. The practical consequence: search queries keep using `category` as before, while the `terms` aggregation must switch the FIELD NAME in its query to `category.keyword` — no need to change already-indexed data, just re-index with the new mapping (since mapping can't be changed for an existing field) and change the field name in the aggregation query. Note: avoid enabling `fielddata: true` directly on the `text` field as a quick fix — it's significantly memory-expensive and should only be used when truly necessary; a multi-field is the standard correct solution.

prompt: You need to instrument an API to cover Google SRE's 'Four Golden Signals': Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation. For each signal, pick the CORRECT Prometheus metric type (counter, gauge, or histogram) and explain why the other types don't fit.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The four golden signals map onto the three metric types as follows. Traffic (request volume) and Errors (error rate) both use a **Counter**: just a monotonically increasing total of events (`http_requests_total`), always read via `rate()` to get "events per second"; Errors is the same counter filtered by an error `status_code`. Latency uses a **Histogram**: each latency value is distributed into pre-declared fixed buckets, allowing quantiles (p95/p99) to be computed at query time via `histogram_quantile` — a counter cannot store the shape of a distribution, only a total, so it can't answer "95% of requests were faster than how many ms." Saturation (resource saturation level) uses a **Gauge**: a free-moving instantaneous state like CPU, heap, or current connection count — not a cumulative event so a counter is the wrong fit, and no distribution is needed so a histogram is overkill. Picking the wrong type breaks things in specific ways: a gauge for Traffic loses the ability to compute an accurate rate across multiple instances/restarts (a counter's `rate()` automatically handles resets; a gauge has no such semantics); a counter for Latency only has a total, so p95/p99 becomes impossible, losing all distribution information. One operational note: a histogram's buckets must be declared FIXED before any data exists — changing the boundaries mid-way once production is running breaks the accumulated time-series.

prompt: You have 3 services subscribed to the `order.created` topic: `inventory-service` (decrements stock), `notification-service` (sends emails), and 2 instances of `inventory-service` itself running side by side to share load. Explain: (1) why `inventory-service` and `notification-service` both receive EVERY event, and (2) why the 2 `inventory-service` instances do NOT both process the same event.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
This entire distribution behavior is decided by a single field: `groupId`. The rule: different `groupId` → broadcast, each group independently receives every message in full; same `groupId`, multiple instances → Kafka splits the topic's partitions across the instances in that group, each message going to exactly ONE instance (sharing work, not duplicating). Applying it to the scenario: `inventory-service` and `notification-service` are two different `groupId`s, so both fully and independently receive every `order.created` event — matching the need for both to know about new orders, but to do two different things (decrement stock vs. send email). The 2 `inventory-service` instances share the SAME `groupId` (since they're replicas of the same service, sharing load) — Kafka treats them as ONE group, splitting the topic's partitions across both instances, so each event is processed by exactly one of the two, avoiding a scenario where both decrement stock for the same order.

prompt: The interviewer asks: 'What is the CORE difference between synchronous (request/response) and asynchronous (event-driven) communication — not just "waiting or not"?'. Answer this and state the cost of moving to asynchronous.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
The core difference isn't 'waiting or not' but temporal coupling — being hard-coupled in TIME between the two sides. Synchronous communication (request/response) forces the caller to wait until the callee finishes before getting a result and moving on; the consequence is that if the downstream dies or slows down, the entire calling flow hangs or fails too, even if the caller itself has no problem. Asynchronous communication (event-driven) decouples the two sides in time: the producer publishes an event and moves on IMMEDIATELY without waiting for anyone to process it, while the consumer processes that event later, at its own pace — the two sides no longer depend on whether the other is running or busy at that exact moment. The cost of moving to asynchronous is losing immediacy: the caller no longer knows the result right away, and the whole system shifts from immediate consistency to eventual consistency — accepting a delay before everything converges to the correct state. This isn't asynchronous being absolutely 'better' than synchronous — it's a deliberate trade-off: giving up immediacy for higher fault tolerance and availability.

prompt: A teammate wonders: 'If the count-consumer container restarts, does it re-read the ENTIRE topic from the beginning? If so, the count would double!'. Explain how Kafka's `groupId` + offset mechanism actually addresses this concern, and the role `clickId` dedup plays in that picture.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
This concern is intuitively reasonable, but Kafka is designed to avoid exactly this situation — though not entirely, not absolutely.
