Kafka stores committed offsets keyed by CONSUMER GROUP (`groupId`), not per individual container/instance: every time count-consumer finishes processing a message, it commits that group's offset to the broker. If a container dies and restarts with the SAME `groupId`, Kafka returns the exact previously committed offset, so the consumer RESUMES from where it left off — it does not re-read events that were both processed AND had their offset successfully committed, so the count is not doubled for that portion. The `fromBeginning: true` flag only ever applies exactly once — on the group's VERY FIRST run when no offset has been committed yet (to read the entire log history from the start); on every subsequent restart, the committed offset always wins, and this flag never forces re-reading from the beginning. However, a real gap still exists: if a consumer has FINISHED processing a message (already incremented the `adId` counter in memory) but CRASHES right BEFORE committing that message's offset, then on restart, Kafka has no idea that message was processed — it will be re-read from the old (uncommitted) offset. This is precisely where `clickId` dedup at the consumer level kicks in: the consumer checks whether `clickId` is already in the `seen` set BEFORE incrementing the counter, so even if the message gets re-read due to this commit-offset gap, the counter is not incremented again. The two mechanisms work together, neither alone is sufficient: per-group offset minimizes the need to re-read (an optimization, avoiding reprocessing the entire history on every restart), while `clickId` dedup is the final safety net guaranteeing CORRECT counting despite the remaining gap between 'finished processing' and 'offset committed'.

prompt: A developer stores a user profile by running `SET user:1 '{"name":"Alice","age":30,"city":"HN"}'` — stuffing the whole object as a JSON string into a Redis string. Every time the user's age changes, the code must `GET`, `JSON.parse`, edit the `age` field, `JSON.stringify`, then `SET` the whole thing back. How do you push back on this proposal, and when is a Redis hash the right choice instead?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The string+JSON approach forces every single-field edit to read the whole thing, parse, edit, re-serialize, then overwrite the whole object — wasting CPU/bandwidth unnecessarily, and it has a race condition: if two requests concurrently edit two different fields (one edits `age`, one edits `city`) via an application-level read-modify-write, the later write overwrites the earlier one's change because both write back the full object based on a stale read. A Redis hash solves exactly this: `HSET user:1 age 31` updates exactly one field, no need to read/re-serialize the whole object, and the operation is atomic at the Redis level, so two different fields edited concurrently don't stomp on each other. A hash is also more memory-efficient for small objects thanks to internal encoding. Bottom line: use a hash when you need to read/edit individual fields of an object; only use string+JSON when the application always treats the whole object as a single block.

prompt: A teammate suggests: 'The `POST /notifications` API should call the provider (email/SMS/push) directly and only respond after that, so the client KNOWS FOR SURE the notification was sent successfully instead of just knowing it was enqueued'. Do you agree? Analyze the pros and cons versus the current design (enqueue and return immediately, actually send in a separate worker).
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
This proposal should not be applied to a high-throughput notification system. If the API calls the provider directly before responding, the API's response time becomes directly BOUND to the provider's speed — a slow provider (a congested email server) or a down one will make the API hang, and during a large traffic burst, the API will bottleneck at exactly the provider's slowest pace, potentially causing mass client-side timeouts. The current design decouples 'receiving a request' from 'actually sending': the producer only pushes work into the queue and returns IMMEDIATELY, so the API never waits on the provider — a large traffic burst only makes the queue longer, never hanging or timing out the API. For a request targeting multiple channels (say, both email and SMS and push), the producer also performs a fan-out: creating MULTIPLE independent jobs, one per channel, so each channel sends and retries COMPLETELY INDEPENDENTLY — if the SMS provider is down, it doesn't drag down or block sending email/push. There's a real trade-off worth acknowledging: with the enqueue-then-return design, the client only gets confirmation that the notification was 'ACCEPTED for sending' (accepted/enqueued) at response time, NOT certainty that it actually sent successfully at that moment — to know the real outcome (delivered/failed), the system needs an additional channel like a webhook callback when the worker finishes, status polling by `requestId`, or a WebSocket push. Conclusion: for a high-throughput system, low and stable API latency (independent of the provider) matters far more than the client immediately knowing the send result — calling the provider directly only makes sense for a very-low-throughput system where high latency is acceptable.

prompt: A code reviewer suggests: 'Why not optimize by checking if the recipient is connected to THIS exact node — if so, emit directly in-memory for speed, and only publish to Redis when the recipient is actually on a different node?'. Do you agree with this optimization? Analyze it.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
This optimization should not be applied in most cases. To branch on 'is the recipient on this node', the node itself would need to know in advance where the recipient's socket lives across the WHOLE cluster — exactly what the backplane architecture is deliberately designed to avoid needing (each node only needs to know who's in its OWN local room). Adding this branch means two code paths handle the same job: one that emits in-memory for same-node, one that publishes/subscribes for cross-node. Any future change to delivery logic — e.g. adding a `deliveredBy` trace for routing debugging, changing the envelope format, adding a validation step — has to be made in BOTH places, and it's very easy for one branch to be missed, causing same-node and cross-node behavior to silently drift apart in ways ordinary tests rarely catch (since tests usually exercise only one branch at a time). Meanwhile, the cost of ALWAYS publishing is just one publish/subscribe round-trip through Redis — which is an in-memory broadcast on Redis's side, extremely fast, and nearly negligible compared to the operational and maintenance cost of two parallel code paths. Conclusion: this is a premature optimization that trades something cheap (a small amount of latency) for something expensive (complexity and hidden-bug risk) — only worth considering if you've actually profiled and proven the Redis round-trip to be a real bottleneck.

prompt: Someone writes `if (computedSignature === receivedSignature)` to verify a webhook signature. The interviewer says this line has a subtle security hole even though the logic is completely correct. Explain what that hole is, and what mechanism fixes it.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
The hole is a timing side-channel. The `===` string comparison short-circuits: it stops at the very first differing byte, so the CPU time needed to return `false` depends on how many leading bytes matched — the more leading bytes match, the slightly longer the comparison runs before it stops. A patient enough attacker can time thousands of requests, each trying a different guessed byte at the same position: whichever guess produces a slightly longer response time (meaning the comparison went further before failing) is the correct byte. Repeating this for every position, the attacker recovers the entire valid signature without ever knowing the secret — the function's logic is completely correct, yet it's an operational security hole. The fix is a CONSTANT-TIME comparison function like `crypto.timingSafeEqual`: it always compares the entire buffer regardless of where the mismatch is, so response time carries no signal for an attacker to exploit. One edge case worth remembering: `timingSafeEqual` throws if the two buffers have different lengths (since a forged signature could be any length), so you must compare the hex length first and treat a length mismatch as an immediate mismatch — never let that exception leak out as an unintended 500. This is exactly the boundary between "logically correct" (passes every functional test) and "operationally secure" (leaks no information through a side channel).

prompt: The interviewer asks: 'readinessProbe and livenessProbe sound similar — what's the difference? If you forget to declare readinessProbe, what happens during a rolling update?'. Explain the role of each probe clearly, and the concrete consequence of missing a readinessProbe.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
The two probes serve completely different purposes despite sounding similar. `livenessProbe` answers 'is this Pod still alive or stuck?' — if it fails repeatedly, Kubernetes considers the Pod logically dead and RESTARTS it. `readinessProbe` answers a different question: 'is this Pod READY to receive traffic?' — only a Pod currently in the ready state gets added to the Service's Endpoints list to receive requests; a not-yet-ready Pod (even if its process is `Running`) is excluded from Endpoints. If you forget to declare `readinessProbe`, Kubernetes defaults to considering the Pod ready as soon as the container is `Running` — regardless of whether the app inside has finished connecting to the database/cache. The concrete consequence during a rolling update: a new Pod that just came up gets pushed into Endpoints right away even though the app is NOT yet ready to serve, so some requests in that window hit exactly that not-ready Pod and get a transient 5xx — losing the very 'zero-downtime' benefit rolling updates are designed to provide.

prompt: The interviewer asks: "Why not just keep a single `balance` column on the account table, and `UPDATE balance = balance ± amount` on every transfer? Why does every fintech ledger use double-entry bookkeeping — writing two immutable DEBIT/CREDIT rows — instead of updating the balance directly?" Answer, and be explicit about what a single-column balance loses and what double-entry buys you.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
A direct `UPDATE balance` is an overwrite: it loses history. When a customer disputes a charge or an auditor asks "which transfer added N to this balance", a single numeric column can't answer — the new number has already overwritten the old one. Double-entry bookkeeping solves exactly that by storing every money movement as an immutable row pair — one DEBIT and one CREDIT — turning the ledger into an event log, and that ledger becomes the single source of truth; `account.balance` is just a derived cache, always recomputable as `SUM(CREDIT) - SUM(DEBIT)`. This unlocks two things: auditability — every transfer is traceable, and balance can be rebuilt from scratch by replaying the whole ledger; and a checkable invariant — total DEBIT across the entire system must always equal total CREDIT, a simple query that proves no transaction ever created or destroyed money. The cost is more rows, and fast balance reads need a cache updated inline with every transfer — but that's a small price for a complete audit trail that a single-column balance can never give you.

prompt: A junior teammate proposes leader election using a simple binary lock: whichever node successfully `SET NX` becomes leader, with no TTL, requiring an ops script to manually delete the key when the leader is deemed "dead." Explain the problem with this design and why a lease (with TTL) is better.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The problem with a TTL-less binary lock is that when the leader (lock holder) crashes, the lock gets stuck FOREVER — nothing automatically releases it, so the cluster completely loses the ability to elect a new leader until someone manually intervenes to delete the key. The proposal of "an ops script deletes the key when the leader is dead" carries an even more serious risk: deciding "the leader is dead" relies on human judgment or an external monitoring system, and that judgment can be WRONG — the leader might just be temporarily slow (a network blip, a GC pause), not actually dead. If the script deletes the key while the old leader is still alive and will wake up later, you immediately get split brain: two nodes both believing they're the leader. A lease solves both problems by baking in a TTL: the leader must actively renew before the lease expires to keep its role; if it crashes and fails to renew, the lease AUTOMATICALLY expires after exactly the TTL with no intervention needed — the cluster recovers within a BOUNDED, precisely measurable window (`leaseTTL + renewInterval`), instead of depending on how fast a human reacts or how accurate an external monitoring system is. This is exactly why production systems like Kubernetes' ControllerManager use a `Lease` object with bounded renewal, rather than a lock requiring manual cleanup.

prompt: A junior teammate implements crawler politeness by keeping `lastFetched` (each host's most recent fetch time) as an in-memory variable inside each fetcher pod. With 5 fetcher pods running in parallel, what happens to a host with `Crawl-delay: 1` second?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The problem is that `lastFetched` in each pod's RAM is PRIVATE data, not shared — each pod only knows to space out ITS OWN requests according to `Crawl-delay`, with zero awareness that 4 other pods are also fetching the same host. With 5 fetcher pods running in parallel and `Crawl-delay: 1` second, the host ends up receiving up to 5 requests per second — one from each pod, each pod confident it correctly respected the 1-second spacing — instead of exactly 1 request/second as required by policy. That's a 5x policy violation, and the number scales linearly with pod count. The correct fix is moving `lastFetched` into shared state, e.g. a `host:lastFetched` key in Redis that every pod reads/writes; the wait formula `wait = delay - (now - lastFetched)` then correctly measures the gap BETWEEN ANY TWO REQUESTS to the same host on a shared clock, correct regardless of worker count. This problem gets worse as pod count grows — precisely because a crawler needs to scale horizontally to handle millions of URLs, a RAM-local design is completely unacceptable in production, even though it might "look correct" when tested with a single pod.

prompt: A junior teammate proposes simplifying file metadata storage: a single `file` table with one JSON column holding the whole chunk array (index, sha256, size). Do you agree? Compare it with splitting into two relational tables, `file` and `chunk` (1 file → N chunks).
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
I disagree with cramming the whole chunk array into one JSON column on `file`. The first problem is resumable upload needs to answer "which chunk indices exist, which are missing" — with a JSON column you must read and parse the entire array on every check, with no way to query a single element directly. The second problem is dedup needs to answer "does this sha256 already exist anywhere in the system" — that's nearly impossible to index efficiently on an array nested inside JSON, whereas a flat `sha256` column on a relational `chunk` table indexes like any other column. Splitting into `file` (1) → `chunk` (N) solves both: each chunk is an independent row, so querying/updating one chunk doesn't require a read-modify-write of the whole array, and `chunkCount` can be derived via `COUNT(*)` from real data instead of being manually kept in sync with a JSON array's length (which drifts easily if you forget to update it). JSON columns aren't always wrong — for data that doesn't need per-element lookups they're perfectly reasonable — but here, the need to index by `sha256` and query by `chunkIndex` makes relational normalization the right call.

prompt: A teammate implements a rate limiter like this: `GET` the remaining token count from Redis, if any remain subtract 1 and `SET` it back, otherwise return 429. When 20 requests from the same user hit a capacity-5 bucket concurrently, the system ends up granting more than 5. Explain why.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The root cause is that reading the token count, computing, and writing it back are three separate operations rather than one atomic operation — a classic "check-then-act" bug. Under concurrency, when 20 requests call `GET` at once, all of them read the same stale snapshot (say, "5 tokens left") because none has written the new value yet; each sees tokens available and proceeds to subtract on its own. This is a **lost update**: subsequent writes overwrite each other based on the same stale read, so the bucket ends up spent far past 5 even though the per-request logic looked correct. The right fix isn't adding another check at the application layer — it's wrapping the whole read-refill-subtract-write chain into one Lua script called via `EVALSHA`. Redis runs a script as a single command on one thread, so two concurrent requests can never read the same stale snapshot again; the second request always sees the first request's write.

prompt: In the interview, the interviewer says: 'Your dashboard reports an average latency of just 20ms, sounds great — so why do I still make you track P95, P99?'. How do you answer? Explain why average latency is a trap at scale, what P99 tells you about user experience, and clearly distinguish latency from throughput.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Average latency is a trap because it is dragged flat by the majority of fast requests, hiding the slow tail: a 20ms average can still be hiding a group of requests taking hundreds of ms. At millions of users, the slowest 1% is already tens of thousands of customers — enough to churn. P99 says: '99% of requests are faster than threshold X, only 1% slower' — it shines a light exactly on the worst user group the average hides, so it reflects real experience far more faithfully. Latency and throughput are different axes: latency is the time one request takes end-to-end (measured at P95/P99), throughput is requests per second (RPS). They also trade off — batching raises throughput but raises latency; spreading load across nodes raises total throughput while keeping latency low. That is why serious SLOs always commit on P95/P99, not on the average.

prompt: One document mentions "redis" 50 times because it's a huge log file covering all sorts of topics, while another document is short and squarely about Redis, mentioning "redis" only 4 times. If you simply counted raw term occurrences, the 50-times document would win. Explain how BM25 avoids this wrong outcome, walking through all three components of the formula.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Raw term counting would let the 50-times document win, but BM25 avoids that by combining three components correctly. First, **IDF** gives a rare term more weight than a common one — not what directly fixes this example, but the foundation for measuring a term's distinguishing power. Second, **term-frequency saturation** (the `K1` parameter): the first few occurrences contribute most of the score, later ones add almost nothing — so 50 mentions doesn't beat 4 mentions by 12.5x, the gap gets compressed significantly. Third, **length normalization** (the `B` parameter with the `dl / avgdl` ratio): the longer a document is relative to the corpus average, the more its score is discounted — a huge log file mentioning "redis" 50 times simply because it's LONG gets penalized exactly for that length, while a short, on-topic document isn't penalized at all. Combining all three, a short, on-topic document (4 mentions) can fully outscore a long, diluted one (50 mentions), because BM25 measures topical FOCUS, not raw repetition count — this is precisely the mechanism that neutralizes keyword stuffing.

prompt: The team is setting up Grafana Loki for centralized logging, and is debating whether `trace_id` (a value unique per request) should be attached as a log stream LABEL or kept in the log content. How do you advise them, based on how Loki's indexing differs from Elasticsearch's?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Loki does NOT do full-text indexing like Elasticsearch — it only indexes a small set of LABELS (e.g. `app`, `env`) and stores the log content as compressed chunks, many orders of magnitude cheaper than Elasticsearch. But the price paid is: every unique label combination creates its own STREAM in Loki. `trace_id` is a value unique to each request, so making it a label means every request spawns a new stream — at meaningful traffic, this reaches millions of streams, slowing down both log ingest and query speed while inflating storage cost. So `trace_id` must live in the log CONTENT (typically structured JSON), queried back with a line filter (`{app="x"} |= "trace-123"`) or a JSON parser (`{app="x"} | json | trace_id="trace-123"`) — searching content is a sequential scan AFTER the label filter has already narrowed things down, but it's still fast because the candidate set has already shrunk. Rule of thumb for choosing labels: a label should only describe the SOURCE of a log — service, environment, region — values with low cardinality that stay stable over time, not a per-request attribute.

prompt: Your video service serves 10 million global users through a CDN edge (NGINX `proxy_cache`) in front of an origin. The diagram below shows the current request flow. You set `Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=31536000, immutable` on EVERY response — including the HLS manifest (`.m3u8`), which gets re-encoded with a new rendition every few minutes. After deploying, viewers report that even after a new rendition finished encoding, the player still only sees the old 2 quality levels for months. What's happening, and how would you fix the cache policy so it matches each content type correctly?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The cause is applying one cache policy to every content type. `s-maxage=31536000, immutable` is correct for **static** assets — an already-encoded `.ts` segment never changes content at that URL, so the CDN holding it for a year is safe. But the `.m3u8` manifest is **dynamic**: it can be rewritten when a new rendition is added, so giving it the same one-year TTL means the edge keeps serving the old HIT for a whole year — exactly why viewers never see the new rendition even though the origin updated long ago. Fix it by splitting the policy: the manifest and any endpoint that can change should use `Cache-Control: public, max-age=5, s-maxage=10, stale-while-revalidate=5` — the CDN holds it for just 10 seconds then revalidates, short enough to stay close to the real state while still absorbing most of the repeat load within that window. If an update needs to land immediately (without waiting the 10s), the origin calls a purge endpoint that sends HTTP `PURGE` to the CDN edge to evict that specific entry, forcing the next request to MISS and pull the fresh copy from the origin.

prompt: Your team is designing a queue for processing payment orders, where an acked message must ABSOLUTELY NEVER be lost. A teammate proposes a classic mirrored queue because 'it sounds familiar, we've used it for a long time.' Push back on this and explain which mechanism should be chosen for this situation.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
Proposing a classic mirrored queue because it's 'familiar' overlooks a crucial fact: as of RabbitMQ 3.13, the classic mirrored queue has been DEPRECATED — it shouldn't be chosen for a new system, especially a payment-processing system that absolutely cannot lose data. The replacement mechanism is the quorum queue, using the Raft consensus protocol: a record is only ACKNOWLEDGED to the client once the MAJORITY of replicas (e.g. 2 out of 3 nodes) have successfully written it to disk — this is a genuine durability guarantee, not 'send it and hope the other node syncs in time.' The core difference is most visible during failover: with a quorum queue, an already-acked message is guaranteed to survive a node dying, because it was already on the majority of replicas before the ack was returned, and the leader-election process when the primary node dies follows the predictable Raft mechanism. In contrast, the (older) mirrored queue mechanism can LOSE a message that hadn't finished syncing to a replica when the primary node dies abruptly — exactly the risk a payment system is not allowed to accept. The trade-off to accept: quorum queues cost higher write latency (waiting for majority consensus) and more memory per message compared to an ordinary classic queue — but this is a reasonable price, not a free lunch, for the guarantee that 'an acked message is never lost.'

prompt: The aggregator currently buckets clicks into 1-minute tumbling windows using an in-memory `Map<string, number>` (keyed by `${adId}|${windowStart}`), flushing periodically every 10 seconds to ClickHouse. At 10:05:34, the aggregator is bucketing window `10:05:00` (already counted 340 clicks) when the container gets suddenly killed by Kubernetes (OOM). What happens to those 340 clicks, and how would you redesign this to minimize the data-loss risk?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
If those 340 clicks hadn't been flushed to ClickHouse yet at the moment of the crash, they are PERMANENTLY LOST from the report — the entire aggregation state (`buckets: Map<string, number>`) exists only in the process's memory, with nothing making it durable between two flushes 10 seconds apart, so when the container is suddenly killed by Kubernetes (OOM), the `Map` disappears entirely along with whatever was counted but not yet written to ClickHouse. The problem is even worse if the Kafka offset for these 340 clicks WAS already committed before the crash (depending on when the commit is designed to happen): in that case, Kafka believes these messages were ALREADY processed, so a newly restarted consumer will NOT re-read them — the 340 clicks vanish without a trace, with no way to recover them. The first (weaker) mitigation is to shorten the flush interval, e.g. from 10 seconds to 2 seconds, to narrow the risk window — fewer clicks could get stuck in memory per crash, but this only reduces the probability, never eliminating the possibility of data loss entirely. The stronger mitigation is to reverse the order: ONLY commit the Kafka offset AFTER successfully flushing to ClickHouse, not the moment a message is counted into the in-memory bucket. With this ordering, if a crash happens mid-way (counted into the bucket but not yet flushed, so the offset isn't committed either), Kafka treats those messages as NOT YET processed and redelivers exactly that segment to a new consumer — recovering exactly those 340 clicks instead of losing them permanently. The key point that makes this SAFE rather than causing double-counting: the `ad_click_counts` table uses `ENGINE = ReplacingMergeTree() ORDER BY (adId, windowStart)`, so re-reading and re-flushing the exact same `(adId, windowStart)` pair is treated by ClickHouse as an OVERWRITE on the same key (idempotent upsert), not an accumulation into two separate rows — this is exactly why `ReplacingMergeTree` was chosen instead of a plain insert-only table.

prompt: Node A is the current leader (holds the lease in `leader_key`). A 2-second network blip prevents A from renewing in time; the lease expires and node B wins, becoming the new leader. Right after, A's network recovers and it tries to renew as usual (unaware it lost the role). The system renews via CAS (`if GET == myId then PEXPIRE`). What happens to A, and why is there no split brain?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
At the moment A tries to renew after its network recovers, the value in `leader_key` is no longer A's ID — it's now B's ID, since B won the `SET NX` quorum right after A's lease expired due to the network blip. A's renewal runs the Lua CAS: `if GET == myId then PEXPIRE`, checking whether the CURRENT value in the key equals A's own ID BEFORE renewing. Since the value is now B's ID, the condition `GET == myId` is false for A, so the Lua returns `0` and absolutely does not renew the TTL of a key that now belongs to B. A receives that `0` result — a clear OBSERVABLE signal that it's no longer the leader — and by correct design, A proactively steps down to become a follower instead of continuing to act as leader. There's no split brain at this moment because Redis always holds exactly ONE value in `leader_key`, and the CAS mechanism ensures no node can renew a key whose current value doesn't belong to it — the "exactly one leader" invariant holds even under this exact contention scenario. If renewal instead used a blind `PEXPIRE` (no CAS check), A would inadvertently renew the TTL of a key now belonging to B, causing both A and B to believe they're the leader — that would be actual split brain.

prompt: The news feed system currently uses pure fanout-on-write (push) for EVERY account. A KOL account with 8 million followers just posted, and the team discovers the fanout queue is severely backed up, affecting even the fanout of posts from ordinary users sharing the same queue. How do you analyze the cause and propose a solution?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The correct cause is: the push model (fanout-on-write) is safe when F (follower count) is small, but when F reaches millions like this KOL account (8 million), write amplification far exceeds acceptable limits — a SINGLE post spawns 8 million writes, enough to completely jam the fanout queue. Because the KOL's fanout and ordinary users' fanout go through ONE shared queue, the KOL's 8 million jobs consume all processing bandwidth, delaying even ordinary users' posts (only a few hundred followers) in a cascading chain — one account jamming the entire system. The core solution is to NOT use pure push for EVERY account: classify authors by a follower threshold (or an `isCelebrity` flag read from the DB), keeping ordinary users on the push-to-followers route (small F, acceptable write amplification, fast reads in exchange), while KOLs switch to a pull-at-read-time route (`expectedWrites = 1` — the post is only written once, no mass fanout). When reading a feed, the system needs MERGE-AT-READ: combine the already-pushed timeline (from ordinary authors followed) with a directly-pulled timeline from followed KOLs, then sort them together by descending `createdAt` — this is exactly the hybrid fanout model that Instagram, Twitter/X, and TikTok all operate a variant of. Beyond classifying authors, it's also worth separating ordinary-user fanout into its OWN dedicated queue away from other heavy tasks (e.g. by priority tier), so a future incident — even a smaller one — can no longer jam the whole system through a single shared queue.

prompt: `payment-service` orchestrates a transfer saga: debit the sender's wallet on `wallet-service`, then credit the receiver's. In one real run, the credit step returns an error (the receiver-side service is momentarily overloaded). Walk through the full flow: what should the orchestrator do next, what does the `saga_step` audit table record, and does the system end up committed or not.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
When the debit step runs, the orchestrator writes a `saga_step` row with status `started` before the HTTP call, then updates it to `ok` once wallet-service confirms — so the moment credit fails, the audit trail already tells you: debit succeeded, credit did not. The orchestrator responds by running a `compensate_debit` step — which under the hood is just another ordinary credit call to wallet-service, this time crediting the sender back for exactly the amount just debited. This is not a special rollback mechanism but a reversing business action, expressed in the same business vocabulary (debit ↔ credit). This compensating step is written `started` then `ok`/`failed` like every other step. The saga's final result is `status: "compensated"`: the sender is restored to their original balance, the receiver gets nothing — the system converges to a consistent state even though the transfer didn't complete, with no distributed rollback needed. What must be planned for: if the compensating step itself fails (say wallet-service is down at that exact moment), the saga is left stuck in an inconsistent state — the sender's money is gone but not yet refunded — so production must retry the compensation with backoff and alert ops via a "stuck sagas" dashboard, never silently swallow that failure.

prompt: A client is uploading a large file resumably (tus-protocol style): the server keeps a committed `Upload-Offset` per session. The client PATCHes a chunk with its offset, but due to a dropped connection, it re-sends the exact chunk that just succeeded (a stale offset). How should the server respond, and how should the client handle that response to keep uploading correctly?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The server keeps a "committed" offset per session and only accepts a PATCH when its offset exactly matches what it's waiting for. Since the re-sent chunk carries a stale offset — smaller than what the server already advanced to after the previous successful PATCH — the server must reject with HTTP 400 plus `expectedOffset`, never silently accepting it (which would duplicate data) or overwriting the offset (which would corrupt committed progress). Upon receiving that 400, the correct client behavior is to read `expectedOffset` (or call GET to ask for the session's current offset), then continue sending the next PATCH from that exact position — not re-sending what already succeeded, and not treating 400 as a hard failure that forces aborting the whole upload. This is precisely the intended, correct behavior: since the server never overwrites data when the offset is off, the operation is data-level idempotent — no matter how many times the client re-sends a stale chunk due to network errors, the final result stays consistent. It's not a bug to patch server-side.

prompt: A submarine cable is cut, completely separating the database between the US and SG regions. You are designing the money-transfer flow of a banking system. The interviewer asks: 'Right now, do you let users keep transacting on stale data, or return an error to protect correctness?'. Walk through the CP vs AP decision for this situation: which metric do you sacrifice, what mechanism produces that behavior, and the concrete risk if you choose wrong (e.g. double spending).
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
When the cable is cut, partition is an unavoidable fact and the US node cannot distinguish 'SG dead' from 'SG network-severed' — so it must choose C or A on the spot. For bank transfers, the answer is CP: sacrifice availability. Mechanism: in CP mode the transfer function synchronizes to the peer BEFORE adding to balance; on partition the sync times out (deliberately set low ~2s) → it throws and returns 503 'Network Partition Detected... transaction aborted to protect data'. If you wrongly pick AP, the system commits locally first then fires-and-forgets the sync: both US and SG accept writes, balances diverge, and an attacker can withdraw the same balance in both regions — that is double spending, unacceptable for money. The cost of CP is that users temporarily cannot transact during the partition, but that is the right trade-off for finance; AP only fits Facebook likes or Amazon carts, where eventual consistency is enough.

prompt: Your waiting-room system runs 5 API instances behind a load balancer (diagram below). Each instance, on receiving an enqueue request, calls `ZADD queue Date.now() userId` — using ITS OWN OS clock as the score. After going to production, users report the queue order is "unfair": someone who arrived 2 seconds later sometimes gets served BEFORE someone who arrived earlier. Explain the root cause, and redesign it to guarantee true FIFO regardless of how many instances there are.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The root cause is **clock skew**: each of the 5 instances reads `Date.now()` on its own machine's OS clock, and physical machine clocks always drift relative to each other (typically tens to hundreds of milliseconds even with NTP sync). So "arrived earlier" per node 1's clock isn't equivalent to "arrived earlier" per node 3's clock — a user served by a node whose clock runs slow can end up with a smaller score even though they actually arrived later, causing `ZPOPMIN` to admit them ahead of someone who arrived earlier but happened to be served by a fast-clock node. The fix is to stop trusting any node's local clock — derive the score from a SINGLE shared time/ordering source: call Redis `TIME` (Redis's own clock, one single point every node reads) as the score, or use an atomic Redis `INCR` as a monotonically increasing sequence number instead of a timestamp. Because `ZADD`/`INCR` on Redis's side are already atomic and all 5 nodes write to that same single source, ordering becomes consistent and monotonic — no longer dependent on which node behind the load balancer happened to handle the request.

prompt: You need to build a type-ahead search suggestion bar with instant feedback for a dictionary of 1 billion learned keywords from search history. A teammate proposes using SQL `WHERE keyword LIKE 'user_input%' ORDER BY frequency DESC LIMIT 10` with a B-tree index on the `keyword` column. How do you evaluate this proposal versus using a Trie structure, especially regarding complexity as the dictionary grows to 1 billion words?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
`LIKE 'prefix%'` with a B-tree index is NOT as bad as `LIKE '%X%'` — since a B-tree keeps data sorted, a prefix match (the sought string is at the START) leverages that structure, giving O(log N) complexity to locate the starting position over a dictionary of size N. But this is exactly the core difference from a Trie: looking up a prefix in a Trie costs only k steps down the tree (k = the length of the typed prefix), COMPLETELY INDEPENDENT of N — whether the dictionary has 1 thousand or 1 billion words, the step count stays k. As N grows to 1 billion, the difference becomes stark: the B-tree's O(log N) still GROWS with N (even if slowly, being logarithmic), while the Trie's O(k) doesn't change at all. For the exact type-ahead use case (only a few characters typed, k very small and fixed), a Trie keeps latency stable regardless of how large the dictionary gets, while a B-tree still pays a cost tied to N on every subsequent keystroke. Beyond lookup speed, a Trie also offers a ranking benefit SQL doesn't have out of the box: frequency is stored RIGHT ON the terminal node of each word, so locating a prefix (which is exactly a subtree in the tree) both gathers all candidates AND has the scores ready to sort in the SAME DFS traversal pass over that subtree — no separate `ORDER BY` step needed after filtering, as SQL requires. It's worth acknowledging nuance: if type-ahead frequency is low (autocomplete isn't the system's primary use case) or the dictionary isn't very large (a few million words), a B-tree + `LIKE 'prefix%'` solution remains simple and fast enough, without necessarily needing to build and operate a separate Trie structure.

prompt: Your team implemented a 3-step order saga (order → payment → inventory) using choreography (each service listens to events and decides its own reaction, no coordinator). After a few months, the saga grew to 8 steps (adding shipping, notification, loyalty points, fraud check...), and the team increasingly can't answer 'which step is a specific order stuck at'. Analyze why choreography starts showing problems at this scale, and propose a fix.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
Choreography has no central coordinator — each service listens to events and decides its own reaction, so the saga's entire logic is scattered across many different consumers, with no single place holding the 'full picture' of the flow. With a 3-step saga, this scattering is still easy to track by eye or scattered logs. But once it grows to 8 steps, no service — and no coordinator, since choreography has none — knows which step a specific order is currently at overall; this is exactly choreography's observability weakness as complexity grows, not a business logic bug at all. A short-term mitigation without changing architecture: attach a correlation id (e.g. `orderId`) to EVERY event emitted in the saga, so you can aggregate logs/tracing by that `orderId` and reconstruct a timeline after an incident, even without any central state. But once the saga is complex enough (8 steps and growing), a more thorough fix is to switch to orchestration: build a central coordinator that issues each step in the right order, actively calls compensation when a step fails, and — most importantly — clearly EXPOSES the current step of each saga instance for easier monitoring/debugging. Trade-off: the coordinator becomes a centralized logic point — and without redundancy for that coordinator itself, it can become a new single point of failure.

prompt: The diagram below shows the current driver-search flow: always `GEOSEARCH` with a fixed 500m radius around the pickup point. In the dense downtown area, this works fine. But in sparse suburban areas, many requests get "no ride found" even though a driver 1.2km away is actually available and willing. Product doesn't want to raise the fixed radius to 2km for EVERY request, since downtown would then have to scan far more unnecessary candidates. Redesign the driver-search flow to handle both areas.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The problem is that a FIXED radius doesn't match driver density that varies by area: 500m suffices downtown but misses drivers in sparse suburban areas even though they're within a reasonable service range. The right fix is **expanding-ring search**: start at a narrow radius (500m), and if `GEOSEARCH` doesn't return enough candidates, widen to the next level (1000m → 2000m → 5000m) and re-query, stopping IMMEDIATELY once enough drivers are found instead of always scanning the largest radius. This solves both areas correctly: in the dense area, the first ring (500m) is already enough so it stops right away — cost stays exactly as it was before, no increase at all; in the sparse area, the system automatically widens through subsequent rings until a driver is found, instead of forcing every request (even downtown ones) to pay for an unnecessarily large radius. Trade-off: expanding-ring costs more calls in sparse areas (one `GEOSEARCH` per ring), but each call is cheap and most stop early at an inner ring; an outermost ring is needed as a hard stop (e.g. 5000m) to avoid scanning forever when an area genuinely has no drivers.

prompt: Currently `service-a` calls `service-b` over plain HTTP inside the internal VPC — the team confidently says 'we're already inside a private VPC, so services can trust each other, no need for extra encryption or authentication between them.' One day, a pod gets compromised via a dependency vulnerability. Analyze the risk of the current model, and explain what mTLS changes FUNDAMENTALLY.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The current model is "trust by network location" (perimeter security): any traffic originating FROM INSIDE the VPC is treated as trustworthy by other services, with no step actually verifying the caller's identity. Once a pod is compromised via a dependency vulnerability, the attacker gets exactly what the system trusts — a valid NETWORK LOCATION inside the VPC — so every request it sends is accepted unconditionally by other services, even though the attacker holds no valid credential whatsoever. "Being inside the network" has been exploited into "being authorized." mTLS changes this FUNDAMENTALLY: it shifts the trust axis from NETWORK LOCATION to CA-BACKED IDENTITY. A shared internal CA issues a cert to each service; during the TLS handshake, instead of only the client verifying the server (one-way TLS — sufficient for public web), mTLS adds the reverse direction: the server ALSO requests and verifies the client's cert. For the exact compromise scenario above, the consequence is clear: a compromised pod that does NOT hold a valid private key + cert issued by the internal CA gets blocked right at the TLS handshake, before any business request ever touches application logic — "inside the network" no longer means "authorized." One important implementation note: the switch enforcing client authentication lives on the SERVER SIDE (`requestCert + rejectUnauthorized` in Node, `client-auth=need` in Envoy/Istio style, `RequireAndVerifyClientCert` in Go) — without this switch, sending a client cert is merely optional (the server doesn't enforce it), and zero-trust isn't truly achieved even with TLS enabled.

prompt: Your team has two systems that need rate limiting: (1) a billing API that charges per request, where miscounting even one request is unacceptable; (2) a public API with a limit of 1 million requests/minute/key across hundreds of thousands of keys. Would you pick sliding window log or sliding window counter for each, and why?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
For the billing API, pick **sliding window log**: it stores each request's timestamp in a ZSET, evicts timestamps outside the window via `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE`, then counts what's left with `ZCARD` — exactly accurate, matching the requirement that not even one request may be miscounted, not even by 0.003%. For the public API at 1 million requests/minute across hundreds of thousands of keys, pick **sliding window counter**: each key costs only two integers (current bucket + previous bucket) no matter how high the limit, so memory is O(1) per key — multiplied across hundreds of thousands of keys, it's still manageable. Using log here instead, each key could hold up to millions of timestamps in a ZSET, turning into a big key and making `ZCARD`/`ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` cost O(N), which can block Redis's single-threaded event loop. Conversely, using counter for billing means a ~0.003% estimation error that, however small, still violates the absolute-accuracy requirement of a charging system. In short: need exact accuracy at moderate scale → log; need massive scale and can tolerate a tiny error → counter.

prompt: Your service just committed a new order to the database when the process got killed RIGHT BEFORE sending the webhook notifying the payment partner. The order genuinely exists, but if you only "commit then send HTTP", the partner will never know about it. Design this with a transactional outbox: where is the event written, who actually pushes it out, and why does this design survive a crash at that exact moment.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
The root problem is that "commit DB then send HTTP" has a window between the two steps that can't be eliminated if they're two separate actions: if the process dies right in that window, the order genuinely exists but the webhook is never sent — the event is silently lost. (The reverse — sending HTTP then committing — is just as bad, because it can double-send if the DB rolls back after the send already happened). A transactional outbox solves exactly this by making "intent to send" part of the same ACID transaction as the business write: when inserting the order, also write a row into an `outbox_event` table (status `pending`) INSIDE THAT SAME transaction. Because both writes commit or roll back together, there's no window where the order exists but the event vanishes, or the event exists but the order never really happened. Actually sending the HTTP request is fully decoupled into a separate poller/worker that periodically reads `pending` rows and pushes them out — this is independent of the transaction that wrote the event. When the original process is killed right after commit, the `outbox_event` row is still sitting in the database in `pending` status; when the service restarts (or another poller is already running), it sees that row and sends the webhook — the event is never lost as long as the original transaction had already committed, no matter when the process dies afterward. This is an at-least-once guarantee: the poller could send an event more than once if it crashes between sending and updating status — preventing a duplicate effect on the receiver side is the job of an idempotency-key, a mechanism entirely separate from the outbox.

prompt: A user types the query "how does a service recover on its own when it hangs" but the best matching document in the system reads "configure health checks and auto-restart for the container" — the two sentences SHARE NOT A SINGLE WORD. The current full-text search (BM25 over an inverted index) returns 0 relevant results because no tokens match. The diagram below shows the flow you're proposing to add for this case. Explain the mechanism that lets it find the document despite sharing no keywords, and what must hold true for it to work reliably.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Full-text search fails because BM25 ranks by **token overlap** over an inverted index — with no shared words between "self-heals when hung" and "health check + auto-restart," the score is 0, even though the two sentences say the SAME THING at their core. Vector search solves exactly this by changing the unit of matching: both the query and the document are mapped by an **embedding model** into a dense vector in the SAME numeric space; two sentences with the same meaning are placed CLOSE TOGETHER in that space regardless of which words they use, so cosine distance is small and they match despite sharing no tokens. The lookup mechanism uses **HNSW** — a multi-layer graph for approximate nearest-neighbor search at close to O(log N), instead of sequential cosine comparison against every document (O(N)). The required condition for all of this to be reliable: the document and the query must be embedded by the EXACT SAME model and version — if one side uses model A and the other uses model B (or a different version), each falls into its own separate embedding space, and comparing cosine across two different spaces is completely meaningless: search still "runs" with no error but silently returns garbage.

prompt: You created an index on the `is_active` (boolean) column of the `users` table, expecting `WHERE is_active = true` to run faster. But `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` still shows the planner picking a `Seq Scan`, completely ignoring the index you just created. Explain why the planner 'ignores' an available index, whether this is a bug, and what you'd do next.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
This isn't a bug — it's correct behavior from a cost-based query planner. `is_active` is boolean with only 2 distinct values, so each value typically covers a large share of the table (low selectivity) — if 90% of users are active, filtering `is_active = true` still keeps 90% of the rows. When a filter keeps most of the table, hopping through the index and then randomly jumping (random I/O) into the heap to read each matching row is far more expensive than a single sequential scan over the whole table, so the planner estimates the cost and deliberately picks `Seq Scan` — the index exists but is intentionally skipped. What to do next: if this index was never used by any other query (check via system statistics), drop it, since it only costs write overhead without any read benefit. If you still need to speed up filtering by `is_active`, the right fix is a partial index — indexing only the rare value group (e.g. only `is_active = false` users if that's the minority) so that index's selectivity is genuinely high.

prompt: A digital wallet system publishes 3 consecutive events for the SAME account: `MoneyDeposited(100)`, `MoneyWithdrawn(30)`, `MoneyDeposited(50)`. The team discovers the consumer sometimes receives and processes these 3 events OUT OF ORDER, causing the computed balance to be wrong. The producer currently publishes WITHOUT a key. Explain why the order gets scrambled, and to what extent Kafka guarantees ordering.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
Kafka only guarantees ordering (FIFO) WITHIN ONE partition, not at all across the entire topic. The cause of the balance mismatch: since the producer publishes these 3 events WITHOUT a key, Kafka spreads them round-robin across multiple different partitions — `MoneyDeposited(100)` might land in partition 0, `MoneyWithdrawn(30)` in partition 1, `MoneyDeposited(50)` in partition 2. Nothing forces the consumer to read these three partitions in the chronological order they were published — each partition is consumed independently, so the order OBSERVED at the consumer can be completely different from the order things actually happened, causing an incorrectly computed balance (e.g. applying a withdrawal before its corresponding deposit). The fix: publish every event for an account with a stable PARTITION KEY — here, `accountId`. Kafka hashes this key value to pick a partition, so for the same key, ALL events always land in exactly ONE fixed partition; and since FIFO is guaranteed within a partition, the three events for the same account are now processed CORRECTLY in the order published. Trade-off: no total order across the whole topic (events for DIFFERENT accounts can still freely interleave across partitions), but that's acceptable since ordering is only genuinely needed within ONE account, not between different accounts.

prompt: A user opens the chat app on their phone (connected to node-1) and on their laptop (connected to node-2) at the same time. A few minutes later, the user closes the laptop tab but leaves the phone open. The current presence system uses a Redis bitmap `presence:online` with `SETBIT`/`BITCOUNT`, and each node runs `SETBIT userId 1` on connect and `SETBIT userId 0` immediately on disconnect. What happens to this user's 'online' green dot, and how would you redesign this mechanism to be correct?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
With the current design, this user's green dot will incorrectly TURN OFF the moment the laptop tab closes, even though the phone still has the app open with a live connection — because every disconnect calls `SETBIT userId 0` right away without checking whether the user has any other active connection. The root problem is that one user's online state is really the union of MULTIPLE connections (phone, laptop, multiple tabs), which can be scattered across different nodes — so 'has the user really gone offline' is a GLOBAL decision, not something inferable from a single local disconnect event happening on exactly one node. The correct fix is to add a reference-counting layer stored IN REDIS (not a per-node memory variable, since the same user's two connections can be on two different nodes): a counter `presence:conn:<userId>` — `INCR` on every connect, `DECR` on every disconnect. Only when the counter transitions from 0 to 1 (the first connection) does it actually `SETBIT userId 1`; and only when the counter drops to 0 or below (the LAST connection just left) does it `SETBIT userId 0`. In the scenario above: the phone connects first (counter 0→1, bit turned on), the laptop connects after (counter 1→2, bit unchanged since it's already on); when the laptop disconnects (counter 2→1, still one live connection, so the bit is NOT cleared) — the user still correctly shows as online until the phone itself also disconnects (counter 1→0, only then is the bit cleared). To confirm the fix, replay this exact scenario (two connections on two nodes, close one) and verify `BITCOUNT` stays unchanged until the last connection actually leaves.

prompt: A marketing campaign just enqueued 500,000 SMS jobs nearly at once, bloating the SMS queue. Right after, a user clicks 'resend OTP code' to log in — their OTP SMS job gets enqueued AFTER those 500,000 marketing jobs. If the worker processes jobs in strict FIFO queue order, that user would have to wait a very long time to receive their OTP — unacceptable. Design a mechanism so OTP is always sent nearly instantly regardless of how bloated the marketing queue is.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The root problem is that if the system relies solely on FIFO (enqueue order) to process jobs, an extremely urgent OTP job enqueued AFTER 500,000 marketing jobs would always have to wait behind all of them — FIFO has absolutely no concept of 'this job matters more than that one'. The correct fix is to attach a NUMERIC `priority` field at the QUEUE LEVEL to each job at enqueue time: BullMQ already supports `opts.priority` (the smaller the number, the sooner a worker picks it up), so when enqueuing the OTP job we assign it a LOWER (higher-priority) value than marketing. The key point is priority must live AT THE QUEUE LEVEL, not implemented as if-else logic inside the worker ('if this job is OTP, prioritize it') — because the worker can only PULL jobs out of the queue in the exact order the queue itself has already arranged; if the worker decides priority after already pulling a job via FIFO, it's already too late, since the OTP job hasn't even reached its turn to be pulled and seen by the worker. Rate-limiting (a token bucket by `user × channel`) plays a COMPLETELY DIFFERENT role here: it blocks spam by REJECTING a request once a user/channel exceeds a threshold within a time window — it never changes the processing ORDER of jobs already accepted, so on its own it does not solve 'OTP stuck behind the marketing queue'. The two mechanisms must work together: rate-limit gates BEFORE enqueueing (blocking abuse), priority decides ORDER AFTER enqueueing (ensuring urgency gets processed first). To confirm the design is correct, publish a batch of low-priority jobs (marketing) first, then publish a high-priority job (OTP) right after, and verify the worker processes the OTP job FIRST even though it entered the queue LATER — proving priority beats enqueue order.

prompt: A site's `robots.txt` has two rules: `Disallow: /admin` and `Allow: /admin/public`. Your crawler needs to decide whether it may fetch `/admin/public/report.html`. Apply RFC 9309 correctly and explain the decision.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Both rules match `/admin/public/report.html`: `Disallow: /admin` matches because it's a prefix of the path, and `Allow: /admin/public` also matches because it too is a prefix. Per RFC 9309, when multiple rules match one path, the rule with the MORE SPECIFIC — that is, longer — path wins, regardless of whether it's `Allow` or `Disallow`. Here `/admin/public` (longer) beats `/admin` (shorter), so the crawler IS ALLOWED to fetch `/admin/public/report.html` even though it sits under the disallowed `/admin`. The design rationale for longest-match: a longer path expresses a MORE SPECIFIC intent from the site owner — here clearly "block the whole /admin area, but reopen specifically the /admin/public area for crawlers." If rules were applied by order of appearance in the file (e.g. the first rule wins) instead of by length, the outcome wouldn't reflect the site owner's actual intent and would depend arbitrarily on how they happened to write the file.

prompt: You need to store 'which users liked which posts' to serve two queries: (1) quickly check whether a specific user liked a specific post, and (2) find users who liked BOTH post A and post B (to suggest friends with shared interests). A teammate proposes using a Redis list, one list per post containing the userIds who liked it. How do you evaluate this proposal, and which structure fits better?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
A list is the wrong fit: checking whether a userId is in the list requires a linear O(N) scan, and a list does not auto-dedupe — wrong both on complexity and on correctness for a membership problem. A Redis set is the right structure: members live in a hashtable, so `SADD` and the membership check `SISMEMBER` are both O(1), and duplicates are auto-rejected. For query (2), "who liked both A and B," `SINTER likes:postA likes:postB` computes the intersection right on the Redis server and returns the shared users directly — instead of pulling both lists into the application and looping to compare pairs, this pushes the set computation down to where the data lives. Two caveats: a set does not preserve like-time ordering, so if "most recent likes" is needed later you must move to a sorted set with score = timestamp; and for an extremely hot post with millions of likes, avoid `SMEMBERS` reading the whole set (an O(N) command that can block Redis) — use the set only for membership and set algebra (`SINTER`/`SUNION`/`SDIFF`), never to enumerate everything.

prompt: Your system has 12 microservices running on a managed cloud Kubernetes cluster, where only 2 services (the main API and a webhook service) need to be reachable from the internet, and the other 10 only call each other internally. A teammate proposes: 'To be safe, let's just declare `type: LoadBalancer` on all 12 Services.' Push back on this proposal and redesign the Service-type choices sensibly.

:::muted
Chốt

The 'just LoadBalancer everything to be safe' proposal is wrong on both cost and security. The three Service types have different access scopes: `ClusterIP` (default) is only reachable FROM INSIDE the cluster — exactly what service-to-service communication needs; `NodePort` opens a fixed port on every node, good for dev/test or when you run your own load balancer in front; `LoadBalancer` provisions a REAL load balancer from the cloud provider with a public IP — each one typically costs money and is an internet-facing exposure point. Declaring `LoadBalancer` for all 12 services means 10 services that should only talk internally also get exposed to the outside — wasting cost (12 IPs/LBs instead of far fewer needed) and needlessly widening the attack surface. The sensible design: keep `ClusterIP` (default) for the 10 internal services since they only need to call each other within the cluster; for the 2 internet-facing services, put an `Ingress` in front to route by host/path to the corresponding ClusterIP Services, and you only need ONE `LoadBalancer` at the edge for that Ingress — saving IPs/cost while consolidating TLS termination and HTTP routing logic into a single managed point instead of scattering it across many separate LoadBalancers.

prompt: The team reports something odd: the dead-letter table keeps filling up with events the receiver NEVER actually rejected — they got parked exactly while the circuit breaker was `open`. Below is the code that handles a job when the circuit blocks the request. Find the bug and explain precisely why it produces this symptom.

:::muted

The bug is the order of two lines: `throw new DelayedError()` is called BEFORE `await job.moveToDelayed(...)`, so the `moveToDelayed` line is dead code — it can never execute because the function has already thrown on the previous line. BullMQ's real contract is "I already moved the job, don't count this" — `DelayedError` only has that effect when the job has genuinely been rescheduled via `moveToDelayed` beforehand. Here the job was never moved, so as far as BullMQ is concerned it's still stuck in the `active` state with no worker actually processing it anymore. After a while, BullMQ's stalled-job detector notices this "active" job has no heartbeat and automatically re-queues it for retry — and that automatic retry IS counted as a real failed attempt, exactly as if the receiver had rejected the request. Repeat across a few `open` cycles and the event exhausts its `attempts` and gets parked into the dead letter table — even though the receiver never actually saw that request. Fix: swap the order — `await job.moveToDelayed(Date.now() + 5000, token)` first, then `throw new DelayedError()`, matching BullMQ's real contract.

prompt: QA reports: when a request sends a notification to BOTH email and SMS with the same `messageId`, only the email actually gets sent — the SMS is silently skipped by the worker even though it was never sent at all. Below is the producer code that attaches `messageId` to each job. Find the bug.

The bug is that jobs for both channels (email and sms) are stamped with the SAME `messageId: baseMessageId` value, with nothing in the key distinguishing the channel. At the worker level, before dispatching, the system calls `dedup.tryAcquire(messageId)` using `SET NX` to prevent duplicates: the email job (assume processed first) calls `tryAcquire(baseMessageId)`, succeeds since that key never existed, so email sends normally. Right after, the sms job also calls `tryAcquire(baseMessageId)` — with the EXACT SAME key email just used — but that key has already been claimed by email, so `tryAcquire` returns `false`, and the processor treats this as 'already processed (duplicate)' and skips it, even though sms was never actually sent. The core issue: the dedup mechanism is working EXACTLY as designed (blocking two uses of the same idempotency key), but it's applied at the WRONG SCOPE — it should only block RESENDING the same channel (e.g. BullMQ redelivering the email job twice), not treat two different channels (email vs sms) of the same logical `messageId` as 'duplicates of each other'. The correct fix is to namespace the idempotency key PER CHANNEL: `messageId: \`${baseMessageId}:${channel}\``, so email gets key `abc:email` while sms gets `abc:sms` — two completely independent keys, each channel deduping within its own scope without colliding with any other channel. To confirm the fix, test a request with `channels: ["email", "sms"]` and the same `messageId`, and verify both jobs actually reach the provider (neither skipped as 'duplicate'); then separately test BullMQ redelivering the same job (same channel) to confirm dedup still correctly blocks the case it's actually meant to block.

prompt: Production is throwing `deadlock detected` errors from Postgres at random, always when two opposite-direction transfers (A→B and B→A) run nearly at the same time. The transfer code below is the culprit. Debug it: pinpoint exactly where the deadlock comes from, explain the ABBA mechanism, and fix it correctly.

:::muted
Chốt
:::
The bug is that both `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` calls lock in the exact order the function's parameters arrive — `fromId` first, `toId` second — instead of a deterministic order like id. When an A→B transfer runs, it locks A first then waits on B. If, at that same moment, a B→A transfer is running, it has already locked B and is waiting on A. The two transactions are now waiting on each other: the first holds A while waiting on B, the second holds B while waiting on A — a classic wait cycle called an ABBA deadlock. Postgres detects this cycle after a delay and proactively rolls back one of the two transactions with a `deadlock detected` error — this isn't a random stroke of bad luck but an inevitable consequence whenever two opposite-direction transfers touch the same pair of accounts nearly simultaneously. The correct fix is to acquire locks in a DETERMINISTIC ORDER independent of transfer direction — typically `const ids = [fromId, toId].sort()` then lock in that sorted order (or a single `SELECT ... WHERE id = ANY($1) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE`). With this, regardless of whether the transfer goes A→B or B→A, both concurrent transactions always try to lock the smaller-id row first — the one that arrives second simply waits cleanly for the first to commit, and a wait cycle can never form.

prompt: QA reports: the late-data detection NEVER marks any event as `late`, even when deliberately sending an event with an `eventTime` 5 minutes old while other events arrive with the current time. Below is the watermark-handling code. Find the bug.

The bug is that the line `this.watermarkMs = eventMs` runs BEFORE the lateness check, causing the watermark to be updated by the very event BEING EVALUATED before it's used to judge that SAME event. For an event whose `eventTime` is newer than the current watermark (the most common case when tests send events in chronological order), the watermark gets pulled up to EXACTLY that event's `eventMs` BEFORE the comparison — so the condition `eventMs < watermarkMs - tolerance` is always false for that event (since `watermarkMs` now equals `eventMs`), and it never marks itself late — this by itself is CORRECT and not a bug. The real bug surfaces in the situation contrary to the design's intent: the watermark is supposed to represent 'the latest timestamp seen FROM PRIOR events', used as the baseline to judge whether a NEWLY arriving event should be considered late relative to what's already been seen — but because the code updates the watermark using this SAME event's `eventMs` before the comparison, the watermark no longer represents 'the past' but blends in 'the present', so the lateness comparison loses all real meaning (an event always gets compared against its own value, not against a watermark set by OTHER events). The correct fix is to reverse the order: check lateness FIRST (comparing `eventMs` against the CURRENT watermark, i.e. the watermark set by PRIOR events), and ONLY AFTER deciding late or accepted, advance the watermark using this event's `eventMs` — so that SUBSEQUENT events have a properly meaningful watermark to compare against. This is exactly the `if (late) {...} else { advance watermark; ...fraud check... }` structure in the lesson's original code. To test correctly: send sequentially an event with `eventTime = now`, then an event with `eventTime = now - 5 minutes`, and assert the second event has `status: "late"` — the buggy version fails this because the watermark gets pulled up by the second event itself (if its `eventMs`, despite being old, is still greater than the initially very low watermark) before the comparison happens.

prompt: The team reports that occasionally an order is created successfully (it exists in the `orders` table) but inventory-service NEVER receives the event to decrement stock — with no error log at all on order-service. Read the code below, identify the bug, and propose a thorough fix.

:::muted
Chốt
:::
This is the classic dual-write bug: writing to the database (`orderRepository.save`) and publishing an event (`kafkaProducer.send`) are TWO separate operations on two different systems (Postgres and Kafka), with no transaction spanning both. The failure scenario: if the process dies — crash, connection drop, pod killed — RIGHT AFTER the DB write commits successfully but BEFORE `kafkaProducer.send` gets to run, the order is already in the `orders` table but the `order.created` event never exists. This is exactly why there's no error log: the code simply never reached the publish line, it didn't throw and get swallowed. The thorough fix is Transactional Outbox: instead of publishing directly to Kafka within the request, write BOTH the `order` AND an event record representing it into ONE `outbox` table within the SAME database transaction as creating the order — meaning either both commit or both roll back, closing the gap between the two operations. A separate relay process (periodically polling the `outbox` table, or using CDC like Debezium reading the WAL directly) reads unsent outbox records, pushes them to Kafka, then marks them sent — if the relay itself dies mid-way, it just re-reads unmarked outbox records on the next run, losing no events. Verify by simulating a crash RIGHT AFTER the DB write step in a test environment and confirming the event still gets relayed to Kafka after the system restarts.

prompt: The team reports: two actions `UserSuspended` and `UserReactivated` for the SAME user are sometimes processed by the consumer out of order — a user who was just suspended appears reactivated first, causing a serious business bug. Read the producer code below and identify the bug.

:::muted
Chốt
:::
The bug is that `kafkaProducer.send` does NOT pass a `key` for the message. Without a key, the Kafka client defaults to round-robin message distribution across the topic's partitions — so two consecutive `SUSPENDED` and `REACTIVATED` events for the SAME `userId` can easily land in two DIFFERENT partitions. Since Kafka only guarantees FIFO (order preservation) WITHIN a partition, two events sitting in separate partitions have no ordering constraint between them at all — the consumer can perfectly well read and process `REACTIVATED` BEFORE `SUSPENDED` even though it was published later, exactly matching the reported symptom (a user's status flipping backwards). The fix: add `key: userId` when sending the message. Kafka hashes this `userId` value to pick a partition, so for the same `userId`, EVERY event always lands in exactly ONE fixed partition — and since FIFO guarantees correct order within that partition, the two `SUSPENDED` → `REACTIVATED` events for the same user are now always processed in publish order. Verify by publishing several status pairs for the same `userId` in a row after the fix, running it repeatedly, and confirming the consumer ALWAYS receives them in the same order they were published — no longer at the mercy of round-robin luck.

prompt: This is a TypeScript illustration (the module is multi-language). The team reports two nodes both claiming to be leader at once and both running the job — even though each node believes it "renewed successfully." Find the bug in the renewal code below.

:::muted

The bug is in `renewLeadership`: it calls `redis.pexpire("leader_key", leaseMs)` BLINDLY, never checking whether the current value of `leader_key` actually equals `myId` before renewing the TTL. The split-brain scenario: old leader A gets paused (network/GC) past its lease, the key expires, node B wins `SET NX` and becomes the new leader with `leader_key = B`. When A recovers and calls `renewLeadership(A_id, ...)`, the blind `PEXPIRE` still executes successfully — it only renews the TTL of the current key, WITHOUT CARING what value is inside — so the TTL of a key now belonging to B gets extended. Both A and B end up believing they hold the valid leader role: A because renewal "succeeded," B because it genuinely just won quorum — that's split brain. The correct fix is replacing the blind `PEXPIRE` with a Lua CAS: `if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[2]) else return 0 end`, run via `EVAL`/`EVALSHA` so the read-and-renew happens in ONE atomic operation — A's renewal call now returns `0` since the key's value is `B`, not `A`, and A steps down instead of continuing to act as leader. The "skip CAS to renew faster" comment doesn't hold up: the CAS check only adds one `GET` INSIDE the same Lua script, still a single Redis round-trip, with no meaningful slowdown compared to a plain `PEXPIRE` — while the trade-off is eliminating the split-brain risk entirely.

prompt: The interviewer says: 'Design me a URL shortener that handles 100 million new URLs per month, redirects must be fast and almost never fail'. Walk through how you approach it with the 4-step process (clarify requirements → estimate → high-level design → deep dive). In particular: estimate rough write QPS / read QPS / peak QPS from the 100M/month figure and show how that very number leads to the conclusion 'we need a distributed store + cache'.

:::muted
Bottom line

Follow the 4 steps, and the key is to let the numbers drive the architecture. Step 1 (clarify): functional = shorten URL + redirect (+ custom alias, link expiration); non-functional = 99.99% availability (redirects must not fail), redirect < 50ms, and read-heavy at 10:1 — lock that ratio early because it drives every calculation. Step 2 (estimate): writeQps ≈ 100M / (30×24×3600) ≈ 39; readQps = 39 × 10 = 390; peakQps = (39+390) × 5 ≈ 2145; 10-year storage ≈ a few TB. peakQps ~2145 crossing the ~1000 threshold is the tipping point: conclude we need distributed NoSQL (Cassandra/DynamoDB) + Redis cache — whereas at just 1M/month peakQps ~55, one Postgres with a read replica is enough. Step 3 (high-level design): Load Balancer → API nodes → distributed key-value store + distributed cache (Redis) in front of the DB for read-heavy + a hash generator (Base62). Step 4 (deep dive): every bottleneck gets a remediation — write contention → sharding; synchronous heavy tasks → message queue for async; don't jump to microservices early (start with monolith if MVP). And remember the process is a loop: a new constraint in step 4 sends you back to step 2.

prompt: The team reports the `order.process` queue is completely STALLED — consumer CPU spikes, throughput drops to 0, even though the broker is healthy. Read the consumer code below and identify the cause.

Chốt

The cause is a poison message — a message the consumer can NEVER successfully process, e.g. a schema mismatch making `JSON.parse` always throw, or a business logic bug that always throws for this exact payload — combined with the `catch` treating EVERY kind of error identically with `channel.nack(msg, false, true)`. `requeue=true` puts the message back at the FRONT of the queue for redelivery; if that message always causes an error, it gets pulled out and reprocessed, throws again, gets nacked with requeue=true again, looping INFINITELY — this loop consumes all consumer CPU (continuously parsing and processing) and blocks every other VALID message behind it in the queue from ever being reached, exactly matching the 'CPU spikes, throughput drops to 0' symptom. The fix: configure `x-dead-letter-exchange` (DLX) on the main queue, and in the error branch, call `nack(msg, false, false)` — i.e., do NOT requeue — so RabbitMQ automatically routes the bad message to a separate dead-letter queue instead of looping it infinitely on the main queue. With a quorum queue, you can additionally use `x-delivery-limit` to cap the number of redeliveries before auto-dead-lettering, avoiding the need to manually count retries in code. Verify by publishing a message with a deliberately malformed schema and confirming it appears exactly ONCE on the dead-letter queue, no longer looping and stalling the main queue.

The team traces it to the code below, which runs every minute as a cron job to export an 'all online users' report. The cause is `SMEMBERS` — an O(N) command that reads the ENTIRE set (here, ~3 million members) in a single call. Because Redis processes commands on ONE thread, while `SMEMBERS` runs, the event loop is entirely occupied until it finishes reading the whole set — every other client, even simple O(1) commands like `GET`/`SET`, must queue and wait. Fix it by replacing `SMEMBERS` with `SSCAN` using a cursor: read the set in small batches (e.g. COUNT 100 per call), and between batches Redis can still serve other clients — trading a slower report job (more round-trips) for never blocking the whole system. prompt: Since last week, some new documents have been failing to index into Elasticsearch with the error `mapper_parsing_exception: failed to parse field [price] of type [long]`, even though indexing worked fine for months before. The indexing code has NOT changed. Debug it: what's the root cause, and how do you fix it so it doesn't happen again?

:::muted
Bottom line
