The root cause is DYNAMIC MAPPING: `indexProduct` declares no explicit mapping at all, so Elasticsearch guesses each field's data type based on the FIRST document ever indexed into the `products` index. The first document (`price: 100`) is an INTEGER, so ES guessed `price` as type `long` and LOCKED that mapping for the entire index. Months later, a new document with `price: 99.99` (a DECIMAL) gets force-parsed against the already-locked `long` mapping — and `long` cannot hold a decimal part, causing the `mapper_parsing_exception`. This is NOT an indexing code bug (the code hasn't changed, as stated) but an inevitable consequence of letting dynamic mapping guess the type from the very first document: once a field's mapping is locked, it CANNOT change type on a running index — a ticking time bomb waiting for a document shaped differently from the first one to appear. Fix going forward: declare an EXPLICIT mapping for `price` as `double` (or `scaled_float` if tighter currency precision control is needed) BEFORE indexing any document — always `PUT /index/_mapping` with an explicit schema before writing real data, entirely removing the dependency on "what the first document happens to look like." Remediation for the CURRENT index that already has the wrong mapping: mapping CANNOT be fixed in place — you must create a new index with an explicit `price: double` mapping, reindex all old data (using the `_reindex` API) into the new index, then switch the read/write alias to point at the new index.

prompt: This is a TypeScript illustration (the module is multi-language). The team reports a small number of URLs getting enqueued TWICE into the ZSET frontier despite using a bloom filter for dedup. Find the cause in the code below and assess its severity.

The cause is that `BF.EXISTS` and `BF.ADD` are two separate Redis commands, not wrapped in one atomic operation. When two workers call `enqueue` for the same brand-new URL nearly simultaneously, both can see `BF.EXISTS = 0` before either manages to run `BF.ADD` to mark it seen — both proceed and both `ZADD` the URL into `frontier:queue`, resulting in a duplicate enqueue even though the bloom filter ends up recording it as "seen" exactly once. If the system genuinely requires strict "exactly-once" enqueue (e.g. per-URL fetch cost is very expensive), the correct fix is to merge all three operations `BF.EXISTS + BF.ADD + ZADD` into ONE Lua script called via `EVAL`/`EVALSHA` — Redis runs the script as a single command on one thread, so the whole check-and-set chain becomes atomic with no race window left. prompt: After deploying, ops reports that some drivers in Ho Chi Minh City "vanish" from search results even though their app keeps pinging normally (no errors, no exceptions in the logs). Read the location-update function below and find the bug — nothing crashes, but the data is silently wrong.

:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The bug is the `GEOADD` parameter order. Redis GEO follows the mathematical `(x=longitude, y=latitude)` convention, so the correct call is `GEOADD key longitude latitude member`. The current code calls `geoadd("drivers:geo", ping.lat, ping.lng, ping.driverId)` — reversed to `(lat, lng)` instead of `(lng, lat)`. This is a classic silent bug: Redis does NOT validate or error when given swapped coordinates — it "succeeds," just placing the driver at a completely different point on the map (swapping the x/y axis roles typically shifts the point far away, sometimes into an ocean or another country depending on the magnitude of lat/lng). Since `updateDriverLocation` never throws, the logs stay clean, but every `GEOSEARCH` around the driver's real location will never find them because the data was wrong from the moment it was written. Fix: swap the order back — `geoadd("drivers:geo", ping.lng, ping.lat, ping.driverId)`. To prevent recurrence, wrap the geoadd call in a SINGLE helper function taking a clearly-named object (`{ lat, lng }`) that reorders internally, instead of every call-site having to remember Redis's `(lng, lat)` convention.

prompt: A teammate just edited the function that calls purge on the NGINX edge — they added an `Accept-Encoding` header to the PURGE request "for consistency with the other GET requests." After deploying, some keys purge fine while others get an unpredictable `412 Precondition Failed` from NGINX. Read the code below and pinpoint exactly why adding this header causes the error, based on how `proxy_cache_key` is configured.

:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The bug is treating PURGE like GET. NGINX is configured with `proxy_cache_key "$request_uri"` — the cache key is a plain URI, with no `Accept-Encoding` factored in. When the purge request attaches `Accept-Encoding: gzip`, it doesn't match the stored entry (which may be cached under a different encoding variant), and NGINX/`ngx_cache_purge` returns `412 Precondition Failed` because it treats this as an unmet request condition rather than a valid delete-by-key. "Consistent with GET" is the wrong intuition: GET needs `Accept-Encoding` for content negotiation to pick the right compressed variant, while PURGE only needs to match `$request_uri` to identify the RIGHT entry to delete — an extra header only throws that off. Fix: drop `Accept-Encoding` entirely from the PURGE request, keep `decompress: false`, and don't attach any other Vary-related header. Verify by creating two cached variants (two different `Accept-Encoding` values for the same key), calling a clean PURGE (no headers), then confirming the next GET returns `X-Cache-Status: MISS` for both variants.

prompt: After a developer added `request_id` to a metric's labels 'to make tracing individual requests easier in Prometheus', Prometheus's RAM kept climbing for hours until the container got OOM-killed. Debug it: why does adding ONE label cause this, and how do you fix it while still being able to trace individual requests without crashing Prometheus?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
Prometheus treats EVERY unique label-value combination as its own time-series, kept entirely in memory. `method`, `route` (already resolved to a template), and `status_code` inherently have low, finite cardinality — the total number of combinations is a fixed number no matter how many requests occur. But `request_id` is a freshly generated UUID on every request, never repeating — adding it to the labels means EVERY request creates a brand new series. So the total series count is no longer bounded but grows exactly with the NUMBER OF REQUESTS processed — this is High Cardinality, and since series are never stopped from being created, Prometheus's RAM keeps climbing until it gets OOM-killed, matching the observed symptom exactly. This is not a logic bug (`inc()` still increments correctly), but a label DESIGN bug: confusing "something to filter/group by on an aggregate metric" (a label — must be bounded) with "a unique identifier of a specific event" (belongs to a log or trace, not a metric). Fix it by removing `request_id` entirely from `labelNames`; if you still need to trace a specific request, put `request_id` into a structured log line or a distributed-tracing span — where each record is independent and does not accumulate as a time-series in Prometheus's memory. Verify by reading `/api/v1/status/tsdb` to check `numSeries`: before the fix it grows unboundedly with request count, after the fix it's bounded only by the finite `method`×`route`×`status_code` combinations.

prompt: A user reports: 'I just followed an account, but my feed shows NONE of their old posts, even though they posted a lot before I followed them — only posts made AFTER I followed show up.' The system uses pure fanout-on-write (push). Debug the cause and fix the `follow` flow to meet expectations.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The cause matches the symptom exactly: the push model (fanout-on-write) ONLY fans out a post AT THE MOMENT it's published — `publishPost` only writes the postId into the timelines of followers that ALREADY EXIST in the `follows` table right when the function is called. `followUser` currently ONLY records the follow relationship in the DB without touching the ZSET `feed:{followerId}` of the person who just followed — so any post published BEFORE the follow moment (when the follow relationship didn't exist yet, so `publishPost` never fanned it out to this person) will PERMANENTLY never appear in their feed, matching exactly the user's reported symptom: only posts made after following show up. Fix it by adding a BACKFILL step to `followUser`: after recording the follow relationship, actively fetch the N MOST RECENT posts of `authorId` (from Postgres, `ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT N`) and `ZADD` each into `feed:{followerId}`, so the new timeline immediately has a reasonable amount of historical content instead of being empty. A reasonable trade-off is needed: if the just-followed author has tens of thousands of old posts, do NOT backfill the ENTIRE history — that would cost reverse write amplification (one follow spawning tens of thousands of ZSET writes), and most old posts have no display value in a real-time feed anyway; backfilling only the N MOST RECENT posts (e.g. N=20-50) is enough for the "see content immediately" experience. Verify with a test: call `publishPost` a few times BEFORE calling `followUser`, then read `feed:{followerId}` with `ZREVRANGE`, asserting posts published before the follow moment (within the N limit) all appear, not just posts published after following.

prompt: This is a TypeScript illustration (the module is multi-language). After a Redis restart for maintenance, ops discovers every in-progress upload session is now treated as "zero bytes uploaded" even though clients had actually sent over half their files. Find the bug in the PATCH handler below.

This is really a desync between "hot state" (Redis) and "committed state" (the actual file data), not file data loss, but the client-facing consequence is being forced to re-upload from scratch. The correct fix: every successful PATCH must write to both — Redis for O(1) read/write on subsequent PATCHes, and Postgres (the `uploadOffset` column on `upload_session`) as the durable source of truth. When reading the offset and Redis has no key, fall back to reading Postgres and reload it into Redis, instead of assuming offset zero. Verify with a test: PATCH a few chunks, simulate the Redis key being lost, PATCH again, and assert `expectedOffset` matches the real value in Postgres.

prompt: After adding 50,000 new documents (much shorter than the existing corpus) to the search system, QA reports that relevance scores for ALL the OLD documents suddenly shifted, even though nothing in the BM25 formula changed. Read the code below and pinpoint the bug that lets adding new documents corrupt the scores of OLD ones.

Bottom line

The bug is in `ensureAvgdl`: it computes `avgdl` exactly ONCE — guarded by the `this.initialized` flag — on the very first `search` call, and never recomputes it no matter how many more times `addDocument` is called afterward. So `avgdl` is frozen at the corpus's value AS OF that first search. When 50,000 new (shorter) documents are added, the corpus's true average length changes, but `this.avgdl` still holds the old value. Because the BM25 formula uses `B * (dl / avgdl)` to normalize length for EVERY document (including old ones that never changed), a stale `avgdl` corrupts the score across the whole corpus — not because the formula is wrong, but because the `avgdl` input fed into it is out of date. Fix: drop the "compute once and lock" pattern entirely — recompute `avgdl` from the current `docs` map EVERY time `search` is called, or maintain `avgdl` incrementally right inside `addDocument` (keep a running total length + document count, dividing when needed) so it always reflects the corpus's latest state.

prompt: A teammate thinks the code below is "safe" because it's wrapped in a `transaction` — but load tests still show oversell. Read the code and pinpoint exactly what hole remains, despite the transaction.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
`transaction` does NOT automatically lock the row being read — it only guarantees that everything inside the block commits or rolls back TOGETHER (block-level atomicity), saying nothing about who gets to read which row before whom. `manager.findOne` here is a plain (unlocked) `SELECT`, so two transactions running concurrently can both read `stock = 1` before either one commits — each transaction independently sees "still in stock," decrements, saves, and both commit successfully despite fighting over the same last unit. Wrapping it in a `transaction` just makes the bug LOOK safe without solving the actual race condition. The right fix: explicitly request a pessimistic lock on read — `manager.findOne(InventoryEntity, { where: { productId }, lock: { mode: "pessimistic_write" } })`, equivalent to `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` — so the second transaction must WAIT for the first to commit/rollback before reading that row, closing the read-then-write gap entirely. A simpler alternative is to skip the read-then-compare step altogether and fold the condition directly into `UPDATE inventories SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE product_id = ? AND stock > 0`, checking `rows affected`.

prompt: Table `products` has a composite index `(category, price)`. A teammate reports the query below is still slow even though 'there's already an index'. Read the SQL, explain why the `(category, price)` index is NOT used by the planner here, and propose a fix.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
The composite index `(category, price)` is a B-tree sorted by `category` first, then by `price` within each category group — like a phone book sorted by last name then first name. The query in question filters ONLY by `price >= 500`, completely skipping `category` — this violates the leftmost prefix rule: since the B-tree doesn't know where to start without a condition on the leftmost column, it can't jump straight into a `price` range and is forced to scan the whole table (`Seq Scan`), exactly as the plan shows. The fix is NOT to reorder the columns of the existing index — that would break other queries that filter by `category` first. If filtering by `price` alone is actually a real hot query pattern, the right solution is to create a separate index starting with `price` (e.g. `CREATE INDEX idx_price ON products (price)`), so this new B-tree serves that specific query shape. After creating it, re-run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to confirm the plan switches from `Seq Scan` to `Index Scan`/`Index Only Scan` and `Execution Time` drops significantly — measure again rather than just trusting the theory.

prompt: This is a TypeScript illustration (the module is multi-language). The team ships the hierarchical quota to production on a 3-node Redis Cluster and starts seeing intermittent `CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot` errors whenever the Lua cascade runs — even though everything worked perfectly in dev against a single-node Redis. Find the bug in the key-building code below and explain why dev never caught it.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The bug is in `buildKeys`: the three keys share no common hash-tag, so on Redis Cluster, CRC16 is computed over each key's entire string — they will almost certainly land on three different slots on three different nodes. Since the Lua cascade touches all three keys in one `EVALSHA` call, Redis Cluster immediately rejects it with `CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot`. In dev against single-node Redis, the notion of a slot doesn't exist in any distributed sense — every key lives on the same instance, so the script always runs, completely hiding this bug until it hits a real cluster. The fix is to add a hash-tag `{q:<tenantId>}` wrapping the tenant's shared part into all three keys, e.g. `{q:<tenantId>}:u:<userId>:<bucket>`, `{q:<tenantId>}:t:<bucket>`, `{q:<tenantId>}:g:<bucket>` — Redis Cluster only hashes the content inside the first `{...}`, so all three always map to the same slot regardless of `userId`/`bucket`. Verify with `CLUSTER KEYSLOT` on all three keys before and after the fix, and always test the cascade against a real multi-node cluster instead of trusting single-node results.

prompt: QA reports: a user with two browser tabs open (both connected to the same node) sometimes shows as 'offline' while one tab is still open. Here's the `disconnect` code. Find the bug.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The bug is that `await this.redis.setbit(this.onlineBitmapKey, userId, 0)` sits RIGHT AFTER `DECR` with no guard condition — it runs on EVERY call to `disconnect`, regardless of whether `liveConnections` after the decrement is still greater than 0. For a user with 2 tabs on the same node: closing the first tab makes `DECR` return `liveConnections = 1` (still exactly one live connection — the second tab), but the `SETBIT ... 0` line above still executes unconditionally, clearing the bit immediately even though the second tab hasn't closed — exactly the symptom QA reported. Running `SETBIT ... 0` again when the second tab closes (when `liveConnections = 0`) doesn't fix anything, because the bit was already incorrectly cleared on the very first disconnect. The correct fix is to move the `SETBIT ... 0` line INSIDE the `if (liveConnections <= 0)` branch, so it only runs when it's genuinely the last connection that just left — symmetric with `connect()`, which only calls `SETBIT ... 1` when the counter transitions exactly from 0 to 1. To catch this class of bug in the future, the test needs to replay EXACTLY the multi-connection scenario: open 2 connections for the same userId, close one and assert the bit is still 1, then close the other and assert the bit flips to 0 — a test that only opens/closes a single connection would never expose this bug.

prompt: A security audit finds that ANY user can promote themselves to admin and view other people's sensitive data, just by sending an extra header on API calls — even though the OPA policy (`default allow := false`, role-based RBAC) looks correctly written. Debug it: where does the flaw live in the PEP → OPA pipeline, and how do you fix it?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The flaw is not in the Rego logic (the policy may still correctly implement RBAC with `default allow := false`) but in the PEP itself (`AuthzGuard`): it reads `user.id`/`user.roles` DIRECTLY from HTTP headers (`x-user-id`, `x-user-roles`) sent by the CLIENT ITSELF, with absolutely no signature or provenance check on these headers. Since HTTP headers are data fully controlled by the client, anyone can simply add `x-user-roles: admin` to their own request — OPA receives exactly that input, sees "this user has the admin role," and correctly allows per the logic as written. This is privilege escalation via injected identity: default-deny is still correct about "a forgotten rule fails closed," but it does not protect against the case where the INPUT DATA fed to the rule was itself forged from an untrusted source — OPA only correctly evaluates the input it receives; it has no way of knowing whether that input is trustworthy. Fix it by deriving identity from an AUTHENTICATED source: verify the signature of a JWT signed by the identity provider (Keycloak) in a guard/middleware that runs BEFORE `AuthzGuard`, taking `roles` from the VERIFIED token's claim (`realm_access.roles`) — the JWT signature guarantees that claim cannot be altered by the client without breaking the signature — then build OPA's input from those trusted claims, NEVER from raw client headers. Verify with a test: send a request with no valid JWT but WITH a forged `x-user-roles: admin` header — the request must be rejected with 401/403 right at the JWT-verification step, before the input ever reaches OPA.

prompt: The team reports that every time a new version is deployed, users get scattered 502/503 errors for about 5-10 seconds, even though `kubectl rollout status` reports success and no Pod crashed. Read the Deployment manifest below, identify the bug, and propose a fix.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
The bug is that the Deployment does NOT declare a `readinessProbe`. Without it, Kubernetes defaults to considering a new Pod ready to receive traffic as soon as the container turns `Running` — regardless of whether the NestJS app inside has finished connecting to the database/cache. `kubectl rollout status` doesn't catch this because it only tracks whether Pods are `Running` and the replica count is satisfied, with no idea whether the app inside is ACTUALLY able to serve requests — that's why the rollout 'reports success' while users still see transient errors. The fix: add a `readinessProbe` to the container spec, e.g. an HTTP GET to a health-check endpoint that only returns `200` AFTER the app has connected to every required dependency. With that in place, a new Pod only gets added to the Service's Endpoints once the probe passes, completely closing the 'running but not ready' window that was causing the 502/503s. Confirm by monitoring the 5xx rate across subsequent rolling updates (should drop to zero) and checking `kubectl get endpoints` to see new Pods appear only AFTER the readinessProbe passes, not right when they become `Running`.

prompt: This is a SQL illustration (the module is multi-language). A teammate opens a PR changing how the `page_link` table (a page's outlinks) is written, from `DELETE FROM page_link WHERE from_url = $1` followed by bulk `INSERT`, to `UPSERT` (`ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`) to "avoid the expensive delete-then-rewrite." Review this change.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
This PR is semantically WRONG and should not be merged. A page's outlinks are a SET at the current parse time, not a cumulative historical log — if a previous parse had `a` linking to `b`, and this parse has `a` linking only to `c`, the row `a → b` must DISAPPEAR from the table to reflect the page's true current state. UPSERT (`ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`) only updates or inserts rows present in the new INSERT batch, but never deletes old rows that no longer appear — the row `a → b`, even though it no longer really exists, stays in the table forever. The direct consequence for PageRank: the graph can only grow over time, never shrinking when an outlink is removed, so rank ends up computed on links that don't actually exist anymore — results become wrong and drift further from reality with each cumulative re-parse. The "avoid the expensive delete-then-rewrite" justification isn't valid to trade away correct semantics: `DELETE-then-INSERT` is more expensive to execute but gives the correct REPLACEMENT semantics the problem requires; if performance is a concern, optimize the execution (wrap it in a transaction, batch the insert) rather than switching to UPSERT and getting the wrong result. Verify: parse `a` with outlinks `{b}`, re-parse `a` with outlinks `{c}`, then assert the table no longer has row `a → b` — the current PR would certainly fail this test.

prompt: The team uses Debezium to capture changes from Postgres, pushes them through Kafka, and a consumer syncs to Elasticsearch using the code below. After a Kafka consumer group had to rebalance (one consumer crashed and restarted), the team sees a burst of document 409 Conflict errors in the logs, even though the final data ends up correct. Review this: what's the cause, and how would you fix the consumer?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The cause of the 409 error is Kafka's AT-LEAST-ONCE delivery guarantee: when the consumer group rebalances after a crash, an uncommitted offset causes the consumer to RE-CONSUME some messages it already processed — including `op: "c"` (create) events that already succeeded. `esClient.create` isn't idempotent in the way this pipeline needs: it actively FAILS with 409 Conflict if a document with that `id` already exists (correct semantics for "create = only create, never overwrite"), so any re-consumption of an already-processed `c` event causes an error, even though nothing is actually wrong with the DATA (the document already exists with the correct content). Fix it by changing `create` to `index` (PUT by `id` — create OR overwrite if it exists) for both the `c` AND `u` branches, since both ops fundamentally only need "make sure the document ends up matching the latest `event.after`" — using `index` makes processing an event any number of times (once, or repeatedly due to re-consumption) produce the SAME final result, the idempotency property required for an at-least-once consumer. The `delete` branch needs the same scrutiny: deleting an `id` already deleted before (due to re-consuming a duplicate `d` event) returns a 404 error — wrap it in a `try/catch` that specifically catches 404 and treats it as HARMLESS (idempotent in the sense "deleting something already gone counts as goal achieved, not an error"). Verify with a test: call `handleCdcEvent` with the SAME `c` event twice in a row, asserting the second call doesn't throw and the ES result is identical to the first call; do the same for a `d` event called twice.

prompt: A teammate implemented the WAF middleware below and reports 'I've blocked SQL injection — payloads in the JSON body all get blocked in testing.' Review it: does this middleware actually protect enough, what gaps remain, and what would you fix/add?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
This middleware is NOT sufficiently protective, even though testing a JSON-body payload appeared to pass. The first problem: it ONLY inspects `req.body`, missing every other user-controlled input surface — query string, headers (especially `X-Forwarded-For`, `Referer`, which are classic injection vectors), cookies, and path parameters. An attacker only needs to put the payload in the query string instead of the body to bypass this middleware entirely. The second problem is false positives: the current regex (`OR`, `UNION`, `'`, `--`, `;`) would incorrectly block a platform that allows free-text content (a blog, comments) if a user DISCUSSES SQL in prose — e.g. "use UNION SELECT to merge rows" — because the regex can't distinguish real SQL trying to inject from the word SQL appearing in descriptive text. The third, most important, conceptual problem: a WAF is a **defense-in-depth** layer at the edge, and it NEVER replaces the real fix at the application layer — truly preventing SQLi requires **parameterized queries** (parameterized, never directly concatenating SQL strings from input); the WAF is only a safety net buying time against zero-days and known patterns, and a determined attacker can still encode/obfuscate around any regex blocklist. Fix it by: (1) expanding the middleware to inspect ALL input surfaces (query + sensitive headers + body), capping the size of input inspected so the inspection itself doesn't become a DoS amplifier on huge bodies; (2) scoping rules per route/field — don't run the SQLi rule against a free-text markdown field; (3) running in LOG-ONLY mode against real traffic for a while to measure false-positive/false-negative rates before switching to enforce; and (4) never treating "WAF passed" as sufficient — the application layer must still use parameterized queries everywhere it touches the database.

prompt: The team has integrated both Winston (pushing logs to Loki) and Sentry (error tracking) for an `OrdersService`. A developer wrote the code below and confidently reports 'I've logged the error fully, Sentry will catch it automatically.' Review this: is that true, and if not, how do you fix it so both the logging and error-tracking pillars work correctly?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The developer's claim is WRONG. `logger.error(...)` only pushes a log line to Loki — that's the LOGGING pillar, entirely separate from ERROR TRACKING. Sentry only catches an incident when an UNHANDLED exception bubbles up to the framework's global filter (e.g. `SentryGlobalFilter`). In this code, the `catch` SWALLOWS the error entirely: no re-throw, no Sentry call, just a log line before the API returns a "pending" status as if nothing happened. Consequence: Sentry is completely BLIND to this payment error — no stack trace, no auto-grouping by error type, no alerting when the error frequency spikes — even though the log line sits somewhere in Loki that no one is actively searching. Fix it by actively calling `Sentry.captureException(err)` right in the `catch` branch, alongside (not instead of) the `logger.error` line, so the exception is still reported to Sentry with full context even though it's not re-thrown up the stack. Boundary to remember: Logging answers "what happened" — recording every event, even errors handled gracefully; Error tracking answers "what's broken and how often" — only cares about real exceptions and auto-groups them by issue. Missing either blinds you to half the operational picture. Verify with a test: simulate `paymentGateway.charge` throwing, then assert `Sentry.captureException` was called exactly once with the right error object, not just that the log message appeared.

prompt: A teammate wrote the money-transfer function below between two Redis accounts and confidently says 'I checked there's enough balance before deducting, so it can never go negative'. Review this code: is it as safe as they think, where's the flaw, and how would you fix it to be atomic?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The teammate is WRONG: the three commands `GET`/`DECRBY`/`INCRBY` are three separate round-trips, not atomic together. Concrete scenario: `fromAcct` has 100, two calls `transfer(fromAcct, X, 80)` and `transfer(fromAcct, Y, 80)` run nearly simultaneously — both `GET` 100, both evaluate `100 < 80` as false (enough balance), then both `DECRBY 80` → final balance is 100 - 80 - 80 = -60, negative, even though each request individually "checked enough balance before deducting." Wrapping the three commands in `MULTI/EXEC` does NOT fix this: `MULTI/EXEC` only batches commands sent in one round-trip to the server; it does not allow reading a value and branching (if) on it inside the same transaction. The correct fix is a Lua script: fold "GET balance — compare — DECRBY — INCRBY" into ONE `EVALSHA` call. Because Redis runs a Lua script as a single uninterruptible command (thanks to its single-threaded model), the "enough balance or not" decision is always based on the balance AT THE EXACT MOMENT of deduction — no request can slip in between. Verify with a test that fires concurrent transfers from an account with a limited balance and asserts the final balance is never negative and the sum across both accounts is preserved.

prompt: Your API receives requests to generate PDF reports; each valid request pushes a job to BullMQ so a worker can call a third-party service (limited to 10 requests/second per contract). A marketing campaign causes API traffic to spike 20x within minutes. The team only set up rate limiting at the API layer (429 if over the threshold) and thinks that's enough to protect the downstream. Assess this design and propose additions if needed.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
A design that only rate-limits at the API layer is NOT enough to protect the downstream, because these two layers solve two independent problems. The edge layer (Token Bucket at the API) blocks requests OVER the allowance with a 429, protecting the API itself from being spammed — but a burst still WITHIN the allowed capacity (e.g. a Token Bucket sized large enough to absorb a 20x spike over a few minutes) can perfectly well generate a huge number of jobs pushed into BullMQ almost simultaneously. If the worker just pulls and calls the downstream as soon as jobs arrive, a downstream with a HARD contractual limit of 10 requests/second would be exceeded, causing errors or getting blocked by the third party. A SECOND rate-limit layer is needed at the worker layer: configure BullMQ's `limiter: { max: 10, duration: 1000 }` to cap the job PROCESSING rate at exactly 10 jobs/second, fully decoupling the RECEIVING rate (edge, already handled) from the PROCESSING rate down to the downstream (worker) — allowing the system to absorb bursts quickly (already durably stored in Redis via BullMQ) while still releasing jobs to the downstream at the allowed pace, honoring the contract. An important point when scaling to multiple worker instances: BullMQ's `limiter` is implemented via a Lua script in Redis, so ALL workers share ONE common counting budget — if you only limit local per-worker concurrency (without a shared `limiter`), the combined throughput of N workers can still far exceed 10 req/s, breaking exactly the limit you need to protect.

prompt: Topic `payment.events` currently has 4 partitions, and `payment-processor-service` runs 4 instances in the same group (matching the partition count). Traffic is projected to triple over the next 6 months due to market expansion. The team proposes: 'Just scale up more instances, Kubernetes autoscaling handles it.' Push back on this proposal and design the correct capacity roadmap.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
The 'just scale instances, Kubernetes handles it' proposal misses the exact core bottleneck: each partition is assigned to AT MOST ONE consumer instance within the same group at any time. With a topic currently at 4 partitions, if Kubernetes autoscales `payment-processor-service` instances up to 12 (to 'keep up' with 3x traffic), 8 extra instances would be completely IDLE — assigned no partition at all — so throughput genuinely doesn't increase one bit beyond the original 4 instances. The real parallelism ceiling is the PARTITION COUNT, not consumer instance count; infrastructure autoscaling doesn't solve this bottleneck. The correct roadmap: increase the topic's `numPartitions` FIRST (based on a 3x traffic estimate, with buffer rather than exactly 3x), THEN scale consumer instance count to match the new partition count. But increasing partitions on a RUNNING topic carries a side risk: the `hash(key) % numPartitions` formula changes with N, so the same key (e.g. `accountId`, if the topic needs per-account ordering) can map to a DIFFERENT partition after N changes — old events (in the old partition under old N) and new events (in the new partition under new N) for the same key get separated, breaking cross-time ordering. So this partition increase should happen during a low-traffic window, and if strict ordering is a critical requirement (as with this payment system), consider provisioning a large-enough partition buffer from the start to avoid needing to resize later, or plan a new-topic-plus-drain strategy instead of resizing the production topic directly.

prompt: Your system uses database-per-service: `orders` lives in order-service's PostgreSQL, `products` lives in inventory-service's MongoDB — no cross-database JOIN possible. You need to build an 'Order Detail' page showing order info MERGED with product info (name, image, description) for EACH item in the order, and this page gets high traffic from end users. Design how to fetch the data, compare two feasible approaches, and pick the one that fits this situation.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
Since you can't `JOIN` across databases directly, there are two feasible approaches. Approach one — API composition: call the `orders` API to get the order, then for EACH item in it call the `products` API for name/image/description, merging results at the application layer (gateway/BFF). Its advantage is simplicity and always seeing the latest data at call time; its disadvantage is N+1 round-trips (one for the order, N for each item) and latency dependent on the slowest service in the chain — not suited for a HIGH-TRAFFIC page. Approach two — CQRS read model: a dedicated service (or order-service itself) listens to events (`order.created`, `product.updated`...) and pre-materializes a merged read view — the order with product info embedded — into a read-optimized store (e.g. Elasticsearch or a denormalized table). The order-detail page then only needs to read from ONE source, no round-trip to inventory-service at request time. Trade-off: accepting eventual consistency — if a product just changed its name/image, the read model may lag a few seconds before updating, and you must build and maintain that read model. For exactly this situation — a high-traffic page, displayed repeatedly many times — the CQRS read model is the more sensible choice: trading a small, acceptable delay in product info for stable read performance no longer dependent on whether inventory-service is alive or fast at that exact request moment.

prompt: The ops team wants to scale count-consumer from 1 instance to 3 instances to increase Kafka read throughput (each instance reads a separate set of partitions in the same consumer group). Review the dedup code below before scaling — will it still work correctly with 3 instances running in parallel?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
This code WILL BREAK when scaled out to 3 parallel instances — it should not be scaled before this is fixed. The root problem: `seen` is an in-memory `Set<string>`, living entirely within EXACTLY ONE process's memory — running 3 instances means each has its OWN completely separate `Set`, sharing nothing with the other two. The consequence: if for any reason (a Kafka rebalance at a partition-reassignment boundary, or a producer sending a duplicate) the same `clickId` gets read by two different instances, each instance only checks its own local `Set` — both see this `clickId` as 'never encountered' and both increment the corresponding `adId` counter, causing a DOUBLE COUNT that the current dedup mechanism cannot detect at all (since each instance only 'knows' its own history). There's a second, independent-but-related problem: `counts: Map<string, number>` is also only local per instance — with 3 instances, a report of 'total clicks for adId X' has to manually aggregate figures from all three separate instances (no single centralized data source), and if one instance restarts, its own portion of the count entirely disappears. The correct fix is to move BOTH structures out of process memory into a store SHARED across every instance: `seen` becomes a `SET NX` check on Redis keyed by `clickId` (or a centrally queryable DB/RocksDB), so whichever instance processes a message checks the SAME single source of truth for 'has this clickId already been counted' — no longer dependent on which instance happens to receive it. To test correctly, simulate 3 instances (or 3 independent objects of the same class) all receiving the exact same `clickId` and assert the total count for the corresponding `adId` increases by EXACTLY ONE — the current in-memory version would definitely fail this test, showing a count increased by three.

prompt: A new teammate opens a PR replacing the complex Lua token-bucket script with 'more readable' JavaScript code, running across multiple parallel producer instances. Review the code below — does it correctly hold the rate-limit threshold when running multiple concurrent producer instances?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
This PR should NOT be merged. The problem is that `GET` then `SET` are TWO separate Redis commands, not atomic with each other at the application level — between the moment `tokens` is read (step 1) and the moment `tokens - 1` is written back (step 2), a DIFFERENT request (from another producer instance running in parallel) can slip in and read the EXACT SAME old value, since that request hasn't yet seen the decremented value. Specifically: if the bucket has exactly 1 token left and two requests arrive nearly simultaneously on two different instances, both `GET` a `tokens = 1`, both see `tokens > 0` so both return `true` (allowed), then both `SET` back `tokens - 1 = 0` — the result is TWO requests let through when the bucket should have allowed exactly ONE, silently exceeding the real rate limit. This is exactly the classic 'check-then-act' race condition (time-of-check to time-of-use): any design that splits reading state and acting on that state into two separate commands, when run across multiple parallel instances, has exactly this flaw. The correct fix — and precisely why the original design chose a Lua script instead of separate JS code — is to merge the entire 'read → check → decrement → write' sequence into ONE Lua script run ATOMICALLY on Redis's side (via `redis.eval`): since Redis only executes one command at a time (single-threaded), a Lua script is treated as one indivisible unit, so there's no gap for another request to read the stale value. To confirm, test by simulating N nearly-simultaneous requests for the same `recipient`+`channel` with a bucket holding only 1 token, then assert that EXACTLY ONE of them returns `true` — this 'simplified' GET/SET version would fail that test (returning more than one `true`), while the atomic Lua version would pass.

prompt: A teammate opens a PR "optimizing" the `accept` function responsible for assigning a sequence number (`seq`) to messages and deduping by `messageId`. They swap the order: claim `seq` via `INCR` FIRST, then check for duplicates via `SET NX`, reasoning 'INCR is cheap so do it first to shave latency off the happy path'. Review the code below.
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
This PR should NOT be merged. The problem is that `INCR` claims `seq` BEFORE `SET NX` checks for a `messageId` duplicate — meaning EVERY call to `accept`, even ones later discovered to be duplicates, has already burned a new `seq` before knowing that. The direct consequence: a client resending the same `messageId` three times due to a flaky network makes the room's seq counter jump by two extra units even though exactly one message is actually written to the log (`ZADD`) — those wastefully burned seqs never get assigned to any message, leaving fake gaps in the seq sequence. This is serious because clients use seq precisely to detect 'what have I missed' on reconnect (via `missedSince`/`ZRANGEBYSCORE`) — these fake gaps make the client mistakenly believe real messages were lost, when in fact the seq was simply wasted on a duplicate request. There's also a subtler second bug: when `reserved === null` (duplicate) is detected, the branch only re-reads `existing` without ever rolling back the seq that was already `INCR`'d — that seq is permanently lost, unrecoverable. The correct fix is to REVERSE back to the original order: `SET NX` (the idempotency gate) must run FIRST, and only when it confirms this is the FIRST request for this `messageId` (not a duplicate) should `INCR` be called to assign a seq — guaranteeing one logical `messageId`, no matter how many times resent, only ever burns exactly one seq. The PR's "latency optimization" reasoning also doesn't hold up: both `INCR` and `SET NX` are extremely fast atomic Redis commands (sub-millisecond), so reordering them barely improves latency, while the cost is breaking the single most important invariant of the system — every seq must correspond to exactly one real message.

prompt: A teammate opens a pull request that adds a second poller to increase throughput reading `outbox_event`, and refactors the claim function into two separate steps for 'clarity'. Review the code below: does it behave correctly with a single poller, and what happens once you run 2 poller instances in parallel, as this PR intends?
ideal:
:::muted
Bottom line
:::
This PR works correctly with ONLY ONE poller, but breaks the moment it runs in parallel — exactly the scenario the PR is trying to enable (more throughput via multiple pollers). The problem: `readPendingBatch` opens transaction 1, runs `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, then `COMMIT`s immediately — that `COMMIT` releases the row-lock right there. Only afterward does `markInFlight` run `UPDATE status = 'in_flight'` in a completely separate transaction 2. Between those two steps there is a gap: the lock is gone but the status in the database is still `pending`. If poller B ticks at that exact moment, its `SELECT ... SKIP LOCKED` sees no lock held on those rows (transaction 1 from poller A already committed), so B reads the SAME batch A just read — both pollers now believe they own those rows and will send duplicate webhooks for the same events. This is exactly what `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` was designed to prevent, but the 'split into two steps for clarity' refactor accidentally broke that invariant. Fix: merge it back into one transaction — `BEGIN`, `SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, `UPDATE status='in_flight' WHERE id = ANY(...)` on the exact ids just read, then `COMMIT`. Because the status flip lives INSIDE the transaction holding the lock, the lock is only released AFTER the status has moved away from `pending` — the next tick of any poller can never see these rows as claimable again.

prompt: The team runs a PostgreSQL primary + 2 replicas in Kubernetes using a `Deployment` with `replicas: 3` for simplicity. After a node gets OOM-killed and Kubernetes recreates the Pod, the team discovers: the new database Pod has NO old data, and it's unclear which Pod is currently primary. Explain why using a Deployment for a database is the wrong choice, and redesign it with the right Kubernetes tool.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
Using `Deployment` for a database is wrong because Deployment treats every Pod as EQUIVALENT and interchangeable — correct for stateless services but completely wrong for a database. A Deployment's Pods come up with random names and no disk stably attached per Pod; when a node gets OOM-killed and Kubernetes creates a replacement Pod, that new Pod doesn't 'inherit' the old Pod's data or role (primary/replica) at all — exactly matching the symptom the team hit. A database is a stateful workload needing two things Deployment doesn't provide: (1) a stable identity per Pod, to know for sure which Pod currently holds the primary role and which are replicas; (2) storage that must survive every restart/reschedule AND stay attached to that exact Pod, not some vague shared disk. The right tool is `StatefulSet`: it gives each Pod a stable, ordered identity (`postgres-0`, `postgres-1`, `postgres-2`), and each Pod gets its OWN `PersistentVolumeClaim` that always follows that exact Pod even if it's restarted or rescheduled to another node — `postgres-0` dying and coming back reattaches to the SAME volume, with no data loss. Pair it with a Headless Service so DNS resolves precisely to each Pod by name (instead of one vague shared ClusterIP), letting the application know exactly which node is currently primary in the replication topology.

prompt: A junior teammate wrote the code below to prevent double-debit when a client retries a transfer, using an in-memory `Set` to store processed `txnId`s. Review this code: does it actually prevent double-debit in every production scenario, and what would you propose fixing?
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
This code is NOT safe for production, for two independent reasons. First, the in-memory `Set` only lives in one process's memory: when the service runs multiple instances behind a load balancer (which is nearly certain in production), two retries of the same transfer can easily land on two different instances — each seeing its own `Set` without this `txnId`, so both run `UPDATE` and a double-debit happens. Second, even running on a single instance, the pair `has()` then `add()` is not atomic: if two requests carrying the same `txnId` arrive nearly simultaneously, both can read `has()` as `false` before either finishes calling `add()` — a classic check-then-act race condition. On top of that, the `Set` is wiped on process restart, so a retry arriving right after a restart is no longer blocked even though the original transfer already succeeded. The correct fix is to place idempotency at the DATABASE layer instead of the app: add a `UNIQUE` constraint on `txnId` (or `(txnId, accountId, direction)` if using a double-entry ledger). When two racing requests hit the database at the same time, only one `INSERT`/`UPDATE` succeeds; the other gets a unique-violation that the code catches and converts into `"replayed"` — this mechanism is atomic, shared across every instance, and survives restarts, because the database — not one process's RAM — is the single source of truth.

prompt: This is a TypeScript illustration (the module is multi-language). A teammate opens a PR to "reduce Redis load" by renewing the lease less often — changing `renewIntervalMs` from 1000 to 2800 while keeping `leaseMs = 3000` unchanged. Review this change.

:::muted
Bottom line
:::
This PR VIOLATES the standard "renew at least 3 times per lease" rule (`renewInterval <= leaseMs/3`). With `leaseMs=3000`, the safe threshold is `renewInterval <= 1000` — the old config (`1000`) sits right at this threshold, while the PR sets `2800`, meaning across a lease's 3000ms lifetime, the node only gets about one renewal OPPORTUNITY, with no backup buffer left. Consequence: just ONE delayed or missed renewal — due to a GC pause, temporary Redis slowness, or ordinary network jitter — causes the lease to expire BEFORE the next renewal tick can run, since there's no backup renewal left to compensate. In practice this manifests as a noticeably higher false step-down rate: a perfectly legitimate leader, running normally, gets treated as "dead" and replaced just because one renewal process was briefly delayed rather than actually crashing — triggering unnecessary failovers that end up more costly than renewing frequently. The PR's "reduce Redis load" justification is disproportionate: renewal is a cheap Lua script (`GET` + `PEXPIRE` in one round-trip); cutting frequency from once/second to once/2.8s saves negligible Redis load, while the trade-off is a significant increase in false step-down risk — an unreasonable trade. Keep or tighten `renewIntervalMs <= leaseMs/3` (e.g. 800-1000ms for a 3000ms lease).

prompt: This is an nginx config illustration (multi-language module, shared edge tier). A teammate opens a PR changing `proxy_cache_key` to "boost hit rate" by dropping the detailed path, keeping only `fileId`. Review this change: is it safe, and what's the consequence if it's wrong?

:::muted
Bottom line

This PR is NOT safe and should not merge as-is. The new cache key drops `$http_accept_encoding`, so a request with `Accept-Encoding: gzip` and a request without gzip support, both for the same `fileId`, now share ONE cache entry — a client without gzip support could well receive the compressed body and hit a decoding error, or conversely waste bandwidth receiving the uncompressed body when it supports gzip. The new key also drops any path/query beyond `fileId`: if the same `fileId` gets reused across different routes/variants (e.g. an image resize, a different version of the same file), those variants get served to each other by mistake — this isn't "higher hit rate" in the good sense, it's a false hit rate: the cache is serving the wrong content faster, not the right content faster. The correct fix: to legitimately raise hit rate, only collapse dimensions that DON'T affect the response body (e.g. normalizing the order of query params that don't influence content selection), while every dimension that genuinely distinguishes the returned content — `Accept-Encoding`, the full path/route, version — must stay in the cache key or be declared correctly via the `Vary` header. Verify by sending two requests with the same `fileId` but different `Accept-Encoding` and confirming they receive two separate cache entries.

The PR removes both `DECR` calls (in the `TENANT` and `GLOBAL` branches) to be "leaner," but the consequence is: when the tenant tier rejects, the user tier has already been bumped (`user_v`) and is never refunded — a blocked request silently spends a user quota slot despite never being served at all. Over time this leaks quota cumulatively: the limiter grows progressively stricter than designed, and legitimate users start getting wrongly rejected even though real traffic hasn't increased. The "later tier rarely blocks" justification doesn't hold up: the cost of DECR only occurs exactly when a rejection happens — already the rare branch — so the performance overhead is negligible compared to the risk of a silent counting leak. prompt: A teammate submits a PR "upgrade the embedding model for speed" — it only changes the model used at QUERY time, leaving the document-indexing pipeline untouched. Read the two snippets below (indexing service and query service) and say whether you'd approve it.

This shouldn't be approved. `indexing.service.ts` still uses `text-embed-v1` to embed every document stored in `vectorStore`, while the PR switches `query.service.ts` to `text-embed-v2` for query embedding — two different models create TWO incompatible embedding spaces. The query vector (v2 space) and document vectors (v1 space) don't share the same semantic coordinate system, so comparing cosine between them doesn't reflect real relevance at all — `search` still "runs" with no error, no exception, but returns near-random results. This is the most dangerous kind of bug: there's no error signal to catch it besides search quality mysteriously getting worse. Swapping the embedding model isn't a localized change in the query service — it's a change that affects the ENTIRE index, since every stored document must be re-embedded with the NEW model before queries can safely use it. The correct procedure: run a job that re-embeds the whole corpus with `v2` into a NEW index (parallel to the old `v1` one), verify quality, then only switch the query service to use the new index — never swap the model on one side (indexing OR querying alone) ahead of the other.

prompt: A teammate's PR adds a nearest-driver endpoint. Read the code below and say whether you'd approve it — pinpoint the specific gap and the user-facing scenario if it's merged as-is.

:::muted

This shouldn't be approved as-is. `GEOSEARCH` only reads from the GEO set — a coordinate sorted set with NO per-member TTL — so a driver who closed the app long ago still sits in `drivers:geo` at their old position, and `findNearbyDrivers` returns a list mixed with offline drivers. Concrete harm: a rider gets matched with a driver who closed the app 20 minutes ago, gets sent an invite, the driver never responds — the rider waits pointlessly instead of being matched immediately with a driver who's actually online nearby. The right fix: every driver ping must also write a dedicated heartbeat key with a short TTL (`SET driver:heartbeat:<id> EX 30` — expires if no ping for 30 seconds); `findNearbyDrivers` should then filter the raw `GEOSEARCH` results with `EXISTS driver:heartbeat:<id>` per candidate, returning only drivers whose heartbeat is still valid. It should also run a periodic sweeper that `ZREM`s driverIds whose heartbeat expired long ago from `drivers:geo`, so the set doesn't accumulate millions of "ghost" drivers over time — both wasting memory and slowing down every future GEO query.

prompt: A teammate's PR adds an idempotency key to the order-creation endpoint. Read the code below and say whether you'd approve it — if not, pinpoint exactly what's missing and the scenario where it causes harm.

This shouldn't be approved as-is. The code only checks "does this key already have a cached result" and completely ignores whether the current call's body matches the body that produced that cached result. Concrete harm scenario: a client sends an order with `quantity: 1` and key `K`, gets a stored result; later (a retry bug or a user mistake) it resends the exact same key `K` but with `quantity: 5` — the API still returns the old `quantity: 1` result with no error at all, leaving the client believing 5 were ordered when the system only ever created 1. This is silent data corruption, not a minor nitpick. Fix: store a **fingerprint** (SHA-256 hash) of `body` alongside the result when writing to Redis; when the same key arrives, compare the current fingerprint against the stored one — a match means it's safe to replay (true idempotency: same request, same result), a mismatch should return `422 Unprocessable Entity` to flag "key reused incorrectly" instead of silently returning the old result or silently processing the new body (both break the idempotency contract). Require the author to add the fingerprint comparison and a test sending the same key with two different bodies before merging.

prompt: An intern's pull request adds an endpoint that serves HLS segments from disk. You're reviewing the `resolveFile` snippet below before merging. Point out the specific security hole in how the path is resolved, describe an exploit scenario (what `quality`/`segment` value an attacker might send), and say what you'd require fixed before approving.

:::muted
Bottom line

This is a classic **path traversal** vulnerability. `path.join(this.streamsDir, videoId, quality, file)` normalizes `..` segments in the string but never stops the final result from escaping `streamsDir` — if `quality` or `file` (taken straight from a route param, controlled by the client) contains `../../../../etc/passwd` or an encoded `..%2F`, `target` can end up pointing at any system file. Because the function only does `fs.existsSync(target)` and hands that path to `res.sendFile` in the controller, there's no step checking "does this path still live inside the video directory" — if the file exists and the process can read it, it gets returned to the client as if it were a valid segment. The required fix: after `path.join`, `path.resolve` both `target` and the root directory `path.join(streamsDir, videoId)`, and only treat it as valid if `path.resolve(target).startsWith(path.resolve(root))` — otherwise return `null` so the controller returns 404. This is exactly why input from a route param must always pass through an explicit boundary-validation layer — you can't trust path-joining to protect itself. Before merging, there needs to be a test that sends a traversal `../` and confirms a 404.

prompt: The team implemented hybrid fanout (push for ordinary users, pull for KOLs) and a teammate wrote the `getHybridFeed` function below. Some users report occasionally seeing ONE post appear TWICE, right next to each other, in their feed. Review the code, identify the cause, and propose a fix.

:::muted

`getHybridFeed` merges `pushedPosts` (from the already-pushed timeline) and `pulledPosts` (pulled directly from KOLs) then sorts by `createdAt`, but NEVER deduplicates by post `id` before returning. The specific scenario causing duplication is ROLE DRIFT: an author who JUST switched from ordinary user (push) to KOL (pull) — or vice versa — due to the `isCelebrity`/follower-count threshold changing over time. Their post was ALREADY pushed to `feed:{userId}` BEFORE the switch (while they were still an ordinary user), and is now ALSO pulled again via `getFollowedKols` since they're CURRENTLY classified as a KOL — the same `postId` appears in both the `pushedPosts` and `pulledPosts` arrays, so after merging and sorting, it shows up TWICE in a row in the final result. Direct fix: add a DEDUPLICATION step by `id`/`postId` AFTER merging the two sources, BEFORE sorting and slicing to `limit` — e.g. use a `Map<id, Post>` (keyed by `id`) to keep exactly ONE record per duplicate `id`, then `Array.from(map.values())`, sort, and slice. A more root-cause fix (not just patching the symptom): when an author transitions from push to KOL, actively clean up their OLD push entries from EVERY follower's timeline — or more simply, let those entries expire naturally via TTL — so long-term there's no longer both an old push copy and a new pull copy coexisting for the same author. Verify with a test: simulate a `postId` appearing in BOTH the `pushedPosts` and `pulledPosts` input lists, call the merge function, and assert the result contains EXACTLY ONE record of that `postId`.

prompt: Your system reads 20 times more than it writes, and the primary database is overloaded handling both. You add a read replica and split traffic: writes go to primary, reads go to the replica. Right after shipping this, a user reports a bug: 'I just updated my profile, hit refresh, and I see the OLD data.' Explain why this bug happens even though the system is 'working as designed', and propose a fix that doesn't throw away the whole benefit of the read replica.
ideal:
:::muted
Chốt
:::
This isn't a logic bug — it's the correct behavior of read/write split with an asynchronous replica. The primary writes the change, commits, and answers the client RIGHT AWAY without waiting for the replica; the replica syncs by replaying that change after some delay (a measurable replication lag, e.g. an LSN difference). When the user updates their profile (write to primary) and hits refresh almost immediately (read from replica), there's a real, if short, window where the replica hasn't finished replaying yet — this is exactly a read-your-writes violation, an inevitable consequence of eventual consistency, not a code error. The right fix isn't to remove the read replica (losing all the read-scaling benefit), but to handle it TARGETEDLY: identify sensitive flows that need to see just-written data immediately (like a 'view profile after save' page) and route just those reads to the primary, while ordinary read flows (feeds, lists, reports) keep going through the replica as before. If a more critical piece of the business (e.g. finance) needs a stronger guarantee for a SPECIFIC slice of data, you can enable synchronous replication for that slice — the primary waits for at least one replica to acknowledge before committing — but this is a deliberate write-latency trade-off, applied only where truly needed, not everywhere.

prompt: This is an illustration in TypeScript (this module is multi-language). In CP mode, the peer-sync function uses `Promise.all(peers.map(...))` to wait for every node to confirm before committing. A teammate finds the 503 error on cable cut annoying and proposes changing `Promise.all` to `Promise.allSettled` so 'we stop getting errors'. Evaluate this proposal: which property of CP mode does it break, what behavior does it turn the system into, and in a money-transfer context what is the consequence?

:::muted
Bottom line
:::
The proposal is fundamentally wrong. `Promise.all` is fail-fast: when one peer times out after 2000ms on a cable cut, it rejects immediately, the error propagates up to `transfer` and aborts the transaction with a 503 — this 'sync every peer BEFORE committing' mechanism is exactly what creates CP mode's strong consistency. Switching to `Promise.allSettled` breaks that very property: `allSettled` never rejects, always resolves even when every peer fails, so `syncToPeers` returns a fake 'success' and `transfer` still adds to the local balance even though no peer received it. The system silently turns from CP into AP. In a money-transfer context the consequence is loss of consistency, balance divergence between regions, and the door open to double spending — the exact thing CP was built to prevent. The 503 is not a bug but a safety contract: removing it requires consciously changing the business requirement to AP + eventual consistency, not swapping `all` for `allSettled` to hide the error. Easy to verify: cut the network, transfer on US, compare the SG balance — divergence appears immediately.

prompt: inventory-service listens to `order.created` events from Kafka to decrement stock. Production reports: some products get their stock decremented TWICE for the same order, even though order-service only publishes the event exactly once. Review the consumer code below and explain the vulnerability.
